Part I
Overview and Foundations

1
Introduction to Physical AI
For decades, artificial intelligence (AI) operated inside computers primarily, processing digital data
and generating symbolic outputs without directly altering the physical world. Recent advances
extend AI beyond this digital boundary by enabling it to perceive and understand physical en-
vironments, reason about them, and act within them. This emerging capability has given rise to
physical AI, which studies how artificial systems shall interact with the physical world. Yet, what
exactly is physical AI? What does its technical landscape look like, and what core challenges does
it entail? And, what are typical application scenarios of physical AI? This chapter addresses these
questions by tracing AI’s expansion from digital to physical space, defining physical AI and its
boundaries with neighboring fields, and examining its core characteristics, system architectures,
and application domains.
1.1
Background: A Paradigm Expansion of AI
1.1.1
Digital AI and Physical AI
Artificial intelligence has developed through several complementary traditions, from symbolic
reasoning and knowledge representation to statistical learning and deep neural networks. Deep
learning substantially advances the ability of computational systems to extract useful representa-
tions from complex data, with major improvements in speech recognition, visual recognition, and
related information-processing tasks. These achievements establish representation learning as a
central methodological foundation of contemporary AI (LeCun et al., 2015).
In this chapter, Digital AI refers to capabilities that operate directly on digital representations, such
as text, images, software, and structured records. This definition emphasizes the system’s oper-
ational interface over the origin of its data. For example, while an image may depict a physical
scene, recognizing its contents does not require the system to actually interact with that environ-
ment. Physical AI, in contrast, applies intelligence to perceive, influence, and adapt to physical
processes through direct interaction. Definition 1.1 in Section 1.2 further clarifies this fundamental
distinction.
The distinction becomes apparent when comparing the description of an action with its execution.
An AI system may correctly explain how to pick up a glass while remaining unable to estimate its
mass, establish a stable grasp, detect incipient slip, or adjust contact forces. Successful manipu-
lation depends on relationships among geometry, material properties, sensing, and actuation that
cannot be assessed solely through the linguistic plausibility of a response. The relevant criterion is
whether the system produces the intended physical outcome under the conditions encountered.
This distinction is related to the symbol grounding problem of how symbols can acquire meaning
through a system’s own capacities rather than solely through interpretation by an external observer.
The formulation by Harnad (1990) identifies the limitations of defining symbols only through other
symbols and motivates their connection to nonsymbolic representations. For physical AI, the cor-
responding engineering problem is to connect concepts such as support, contact, and stability to
observations and action consequences.
Grounding should not, however, be reduced to a categorical claim that digital models possess no
physical knowledge. Models trained on descriptions, images, videos, or simulated trajectories can
acquire useful regularities concerning the physical world. The unresolved issue is whether these
regularities support reliable intervention across changes in objects, environments, and operating
conditions. Semantic competence, predictive accuracy, and physical competence are related but
distinct properties.
Figure 1.1 summarizes this expansion from digital tools and simulated agents to real-world single-
agent systems, multi-agent collaboration, and infrastructure-level physical AI. Across these phys-
ical deployments, the unit of analysis extends from an isolated model to the integrated system
of computation, sensing, actuation, communication, and environment. This perspective has im-
portant historical precedents. Brooks (1991) demonstrates an approach to robotics in which intel-

representations, scalable training, and predictive models.
1.1.2
Core Characteristics
Physical AI operates under constraints that cannot be removed by increasing model capacity alone.
Three characteristics are particularly important, namely, consequential interaction under uncer-
tainty, perception of evolving physical states, and the integration of empirical learning with physi-
cal structure.
Consequential Interaction Under Uncertainty
Physical systems are only partially observable.
Object properties, external disturbances, and equipment conditions may be unknown or change
during execution.
Actions also affect the evidence available to the system.
Moving a camera
changes visibility, probing a surface reveals compliance, and applying force may alter an object’s
configuration. Perception and action consequently form an interdependent process.
Physical interaction can incur recovery costs and irreversible consequences. A simulated episode
can often be restarted from a saved state, whereas a spilled chemical, damaged component, or
contaminated sample may require substantial intervention or may be impossible to restore. The
operational distinction is that physical systems generally lack an exact, inexpensive reset mecha-
nism. Planning must therefore consider the recoverability of future states as well as the likelihood
of immediate task success.
Perception of Evolving Physical States
Physical AI requires observations that are temporally
and spatially meaningful. Vision can describe appearance and geometry, while force, touch, pro-
prioception, temperature, pressure, and other measurements reveal complementary aspects of in-
teraction. A manipulation system, for example, may need to distinguish visual contact from load-
bearing contact and a completed motion from a successfully transferred object.
Although sensors typically produce sampled digital measurements, the processes they measure
evolve in continuous time and may include discrete events such as impact, grasp release, or equip-
ment switching. Reliable interpretation therefore depends on sampling rates, calibration, synchro-
nization, coordinate frames, and measurement uncertainty. A correct estimate obtained too late
may be unusable for control. More generally, computation and physical dynamics must be ana-
lyzed together because execution timing can affect system behavior (Lee, 2008).
12


Learning Informed by Physical Structure
Data provide evidence about real operating condi-
tions, including effects that are difficult to model analytically. Physical knowledge provides struc-
ture that can restrict implausible predictions and reduce the burden of learning. Conservation
relationships, symmetries, geometric constraints, and governing equations can be incorporated
through model architectures, training objectives, simulation, or constrained decision procedures.
Physics-informed machine learning formalizes several ways of combining observations with math-
ematical descriptions of physical processes (Karniadakis et al., 2021).
The appropriate balance depends on the task. Explicit models may be effective when governing
relationships are sufficiently understood, whereas learned components can represent uncertain in-
teractions or compensate for model mismatch. Physical priors are themselves conditional on as-
sumptions and operating regimes. For example, an inaccurate friction model or an inappropriate
rigid-body approximation can produce systematic errors. Physical consistency therefore requires
validation within the task’s operating regime, regardless of the model family.
Together, these characteristics shift evaluation toward closed-loop performance. Relevant measures
include task completion, robustness to disturbance, response time, resource consumption, and re-
covery from failure. Prediction accuracy remains valuable, but its practical significance depends
on how prediction errors propagate through decisions and physical execution.
1.1.3
Why Physical AI Is Needed and Increasingly Feasible
Physical AI is motivated by tasks that require systems to act on the physical world. Flexible man-
ufacturing requires adaptation to variations in parts and processes. Transportation and energy
systems require coordinated responses to changing demand and operating conditions. Scientific
experimentation requires procedures to be adjusted in response to measurements. Furthermore,
extreme environments, such as deep space and the deep sea, drive the need for local autonomy, as
communication constraints and physical hazards severely limit continuous human intervention.
These demands do not imply that established automation is inadequate in every setting. Carefully
engineered automation remains effective where tasks and operating conditions can be specified in
advance. The additional research challenge is to preserve useful performance when relevant con-
ditions change and exhaustive preprogramming becomes impractical. Physical AI addresses this
challenge by integrating interactive learning with perception, inference, prediction, and adaptation.
Several technical developments support this direction. Sensing and local computation provide
the practical interfaces for observing and influencing physical processes. Simulation supplies con-
trolled environments for training and evaluation, while methods for transfer from simulation to
reality reduce dependence on collecting every training example on physical hardware. For exam-
ple, Tobin et al. (2017) demonstrate that varying simulated visual conditions can support transfer
of a vision model to real robotic tasks. Such results establish a useful transfer mechanism, while
leaving its effectiveness dependent on the relationship between training variation and deployment
conditions.
Learned physical models provide another foundation. Graph network simulators have demon-
strated the ability to represent interacting particles and predict dynamics across fluids, rigid solids,
and deformable materials within evaluated settings. These models illustrate how structured learn-
ing can support physical prediction beyond a single fixed configuration (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al.,
2020). For autonomous action, their potential value lies in evaluating candidate interventions be-
fore execution, provided that prediction errors and operating limits are understood.
Large pretrained models also offer reusable semantic knowledge. For example, RT-2 shows that
vision-language pretraining can be combined with robot demonstrations to support robotic action
and improve generalization in the reported experiments (Zitkovich et al., 2023). This provides
evidence that capabilities developed through digital learning can contribute to physical interaction
when connected to appropriate action data and interfaces.
13


These developments make it increasingly feasible to combine digital capabilities, physical models,
and control mechanisms to study how systems acquire transferable physical skills while maintain-
ing measurable performance within specified operating conditions.
1.2
Physical AI: Definition and Boundaries
1.2.1
A Broad Definition of Physical AI
At its most general, physical AI concerns the capacity of an artificial system to interact with the
physical world. This monograph uses physical AI for this artificial-system scope. The term physical
intelligence is retained for general capacities, bodily mechanisms, and source-specific usage. The
following definition makes the notion precise.
Definition 1.1 (Physical AI). Physical AI is the capacity of an artificial system to perceive physi-
cal environment states, maintain task-relevant representations of physical relationships and action
consequences, and select and execute interventions through physical interfaces, using feedback to
achieve objectives under physical, operational, and computational constraints.
PHYSICAL AI

Fig. 1.2 Physical AI as closed-loop interaction between artificial systems and the physical world.
Systems observe physical states, maintain task-relevant representations of physical relationships
and action consequences, and select and execute interventions through physical interfaces. Out-
come feedback guides adaptation toward objectives under physical, operational, and computa-
tional constraints
This definition identifies a functional scope rather than a particular architecture. Representations
may be explicit, implicit, or distributed across several components. They need not constitute a
complete internal simulator, and action selection need not depend on symbolic reasoning. What
matters is whether the integrated system can use information about physical conditions to guide
and revise its behavior.
Four implications clarify the definition. First, physical grounding requires observations to be con-
nected to relevant quantities, events, or conditions in the world. Second, the system must have
a path for intervention, whether through direct actuation or commands to controlled equipment.
Third, feedback must inform subsequent behavior, allowing discrepancies between expected and
observed outcomes to affect execution. Fourth, claims of intelligent capability should be supported
by evidence of task-relevant inference, prediction, planning, or adaptation, rather than inferred
merely from the presence of sensors and actuators.
14


These criteria define a continuum of capability. A fixed feedback regulator and a system that adapts
across changing tasks may share essential control principles, yet differ substantially in the breadth
of conditions they can handle. The distinction between automation and Physical AI is therefore
most useful when expressed through demonstrated capabilities and operating assumptions, rather
than an absolute technological boundary.
Terminological care is also necessary because physical intelligence has an established, more specific
usage in mechanics and robotics. Sitti (2021) uses the term to describe functions such as sensing, ac-
tuation, memory, and computation physically encoded in an agent’s body. The broader definition
of Physical AI adopted here includes such contributions while also encompassing computational
and distributed systems that interact with physical processes. It should be understood as this chap-
ter’s organizing framework, rather than a claim that the literature has converged on one definition.
Finally, key components should be distinguished from a complete system. A learned simulator,
perception model, or action planner may provide an essential Physical AI capability. In isolation,
however, it does not satisfy the system-level requirement for closed-loop physical intervention.
This distinction allows purely digital modules to be recognized as enabling technologies without
attributing autonomous physical competence to them prematurely.
1.2.2
Physical AI vs. Embodied AI
Embodied AI posits that artificial intelligence requires a body to house the system and drive its
active sensorimotor relationship with the environment (Pfeifer and Iida, 2004). The concept of em-
bodiment focuses on how this morphology, along with sensing and action capabilities, directly
shapes environmental interactions and guides behavior. Importantly, embodiment is by no means
limited to humanoid or biologically inspired designs. For physically deployed agents, research fur-
ther highlights how mechanical structures and material properties can intrinsically support adap-
tive behavior, thereby reducing the control burden on a centralized controller (Pfeifer et al., 2007).
Nor does embodied AI necessarily require a deployed physical robot. Simulated agents are widely
used to study navigation, interaction, and learning under embodied constraints (Shridhar et al.,
2021). Habitat, for example, was introduced as a platform for training and evaluating virtual em-
bodied agents in three-dimensional environments (Savva et al., 2019). Embodied AI therefore in-
cludes both simulated and physically deployed agents.
Within this chapter’s framework, physically deployed embodied AI constitutes a major realization
of physical AI. Its characteristic analytical focus is the agent and its particular sensing and action ca-
pabilities. Physical AI adopts an additional system-level perspective, encompassing arrangements
in which sensing, decision-making, and actuation are distributed across infrastructure. Figure 1.3
summarizes these distinctions and their overlap.
Consider an adaptive traffic-management system that estimates network conditions, changes sig-
nal timings, and evaluates the resulting traffic flows. Its interaction with the world is mediated
by distributed detectors, communication links, and signal controllers rather than a single mobile
body. Similar arrangements can be considered for factory coordination or power-system operation,
provided that the system actually closes the loop between observations, decisions, and physical
consequences. These are illustrative applications of the proposed definition, not claims that every
traffic controller, factory scheduler, or grid-management platform possesses advanced intelligence.
Scientific equipment provides a concrete research example. Degrave and colleagues demonstrated
deep reinforcement learning for magnetic control of plasma configurations in the TCV tokamak.
The controller interacts with a physical process through the machine’s measurement and actuation
infrastructure (Degrave et al., 2022). Under the present framework, this qualifies as Physical AI
even though the system lacks the conventional form of a mobile or manipulative robot.
Such systems are not independent of physical embodiment in the broadest sense, because sensors,
actuators, and material processes remain indispensable. Their distinguishing feature is that the
physical interface is distributed across an installation or network. Within this monograph’s frame-
work, embodied AI emphasizes how an agent’s body shapes sensing and action, while physical

1.2.3
Physical AI vs. Cyber-Physical Systems and Digital Twins
Physical AI intersects closely with cyber-physical systems (CPS), but the concepts describe different
aspects of a system. CPS concerns the integration of computation with physical processes, includ-
ing the consequences of timing, concurrency, and interaction between software and its physical
environment (Lee, 2008). Physical AI concerns the capabilities exercised through that integration,
including interpreting conditions, anticipating consequences, choosing interventions, and adapting
behavior.
A CPS may operate effectively through fixed control logic without possessing broad inference or
adaptation capabilities. Conversely, a physically intelligent system depends on the engineering
properties of its computational and physical infrastructure, including dependable sensing, timely
communication, and executable control. Physical AI can therefore be understood as a capability
layer within many CPS architectures. Describing it as a possible development toward greater au-
tonomy is useful, provided that this does not imply that CPS research excludes advanced cognition
or that learning automatically improves an engineered system.
Digital twins occupy a different position. They provide digital representations associated with
identifiable physical counterparts, with connections that support updating and comparison be-
tween physical and digital states. The literature identifies multiple characteristics and implemen-
tation choices, making it important to specify how a proposed twin is connected to its physical
counterpart (Jones et al., 2020).
Within a Physical AI architecture, a predictive digital twin can support state estimation, diagnosis,
and evaluation of alternative interventions. It may help estimate how a production line would
respond to a schedule change or how equipment behavior would change under another operating
condition. Such uses require more than a visually accurate replica. The representation must capture
the variables and dynamics relevant to the decision.
16


A digital twin does not necessarily select or execute actions autonomously, and a Physical AI sys-
tem need not maintain a comprehensive twin. A compact learned dynamics model may be suffi-
cient for a particular control task. Likewise, a generic world model becomes a digital twin only
when it is meaningfully associated with a specific physical counterpart and maintained through an
appropriate update relationship. Counterfactual predictions remain conditional on the validity of
the model and its assumptions.
These distinctions establish complementary roles. CPS describes the integration of computational
and physical processes. Embodied AI examines intelligence through situated sensorimotor inter-
action. Digital twins provide representations tied to physical counterparts. Physical AI, in the
framework developed here, identifies the capacity to combine perception, physical understanding,
decision-making, and feedback into effective intervention. This system-level perspective provides
the basis for the architectural elements discussed in the following sections.
1.3
Core Elements of Physical AI
Definition 1.1 characterizes Physical AI as the capacity to perceive physical states, maintain task-
relevant representations, and execute interventions through feedback. In practice, this capacity
takes the form of a persistent closed loop. Information processing and decision-making must be
translated into physical actions, and subsequent behavior must be revised according to observed
outcomes. Physical AI therefore operates through a cycle of perception, modeling, prediction,

As Section 1.2 emphasizes, Physical AI is not synonymous with robotic intelligence. Whether a
system exhibits it depends on its ability to close the loop between perception and action, not on
its morphology. The elements discussed in this section apply equally to autonomous vehicles,
industrial equipment, automated experimentation platforms, intelligent buildings, and energy in-
frastructures. In such systems, perception, computation, decision-making, and execution are often
distributed across devices, edge nodes, cloud platforms, and physical facilities rather than concen-
trated within a single device.
Operating in a continuously changing and uncertain world also means that actions are constrained
by dynamics, geometry, time, energy, materials, and safety requirements, and that their conse-
quences are not always reversible, as Section 1.1 discusses. A physically intelligent system must
therefore answer not only “What should be done?” but also “Can it be done under the current con-
ditions?”, “How can it be done safely?”, and “Does the execution produce the intended outcome?”
Organized around these questions, Physical AI comprises four closely related elements, includ-
ing physical state perception and estimation, physical world models, physical decision-making
together with planning and control, and closed-loop feedback and multiscale adaptation. They
correspond respectively to perception, representation, intervention, and feedback in the definition.
The first three together constitute the physically intelligent agent, while the fourth connects the
agent with the physical world into a continuously running loop. The relations among these ele-
ments, together with the data, hardware, and physical world on which they depend, are illustrated
in Figure 1.4.
1.3.1
Physical State Perception and Estimation
Physical AI begins with information about the environment, task-relevant objects, and the system
itself. Vision conveys identity, pose, geometry, and motion. Force and tactile sensing reveal contact,
friction, and material properties (Dahiya et al., 2010), while acoustic sensing detects collisions and
vibrations. Proprioception measures the system’s own configuration and load, and industrial sys-
tems add process variables such as temperature, pressure, and current. Chapter 9 treats the sensors
themselves. The concern here is turning their signals into an estimate of physical state.
Measurements are incomplete, noisy, delayed, and often misaligned across modalities, so calibra-
tion, multimodal fusion, and state estimation are needed to obtain a temporally consistent state
with explicit uncertainty (Kalman, 1960a; Baltrušaitis et al., 2019). Perception also supports active
information acquisition. When observations are insufficient for a decision, the system can change
its viewpoint, reposition sensors, or probe objects to estimate mass, stiffness, or friction, folding
information acquisition into the decision loop (Bajcsy, 1988).
1.3.2
Physical World Models: Representation and Prediction
State estimates are organized into a world model, which describes the environment, the actions
available to the system, and how physical states evolve over time (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018;
LeCun, 2022). It has two interdependent aspects. Representation captures what the model holds
about the current world, and prediction anticipates what the world becomes after a given action.
Physical representations cover objects, poses, geometry, and spatial relations, together with veloci-
ties, masses, contacts, forces, material properties, affordances, and task constraints. A cup is at once
a shape with a pose and an object that can be grasped, holds liquid, and spills when tilted. Rep-
resentations may be explicit (maps, object lists, equations of motion, relational graphs), implicit
(learned from data), or hybrid, combining physical priors with learning to retain interpretability
while correcting for unmodeled effects. An effective world model is updated with each new obser-
vation and distinguishes directly observed, estimated, and unobserved states.
Prediction estimates the consequences of a particular action, covering trajectories, contact out-
comes, equipment conditions, task success, and safety hazards over time scales from milliseconds
18


to hours. Predictions may come from physical equations and simulators (Raissi et al., 2019) or from
transition patterns learned from data (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020). Practical systems combine
the two and revise predictions and their uncertainty online. In scenario simulation, the decision
process submits candidate actions and the world model returns predicted outcomes with their un-
certainty, enabling counterfactual comparison before anything is executed. This simulation runs
online, unlike the physics engines and generative environments of Chapter 4, which are used of-
fline to produce training data and test policies.
1.3.3
Physical Decision-Making, Planning, and Control
Physical decision-making selects actions from task objectives, the current state, predicted outcomes,
and real-world constraints, usually through a hierarchy (Kaelbling and Lozano-Pérez, 2011; Sutton
et al., 1999). At the top, the system sets goals and constraints and, when several physical agents
share a task, allocates and coordinates subtasks among them. Foundation models for robot manip-
ulation reason about the task and scene, decompose goals into executable steps, and produce action
policies. Foundation models for whole-body motor control provide reusable feedback policies for
executing movement goals and correcting deviations (Zeng et al., 2025; 2026). The levels differ
mainly in time scale, from minutes or hours for task allocation to seconds for policies and mil-
liseconds for motor commands. The boundary separating task-level reasoning and action-policy
generation from motor control and feedback correction varies across systems.
Execution takes many forms, from joints and end effectors to steering and braking, instrument
scheduling, or valves, pumps, and switches. An action is thus best understood as an observable
intervention that changes a physical object, environment, or process. Such interventions must be
feasible, safe, and timely. A logically valid plan can still fail because of collisions, actuator limits,
or latency, so safety checks precede execution, and monitoring and emergency stops stay active
throughout.
1.3.4
Closed-Loop Feedback and Multiscale Adaptation
Physical AI revises behavior according to the observed consequences of action. After each com-
mand, the system perceives again, checks whether the intended result is achieved, and updates its
state estimate together with its world model and plan. When outcomes deviate from predictions,
it identifies the cause and compensates, retries, replans, or terminates safely.
The loop resides in no single module but in the connections among the elements. Perception sup-
plies the state, the world model answers action queries from the decision process, commands act
on the world through actuators, and sensors return the consequences to perception (Figure 1.4).
The loop thus closes through the physical world rather than inside the agent. Fast reactive control,
such as tightening a grip when an object begins to slip, may bypass the world model and respond
directly to the current state.
Feedback operates at three nested scales. The fastest loop connects motor control and feedback
correction with the actuators and sensors, adjusting position, velocity, or force in real time. The
task-level loop connects task-level reasoning and action-policy generation with the world model
and revises plans as the task progresses. The slowest passes through the offline data and simulation
infrastructure, where deployment data drive continual learning (Parisi et al., 2019) and form a data
flywheel. In multi-agent and infrastructure-scale systems these loops may be distributed across
devices that coordinate toward a common objective, and humans may join them by providing
goals, demonstrations, supervision, and intervention.
Physical AI therefore lies not in producing a plausible action or plan, but in sustaining this cycle of
observation, prediction, action, verification, and revision under real physical constraints, whether
the system is a single robot or distributed infrastructure.
19


1.4
The Role of Physical AI in the Evolution of AI
Section 1.1 contrasts digital intelligence, whose objects of computation and evaluation are recorded
content, with the Physical AI defined in Definition 1.1. This subsection develops three claims about
what that contrast means for the trajectory of AI. Physical AI is the stage at which artificial intelli-
gence moves from understanding and generating digital information to perceiving, predicting, and
changing physical processes. It builds on digital intelligence rather than replacing it and provides
one of the important paths toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).
New Capabilities Beyond Digital Intelligence
The first extension concerns what the system per-
ceives. Digital intelligence works on symbols and pixels that come from prior collection, curation,
and encoding. Physical AI deals with physical states directly (Section 1.1), including the pose and
velocity of objects, forces and friction at contact surfaces, pressure and temperature in fluids, and
the composition and structure of materials. These states are continuous and evolve over time. They
can only be partially observed through noisy sensors, and vision, touch, force, and other modalities
must be fused within a common spatiotemporal frame. The object of perception thus shifts from
previously recorded content to the current state of a world that keeps changing.
The second extension concerns what the system produces. Because physical systems lack an inex-
pensive reset (Section 1.1), a grasp, an injection, or a turn of the steering wheel changes the subse-
quent state of the system and often cannot be undone. Physical AI must therefore predict, before
acting, how the world will evolve if a given action is taken. This prediction is interventional in na-
ture and depends on causal relations and dynamics, not merely on statistical correlation (Schölkopf
et al., 2021).
Building on Digital Intelligence
These new capabilities do not make Physical AI a replacement
for digital intelligence. The common-sense and domain knowledge accumulated in foundation
models is the basis on which Physical AI understands and plans tasks (Ichter et al., 2023). In turn,
Physical AI grounds that knowledge in measurable changes of state and tests it through real in-
teraction. A large language model can search the literature, propose a hypothesis, and write an
experimental protocol, but whether the protocol succeeds depends on accurate pipetting, stable
temperature control, and correct sample handling. Only when digital reasoning is closed with
physical execution can AI take part in the full process from posing a question and running an
experiment to drawing a conclusion.
Section 1.1 explains that Physical AI enlarges the unit of analysis from the model to the system,
and this enlargement has concrete consequences for how capability is attributed. The same policy
may perform very differently on robot arms of different precision or in workshops with different
lighting, and task success also depends on engineering conditions such as sensor calibration, fixture
design, and safety interlocks. The shift also changes how general capability should be understood
and measured, which leads to the third claim.
A Path Toward AGI
Benchmarks in digital environments are prone to overfitting, and it is hard
to rule out memorization caused by contamination of the training data. The physical world is open,
continuous, and impossible to enumerate in advance, and whether a task has been completed is de-
cided directly by physical outcomes. Moravec’s paradox points in the same direction, highlighting
that perceptual and motor skills that humans find effortless are among the hardest for machines to
acquire (Moravec, 1988). Physical AI therefore provides a demanding test of generality along four
axes, including generalization to new objects and scenes as well as new task combinations, trans-
fer across embodiments and tasks as well as from simulation to reality (Tobin et al., 2017; OpenAI
et al., 2020), robustness to disturbances and sensor degradation as well as environmental drift, and
long-term autonomy over days or months with little human intervention. Because mistakes in the
physical world are often irreversible, evaluation cannot rest on task success rate alone. Real-time
performance, sample efficiency, energy consumption, risk controllability, and recoverability after
failure must be considered together, and they frequently trade off against one another. Physical
AI is not the only such path, as mathematical reasoning, scientific discovery, and social interaction
20


advance general capability from other directions, but it is the one in which capability is checked
against physical reality.
Locating Physical AI on the Trajectory of AI
Taking the degree of coupling between AI and the
physical world as the axis, the position of Physical AI can be stated more concretely. At the loosely
coupled end, AI acts as a digital tool that assists humans with design, analysis, and decision-making
but leaves execution entirely to them. Next, simulated agents perceive and act in simulators or digi-
tal twins (Jones et al., 2020), where trial and error is cheap and safe but limited by the gap between
simulation and reality. Physical AI proper begins when AI closes the loop in the real world. It
starts with single-agent systems, such as a robot, vehicle, drone, or autonomous laboratory platform,
where most current embodied intelligence research is concentrated. It then extends to multi-agent
collaboration, in which groups of agents accomplish tasks that no single agent can, and finally to
infrastructure-level Physical AI, in which distributed sensing, computing, and actuation resources
embedded in cities, power grids, factories, and research facilities are scheduled and governed
through common protocols. Section 1.5.6 returns to these three stages as the recurring physical
compositions of deployed systems. In a network of autonomous laboratories spread across insti-
tutions, for example, the question is no longer only whether an experiment can be completed, but
also how resources are allocated, how processes are audited, and how data ownership and repro-
ducibility are established. These stages coexist and support one another rather than replacing each
other. Digital tools and simulation continue to supply knowledge, data, and safety validation to
physical systems. Physical AI thus occupies the tightly coupled end of this axis, where the value
of AI is realized as a change in physical processes rather than only as the production of informa-
tion. The application landscape in Section 1.5 makes this coupling concrete across industries, and
Chapter 10 examines Physical AGI as a long-term research goal.
1.5
The Application Landscape of Physical AI
Physical AI connects the interpretation of physical state with decisions that change it, and its ap-
plications span individual robots, autonomous vehicles, instrument networks, factories, cities, and
scientific facilities. These settings differ in scale by orders of magnitude, yet the questions that
determine whether a system is useful remain largely the same, concerning what the task requires,
what the environment allows, what resources are available, and which decisions may be taken
without a human in the loop. Whether a particular configuration amounts to a deployable system
is ultimately reflected in the cost of the valid work it produces. The subsections that follow first
state the closed loop that every application instantiates, together with the four dimensions along
which applications are described, namely task, environment, resources, and autonomy. They then sur-
vey four domains, from industrial operation through everyday services and public infrastructure
to scientific inquiry, and finally extract the system archetypes that recur across those domains.
1.5.1
The Closed Loop and the Distinction from Conventional Automation
Every application of Physical AI instantiates one closed loop as shown in Figure 1.5. Physical per-
ception acquires signals from the environment through sensors. State understanding assembles these
signals into estimates of the objects, agents, and processes present, together with the representa-
tions and world models of how they evolve. Prediction and imagination extrapolate the estimated
state forward and evaluate candidate actions, whether through learned dynamics or explicit phys-
ical simulation. Decision making and planning select and sequence actions under task and process
constraints. Physical action executes the selected behavior through control and actuation, and the
resulting environmental feedback becomes the input to the next cycle of perception. These stages give
Definition 1.1 its operational form. Section 1.3 groups them into four elements comprising phys-
ical state perception and estimation, world modeling for representation and prediction, decision-
making with planning and control, and closed-loop feedback with multiscale adaptation. The loop
as a whole, rather than any single stage, defines an application. A system that perceives with-
out acting merely observes its environment, and one that acts without state understanding merely
executes a prescribed motion.

The four domains illustrate its operation under different conditions. Five system archetypes (three
physical compositions and two cross-cutting modes) and four assessment dimensions apply across
domains
Conventional automation already incorporates feedback control, so the loop itself is not
new (Åström and Murray, 2008). What distinguishes Physical AI is how the loop is sustained
when conditions depart from those anticipated at design time, through adapting to changing con-
ditions, interpreting unfamiliar tasks, and transferring knowledge across operations. Classical con-
trol holds a process near a setpoint under modeled disturbances. Physical AI re-estimates state,
re-plans, and recovers when the task or the environment changes. The distinction is graded rather
than binary. Applications occupy a spectrum from fixed procedures with local adaptation, such as
an industrial manipulator re-grasping a shifted part, to open-ended task interpretation, in which a
system must infer what is wanted from instruction, demonstration, or context (Ichter et al., 2023).
The position of an application on this spectrum is determined by the task rather than by the in-
dustry in which it appears. An application can be characterized along four dimensions, namely
task, environment, resources, and autonomy. Resources include sensing, actuation, computation,
energy, and human support. Autonomy specifies which decisions are delegated and when human
participation is required (Parasuraman et al., 2000). These dimensions distinguish requirements
that industry categories tend to merge. Within one factory, moving sealed containers and manip-
ulating deformable materials impose different demands on contact control and recovery, and a
laboratory may coordinate fixed instruments without a single mobile body. System composition
and decision authority therefore require separate descriptions.
22


1.5.2
From Automation to Autonomous Industrial Operation
Industrial production, logistics, and agriculture involve transportation, manipulation, inspection,
and process regulation. Physical AI offers value when variability makes fixed procedures costly to
maintain. Parts arrive in unfamiliar configurations, crops vary in maturity, or equipment behavior
changes with wear. The underlying pattern is common to these sectors. Fixed, engineered proce-
dures are replaced by state estimation and adapted planning, while the process constraints within
which the adaptation must operate remain fixed.
Flexible Manufacturing and Lights-Out Production
In an adaptive production system, visual
and tactile observations update estimates of object and process state, while planning and control
adjust operations within process constraints (Lee et al., 2015; Monostori et al., 2016). Variability
enters as small batches, frequent product changeovers, and parts presented in unfixtured configu-
rations, and the value is realized when changeover no longer requires re-engineering (Van Brussel
et al., 1998). The benefit is measured by product quality, changeover time, resource consump-
tion, and the effort of setting up a new task, while task variability and the resources required for
changeover are the binding constraints. The limit of this development is the lights-out factory, in
which no standing human presence remains on the floor. Lights-out operation does not eliminate
human work. It moves that work to exception handling, supervision, and maintenance, and the
cost of these activities becomes a primary economic variable rather than an overhead (Bainbridge,
1983).
Warehousing, Logistics, and Supply-Chain Orchestration
Warehouses and distribution net-
works concentrate transportation and manipulation at high repetition rates, including automated
storage and retrieval, mobile-robot fleets, sortation, palletizing and depalletizing, and parcel han-
dling (Wurman et al., 2008). The distinguishing problem is not the execution of any single mo-
tion but orchestration, which involves allocating physical work across many machines as demand
fluctuates, replanning after disruption, and keeping physical flows consistent with the inventory
records and delivery commitments carried by information systems (Gerkey and Matari´c, 2004). Lo-
cal motion competence and network-level coordination are separate achievements. An operation
can automate the former while the latter remains manual, and the gap between the two is closed in
practice either by consistent state estimates or by buffer stock.
Agriculture, Forestry, Fishery, and Animal Husbandry
Agricultural settings concentrate the
constraints of Physical AI, including biological variability, unstructured outdoor terrain, weather-
dependent timing, and long deployment cycles. Operations under development span the produc-
tion sequence, including inspection and patrol, seeding and planting, mechanical weeding, fertil-
ization, plant protection, harvesting, and grading and sorting of produce (Bac et al., 2014), together
with livestock monitoring and aquaculture operations (Berckmans, 2017; Føre et al., 2018). Value
appears in two forms, namely precision, in which seed, chemical, and water inputs are reduced by
acting at the resolution of individual plants or animals, and timeliness, in which operations are per-
formed within short agronomic windows. The acceptance criteria are correspondingly biological
and seasonal rather than volumetric, such as fruit harvested without bruising at the correct matu-
rity, weeding achieved with a specified reduction in chemical use, or illness detected early enough
for intervention.
Energy, Mining, and Resource Systems
Energy and mineral systems are high-risk and large-
scale, including generation equipment, transmission corridors, pipelines, refineries, and open-pit
and underground mines. Applications combine inspection of assets (such as turbine blades, trans-
mission lines, and pipe corridors) (Nguyen et al., 2018), autonomous haulage and drilling (Wang
and Huang, 2017; Marshall et al., 2008), and process regulation distributed across many devices.
Equipment behavior changes with wear, which motivates continuously updated estimates of
degradation in place of fixed maintenance schedules (Jardine et al., 2006). Limited access and the
high consequence of failure shift the economics toward predictive operation and remote super-
vision. In these systems, safety cases rather than throughput determine which functions may be
23


automated, and the allocation of authority between site automation and remote operation centers
is itself a design decision.
1.5.3
Daily Services: From Dedicated Equipment to Embodied Companions
Service applications place Physical AI in environments that are built for people rather than for ma-
chines. At one end are dedicated devices (single-purpose appliances that perform one task under
human setup), and at the other are personalized embodied companions intended to share unstruc-
tured space with untrained users. Consumer-grade embodied products, from desktop companions
to inexpensive legged and humanoid platforms, make this trajectory visible at retail prices, al-
though the distance between demonstrations of interactive behavior and dependable household
service remains substantial (Srinivasa et al., 2012).
Human participation is an explicit design variable in these applications. Supervision, shared con-
trol, and selective delegation assign different responsibilities to users, operators, and machines.
In human-facing services, decision authority and timely assistance matter alongside completion
rates, so evaluation includes service quality, accessibility, and the burden placed on users and care-
givers (Hoffman, 2019; Nikolaidis et al., 2016).
Home and Community Services
A household assistant must accommodate changing layouts and
object locations, because neither residents nor their belongings remain arranged to suit a stored
map (Wisspeintner et al., 2009). Cleaning, tidying, laundry, and meal preparation combine manip-
ulation with continual re-estimation of where things are and what state they are in. Community
services extend the same capabilities into semi-public space, including delivery to doors and lock-
ers, patrol and monitoring, and check-ins on residents who live alone. In these settings, acceptance
is determined not by peak capability but by the frequency and manner in which the system re-
quests help. If a robot completes 90% of its tasks unaided but leaves the remaining 10% unfinished
in mid-task, it shifts the burden to its users rather than removing it (Forlizzi and DiSalvo, 2006).
Medical Rehabilitation and Eldercare
A rehabilitation system must respect clinically established
limits on force, range, and intensity while still challenging the patient enough for therapeutic ef-
fect. Applications include shared-control therapy devices that adjust assistance to measured per-
formance, hospital logistics and delivery, continuous monitoring of activity, and assistance with
activities of daily living (Kyrarini et al., 2021). Clinical deployment adds requirements that are
foreign to industrial settings. Interventions must demonstrate safety and efficacy under the con-
ventions of clinical study (Lo et al., 2010; Esquenazi et al., 2012), responsibility for decisions must
be traceable to accountable parties, and eldercare in particular must weigh privacy and dignity
alongside capability (Broadbent et al., 2009). In this domain, Physical AI cannot be separated from
its regulatory and evidentiary context.
Commercial and Professional Services
Retail, hospitality, professional cleaning, and food prepa-
ration occupy a middle ground, with spaces more structured than homes, because they are de-
signed around service processes, yet occupied by the public and by staff whose cooperation cannot
be assumed. Tasks include shelf monitoring and restocking, floor care, reception and guidance,
and food handling to hygienic standards. Interaction with customers and employees is part of
the task itself rather than a distraction from it, which places interface design and predictable, leg-
ible behavior on the critical path alongside manipulation competence. The economics are those
of semi-structured spaces. Repetition is higher than in domestic service, while the tolerance for
bespoke installation is lower than in industry.
1.5.4
Public Infrastructure: From Single-Vehicle Autonomy to City-Scale Coordination
Transportation, energy networks, and public infrastructure extend the concerns of the preceding
sections across larger spatial and temporal scales. The unit of analysis shifts from one machine to
populations of devices whose local actions must combine into system-level outcomes.
24


Intelligent Transportation
Vehicles and drones combine local perception and control with rout-
ing and coordination (Yurtsever et al., 2020; Murray and Chu, 2015). For road vehicles, the dif-
ficult problems are increasingly systemic rather than vehicular, including mixed traffic in which
autonomous and human drivers share conventions, fleet scheduling together with charging and
cleaning for shared robotaxi operation, and the interfaces between vehicle autonomy and traffic
management (Stern et al., 2018; Varaiya, 2013). For low-altitude aircraft, coordination is the found-
ing problem. Airspace organization, geofencing, and conflict resolution for large numbers of small
vehicles must exist before individual autonomy is useful at scale (Prevot et al., 2016). In both cases,
the binding constraint is the coordination of many local planners toward network-level service
quality.
Urban Operations and Public Facilities
Buildings, power systems, and water networks dis-
tribute sensing and actuation across many devices with no mobile body at all, an arrangement
treated as a distinct system archetype in Section 1.5.6. Model predictive control of building climate,
demand response across a power network, and leakage detection in a water distribution network
illustrate the range (Afram and Janabi-Sharifi, 2014; Siano, 2014; Chan et al., 2018). Communication
capacity and consistent state estimates constrain coordination between local actions and system-
wide outcomes. Value is measured by the reliability and continuity of service, energy and resource
efficiency, and responsiveness to faults, observed over the scales of cities and seasons, which places
a premium on sustained and validated operation rather than on peak performance.
Disaster Response and Public Safety
Extreme environments impose additional restrictions. Dis-
aster response combines difficult access, limited energy, and delayed or unavailable human in-
tervention, making recovery mechanisms and bounded local autonomy particularly important.
Search and rescue in collapsed structures, firefighting and hazardous-material intervention, and
post-disaster inspection all require systems that decide and recover locally within a pre-authorized
envelope and degrade safely when communication fails (Murphy, 2014; Delmerico et al., 2019;
Tranzatto et al., 2022). Public-safety applications sharpen the question of authority more than any
other setting in this chapter. The conditions under which a machine may act, and the parties who
are answerable for its actions, must be specified before capability is deployed rather than after.
1.5.5
Scientific Inquiry: From Automated Instruments to Autonomous Laboratories
Scientific applications use physical action to acquire evidence and guide inquiry. An autonomous
laboratory selects experiments, operates instruments, measures outcomes, and revises subsequent
choices (King et al., 2009; Burger et al., 2020; MacLeod et al., 2020; Dai et al., 2024). Scientific value
depends on measurement validity, sample traceability, and reproducible interpretation, alongside
experimental throughput.
Automated and Self-Driven Laboratories
The A-Lab illustrates this organization within a de-
fined inorganic-materials synthesis workflow, integrating robotic operations, computational infor-
mation, automated characterization, and active learning (Szymanski et al., 2023). Its subsequent
correction underscores the need to validate material identification and novelty claims separately
from successful workflow execution (Szymanski et al., 2026). Workflow autonomy (the reliable
execution of planned operations) and epistemic autonomy (the production of claims that survive
scrutiny) are different achievements, and evaluations in this field tend to measure the former while
the value lies chiefly in the latter. Self-driven laboratory programs accordingly treat the validity
chain from sample to published claim as part of the system to be engineered.
Physical Simulation and Digital Twins
In scientific inquiry, simulation and digital twins, which
Section 1.2.3 distinguishes from generic world models, serve as instruments for experiment design,
parameter estimation, and controlled testing. Validation takes two forms. For policy training, it
concerns whether simulated variation supports performance in reality. For an operational digital
twin, it concerns the accuracy, timeliness, and uncertainty of the estimates used in decisions. The
two uses impose different obligations. A training environment must cover the variations a policy
25


will meet, while an operational twin must declare how far ahead, and with what confidence, its
estimates may be trusted.
Human-Machine Collaborative Scientific Cognition
Autonomous laboratories change the divi-
sion of cognitive labor in science rather than removing the scientist. In deployed systems, objective
setting, prioritization among hypotheses, and the acceptance of evidence remain human responsi-
bilities, while machines contribute breadth of search, uniformity of execution, and complete proce-
dural memory. The interpretability of proposed experiments conditions trust. A suggestion whose
rationale can be examined can also be disputed, and such dispute is one of the mechanisms by
which science corrects itself. The productive design question, familiar from Section 1.5.1, is which
parts of inquiry to delegate. Within a research program, the answer to this question is itself some-
thing to be established experimentally.
Aerospace and Space Exploration
Space exploration combines scientific objectives with the most
constrained communication, energy, and mass budgets in this chapter. Planetary rovers schedule
a sol of activity within command latency (Jet Propulsion Laboratory, 2021), on-orbit systems ser-
vice and assemble spacecraft, and in-situ instruments analyze samples that cannot be returned.
Underwater operations share the pattern of difficult access, limited energy, and delayed or absent
intervention (Wynn et al., 2014). Both settings inherit bounded local autonomy as their organizing
principle of deciding locally within a pre-authorized envelope, recording faithfully, and deferring
the remainder to later analysis. This is the same principle identified for disaster response in Sec-
tion 1.5.4, applied where the return of data is slower still.
1.5.6
System Archetypes across Industries
Beneath the domain labels above, deployed systems assume a small number of recurring physi-
cal compositions, together with two modes that cut across them. Three compositions locate sens-
ing and actuation together with computation in one body, in many bodies, or in the facility itself,
while the two modes place either a human operator or a simulated world inside the loop. These
compositions retrace the progression from single-agent systems through multi-agent collaboration
to infrastructure-level Physical AI described in Section 1.4. Taken together, the five archetypes
span the domains surveyed above, each of which can be read through the four dimensions of Sec-
tion 1.5.1. Figure 1.5 shows both views together.
Single Embodied Agents
The first composition concentrates sensing, actuation, computation,
and energy in a single mobile body, as in the household assistant (Fu et al., 2025), the inspection
quadruped (Miki et al., 2022), the planetary rover, the delivery drone (Loquercio et al., 2021). Its
defining property is that resources and autonomy are co-located and bounded by one morphology,
which in turn fixes the reachable task set. Most public attention attaches to this archetype, although
the surveys above show it to be one composition among three.
Multi-Agent and Swarm Systems
The second composition distributes work across many coop-
erating bodies, as in warehouse fleets, agricultural machine teams, drone formations, cooperative
transport (Dorigo et al., 2021). Capability emerges from task allocation, communication, and con-
sensus rather than from any single member, and the fleet thereby acquires properties that its indi-
vidual members lack, such as tolerance of the failure of one member (Werfel et al., 2014; Tolstaya
et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2024). Assessment correspondingly shifts to fleet-level quantities such as
throughput, availability, and the reliability of the coordination mechanism itself.
Environment-Scale Installations
The third composition embeds sensing and actuation in the fa-
cility itself, as in automated warehouses, lights-out factories, autonomous laboratories (Gao et al.,
2025), intelligent buildings, instrumented grids. No mobile body need exist. The laboratory de-
scribed in Section 1.5.1, which coordinates fixed instruments without any mobile body, belongs to
this composition. Engineering attention shifts from the agility of a body to the interfaces of a fa-
26


cility, including how materials, information, and people enter and leave, and the system boundary
becomes an explicit design decision rather than the surface of a robot.
Capability-Augmenting Tools and Collaborative Systems
The first of the two cross-cutting
modes extends a single person’s capabilities through intelligent hand tools, exoskeletons,
augmented-reality task guidance, and collaborative robot cells (de Looze et al., 2016; Matheson
et al., 2019). The human retains decision making, while Physical AI supplies perception, guidance,
and force at the point of work. Autonomy is deliberately low, and integration with the human
is the design center rather than a constraint. Because responsibility remains with the operator,
this archetype provides the economic baseline against which more autonomous alternatives are
judged (International Organization for Standardization, 2025).
Virtual-Real Interaction Systems
The other cross-cutting mode spans physical and simulated en-
vironments through sim-to-real policy training (Tobin et al., 2017), operational digital twins, tele-
operation with haptic and mixed-reality interfaces (Hokayem and Spong, 2006), and hardware-in-
the-loop test benches. The virtual channel may support development, remain part of operation, or
serve both roles. Action may originate from a human operator, a learned policy, or a simulator, and
its physical effect depends on how the resulting command is executed. The validation questions of
Section 1.5.5, concerning whether simulated variation covers reality and how far estimates may be
trusted, thereby become structural properties of the system rather than external checks.
The archetypes compose rather than compete with one another. An autonomous laboratory, for
example, is an environment-scale installation that contains single agents, is trained through virtual-
real interaction, is maintained by humans with augmenting tools, and is coordinated as a multi-
agent system when replicated across sites. The physical composition fixes much of the resource
profile of an application before any algorithm is selected, and the two modes then determine where
authority resides and how much of the loop runs in simulation. For this reason, the four dimensions
of Section 1.5.1 are best assessed per archetype rather than per industry.
1.6
Summary and Organization of the Monograph
This chapter introduces Physical AI as a system-level capacity to perceive physical states, maintain
task-relevant representations of physical relationships and action consequences, and select and ex-
ecute interventions through feedback under physical, operational, and computational constraints.
It contrasts this capacity with digital intelligence, makes the contrast precise in Definition 1.1, and
marks its boundaries against embodied AI, cyber-physical systems, and digital twins. It then de-
composes the capacity into four interdependent elements (Section 1.3), locates it on the axis of
coupling between AI and the physical world (Section 1.4), and shows how deployed applications
instantiate one closed loop under four assessment dimensions, across three physical compositions
and two cross-cutting modes (Section 1.5). A single criterion runs through these perspectives. What
a system can do is determined less by any individual model than by the integrated loop of percep-
tion, prediction, decision, action, and feedback, and by the physical and operational conditions
under which the loop is sustained.
The remainder of this monograph develops that loop. Chapter 2 assembles the technical foun-
dations shared by all four elements, including mathematical descriptions of the physical world,
control theory and autonomous systems, embodied cognition, and learning and reasoning. The
chapters that follow then take up the elements in order. Chapter 3 covers perception and state
estimation. Chapters 4 and 5 cover physical data, simulation environments, and world models
as resources that support prediction. Chapters 6 and 7 cover the foundation models and motor-
control systems that realize decision-making and execution. Chapter 8 develops the definition,
organization, task execution, and coordination of physical agents. Chapter 9 covers the hardware
and systems that must sustain the loop reliably over long-term operation. The final chapters return
to the questions left open here concerning how far the path toward general Physical AI extends
(Chapter 10), how capabilities are evaluated and governed (Chapter 11), and what development
strategies and longer-term outlook follow from them (Chapter 12).
27


The definitions and distinctions established in this chapter provide the vocabulary for all that fol-
lows. Whether a system amounts to Physical AI, where it sits between fixed automation and open-
ended autonomy, and how much of the loop runs in simulation or under human authority are
judged not by stated architecture but by demonstrated capability under specified conditions.
28


2
Technical Foundations
Building on the framework introduced in Chapter 1, this chapter first establishes foundations of
Physical AI, including the mathematical modeling, control theory, cognitive AI, and usage of ma-
chine learning. These four points are organized around the closed physical interaction loop: obser-
vations inform state estimates, models and goals guide action, physical contact generates feedback,
and learning updates behavior. Particularly, Section 2.1 introduces mathematical descriptions of
geometry, dynamics, state, and uncertainty, which provide a shared language for later discussion.
Section 2.2 explains how the core feedback control is used to build a robust and safe embodied
system. On top of the control theory, Section 2.3 examines how to enable embodiment with percep-
tion, skill, and physical grounding of language and multimodal representations. Finally, Section 2.4
moves towards the modern machine learning-based methods. This closed-loop formulation pro-
vides the shared theoretical backbone for the perception, modeling, control, hardware, and safety
chapters that follow.
2.1
Mathematical Descriptions of the Physical World
Physical AI requires an internal representation of the physical world that enables an agent to
perceive, predict, and interact with its environment. Unlike purely symbolic systems, embodied
agents must reason about continuous geometry, physical dynamics, uncertainty, and interaction
constraints. Mathematical descriptions provide the foundation for this process by defining how
physical entities are represented, how their states evolve over time, and how observations relate to
underlying physical reality.
Classical robotics has developed rigorous mathematical formulations for geometry, motion, and
dynamics, while modern embodied intelligence extends these concepts toward learned represen-
tations of complex environments. Together, geometric representations, physical dynamics, and
predictive state descriptions form the foundation for physical world modeling.
2.1.1
Geometry and Spatial Representation
Euclidean Space and Rigid-Body Transformations
The physical world is naturally described in
three-dimensional (3D) Euclidean space. The position of an object can be represented as a point
xpos ∈R3, while the complete pose of an object requires both translation and rotation.
A rigid transformation is represented as

where R ∈SO(3) is a rotation matrix in the special orthogonal group in three dimensions and
t ∈R3 represents translation. The rotation matrix satisfies
R⊤R = I,
det(R) = 1.
(2.2)
Although rotation matrices provide an intuitive geometric interpretation, they contain redundant
parameters. Unit quaternions provide a compact representation of orientation and avoid singular-
ities associated with Euler angles.
For robotics and embodied systems, rigid transformations in the special Euclidean group SE(3) are
commonly represented as

The corresponding Lie algebra se(3) provides a local representation of transformations and is
