29


Explicit Geometric Representations
A physical environment can be represented using explicit
geometric structures that directly describe spatial entities. Point clouds represent surfaces through
discrete sample sets of the form
Pcloud = {p1, p2, ..., pNpoint},
pi ∈R3.
(2.4)
Point clouds preserve metric geometry and naturally arise from sensors such as light detection
and ranging (LiDAR) devices and depth cameras. They are widely used for localization, mapping,
manipulation, and 3D scene understanding.
Mesh representations describe surfaces using vertices, edges, and faces. Compared with point
clouds, meshes explicitly encode surface connectivity and are therefore important for simulation,
collision detection, and physical interaction.
Implicit Representations of Physical Environments
Instead of explicitly storing geometric ele-
ments, implicit representations describe the environment through continuous functions.
A signed distance function (SDF) represents geometry as the zero-level set of a continuous function:
Ssurf = {xpos| f (xpos) = 0}.
(2.5)
SDFs provide useful geometric properties such as surface distance and occupancy, making them
suitable for collision checking, motion planning, and reconstruction.
Neural implicit representations extend this idea by parameterizing continuous scene functions with
neural networks. Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) represent a scene through a continuous mapping
from spatial coordinates and viewing directions to density and appearance as
(σrad, crgb) = FNeRF
θ
(xpos, d),
(2.6)
where σrad represents density and crgb represents color. Such representations enable high-quality
reconstruction and novel-view synthesis, providing a foundation for simulation-ready environ-
ments (Mildenhall et al., 2020).
Topology and Connectivity
Geometric representations describe where objects exist, but embod-
ied agents must additionally understand how spaces and objects are connected. Topological repre-
sentations abstract environments into nodes and edges, where nodes represent meaningful states
or locations and edges represent feasible transitions.
For navigation, topology captures reachability and connectivity of environments. For manipula-
tion, object topology describes structural relationships among parts and possible interaction paths.
Combining geometry and topology allows agents to reason not only about spatial configuration
but also about possible actions.
2.1.2
Physical Dynamics and Interaction Modeling
Kinematics
Kinematics describes how the configuration of a physical system changes without
considering the forces causing the motion. For articulated robots, forward kinematics describes the
relationship between joint space and task space as
T = f (q),
(2.7)
where q represents joint variables and T ∈SE(3) represents the end-effector pose.
The inverse kinematics problem estimates joint configurations required to achieve a desired pose:
q ∈f −1({T}),
(2.8)
where f −1({T}) denotes the set of joint configurations that reach the desired pose.
Inverse kinematics is fundamental for manipulation, locomotion, and motion planning, but can be
challenging due to redundancy, constraints, and multiple feasible solutions (Khalil and Dombre,
2004).
30


Dynamics and Equations of Motion
Dynamics describes how physical states evolve under forces
and control inputs. For articulated systems, robot dynamics can be expressed as
M(q) ¨q + C(q, ˙q) ˙q + g(q) = τ + J(q)⊤wext,
(2.9)
where M represents inertia, C represents velocity-dependent effects, g represents gravity, and τ
represents actuator torque. The external wrench wext ∈R6 stacks force and moment. The geometric
Jacobian J(q) ∈R6×n maps the n joint rates to linear and angular velocity at the wrench reference
point, expressed in the same coordinate frame.
The Newton-Euler formulation provides an efficient recursive computation of rigid-body dynam-
ics, while the Lagrangian formulation derives motion equations from energy functions:
Lmech(q, ˙q) = Ekin(q, ˙q) −Epot(q).
(2.10)
These formulations provide the mathematical basis for simulation, control, and physical reason-
ing (Featherstone, 2008).
Contact Mechanics and Interaction
Physical AI requires reasoning about interaction between
objects. Unlike free-space motion, contact introduces constraints involving collision, friction, and
force transmission.
The Coulomb friction model relates tangential and normal forces through
∥ft∥≤µ∥fn∥,
(2.11)
where µ denotes the friction coefficient.
Contact dynamics are often formulated as constrained optimization problems involving non-
penetration constraints and friction cones. Accurate contact modeling is essential for grasping,
manipulation, locomotion, and tool use (Posa et al., 2014; Stewart and Trinkle, 1996).
2.1.3
State Representation and Predictive Modeling
State-Space Representation
A physical system is commonly described through a state variable xt
that summarizes the information necessary to predict future evolution. The state transition process
can be represented as
xt+1 = F(xt, ut) + wt,
(2.12)
where ut represents actions and wt represents disturbances.
The observation process connects physical states with sensory measurements through
yt = hobs(xt) + ϵt.
(2.13)
This formulation provides the mathematical foundation for perception, estimation, planning, and
control.
Latent States and Compact Physical Representations
In realistic environments, the complete
physical state is rarely directly observable. Sensors provide incomplete and noisy measurements,
while variables such as object properties, hidden geometry, and contact states may remain un-
known.
Therefore, modern Physical AI systems often learn latent state representations of the form
zt = fθ(ot),
(2.14)
where ot represents observations and zt represents a compact latent description of the environment.
A useful latent representation should preserve task-relevant physical information while discard-
ing irrelevant variations. Such representations provide the foundation for predictive learning and
world models discussed in Section 2.4 and Chapter 5.
31


Uncertainty and Predictive Representations
Physical environments are inherently uncertain due
to incomplete observations, stochastic dynamics, and unknown parameters. Therefore, physical
state representations should incorporate uncertainty:
p(xt | y1:t)
(2.15)
rather than assuming exact knowledge of the state.
Probabilistic state estimation methods, including Kalman filtering and Bayesian inference, pro-
vide classical solutions for uncertainty estimation. Modern learning-based approaches extend these
ideas by learning predictive representations directly from large-scale sensory experience.
These mathematical descriptions provide the bridge between explicit physical models and learned
world models. Classical representations define the structure of the physical world, while learned
representations enable scalable prediction and reasoning in complex environments.
2.2
Control Theory and Autonomous Systems
The mathematical descriptions in the previous section provide models of the physical world, and
control theory in this section explains how an embodied agent can use measurements and actions
to regulate its interaction with that world. Embodied intelligence requires continuous exchange of
energy and information with the physical world. A robot must therefore not only infer an appro-
priate action but also realize it through actuators subject to finite torque, uncertain contact, delayed
sensing, and disturbances that cannot be enumerated in advance. Control theory provides the for-
mal language for this interaction. It asks how measurements should modify action, how models
may be used without being trusted unconditionally, and under what conditions the resulting closed
loop remains stable, accurate, and safe.
This section examines closed-loop autonomous operation, in which sensing, planning, and control
repeatedly respond to the consequences of action. Motor-current and joint controllers react within
microseconds to milliseconds. Whole-body controllers coordinate forces over tens of milliseconds,
and task planners and behavior executives operate over seconds or minutes. Learning systems
may update models over an entire deployment. Although these layers differ in representation and
method, each compares an intended condition with an observed one and acts on the discrepancy.
Feedback therefore connects classical control, optimization, planning, and learning-based auton-
omy rather than belonging to any one of them. The following subsections introduce feedback,
control methods, and hierarchical autonomy. They also analyze stability, robustness, adaptation,
and safety.
2.2.1
Foundations of Cybernetics: Feedback and Steady State
A feedback control system uses measurements of a physical system’s behavior to adjust its con-
trol inputs toward a desired target, which forms a feedback loop of measurement and correction.
This section first introduces this feedback loop, and then discusses its transient and steady-state
behavior, to assess how effectively a system approaches and maintains that target.
Negative Feedback Principle
Wiener (1948) introduces cybernetics as a framework for studying
control and communication in systems whose actions affect the conditions they subsequently ob-
serve. In this framework, a plant receives a control input u(t), evolves under its own dynamics and
external disturbances, and produces an output y(t). For output tracking, a controller compares the
measured output with a reference r(t) and uses the tracking error to determine the next control
command. The error, and the control input in the simplest case of proportional control with gain
KP, are defined as
etrack(t) = r(t) −y(t),
u(t) = KPetrack(t),
(2.16)
where the proportional law is the simplest instance of feedback. Integral and derivative action
extend this relation in the proportional-integral-derivative controller introduced below.
32


Controllers may also use an estimate of the underlying state when the relevant variables are not
directly measured. The loop is called negative feedback when the controller acts so as to reduce the
measured deviation, as when a thermostat increases heating below its set point or a balancing vehi-
cle generates torque opposing body tilt. Feedback is most valuable when the model is incomplete.
If an actuator delivers less torque than commanded, or a manipulator grasps an object of unknown
mass, a precomputed input cannot detect the resulting error. Feedback uses observations of the
changed motion to compensate within the limits of sensing, actuation, and closed-loop bandwidth.
Feedback thereby converts certain forms of uncertainty into observable error and permits repeat-
able behavior from imperfect components.
Negative feedback is not synonymous with stability. A correction whose sign is appropriate at low
frequency may destabilize the loop once sensing, computation, or actuation introduces sufficient
delay. Excessive gain has the same effect, and strong reaction to high-frequency measurement noise
may excite unmodeled flexible modes. Feedback design must therefore shape the magnitude and
phase of the loop response, not merely reverse the sign of the error (Åström and Murray, 2008).
The signals entering the loop must also be distinguished. A reference describes intended behavior,
a disturbance acts on the plant from outside, measurement noise corrupts the information avail-
able to the controller, and model uncertainty denotes the discrepancy between representation and
mechanism. These signals can produce similar visible effects yet require different remedies, so an
embodied controller is a negotiated balance among tracking, disturbance rejection, noise attenua-
tion, actuator effort, and robustness. Feedback further depends on what is measured. Because the
full state is rarely available, practical loops incorporate an estimator that fuses a dynamic model
with sensor streams. Estimation and control become coupled processes in which actions determine
which future observations become available.
Open-Loop and Closed-Loop Control
Two basic control arrangements are open-loop and closed-
loop control, illustrated in Figure 2.1 (Franklin et al., 2019; Dorf and Bishop, 2017; Åström and
Murray, 2008). An open-loop controller selects its input without measurements of the controlled
outcome during execution. Such control is appropriate when the plant and environment are suffi-
ciently repeatable, when feedback is unavailable, or when the maneuver is too fast for a sensor-
to-actuator loop, but it cannot correct errors that become observable only after execution be-
gins. Closed-loop control uses observations to revise action, and its advantage is made precise
by the sensitivity functions. For a single-input, single-output linear system in the standard neg-
ative unity-feedback configuration with plant P(s) and controller C(s), the loop transfer function
L(s) = P(s)C(s) yields
S(s) =
1
1 + L(s),
T(s) =
L(s)
1 + L(s),
S(s) + T(s) = 1,
(2.17)
where T maps the reference to the output, S maps an additive output disturbance to the output, and
measurement noise reaches the output through −T. Where |L| is large and the loop is stable, |S| is
generally small, whereas noise is transmitted through T. The multivariable case is analogous, with
multiplication order significant. Feedback thus does not erase uncertainty but redistributes sensi-
tivity across frequencies, subject to stability margins, delay, and unmodeled dynamics (Skogestad
and Postlethwaite, 2005).
Capable robotic systems combine feedback with feedforward. Inverse dynamics, for example, pre-
dicts the torques required for a desired motion, while feedback corrects residual errors caused by
inaccurate parameters, friction, contact, or estimation error. This two-degree-of-freedom structure
also clarifies the role of learned models, which improve the nominal action while the conventional
loop rejects deviations within a known operating envelope. The open-loop/closed-loop distinction
is therefore a design spectrum rather than a dichotomy. Feedforward motion may be embedded
within a slower feedback loop, and symbolic goals may be issued to feedback controllers with local
termination conditions. Physical feedback also carries costs. Sensors consume power and band-
width, estimation and communication add latency, and a loop may regulate the wrong variable
with high precision, as when position control damages a fragile object because contact force is un-
monitored (Raibert and Craig, 1981; Hogan, 1985).

Steady-State Error and Integral Action
Transient performance describes behavior while a system
approaches its target. For a system that converges to a steady state, steady-state performance char-
acterizes the residual behavior after transients have decayed (Ogata, 2010; Franklin et al., 2019).
For a constant reference r(t), with the tracking error etrack(t) = r(t) −y(t) as defined above, the
steady-state error is
ess = lim
t→∞etrack(t),
(2.18)
provided that the limit exists and the closed loop is stable. A proportional controller may fail to
eliminate this error when a constant input is needed to balance a persistent load. For instance,
a mobile robot ascending a slope requires a constant drive force to balance gravity, and because
proportional action generates its command solely in proportion to the present error, such a nonzero
force can be produced only while a nonzero error persists, so the vehicle settles into a steady climb
at a speed below the reference. Integral action instead accumulates the error in an integrator state
ηI(t) and adds an integral term uI(t) to the control input,
ηI(t) =
Z t
0 etrack(τ) dτ,
uI(t) = KIηI(t),
(2.19)
where KI is the integral gain. A persistent deviation therefore continues to modify the command
and, subject to closed-loop stability and sufficient control authority, is driven to zero. The inter-
nal model principle formalizes this mechanism. Under closed-loop stability and the solvability
conditions of output regulation, exact asymptotic tracking or rejection that is robust to small plant-
parameter variations requires a model capable of generating the reference or disturbance signal
within the feedback path (Francis and Wonham, 1976). The integral action discussed above is the
simplest instance of this principle. An integrator generates constant signals, and a loop containing
an integrator can therefore track a constant reference or reject a constant disturbance exactly. Ro-
bust tracking of sinusoidal references likewise requires the controller to contain a corresponding
oscillatory model at the reference frequency.
34


Integral action has its own failure mode under actuator saturation. An actuator, such as an electric
motor or a hydraulic drive, delivers only bounded torque or force, so the applied control input u(t)
stops following the command whenever the requested value exceeds this physical limit. During
saturation, the integrator may continue accumulating error although additional command cannot
affect the plant, and the stored term produces a large overshoot when the system re-enters the
controllable range. Anti-windup schemes limit or discharge this accumulation by clamping the
integrator, feeding back the difference between requested and applied input, or conditioning in-
tegration on the actuator state (Kothare et al., 1994; Tarbouriech and Turner, 2009). For embodied
systems, saturation must be treated as part of the model rather than as a rare implementation detail.
Note that the significance of zero steady-state error is task-dependent. Contact tasks often tolerate
deliberate pose error in exchange for regulated force, and legged robots accept bounded periodic
error in exchange for lower impact and energy consumption.
2.2.2
Classical and Modern Control Methods
One of the most widely used control systems is proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control. It
maps three interpretable features of the error into control action. In its ideal continuous-time form,
u(t) = KPetrack(t) + KI
Z t
0 etrack(τ) dτ + KD
detrack(t)
dt
,
(2.20)
where KP, KI, and KD are the proportional, integral, and derivative gains, and etrack(t) is the track-
ing error defined above. The proportional term KPetrack(t) responds to the present error, the integral
term KI
R t
0 etrack(τ) dτ to its accumulated history, and the derivative term KD detrack/dt to its local
trend. For position or angle error with force or torque output, proportional action resembles a vir-
tual spring, derivative action resembles a virtual damper, and integral action resembles a slowly
adjusting bias that offsets gravity or friction. In a torque-controlled robot this analogy connects PID
directly to impedance design. It also exposes the hazard of aggressive tuning. A stiff virtual spring
improves free-space positioning while generating unsafe forces after unexpected contact, so that
gains encode a physical interaction policy rather than a numerical convergence rate alone.
In practice, PID implementations modify the ideal equation in several ways. First, the derivative
term is filtered against measurement noise and applied to the output rather than the reference to
avoid derivative kick. Integral action also requires anti-windup. Additionally, actuator dead zones,
quantization, rate limits, and computation delay can dominate performance if ignored (Åström
and Hägglund, 2005). Tuning rules such as Ziegler-Nichols (Ziegler and Nichols, 1942) provide
useful initial gains, but they do not replace validation on hardware. Practical implementations
typically nest current, velocity, and position loops of decreasing bandwidth. When this bandwidth
separation is weak, the independently tuned loops interact and may destabilize the mechanism.
PID control is best suited to regulation tasks with few variables and nearly constant dynamics.
Multivariable coupling, nonminimum-phase behavior, hard constraints, and large changes in the
operating range call for model-based methods instead. Even then, PID often persists at the actuator
interface, because its failure modes are familiar and its behavior is inspectable.
State Space and Optimal Control
Another model is the state-space model, which represents the
internal configuration required to predict future evolution. A linear time-invariant model has the
form
˙x(t) = Ax(t) + Bu(t) + Ew(t),
y(t) = Cobsx(t) + vnoise(t),
(2.21)
where x ∈Rn is the state, u ∈Rm the control input, w a process disturbance, y the measurement,
vnoise measurement noise, and A, B, E, Cobs are matrices of compatible dimensions. A nonlinear
system ˙x = fc(x, u, w) can be linearized about an equilibrium or nominal trajectory. Controlla-
bility describes whether the input can move every state direction over a finite interval, and ob-
servability describes whether the initial state can be recovered from the input-output history. The
weaker properties of stabilizability and detectability suffice for stabilization and estimator con-
vergence, requiring only that every uncontrollable or unobservable mode already be stable. As
a result, no controller compensates for an actuator lacking authority over an unstable direction,
35


and no model complexity recovers a contact state invisible to the measurements (Åström and Mur-
ray, 2008). When the full state is not measured, an observer estimates it. For a linear model with
zero-mean white process and measurement noises of known covariance, the Kalman filter is the
minimum-mean-square-error estimator among linear estimators, and it is the optimal estimator
without that restriction when the initial state and the noises are jointly Gaussian (Kalman, 1960a).
Because estimation error enters the loop as a dynamic signal, estimator bandwidth, outlier han-
dling, and covariance calibration are part of controller design rather than preprocessing details.
The linear-quadratic regulator (LQR) (Kalman, 1960b) renders the trade-off between regulation and
control effort explicit. For the system ˙x = Ax + Bu, it minimizes

tracking applies time-varying LQR to deviations linearized along a nominal trajectory, and apply-
ing the gain to a Kalman estimate yields the linear-quadratic-Gaussian controller under the sep-
aration principle. The principal limitation is constraint handling. LQR does not natively enforce
joint limits, contact, collision avoidance, or torque saturation, and clipping an optimal command
after computation alters the closed-loop dynamics and can invalidate the nominal analysis. Con-
strained quadratic programs impose instantaneous limits, while model predictive control extends
the optimization across future steps.
Model Predictive Control
Model predictive control (MPC) is also commonly used and repeatedly
solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem using the latest state estimate. A representative
nominal discrete-time formulation is

Xterm is a terminal constraint set. Only the first optimized input is applied. The horizon then shifts
forward, a new estimate is obtained, and the problem is solved again. When the optimization re-
mains feasible and is solved as specified, this receding-horizon procedure induces a feedback law
on the current state estimate.
MPC is attractive for embodied systems because constraints are part of the decision problem. A ma-
nipulator can bound joint angles, velocities, torques, or predicted collision distances, and a legged
1A pair (A, B) is stabilizable when every eigenmode of A that cannot be influenced by the input is already
asymptotically stable. Likewise, (A, Q1/2) is detectable when every eigenmode of A that is unobservable
through Q1/2x is already asymptotically stable. These are necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence
of stabilizing linear state feedback and a linear observer with asymptotically stable error dynamics, respec-
tively. Here detectability refers to the cost output Q1/2x.
36


robot can also consider friction and feasible contact forces. For nominal regulation, recursive feasi-
bility and asymptotic stability can be established through a positive-definite stage cost, a terminal
controller that respects the constraints, a positively invariant terminal set, and a terminal cost de-
crease condition, provided that the initial problem is feasible (Mayne et al., 2000). Design choices
are consequential. Short horizons reduce computation but limit how far ahead the controller pre-
dicts. Hard constraints declare violations inadmissible, whereas selected constraints may be soft-
ened with slack variables when requirements conflict. With linear dynamics, linear constraints,
and convex quadratic costs, MPC is a convex quadratic program. Nonlinear MPC typically uses
iterative numerical optimization, often with warm starts and sparse solvers.
Prediction does not eliminate the need for feedback or robustness. Model mismatch grows along
the horizon, particularly during impacts, slip, or deformable contact. Tube MPC, stochastic MPC,
chance constraints, or min-max formulations reserve margins against possible deviations. The sys-
tem must define the response to infeasibility or solver timeout, whether retaining the previous
command, switching to a stabilizing backup, or braking. Controller selection should follow the
structure of the task, and the methods are frequently composed. MPC supplies whole-body refer-
ences, an intermediate controller stabilizes deviations, and embedded PID loops realize actuator
commands.
2.2.3
Hierarchical Architectures of Autonomous Systems
The Classical Sense-Plan-Act Pipeline
Sense-Plan-Act decomposes autonomous behavior into
perception, planning, and control. Perception converts sensor data into estimates of robot and
environment state. Planning selects goals, actions, or trajectories. Control converts plans into ac-
tuator commands while correcting deviations (Gat, 1998). The decomposition is misleading when
read as a one-shot sequence. By the end of a long perception-and-planning cycle, the environment
may have changed and localization uncertainty may have grown. Autonomous operation therefore
requires repeated sensing and replanning, with components running concurrently under explicit
latency budgets, because an accurate estimate of an old state can be less useful than a coarser esti-
mate of the present one.
One design requirement for this pipeline is that information passed between the perception, plan-
ning, and control stages should include uncertainty and validity, not only nominal values (Siciliano
and Khatib, 2016). For example, a pose estimate without covariance encourages downstream mod-
ules to treat perception as certain, and a path without timing assumptions leaves control unable
to distinguish acceptable tracking error from an obsolete plan. Interfaces should include refer-
ence frames, units, update rates, tolerances, and failure conditions, particularly when learned com-
ponents are integrated with model-based control (Brugali and Scandurra, 2009). Feedback paths
should also cross stage boundaries. Control influences perception through active sensing, and a
geometrically valid path may be dynamically infeasible. Finally, real-time performance is gov-
erned by worst-case timing rather than average throughput. Occasionally, a planner that requires
2 seconds may be unacceptable for collision avoidance. A predesigned degradation behavior pro-
vides a backup solution. Also, scheduling priorities must follow physical urgency, because motor
stabilization and contact protection cannot wait for task-level planning.
Behavior Trees and Finite-State Machines
Finite-state machines (FSMs) can also formalize task
execution as discrete modes and transitions triggered by events or conditions, with each state ac-
tivating corresponding controllers or planners. Hybrid automata extend the representation by as-
sociating continuous dynamics with each mode (Henzinger, 1996), a natural description of sys-
tems that alternate among free motion, contact, and impact. However, a limitation of a flat FSM is
combinatorial growth. As recovery cases and task variants accumulate, transitions proliferate and
behavior becomes difficult to inspect. Hierarchical state machines mitigate this growth, but their
interrupt, priority, and concurrency semantics must be specified explicitly. A logically valid transi-
tion may be physically unsafe if it switches references discontinuously or transfers control without
resetting estimator and integrator states.
37


Behavior trees organize task logic through a rooted tree that is evaluated, or “ticked,” repeatedly.
Internal control-flow nodes implement sequences, fallbacks, and parallel combinations. Leaf nodes
evaluate conditions or execute actions. Every node returns one of the three statuses Success, Fail-
ure, or Running to its parent. A sequence ticks its children until one returns Running or Failure. A
fallback ticks its children until one returns Running or Success. Because a subtree exposes a small
status interface, it can be reused across tasks, and repeated evaluation supports reactive switch-
ing (Colledanchise and Ögren, 2018; Iovino et al., 2022). Behavior trees do not themselves solve
planning or control. A leaf labeled grasp object still requires perception, control, and recovery logic,
and apparent modularity can conceal resource conflicts between branches. The choice between
the representations should follow execution semantics. FSMs suit a small number of modes with
well-defined transitions and admit formal verification, whereas behavior trees favor hierarchical
composition and reusable recovery strategies, with an independent monitor retaining override au-
thority for safety-related functions. Task-level switching also interacts with continuous control.
Stability of each mode does not imply stability under arbitrary switching. Common and multiple
Lyapunov functions, dwell-time conditions, guards, and reset maps address different classes of
switched and hybrid systems (Liberzon, 2003), and the task executive and the low-level controller
must share explicit entry, exit, and state-transfer rules.
Coordinating Reactive and Deliberative Systems
Reactive control maps current observations
directly to actions, with little or no explicit look-ahead, whereas deliberative control constructs and
evaluates possible futures. Neither is sufficient alone. Pure deliberation becomes slow or brittle
once its world model is stale. Pure reaction may cycle, become trapped, or sacrifice a long-term
goal. Layered architectures therefore emerged to combine the two (Brooks, 1986; Gat, 1998). A use-
ful architecture separates time scales while preserving channels for intervention. Its layers range
from actuator limits, balance, and contact stability through short-horizon motion generation and
skill selection to mission-level reasoning over goals and resources. Each layer has a character-
istic update rate, abstraction, authority, and failure response. Higher layers parameterize lower
layers, and lower layers report feasibility, progress, and exceptions rather than merely accepting
commands.
Coordination can be expressed through references and invariant sets. A local controller accepts a
high-level goal only if it lies within a verified operating envelope, and it modifies or rejects com-
mands that approach limits of balance, collision distance, or actuator temperature, reporting the
reason. Learned policies fit naturally into this view. A policy may propose task choices, way-
points, residual torques, or complete actions, and its placement determines the consequences of
error, because a high-level proposal can be checked by planning and constrained control whereas
an end-to-end torque policy admits little downstream correction. When layers disagree, summing
commands can produce an action intended by neither. Priority arbitration, constrained optimiza-
tion, and supervisory switching provide explicit alternatives, and hysteresis and minimum dwell
times prevent chattering. The resulting system is a hierarchy of closed loops rather than a lin-
ear pipeline. Each layer monitors variables appropriate to its horizon and receives feedback from
below and from the environment, and autonomy arises when these loops maintain short-term via-
bility while advancing long-term objectives.
2.2.4
Stability and Robustness Theory
Feedback enables a controller to respond to deviations from a reference, while stability and robust-
ness analysis establishes the closed-loop guarantees under specified conditions. This subsection
reviews Lyapunov methods, barrier functions, and robust and adaptive control as formal tools for
making such guarantees explicit.
Lyapunov Stability
The stability of a closed-loop system depends on the specified equilibrium,
trajectory, set, or orbit. For an equilibrium x = 0, Lyapunov stability requires that trajectories
starting sufficiently close remain close, asymptotic stability additionally requires convergence, and
exponential stability specifies a convergence-rate bound (Khalil, 2002). These statements are not
interchangeable, and a local certificate asserts nothing about initial conditions outside its certified
38


region of attraction. Lyapunov’s direct method establishes stability without solving the differential
equation. Let f be locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood DLyap of the equilibrium, with f (0) = 0. If
a continuously differentiable function V : DLyap →R, called a Lyapunov function candidate and
distinct from the terminal cost Vf used in model predictive control above, satisfies
V(0) = 0,
V(x) > 0,
˙V(x) = ∇V(x)⊤f (x) < 0,
x ∈DLyap \ {0},
(2.25)
then the equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable. If these conditions hold on all of Rn and V
is proper and radially unbounded, the equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable. If ˙V is only
negative semidefinite, stability follows, but asymptotic convergence requires additional reasoning
such as LaSalle’s invariance principle (Khalil, 2002). Every stability claim should be paired with its
domain, assumptions, and convergence notion.
For control-affine dynamics ˙x = f (x) + gin(x)u, a control Lyapunov function identifies inputs that
render the derivative sufficiently negative and can be imposed as a constraint in an online opti-
mization that remains close to a nominal command. This construction bridges nonlinear control
and learning. A neural network may propose a command that a model-based filter modifies when
the constraint would otherwise be violated. Claims that a learned certificate renders a neural con-
troller unconditionally stable are nevertheless too broad. The positivity and decrease conditions
must hold over a stated domain, not merely on sampled training points, and verification may re-
quire analytic bounds, interval methods, mixed-integer formulations, sum-of-squares relaxations,
or reachability analysis. Neural representation changes the parameterization of the candidate, not
the logical requirements of the theorem.
Stability also differs from safety. An asymptotically stable robot may pass through an obstacle on
its way to the goal. Safety is commonly formulated as forward invariance of a set Csafe = {x :
hsafe(x) ≥0}. For a differentiable relative-degree-one constraint and control-affine dynamics, a
zeroing control barrier function requires an admissible input u ∈U satisfying
L f hsafe(x) + Lginhsafe(x)u + αsafe(hsafe(x)) ≥0,
(2.26)
where L f hsafe = ∇h⊤
safe f, Lginhsafe = ∇h⊤
safegin, and αsafe is a locally Lipschitz extended class-K
function. If a well-posed feedback law selects such an input and the regularity assumptions of the
barrier theorem hold, trajectories starting in Csafe remain in Csafe (Ames et al., 2017). Feasibility
can fail under input limits or conflicting barriers, so the inequality is not an unconditional safety
guarantee. Lyapunov and barrier constraints can be combined in a quadratic program, with safety
taking priority over convergence when relaxation is necessary. Formal claims must finally encom-
pass computation and implementation. A continuous-time proof may not survive slow sampling,
solver timeout, communication delay, or state-estimation error. A credible assurance case therefore
connects the theorem to timing tests, uncertainty bounds, fault handling, and a validated operating
domain, with formal analysis and empirical stress testing supporting one another.
Robust Control
Robust control studies whether stability and performance persist across a spec-
ified family of plants and disturbances. The uncertainty set is the central object. It may represent
bounded parameter variation, neglected high-frequency dynamics, or uncertain contact stiffness,
and no controller is robust to unspecified uncertainty of arbitrary magnitude. A common objective
bounds the induced gain from a disturbance w to a performance output zperf. In H∞control, the
closed-loop transfer matrix Tzw from the disturbance w to the performance output zperf is designed
so that
∥Tzw∥∞= sup

(2.27)
where ¯σ denotes maximum singular value. For a stable proper linear time-invariant interconnec-
tion with zero initial condition, this is the induced L2-gain bound ∥zperf∥2 < γgain∥w∥2 for nonzero
w ∈L2. Weighting functions specify which signals and frequency ranges matter, and γgain is a cer-
tified performance bound for the chosen interconnection, not a probability of success in an arbitrary
environment (Zhou et al., 1996).
39


Frequency-domain concepts clarify why high nominal performance can erode tolerance to uncer-
tainty. Gain and phase margins describe only particular scalar perturbations in a single loop, sin-
gular values generalize sensitivity analysis to multivariable systems, and structured singular-value
methods distinguish repeated, real, complex, and dynamic uncertainties. Finer uncertainty models
reduce conservatism but demand stronger plant knowledge. The guarantee covers only the uncer-
tainty that analysis has identified and bounded. Robust performance also trades against nominal
agility, and excessive conservatism is itself hazardous when a vehicle cannot maneuver quickly
enough to avoid a collision. Learning reduces model error but introduces new uncertainty. A
residual dynamics model may improve tracking in familiar conditions while extrapolating poorly
after a payload or surface change. A practical pattern lets the learned component improve perfor-
mance inside a confidence region while a robust backup or safety filter limits consequences outside
it, preserving the separation between empirical performance and a separately justified safety mech-
anism (Brunke et al., 2022).
Adaptive Control
Adaptive control changes controller parameters online in response to observed
behavior (Åström and Wittenmark, 1995). It is useful when the dynamics vary beyond what fixed
gains can tolerate, as when a manipulator grasps an unknown payload or tire forces change with
road conditions. A canonical analysis considers dynamics linearly parameterized by an unknown
constant vector θ. The controller maintains an estimate ˆθ, updated from tracking errors and mea-
sured regressors. The control and update laws are designed together so that a Lyapunov argument
establishes boundedness and, under stated assumptions, tracking convergence. This structure is
more specific than unconstrained online learning, because the form of uncertainty, the update sig-
nal, and the stability objective are stated in advance (Åström and Wittenmark, 1995). Gain schedul-
ing selects among precomputed controllers, direct adaptive control updates controller parameters,
and indirect adaptive control estimates plant parameters and redesigns the controller. Guarantees
proved for constant θ do not transfer unchanged to time-varying parameters, where bounded rates
of variation yield ultimate bounds rather than exact asymptotic convergence.
Accurate tracking does not imply parameter convergence. For a regressor ϕPE(t) ∈Rdreg, a stan-
dard persistent-excitation condition requires constants T0 > 0 and µPE > 0 such that
Z t+T0

for all t ≥0.
(2.28)
Under the assumptions of a given adaptive law, such excitation supports convergence because the
data distinguish all parameter directions. A robot holding a constant pose may regulate success-
fully while learning almost nothing about inertial coupling, whereas deliberate excitation improves
identification but may conflict with task performance, comfort, or safety. Actions in adaptive con-
trol therefore influence both immediate regulation and future knowledge (Bar-Shalom and Tse,
1974).
Classical adaptive laws can drift when disturbances, unmodeled dynamics, or sensor bias violate
their assumptions. Projection operators confine estimates to plausible bounds, dead zones pre-
vent adaptation to noise-dominated errors, and leakage or σ-modification discourages unbounded
parameter growth, typically replacing exact asymptotic tracking with uniform ultimate bounded-
ness. Modern learned adaptation extends beyond low-dimensional parameter estimation to latent-
context identification, dynamics-model updating, and policy adaptation, but stability does not fol-
low from low prediction loss alone. A conservative architecture confines adaptation to a nominal
model or policy inside an envelope maintained by independent constraints, monitoring, and fall-
back behavior. Stability, robustness, adaptation, and safety answer distinct questions about what
trajectories do, whether that behavior persists over a bounded uncertainty set, how the controller
changes as information is acquired, and whether forbidden states are avoided. Dependable auton-
omy requires an explicit argument for each property, and it requires every feedback loop to declare
what it regulates, what uncertainty it tolerates, and where its guarantees end.

2.3
Embodied Cognition and the Development of Intelligence
Embodied cognition examines how intelligence depends on the interaction between an agent’s
body and its environment. Perception and action shape one another, and concepts gain meaning
through sensory and motor experience. For Physical AI, this view calls for models and representa-
tions that are developed and tested through physical interaction.
2.3.1
Core Claims of Embodied Cognition
Embodied cognition is not a single theory but a family of claims about the unit of analysis for in-
telligence. Classical accounts often separate sensing, internal reasoning, and actuation. Embodied
accounts emphasize that perception depends on possible movement, bodily dynamics change the
control problem, and action alters the observations available next. Embodied, embedded, enactive,
and extended cognition make distinct claims about bodily realization, real-time environmental de-
pendence, autonomous sense-making, and the possible inclusion of external resources in a cogni-
tive system (Wilson, 2002; Clark, 1997; Varela et al., 1991; Clark and Chalmers, 1998). For Physical
AI, the common methodological lesson is to analyze the coupled agent-body-environment system.
Merely attaching sensors and actuators is not enough. The body and interaction history must ma-
terially organize the capability being explained.
Gibson’s ecological approach shifts perception from recovering detached object properties to de-
tecting information relevant to an acting organism (Gibson, 1979). Its central concept, the affor-
dance, is relational rather than a fixed label. The same ledge may afford stepping, climbing, or no
safe action for bodies with different abilities (Chemero, 2003). An affordance-centered robot must
therefore ask not only “What is this?” but also “What can this body do here under its current kine-
matic, dynamic, and safety constraints?” Sensorimotor theories complement this view by treating
perception as mastery of action-dependent sensory regularities (O’Regan and Noë, 2001). Camera
motion can reveal depth, wrist rotation can disambiguate shape, and tactile exploration can reveal
compliance. Brooks’s situated robotics work in 1991 and subsequent dynamical analyses show how
robust behavior can arise from such tight real-time coupling without an exhaustive central recon-
struction (Brooks, 1991; Beer, 2000). These results challenge mandatory complete world models,
but they do not show that long-horizon planning or reasoning about absent events can dispense
with internal state.
Intelligence also requires the ability to combine learned concepts and apply them to new situa-
tions (Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988). However, these concepts must be connected to real-world expe-
rience. Harnad’s symbol-grounding problem highlights that symbols cannot obtain meaning only
from relations to other symbols (Harnad, 1990). Barsalou’s perceptual-symbol theory suggests that
concepts are grounded in perceptual and motor experiences (Barsalou, 1999; 2008). For example,
the concept of “heavy” can be associated with the effort required to lift an object and the adjust-
ments needed to maintain a stable grip. Thus, intelligent systems need representations that support
reasoning and generalization while remaining connected to perception and action.
A robot’s physical structure can simplify certain movements, while interaction with the environ-
ment provides information that helps it make better decisions (Pfeifer and Bongard, 2006; Wilson
and Golonka, 2013). Rather than replacing internal models, physical interaction can complement
them by providing feedback and helping robots adapt their behavior. This raises the question of
how robots acquire and improve their knowledge and skills through repeated interactions with the
physical world.
2.3.2
Perception-Action Coupling and Development
Action does more than follow perception. It can also improve perception. Action can help to se-
lect viewpoints, create contacts, and determine which perceptual signals may covary. Bajcsy (1988)
formalizes active perception by proposing that sensing strategies be chosen jointly with task goals.
Held and Hein’s 1963 yoked-control experiment further distinguishes receiving visual stimula-
tion from causing it, supporting a developmental role for action-contingent experience under its
41


controlled conditions (Held and Hein, 1963). In robotics, an observation paired with the agent’s
command, proprioception, and resulting state transition contains information absent from passive
video. New motor skills also create developmental cascades. Reaching, locomotion, and tool use
change what can be observed and manipulated, thereby changing the data distribution for later
learning (Adolph and Hoch, 2019).
One aspect of development is learning sensorimotor coordinates and a body schema. Hand-eye
coordination requires image displacement, head pose, arm configuration, joint motion, and contact
to become mutually predictive. Metta et al. (1999) show that an artificial system can refine a vi-
suomotor reaching map through experience without a fully specified prior kinematic calibration.
Body-schema research generalizes this result to revisable relations among commands, configura-
tions, contacts, and sensory consequences (Hoffmann et al., 2010). The exploration policy matters.
Uniform motor babbling may oversample redundant regions, whereas goal babbling selects desired
outcomes and learns the inverse mapping needed to reach them (Rolf et al., 2010). Internal models
and sensorimotor coupling are therefore complementary. A model compactly predicts bodily con-
tingencies, while intervention and feedback recalibrate it after tool use, wear, damage, or payload
change.
The morphology of the physical body can also serve as a dynamical prior for learning and control.
Morphological computation describes how geometry, inertia, and compliance reduce or transform
what a controller must compute (Paul, 2006). McGeer’s passive walkers generate gait structure
from gravity and mechanics under restricted conditions, and minimally actuated descendants in
later work extend the principle to level-ground walking (McGeer, 1990; Collins et al., 2005). Com-
pliant bodies can likewise absorb impacts and provide fading-memory dynamics, although formal
results apply only under specific assumptions (Hauser et al., 2011). These examples show how
a task-matched body supplies a dynamical prior that learning can exploit. The gain is also task-
specific, so morphology and learned control must be co-designed rather than treated as alternatives.
Lastly, self-generated experience creates a final selection problem concerning what the agent should
practice next. Early curiosity systems reward expected improvement of a predictive model, while
learning-progress methods direct attention toward activities that are neither mastered nor irre-
ducibly unpredictable (Schmidhuber, 1991; Oudeyer et al., 2007). Deep curiosity methods extend
action-conditioned prediction error to high-dimensional observations, but evidence from video
games does not resolve physical safety, wear, or stochastic “noisy-TV” effects (Pathak et al., 2017).
Taken together, active sensing determines what to observe, the body determines how action un-
folds, body schemas relate commands to consequences, and intrinsic motivation allocates prac-
tice. These mechanisms explain how a learning trajectory can become structured. Developmental
robotics asks how they can be integrated across an embodied lifetime.
2.3.3
Developmental Robotics
Developmental robotics studies how robots acquire and reorganize their abilities through expe-
rience over time. This subsection examines developmental constraints, lifelong and open-ended
learning, imitation, and social interaction as complementary ways to guide that process.
Developmental robotics views intelligence as a gradual learning process rather than a collection of
independently designed abilities. Autonomous mental development and cognitive developmental
robotics study how robots are used both as constructive tests of developmental hypotheses and as
systems that may benefit from developmental constraints (Weng et al., 2001; Asada et al., 2001; Lun-
garella et al., 2003). Development entails more than ordering examples by difficulty. The learner’s
body, reachable goals, representations, and social relations can all change. Morphological growth
or progressively released degrees of freedom can therefore structure exploration by temporarily
reducing the search space (Lungarella and Berthouze, 2002). Infant development is valuable here
as a source of mechanisms such as self-calibration, staged constraints, and skill reuse, rather than
as a schedule robots must literally reproduce.
Another important research direction is lifelong robot learning, which focuses on how robots
continuously learn new tasks while retaining and reusing previously acquired knowledge and
42


skills (Thrun and Mitchell, 1995; Parisi et al., 2019). Robotics adds active data collection, temporally
correlated experience, and simultaneous change in platform and environment, which static-dataset
protocols often omit (Lesort et al., 2020). Also, retention is only one component of development.
An agent may preserve old task performance without inventing goals, composing skills, or chang-
ing its state and action representations. Open-ended learning therefore adds representational re-
description and goal discovery (Doncieux et al., 2018). Progress-based goal exploration offers one
operational mechanism. Agents generate and order goals according to current learning progress,
allowing acquired skills to become stepping stones for more complex behavior (Oudeyer et al.,
2007; Forestier et al., 2022). A developmental architecture must consequently balance plasticity,
consolidation, and expansion rather than optimize only final reward.
Additionally, individual exploration is expensive in the high-dimensional spaces of humanoid ma-
nipulators. Imitation learning is introduced to reduce this cost by directing attention toward actions
another agent has made relevant. Still, it introduces a correspondence problem between different
bodies, viewpoints, and intentions (Schaal, 1999). Demonstrations should therefore be treated as
priors over goals and action structure, not as trajectories to copy blindly, and embodiment-specific
practice remains necessary.
Lastly, social learning also requires shared reference. Constructive models show how saliency and
sensorimotor regularities can scaffold joint attention (Nagai et al., 2003), while sociable-robot stud-
ies show that timing, gaze, and expression shape the feedback humans provide (Breazeal, 2003).
Language games with AIBO further demonstrate that social feedback can participate in form-
ing shared perceptual categories and words (Steels and Kaplan, 2001). The resulting relation is
reciprocal. Language directs attention and decomposes goals, while action constrains linguistic
meaning (Cangelosi et al., 2010). Developmental robotics thus integrates autonomous exploration,
continual retention, and social scaffolding over one trajectory. In the studies reviewed here, how-
ever, these mechanisms are typically demonstrated separately and over short periods. Evaluation
should measure skill diversity, retention, compositional reuse, adaptation to bodily change, safety
cost, and tutor effort. This social-developmental account also provides the transition to symbols.
Language becomes meaningful when shared expressions are connected to the learner’s evolving
perceptual and action repertoire.
2.3.4
Embodied Grounding and Multimodal Pretraining
For robots to operate effectively in the physical world, they need both broad knowledge of the
world and the ability to perform physical actions. Multimodal pretraining on images, text, and
videos provides useful semantic knowledge and motion priors, but this knowledge alone is not
sufficient for reliable robot control (Bisk et al., 2020). Robots also need embodied experience to un-
derstand which actions are feasible and what consequences they may produce. Embodied ground-
ing aims to connect these two sources of knowledge, linking what robots perceive and understand
to what they can actually do. As illustrated in Figure 2.2, this perspective helps explain the roles of
different embodied AI approaches, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, world-action
models (WAMs), and multimodal agents.
Multimodal pretraining provides a scalable source of prior knowledge. Early systems explicitly
connect speech to visual objects and compositional instructions to executable robot plans (Roy
and Pentland, 2002; Tellex et al., 2011). At greater scale, CLIP learns broad image-language cor-
respondences, while R3M extracts temporally informative representations from human video for
downstream robot learning (Radford et al., 2021; Nair et al., 2023). Image-text data primarily con-
tribute semantic and referential knowledge. Human video additionally conveys motion patterns
and likely object interactions. However, neither directly specifies a particular robot’s reachability,
actuation limits, contact dynamics, or action costs. Such data therefore provide valuable semantic
and motion priors, rather than sufficient evidence of executable competence.
Embodied experience supplies complementary evidence by connecting an agent’s actions with ob-
served outcomes. Robot demonstrations illustrate how tasks can be accomplished with a particu-
lar embodiment, while self-generated interactions reveal feasible actions and their consequences.

Work on intuitive physical prediction, robotic poking, and action-conditioned visual foresight ex-
emplifies the transition from observation toward intervention-based learning (Battaglia et al., 2013;
Agrawal et al., 2016; Finn and Levine, 2017). Modular systems also make the division between
meaning and feasibility explicit.
CLIPort combines pretrained visual-language semantics with
spatial manipulation, and SayCan evaluates language-model skill proposals using embodiment-
specific value functions (Shridhar et al., 2022; Ichter et al., 2023). Yet successful skill selection is not
equivalent to learning new affordances or revising semantic beliefs after failure. Robust grounding
requires both physically informed action and feedback that can improve subsequent decisions.
Recent embodied models increasingly integrate these complementary sources. VLA models learn
language-conditioned control, progressing from RT-1 and RT-2 through heterogeneous cross-robot
training to systems such as π0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025), which co-trains on robot actions,
web data, and semantic subtasks for open-world generalization. EgoScale further explores human
egocentric video as scalable motor supervision (Brohan et al., 2023; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Open
X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026b). WAMs,
including DreamZero and Cosmos Policy, extend action learning by predicting future observations
alongside actions, potentially supporting consequence-aware planning (Wang et al., 2026b; Ye et al.,
2026a; Kim et al., 2026a). General-purpose multimodal agents, as explored in preliminary evalu-
ations of GPT-6 Astra, may instead contribute task-level reasoning, failure diagnosis, and replan-
ning, but are not established substitutes for reliable low-level control (OpenAI, 2026; Su et al., 2026;
Zhang et al., 2026b). These are complementary modeling emphases rather than successive stages.
The shared challenge is to turn broad multimodal priors and embodiment-specific experience into
reliable, adaptive behavior.
2.4
Learning and Reasoning in the Physical World
Physical AI requires more than representing the physical world. A learning-based physical AI
agent must learn the underlying regularities of physical processes, reason about possible future
states, and acquire effective behaviors through interaction. Unlike learning methods that primarily
exploit statistical correlations in static data, Physical AI requires models that respect geometric
constraints, dynamical laws, and causal consequences of actions.
Modern approaches therefore combine three complementary principles. Physical knowledge pro-
vides inductive biases, machine learning extracts unknown structures from experience, and rein-
44


forcement learning enables agents to improve through interaction. Together, these components
provide the foundation for learning and reasoning in physical environments.
2.4.1
Physics-Informed Learning Architectures
Physical Inductive Biases
Physical environments contain strong structural regularities, including
symmetry, conservation laws, locality, and relational interactions. Incorporating these properties
into machine learning models reduces the hypothesis space and improves data efficiency.
A fundamental example is equivariant learning. Physical predictions should transform consistently
under changes of coordinate systems. For a transformation ggroup from a symmetry group, an
equivariant model satisfies

2.4.2
Reinforcement Learning for Physical Interaction
Markov Decision Processes and Physical Interaction
Learning Physical AI requires not only
predicting the world but also selecting actions that influence future states. Reinforcement learning
formulates this process as sequential decision-making.
A Markov decision process (MDP) is defined as
(S, A, Ptr, R, γ),

rewards.

However, physical agents rarely observe complete states. A robot may observe an object’s appear-

noise, occlusion, and delayed measurements further limit the information available for decision-
making.
A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) extends the MDP with an observation

(S, A, Ptr, R, O, O, γ),

where O(ot+1 | st+1, at) specifies the probability of receiving observation ot+1 after action at leads
to state st+1, and γ ∈[0, 1) is the discount factor. The physical state remains Markovian, but an
individual observation need not contain enough information to predict future outcomes.
Decisions therefore depend on both past observations and past actions:

Past actions matter because they help explain subsequent measurements. A change in an object’s
position may result from the robot’s own push or from an external disturbance.
46


The history can be summarized by a belief state
bt(s) = P(st = s | ht),
(2.42)
which represents uncertainty about the current physical state. With a known transition and ob-
servation model, the belief is a sufficient statistic of the history for decision-making, allowing a
policy to be written as π(at | bt). Belief updates combine predictions from the previous action with
evidence from new observations.
Practical systems may approximate this inference using state estimators, recurrent networks, or
policies conditioned on a recent interaction history. For example, lifting an object provides force
measurements that help infer its weight and guide subsequent control. POMDPs thus make explicit
how uncertain perception, memory, and action jointly shape physical decision-making (Sutton and
Barto, 2018).
Reward Design and Task Specification
The reward function defines the objective of an embodied
agent. Designing appropriate rewards is challenging because physical tasks often involve long
horizons and complex constraints.
Sparse rewards provide feedback at infrequent events, such as successful grasping or completion
of a navigation task. Although simple, they create exploration difficulties.
Dense rewards introduce intermediate objectives, such as distance reduction, energy efficiency, or
trajectory smoothness. However, poorly designed dense rewards may lead to unintended behav-
iors.
Curriculum learning gradually increases task complexity and allows agents to acquire complex
physical skills from simpler subtasks.

Offline Reinforcement Learning
Unlike simulation environments, real physical systems cannot
collect unlimited interaction data. Offline reinforcement learning addresses this limitation by learn-
ing policies from previously collected datasets, including demonstrations and robot trajectories.
This paradigm is particularly important for Physical AI because large-scale datasets can provide
diverse physical experiences without requiring unsafe exploration on real hardware.

2.4.3
Predictive Learning and World Models
This subsection develops the predictive-learning mechanisms underlying the action-consequence
relation discussed in Section 2.3. The focus is on constructing internal states, learning how they
evolve under actions, and using predicted outcomes for decision-making. The mathematical notion
of state and the motivation for latent representations are introduced in Section 2.1.3.
Learning Latent Physical Dynamics
Under partial observability, an observation feature and an
internal predictive state serve different purposes. An encoder extracts features from the current
measurement, while a state-update model integrates them with past actions and the previous in-
ternal state:

This recurrent form is one way to summarize the interaction history ht used in the POMDP for-

zt+1 ∼pθ(· | zt, at),
(2.46)
where pθ is a learned transition distribution. A deterministic predictor, ˆzt+1 = Fθ(zt, at), is a sim-

updates and transitions. Known physical structure can constrain these models through the archi-
tectural and loss-based approaches in Section 2.4.1. Their adequacy depends on preserving the
distinctions that affect future outcomes, including uncertainty that remains after observing the in-
teraction history.
Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures
The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA)
approach learns representations by predicting target features from context features. I-JEPA pre-
dicts representations of masked image regions from visible context (Assran et al., 2023), while V-
JEPA extends feature prediction to masked spatiotemporal regions in video (Bardes et al., 2024). A
schematic prediction is
ˆztarget = gϕ(zcontext, mtarget),
(2.47)
where zcontext represents the visible context, mtarget specifies target positions, and gϕ is the predictor.
Predictions are matched to features produced by a target encoder. In these implementations, a stop-
gradient target and an exponentially averaged target encoder help prevent representation collapse.
Such representations can supply observation features for a predictive world model. Learning from
passive images or videos, however, does not by itself identify the effects of executable robot ac-
tions. An action-conditioned dynamics model additionally requires experience linking the agent’s
commands to resulting changes. This distinction separates predictive representation learning from
the action-grounded models needed for physical planning and policy improvement.
World Models, Imagination, and Decision-Making
Given a current internal state, a dynam-
ics model can roll forward candidate actions. For a deterministic model and an action sequence
at:t+Hroll−1 of length Hroll, the rollout is

ˆzt+i+1 = Fθ(ˆzt+i, at+i),
i = 0, . . . , Hroll −1.
(2.48)
A stochastic model instead produces a distribution of possible rollouts. A planner evaluates pre-
dicted outcomes against the task objective and constraints, executes a selected action, and updates
the internal state from new observations. The receding-horizon control principle is developed in
Section 2.2.2.
Model-based reinforcement learning can also use imagined trajectories to improve a policy.
Dreamer learns behavior through rollouts in a learned latent world model (Hafner et al., 2020), and
48


DayDreamer applies world-model-based learning to physical robots (Wu et al., 2023). Prediction
thus supports both selecting actions and learning better action policies. Model errors can accu-
mulate over long rollouts, and a policy may exploit inaccurate predictions, so useful imagination
requires validation against observed physical outcomes.
These mechanisms connect state representation, physical priors, and reinforcement learning
through prediction of action consequences. Chapter 5 develops world-model architectures, training
objectives, uncertainty, and validation in detail. Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 examine their relationship
to learned manipulation and motor capabilities.

3
Perception and Cognition
This chapter dives deeply into perception and cognition. One of the primary differences between
normal AI systems and physical AI systems is that physical AI uses perception and cognition to
bridge the physical environment with the actual AI system. The key part for that bridge is the
multimodal sensing, which brings information about this complex and diverse world into digital
form, and produces a compressed representation.
Therefore, the perception and cognition module aims to obtain a coherent and comprehensive
understanding of the physical environment from raw sensor observations. This understanding
grounds world models in sensory evidence and supports prediction, planning, and action. This
chapter traces that pipeline from low-level multimodal sensing and sensor fusion, 3D spatial and
four-dimensional (4D) spatiotemporal perception, to high-level semantic and interaction reasoning.
3.1

Fig. 3.1 Embodied perception from multimodal observations. A complex physical environment is
sampled through multiple sensors, producing a compressed and incomplete digital representation.
Perception and cognition integrate these observations to infer the environment state relevant to an
embodied agent’s task
Perception provides the fundamental interface between the physical world and embodied intelli-
gence. Unlike symbolic or language-based environments, where information is already presented
to a model in discrete and machine-readable forms, the physical world does not directly expose its
underlying state. It is continuous, high-dimensional, dynamic, and only partially observable. As
illustrated in Fig. 3.1, an embodied agent can access this world only through sensors that trans-
form physical signals into digital observations. Before reasoning, prediction, planning, or action
can take place, these observations must therefore be organized into representations that a compu-
tational model can interpret and use.
This transformation is inherently incomplete. Cameras have finite resolution and fields of view,
depth sensors contain missing or uncertain measurements, force and tactile sensors observe only
local contacts, and all sensing modalities operate with finite sampling rates and measurement noise.
Occlusion further prevents parts of the environment from being observed at a given time. Con-
sequently, the digital observations available to an embodied agent constitute only a partial and
compressed representation of the underlying physical world. Perception must infer task-relevant
structure from this incomplete evidence rather than assuming direct access to the true physical
state.
This distinction makes perception particularly important for Physical AI. Downstream models rea-
son and act on the basis of what has been observed and represented, rather than on the physical
51


world itself. Errors or missing information in perception can therefore propagate to state estima-
tion, prediction, reasoning, planning, and ultimately physical action. A missed obstacle may lead
to a collision. An incorrect depth estimate may produce an invalid grasp. An incorrect estimate of
object or material state may cause an otherwise reasonable plan to fail. Reliable Physical AI thus
depends not only on the capability of downstream models, but also on the accuracy, completeness,
consistency, and uncertainty of the perceptual representations on which they operate.
Physical perception addresses this problem by acquiring multimodal observations and progres-
sively transforming them into representations of the environment that are useful for embodied
tasks. Beyond recognizing what is present, a physical perception system must determine where
entities are, how they move and change over time, what physical and semantic states they are in,
and how they can be interacted with. Perception is therefore not merely a preprocessing stage for
downstream intelligence, but a continuous process of constructing and updating an internal repre-
sentation of the physical world.
Physical perception can be broadly organized into three levels. Low-level perception acquires ob-
servations through sensory modalities. These include color cameras using red, green, and blue
(RGB) channels, together with depth sensors, LiDAR, infrared and event cameras, tactile and force
sensors, and proprioception. These modalities capture complementary aspects of appearance, ge-
ometry, motion, temperature, contact, and the agent’s own physical state. Mid-level perception or-
ganizes these observations into spatially and temporally consistent representations, including 3D
geometry, motion, and dynamic 3D/4D scene structure. High-level perception and cognition further
associates these representations with semantic entities, physical properties and states, functional re-
lationships, affordances, and interaction possibilities, enabling task-dependent interpretation and
reasoning.
Across these levels, physical perception is characterized by multimodality, spatiotemporal consistency,
physical grounding, uncertainty, and interaction-oriented understanding. Multimodal observations com-
pensate for the limitations of individual sensors, while spatiotemporal modeling connects partial
observations across viewpoints and time. Physical grounding associates semantic interpretation
with measurable geometry, state, and physical evidence, and explicit treatment of uncertainty re-
flects the unavoidable incompleteness of sensing. Interaction-oriented understanding further fo-
cuses perception on the information that matters for action, including contact regions, object states,
material conditions, and possible state transitions.
These requirements drive physical perception beyond isolated single-modality recognition toward
integrated systems that continuously combine multimodal sensing, 3D/4D spatial modeling, se-
mantic understanding, physical measurement, and interaction feedback. From this perspective,
perception extends beyond recognition to make the physical world observable, representable, and
actionable to an embodied intelligent system.
3.2
Multimodal Perception and Fusion
3.2.1
Multimodal Sensing and Data Acquisition
Multimodal sensing and data acquisition refer to the processes by which an embodied system mea-
sures the physical state of itself and its environment and converts heterogeneous measurements
into digital observations. Perceiving and interacting with a physical environment require infor-
mation about several complementary properties, including appearance, geometry, motion, tem-
perature, and contact state. No single sensing modality can reliably and completely observe all
of these properties. Embodied systems therefore commonly combine RGB cameras, depth cam-
eras, LiDAR, force and tactile sensors, and proprioceptive sensors. Exteroceptive sensors observe
the external environment, proprioceptive sensors measure the internal configuration and motion
of the robot, and contact sensors characterize physical interaction at the robot-environment inter-
face. Together, these measurements form the observational basis for subsequent perception, state
estimation, reasoning, planning, and control. Section 9.2 provides additional details.
52


RGB Cameras
RGB cameras are the most widely used exteroceptive sensors in embodied intel-
ligence. They measure visible optical radiation and provide dense observations of scene color,
texture, boundaries, and appearance. These observations contain rich semantic cues but do not
directly encode metric depth or contact state.

primary source of exteroceptive information for semantic scene understanding, object localization,

multi-view imagery with language and proprioceptive state. DROID, for example, records three
synchronized stereo RGB camera streams, together with robot states and actions, exterior-camera
calibration, and natural-language instructions across 86 manipulation tasks (Khazatsky et al., 2024).
Generalist VLA models such as π0 and π0.5 similarly combine camera observations with language
instructions and robot state to generate actions across diverse tasks and robot embodiments (Black
et al., 2025a; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Despite their low cost and semantic richness, RGB
cameras do not directly measure metric geometry or physical contact, and their reliability remains
sensitive to illumination changes, saturation, specular reflections, motion blur, and occlusion.
Depth Cameras and LiDAR
Depth cameras and LiDAR provide metric observations of scene
geometry, but their measurement principles and sampling patterns are not determined by the de-
vice category alone. Some depth cameras employ stereo triangulation, whereas others use time-
of-flight principles closely related to LiDAR. A useful distinction is therefore made between axial
depth Zdepth, defined as the coordinate of a scene point along the camera optical axis, and ray range r,
defined as the Euclidean distance from the sensing origin along a viewing or emission ray. The sys-
tems considered here are organized by how distance is inferred, distinguishing triangulation-based
depth sensing from propagation-based optical ranging.
Triangulation-based systems infer depth from correspondences between calibrated rays originat-
ing from spatially separated camera or projector centers. For a rectified stereo pair with baseline
Bstereo, common horizontal focal length fx, and aligned principal points, the horizontal disparity
dstereo(upix) = upix,L −upix,R determines the axial depth. The resulting depth can then be back-
projected into the reference-camera coordinate frame using
Zdepth(upix) =
fxBstereo
dstereo(upix),
pC(upix) = Zdepth(upix)K−1

(3.5)
where fx and dstereo(upix) are expressed in pixels, Kcam is the intrinsic matrix of the reference cam-
era, and ˜upix = (upix, vpix, 1)⊤is the homogeneous image coordinate (Hartley and Zisserman,
2003). The second relation assumes that the depth image stores axial depth rather than distance
along the viewing ray. Passive stereo relies on naturally occurring scene texture to establish corre-
spondence. Active-stereo systems retain the same binocular geometry but project an unstructured
infrared pattern to add texture in weakly textured regions. The pattern assists left-right image
matching and need not be decoded into projector coordinates. The Intel RealSense D400 series is a
representative example (Keselman et al., 2017). Structured-light systems also recover depth by tri-
angulation, but use a calibrated camera-projector pair and establish correspondences between ob-
served image locations and encoded projector coordinates (Zanuttigh et al., 2016). Thus, although
active stereo and structured light employ active illumination, both remain triangulation-based be-
cause depth is inferred from spatial correspondence rather than optical propagation time.
Propagation-based sensors emit optical signals and infer distance from temporal or phase proper-
ties of the returned signal rather than from spatial disparity. For a pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR, the
measured round-trip propagation delay ∆ti determines the range of the ith return. Combining this
range with the calibrated beam direction gives its three-dimensional position as
