on the sensor design, they estimate distance from the direct time of flight of optical pulses or from
the phase shift of modulated illumination (Horaud et al., 2016). The stored value may represent
ray range or may be converted into axial depth according to the sensor’s calibration and output
convention.
The native measurements of these sensors induce different spatial structures. A camera depth im-
age can be back-projected into an organized point cloud whose samples preserve the image lattice,
whereas LiDAR measurements generally form an irregular, sparse point cloud indexed by beam
direction and acquisition time. After calibration and coordinate transformation, either representa-
tion may be converted into voxels, signed-distance fields, or continuous neural implicit fields for
downstream perception and planning.
In embodied systems, depth observations are particularly useful for close-range geometry, includ-
ing object-pose estimation, grasping, and workspace reconstruction. PerAct, RVT, and Act3D, for
example, demonstrate how calibrated RGB and depth (RGB-D) observations can be transformed
into volumetric, multi-view, or continuous three-dimensional representations for robotic manip-
ulation (Shridhar et al., 2023; Goyal et al., 2023; Gervet et al., 2023). LiDAR is more commonly
employed on mobile and field robots, where its typically longer sensing range and direct metric
measurements support localization, mapping, obstacle avoidance, and exploration. CERBERUS
provides a representative example in subterranean environments (Tranzatto et al., 2022). These
modalities nevertheless exhibit different failure modes. Passive stereo correspondence becomes
unreliable in textureless, repetitive, or occluded regions. Active stereo and structured light reduce
texture ambiguity but remain limited by projector range, strong ambient illumination, interference,
and transparent or specular surfaces. Propagation-based ranging can likewise be degraded by
low-return surfaces, strong ambient illumination, multipath interference, and adverse atmospheric
conditions.
Force and Tactile Sensors
Force and tactile sensors provide measurements of physical interaction
that cannot be obtained directly from conventional vision. Force and torque sensors measure the re-
sultant loads transmitted through a robot component, whereas tactile sensors measure local contact
conditions over a sensing surface. This distinction concerns the spatial support and physical inter-
pretation of the measurements rather than the transduction material alone. Resistive, capacitive,
piezoelectric, optical, and magnetic mechanisms may be used in different sensor configurations.
A multi-axis force/torque sensor measures the resultant force and moment acting on a robot com-
ponent, commonly at the wrist, ankle, or end effector. A six-axis sensor reports the wrench, ex-
pressed in a declared sensor coordinate frame, as
wS = [ f⊤
S , τ⊤
S ]⊤,
wS = Ccal(vsens −vsens,0),
(3.7)
where fS ∈R3 and τS ∈R3 are the measured force and torque, vsens denotes the raw electrical
outputs, vsens,0 is the zero-load offset, and Ccal is a calibration and decoupling matrix. The second
relation is a common linear approximation for strain-based sensors, which infer applied loads from
the deformation of an elastic structure (Cao et al., 2021). Such sensors provide accurate aggregate
interaction loads but do not resolve how those loads are distributed across multiple contact points.
Joint-torque sensors and motor currents can also support external-force estimation through a robot
dynamics model, but these indirect estimates should not be treated as equivalent to a directly mea-
sured endpoint wrench.
Tactile sensors measure contact locally at the robot surface. Their outputs may describe contact
location, surface deformation, normal and tangential loading, or slip. According to their domi-
nant sensing and readout mechanisms, tactile sensors commonly used in embodied systems can be
broadly organized into vision-based tactile sensors and taxel-based tactile arrays.
55


Vision-based tactile sensors illuminate a compliant elastomer and use an internal camera to observe
its deformation during contact. Their native digital observation is an image rather than a direct
force measurement:

Because their output is image-like, these sensors also support visual representa-

Some specialized tactile devices additionally measure vibration, acoustic emission, or temperature.
High-bandwidth vibration and acoustic signals can reveal impact, sliding, texture, and incipient

commonly used as standalone tactile modalities in embodied systems and are often incorporated
as complementary channels in multimodal tactile sensors.
The appropriate sensor depends on the spatial scale and information required by the task. Six-axis
force/torque sensors are mature choices for aggregate load feedback in compliant control, insertion,
assembly, and human-robot interaction. Vision-based tactile sensors are particularly attractive in
current robot-learning research because they provide dense contact geometry and can be processed
with image-based models, whereas electrical or magnetic taxel arrays can be integrated into com-
pact fingertips, finger links, palms, and larger-area robotic skin. Force and tactile measurements
support contact detection, grasp stabilization, slip detection, texture recognition, object reorienta-
tion, and dexterous manipulation. RH20T illustrates their role in multimodal robot learning by
recording force together with visual, audio, robot-state, action, and language information across
diverse manipulation skills (Fang et al., 2024b).
These sensing families also have distinct limitations. Force/torque sensors do not localize individ-
ual contacts without additional geometric assumptions. Taxel arrays may exhibit hysteresis, drift,
cross-talk, and limited spatial resolution. Vision-based tactile sensors are sensitive to illumination
and camera-calibration errors, as well as elastomer wear and viscoelastic effects such as hysteresis
and stress relaxation. Their physical estimates additionally depend on calibrated or learned map-
pings from deformation to contact quantities. All tactile modalities have a local field of view and
become informative primarily after contact. They are therefore commonly combined with vision
and proprioception. Vision estimates where interaction should occur, proprioception supplies the
robot configuration, and force or tactile feedback verifies the resulting physical interaction.
56


Proprioceptive Sensors
Proprioceptive sensors measure the internal state and motion of the em-
bodied platform. For an articulated robot, a representative proprioceptive observation is
zprop(t) = [ q⊤, ˙q⊤, τ⊤, i⊤, a⊤
imu, ω⊤
imu ]⊤,
(3.10)
where q and ˙q are joint positions and velocities, τ denotes measured or estimated joint torque, i is
motor current, and aimu and ωimu are specific force and angular velocity from an inertial measure-
ment unit. Depending on the platform, proprioception may additionally include wheel odometry,
base orientation, gripper aperture, actuator temperature, or foot-contact switches.
These signals support forward kinematics, state estimation, trajectory tracking, balance, and body-
aware control. They also provide the configuration needed to transform head-, wrist-, and body-
mounted sensor data into a common coordinate system. Joint torque and motor current can sup-
port external-force estimation through an explicit robot dynamics model, but the resulting estimate
remains sensitive to transmission, friction, and model error. In learning-based embodied systems,
proprioceptive state is commonly combined with visual and language inputs so that action gen-
eration is conditioned on both the external scene and the current robot configuration (Black et al.,
2025a; Khazatsky et al., 2024).
Multisensor Acquisition, Calibration, and Time Synchronization
Combining sensors requires
more than recording their outputs. Different devices use different coordinate frames, sampling
rates, exposure intervals, clock domains, communication paths, and latency conventions. Reliable
fusion therefore depends on calibrated spatial and temporal relationships between measurements.
Spatial calibration comprises intrinsic calibration of each imaging or ranging sensor and extrinsic
calibration between sensor frames. If a point measured in sensor frame Sm is to be expressed in a
reference frame S0, the homogeneous-coordinate transformation is
epS0 = S0TSmepSm,
S0TSm ∈SE(3).
(3.11)
For moving sensors, this transform is composed with the robot kinematic state at the measurement
time. Calibration may also include image rectification, depth-to-color registration, tactile-frame
localization, force-sensor bias estimation, and calibration of the transformation from sensor output
to physical units.
Temporal alignment requires a model of each sensor clock. A common affine approximation relates
sensor time tm to a reference time t0 as
tm = αclk
m t0 + βclk
m ,
(3.12)
where βclk
m is the clock offset and αclk
m represents the relative clock rate. A timestamp must also be
associated with a clearly defined event. For a camera, that event may be the beginning, midpoint, or
end of exposure. For a ranging pulse, it may be emission or reception. A timestamp may also mark
the arrival of a sample at the host computer. Joint estimation of spatial and temporal calibration
is often necessary because an unmodeled time offset during robot motion can be mistaken for an
extrinsic-calibration error (Furgale et al., 2013).
Software synchronization aligns independently acquired streams through timestamps, buffering,
interpolation, and nearest-neighbor association. It is flexible but cannot recover information lost
through inaccurate timestamps or variable transport delay. Hardware synchronization distributes
a common clock, trigger, or pulse-per-second signal and is preferable when the platform undergoes
rapid motion or contact transitions. Even with hardware triggering, an acquisition system should
account for exposure duration, rolling-shutter readout, sensor processing delay, network latency,
and the time required to assemble scanning measurements.
The final synchronized record should preserve the raw measurements, calibrated measurements,
timestamps, coordinate-frame definitions, calibration parameters, and validity indicators. An RGB
image, depth frame, LiDAR return, tactile image, wrench sample, and joint state should either
refer to the same physical instant or carry sufficient timing information to be transformed or inter-
polated to a common instant. This requirement is particularly important for visual-tactile learning,
57


force-guided manipulation, and high-speed navigation, where small temporal errors can associate
observations with different robot poses or contact regimes. Careful acquisition and calibration are
thus integral to perception and determine the reliability of all subsequent multimodal fusion.
3.2.2
Multimodal Fusion for Joint Perception
Multimodal fusion combines complementary observations to estimate the state of the robot, its
surroundings, and their interactions. RGB images describe appearance. Depth and LiDAR provide
geometric measurements. Force, tactile, and proprioceptive signals supply information about con-
tact and robot motion. A useful organizing principle is the stage at which information is combined,
whether at the level of observations, intermediate features, or task-level estimates. These levels
describe possible operations rather than mutually exclusive architectures (Hall and Llinas, 1997;
Baltrušaitis et al., 2019).
Observation-Level Integration and Cross-Modal Enhancement
When measurements have been
spatially registered and temporally aligned, they can be associated in a common coordinate frame.
For example, a registered RGB image and depth map associate appearance with measured distance
at corresponding image locations. RGB-guided depth completion additionally uses image infor-
mation to infer depth where measurements are sparse or missing (Ma and Karaman, 2018). Such
estimates must remain distinguishable from measured depth. An appearance edge need not coin-
cide with a geometric boundary. Validity masks, calibration, and timestamps are therefore part of
the fused observation, especially near occlusions or when the sensors move.
Feature-Level Fusion for Joint Perception
Modality-specific encoders can extract representations
that are then combined through concatenation, learned weighting, or attention. The features may
be aligned on an image grid or mapped into a shared three-dimensional or bird’s-eye-view space.
FuseNet combines color and depth features for semantic segmentation (Hazirbas et al., 2017).
BEVFusion combines camera and LiDAR features in a bird’s-eye-view representation for three-
dimensional perception (Liu et al., 2023c). In embodied systems, visual, tactile, and proprioceptive
features can likewise be related through robot kinematics and contact geometry, even when pixel-
wise correspondence is unavailable. Feature fusion allows task-dependent interactions but can be
sensitive to missing modalities and errors in spatial or temporal alignment.
Estimate-Level Fusion
Alternatively, each sensor stream can produce an estimate, such as ob-
ject pose, occupancy, or contact state, before the estimates are combined. This approach permits
modality-specific processing and can accommodate different sampling rates, provided that the es-
timates refer to compatible states and their uncertainties and dependencies are accounted for (Hall
and Llinas, 1997). Because high-level estimates discard some measurement detail, they may offer
less opportunity to exploit fine cross-modal correspondences. In practice, the fusion level is chosen
according to the perceptual task, available calibration, measurement reliability, and computational
constraints. A system may combine several levels.
3.3
3D/4D Spatial Perception
Three-dimensional spatial perception estimates scene geometry, object locations, and spatial rela-
tionships. 4D perception additionally represents changes over time, including object motion and
deformation. Figure 3.2 illustrates alternative 3D representations of the same object. For an em-
bodied agent, these estimates should support interaction with the physical environment, not only
recognition or novel-view rendering. Because sensors observe only limited, noisy projections of
the world, spatial perception maintains a task-relevant estimate rather than a complete copy of
physical reality.

3.3.1
3D/4D Scene Representation and Modeling
Scene representations differ in the properties they encode and the queries they support. In a cali-
brated pinhole camera, a world point pW projects to image coordinates according to
pC = RCWpW + tCW,
˜upix ∝KcampC,
(3.13)
where RCW and tCW define the transform from world to camera coordinates, and Kcam is the intrin-
sic matrix (Hartley and Zisserman, 2003). Given axial depth Zdepth(upix, vpix), the corresponding
camera-frame point is pC = Zdepth(upix, vpix)K−1

registered to robot or world coordinates, subject to calibration, depth error, and temporal align-
ment.
Point clouds retain measured or predicted surface samples, but do not by themselves define con-
tinuous surfaces, object interiors, or free space. Occupancy grids represent cells as occupied, free,
or unknown, often with probabilistic occupancy. OctoMap is a probabilistic octree-based exam-
ple (Hornung et al., 2013). Signed-distance fields encode distance to a surface, with the zero level
set representing that surface under a chosen sign convention. They support geometric queries such
as clearance and collision checking. Voxblox incrementally constructs Euclidean SDFs for plan-
ning (Oleynikova et al., 2017). Meshes explicitly represent surfaces and can support rendering or
collision queries when constructed for that purpose. None of these representations alone supplies
all physical properties required for interaction, such as friction, mass, articulation, or contact dy-
namics. Their coverage is also limited by sensor visibility and spatial resolution.
NeRFs represent a scene by mapping 3D position and viewing direction to volume density and
view-dependent radiance, (σrad, crgb) = FNeRF
θ
(xpos, d) (Mildenhall et al., 2020). 3D Gaussian Splat-
ting (3DGS) represents a scene using anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized for efficient ren-
dering (Kerbl et al., 2023). These appearance-oriented representations can support high-quality
novel-view synthesis, but rendering quality alone does not establish accurate metric geometry or
collision-ready surfaces.
For dynamic scenes, the representation must also describe temporal change. Time-dependent radi-
ance fields and Gaussian models can reconstruct or render scenes at different times. 4D Gaussian
Splatting is one example that models dynamic scenes with Gaussian primitives and learned de-
formations (Wu et al., 2024a). When motion estimation or interaction prediction is required, the
system must additionally maintain quantities such as object identity, pose or shape trajectories,
and correspondences over time. A temporally plausible rendering does not by itself guarantee
physically valid motion.
Learning-based reconstruction has reduced the need to optimize a separate model from scratch
for every scene. For example, VGGT directly predicts camera parameters as well as geometric
attributes such as depth maps, point maps, and point tracks from one or more images (Wang et al.,
2025a). pixelSplat predicts a Gaussian radiance-field representation from image pairs (Charatan
59


et al., 2024). These predictions can complement geometric reconstruction, but scale, coordinate-
frame alignment, calibration, and task-specific accuracy still require attention. Geometry in regions
not constrained by observations is inferred rather than measured.
World models can combine scene representation with prediction or generation, but these functions
should be distinguished. A renderer that generates plausible views is not necessarily a model that
predicts physically valid outcomes under robot actions. Atlas, for example, is described by its de-
velopers as producing point-cloud or Gaussian-splat outputs from images and generating novel
views. Its developers also state that unseen regions may be inferred to fill gaps (World Labs Team,
2026). A related but distinct capability is tool-assisted 3D authoring. OpenAI reports that GPT-6
Astra can generate computer-aided design (CAD) models from multi-view renders with tools and,
in the reported demonstration, is used to create an editable house scene in Blender and a walk-
through version in Unreal Engine (OpenAI, 2026).2 These developer-reported examples demon-
strate 3D generation and software-mediated modeling. Their use for robot interaction requires
distinguishing generated content from sensor-supported estimates and validating geometry and
motion against physical constraints.
3.3.2
Model-Driven Spatial Perception and Reasoning
Learned models can associate geometric representations with semantic concepts and use these as-
sociations to answer spatial queries or guide actions. The approaches below differ mainly in where
spatial information is retained and how it is grounded in observations.
Models Using Explicit Spatial Representations
An explicit map can associate semantic features
or object labels with points, surfaces, or regions in a common coordinate frame. OpenScene, for
instance, co-embeds features of 3D scene points with image and text features, enabling open-
vocabulary queries about observed space (Peng et al., 2023). Such maps allow geometric grounding
and repeated queries, although their coverage and semantic accuracy depend on observation qual-
ity, registration, and the underlying visual features.
Spatial Perception with Vision-Language Models
Vision-language models can infer object rela-
tions and answer spatial questions directly from images and text without necessarily maintaining
a persistent 3D map. SpatialVLM shows that spatially grounded training can improve qualitative
and quantitative spatial question answering (Chen et al., 2024). These outputs can help interpret
instructions and propose likely relationships, but a linguistic answer should not be treated as a
verified metric measurement or reachability judgment, particularly when viewpoint, occlusion, or
unknown scale creates ambiguity.
Agent-Based Spatial Perception and Reasoning
An agent can couple perception to action. It
maintains a spatial state, chooses where to look or move, and revises its estimates as new obser-
vations arrive. SayNav incrementally builds a 3D scene graph to ground language-model plans
for navigation in unfamiliar environments (Rajvanshi et al., 2024). VoxPoser grounds language
instructions in 3D value maps and uses model-based planning to generate closed-loop manipula-
tion trajectories (Huang et al., 2023a). These examples illustrate how spatial representations and
learned knowledge can inform action. Reliable operation still requires checking proposed plans
against current geometry, robot configuration, collision constraints, and physical limits, and updat-
ing the estimate from feedback during execution.
3.4
High-Level Perception and Cognition
High-level perception organizes sensory observations and spatial representations into entities, at-
tributes, states, and relations that are relevant to a task. Cognition builds on these representations
by integrating prior knowledge, retaining relevant history, reasoning about spatial and physical
2Thomas Ricouard, OpenAI Developers Blog, Architectural Visualization with Astra, September 4, 2026.
60


relationships, and identifying what additional evidence is needed when current observations are
insufficient.
For example, picking up a cup requires more than detecting and localizing it. The system may
need to estimate its contents and physical state, identify an appropriate contact region, and deter-
mine whether the intended interaction is feasible. Similarly, monitoring an automated experiment
requires associating a vessel with the correct sample, interpreting changes in material state, and
relating visual observations to instrument measurements and experimental history. Both cases
require representations that connect semantic understanding with physical evidence and persist
beyond a single observation. This section develops a progression from object- and scene-level se-
mantic perception to the understanding of physical properties, states, and interaction possibilities.
It finally addresses grounded reasoning with vision-language models, memory, measurements, and
active perception.
3.4.1
Object Recognition and Scene Semantic Understanding
Object- and scene-level semantic perception provides the foundation for high-level physical un-
derstanding. It identifies the entities present in an environment, localizes them in observations,
maintains their identities over time, and organizes their semantic and spatial relationships. These
representations provide the targets and contextual structure required for subsequent state estima-
tion, interaction perception, and task-level reasoning.
Fig. 3.3 Illustration of object detection and instance segmentation. Bounding boxes indicate the
locations and categories of detected objects, while colored masks delineate individual object in-
stances at the pixel level
Object Detection, Segmentation, and Tracking
Object detection predicts object categories and
locations, typically represented as bounding boxes. Semantic segmentation assigns category la-
bels at the pixel level, whereas instance segmentation distinguishes individual object instances
within each category, as illustrated in Fig. 3.3. Mask R-CNN jointly predicts object categories,
bounding boxes, and instance masks (He et al., 2017), while DETR formulates object detection as
Transformer-based set prediction (Carion et al., 2020). Tracking extends recognition across time
61


by maintaining object identities using appearance, motion, and geometric information. ByteTrack,
for example, incorporates lower-confidence detections during association to recover partially oc-
cluded objects (Zhang et al., 2022). Together, detection, segmentation, and tracking provide object
categories, spatial regions, and persistent identities that support target selection and state estima-
tion. A cup temporarily occluded by a gripper, for example, should remain associated with the
same contents, physical state, and interaction history after it becomes visible again.
Open-vocabulary recognition extends this capability beyond a predefined set of object categories.
Grounding DINO localizes objects specified through textual descriptions (Liu et al., 2024), while
the Segment Anything Model (SAM) generates segmentation masks from spatial prompts such
as points and bounding boxes (Kirillov et al., 2023). Combining language-grounded detection
with promptable segmentation connects task descriptions to observable image regions, allowing a
system to identify and segment relevant targets without requiring an exhaustive task-specific label
set.
Scene-Level Semantic Perception and Understanding
Recognizing individual objects is only the
first step toward understanding a physical environment. Scene-level perception organizes entities
according to their spatial, semantic, and functional relationships. Scene graphs, for example, rep-
resent objects or regions as nodes and relationships such as support, containment, proximity, or
attachment as edges. These structured relationships provide context for interpreting both indi-
vidual objects and the overall scene. For example, cups and a kettle located on the same coun-
tertop may jointly indicate a beverage-preparation area. In a laboratory, scene relationships may
associate a sample with its vessel, a vessel with an instrument, and an observation with the ex-
perimental stage at which acquisition occurs. Such associations make isolated sensor observations
interpretable within the context of an ongoing task or physical process.
Context can also help resolve ambiguous observations. An object that appears partially behind
a drawer may be contained inside it or merely occluded by it, while a visible liquid region may
belong to one of several overlapping transparent vessels. Scene representations should therefore
retain not only predicted relationships but also the evidence and uncertainty associated with them.
New observations can then confirm, reject, or revise previously inferred relationships.
These semantic representations answer questions about what entities are present, where they are,
and how they are related. Physical interaction, however, requires additional information about what
properties they have, what states they are in, and what actions they afford. These aspects are considered
next.
3.4.2
Object Properties, States, and Interaction Perception
High-level physical perception extends object recognition beyond identifying what an object is to-
ward understanding what properties it has, what state it is in, and how it can be interacted with. Such un-
derstanding requires connecting semantic observations with physical properties, functional struc-
tures, interaction possibilities, and feedback from the environment.
Observable Attributes and Latent Physical Properties
Objects exhibit directly observable at-
tributes, such as color, texture, shape, and visible geometry, as well as physical properties that
are only indirectly observable, including mass, friction, stiffness, compliance, and fragility. Visual
appearance provides useful cues for these properties but is often insufficient for reliable estimation.
Visually similar objects, for example, may differ substantially in mass because of their contents or
internal structure.
Multimodal sensing and physical interaction provide complementary evidence for resolving such
ambiguities. Deformation under load can reveal compliance, object motion during controlled con-
tact can constrain friction estimates, and force measurements during lifting can provide evidence
about mass. These estimates remain dependent on contact conditions, sensing quality, and dynami-
cal assumptions, and should therefore retain uncertainty. Their primary role in physical perception
62


is not necessarily to recover exact physical parameters, but to provide sufficient information for
selecting appropriate contact regions, forces, and interaction strategies.
States, Functional Parts, and Affordances
Recognizing an object category alone does not deter-
mine how the object should be used or manipulated. Object function describes its typical role,
while functional parts identify regions that support particular interactions. A cup, for example,
may function as a container, while its handle provides a functional region for grasping.
Affordances further describe the actions that are possible for a particular agent under the current
physical and task conditions. Unlike object categories or intrinsic properties, affordances are re-
lational. They depend jointly on object geometry, physical state, environmental context, agent ca-
pabilities, and task requirements. A handle may be graspable by one gripper but inaccessible to
another, and an otherwise graspable cup may be unsuitable for lifting when its contents are likely
to spill. In an automated laboratory, relevant affordances may instead concern access to a vessel
opening, available capacity, or whether a valve can be operated in its current state.
Interaction perception connects these semantic and physical descriptions to possible actions and
state transitions. It estimates discrete conditions such as open, closed, grasped, or slipping, as well
as continuous quantities such as deformation and contact force. It also associates functional parts
with candidate interactions and evaluates whether an observed response is consistent with the in-
tended action. Methods such as Where2Act demonstrate how actionable regions and interaction
proposals can be inferred for articulated objects (Mo et al., 2021). Such proposals nevertheless re-
main candidates rather than executable actions and must be checked against reachability, collision,
object state, and task constraints.
Physical interaction also reveals information that may be unavailable from external vision. During
contact, relevant regions can become occluded, while incipient slip, local deformation, and contact
loading may be difficult to infer visually. Tactile and force sensing provide complementary observa-
tions of these conditions. GelSight, for example, demonstrates how vision-based tactile sensing can
capture local contact geometry and deformation (Yuan et al., 2017). Observed slip, deformation, or
unexpected resistance can then update the estimated interaction state and support adjustments to
contact location, grasp force, or subsequent actions.
Material and Process-State Perception
High-level physical perception is not limited to robot-
object contact. In autonomous laboratories and other process-oriented environments, the target of
perception may instead be a material state or a process variable. Relevant observations include
liquid levels, phase boundaries, precipitates, vessel contents, and changes occurring during an ex-
periment. Distinguishing the container from its contents is particularly important because material
regions may lie within, overlap with, or be partially occluded by the surrounding vessel. Reflec-
tions, refraction, foam, transparency, and occlusion can further make visible boundaries ambigu-
ous.
Visual observations should therefore be connected to calibrated measurements and process context.
Estimating a liquid level may require vessel geometry, camera calibration, or a visible scale, while
determining material identity may require sample metadata or analytical measurements. Other
quantities, including temperature, pressure, mass, and spectral measurements, may be obtained
directly from instruments or extracted from their displays. Regardless of the acquisition mecha-
nism, observations should retain their units, timestamps, sample associations, and measurement
quality. Maintaining these relationships allows semantic interpretation to remain grounded in the
physical process being observed.
3.4.3
Grounded Perception and Cognition with Vision-Language Models
Vision-language models (VLMs) provide a flexible semantic interface between visual observations,
task instructions, and prior knowledge. In Physical AI, however, semantic interpretation alone is
insufficient. Model predictions must ultimately be grounded in specific entities, physical states,
spatial geometry, measurements, and interaction history. VLMs should therefore be viewed as
63


one component of a broader perception and cognition system rather than as a replacement for
geometric estimation, physical sensing, memory, or measurement.
Semantic, Property, and Affordance Understanding
VLMs can associate visual appearance with
semantic concepts, material cues, object functions, and typical interactions. This capability is par-
ticularly useful when a system encounters unfamiliar objects or must interpret them in the context
of a task. Given an image and an instruction to move a cup, for example, a ceramic appearance
may suggest fragility and careful handling, while a visible handle may indicate a candidate in-
teraction region. PhysObjects illustrates the use of physical-concept annotations to improve the
understanding of properties relevant to manipulation (Gao et al., 2024).
Such predictions should be interpreted as hypotheses rather than direct physical measurements. A
visual model may suggest that an object is heavy, fragile, or slippery, but quantitative or safety-
critical judgments generally require additional sensing or interaction evidence. Semantic knowl-
edge therefore provides useful priors that can guide subsequent observation and interaction with-
out replacing physical verification.
Semantic knowledge must also be grounded in specific locations in the current environment. Robo-
Point, for example, predicts image-space affordance points from visual observations and language
instructions, linking semantic requests to candidate interaction regions (Yuan et al., 2025). These
predictions help identify where an interaction may occur but do not by themselves specify a feasible
physical action. Depth, geometry, object state, collision constraints, and robot kinematics are still
required to convert semantic interaction targets into executable contact poses and motions.
Reasoning with Geometry, Memory, and Measurements
High-level physical reasoning fre-
quently requires information beyond the current image. Spatial questions may require calibrated
geometry, questions about change require previous observations, and process-state interpretation
may depend on event history or instrument measurements. A grounded cognition system there-
fore combines semantic reasoning with explicit geometric representations, persistent memory, and
quantitative measurements.
Relevant information can be retrieved through object, sample, or task identity and associated with
the current observation. Geometry provides spatial structure, memory provides temporal con-
text, and sensors or instruments provide quantitative physical evidence. VLMs can integrate these
sources to interpret a request, relate observations to the intended task, and identify missing or in-
consistent evidence. Memory management, geometric computation, and numerical measurement
remain explicit system functions even when their outputs are consumed by a multimodal model.
PaLM-E demonstrates one architecture for incorporating visual observations, continuous state es-
timates, and textual representations into an embodied language model (Driess et al., 2023). More
generally, physical information may be provided to a reasoning model through structured records,
tool outputs, or textual representations. Regardless of the interface, physical semantics should be
preserved, including units, timestamps, coordinate frames, object identities, and measurement un-
certainty.
Consider determining whether a vessel has reached a target fill level. Visual perception first identi-
fies the vessel and candidate liquid boundary, while calibration or vessel geometry converts image
evidence into a physical estimate. Memory provides the target level and relevant filling history,
and complementary measurements can be consulted when the visual evidence is ambiguous. The
VLM helps interpret the task and associate the available evidence with the correct sample, while
geometric and measurement tools support the quantitative comparison. This division of roles pre-
vents semantic plausibility from being mistaken for physical certainty.
Active Perception and Feedback-Based Updating
Physical cognition becomes particularly im-
portant when the available observations do not uniquely determine the current state. Rather than
forcing a decision from incomplete evidence, a high-level reasoning module, potentially imple-
64


mented with a VLM, can maintain competing hypotheses, identify unresolved variables, and pro-
pose additional observations or controlled interactions that reduce uncertainty.
The resulting process forms a perception-cognition loop. The system observes the environment,
interprets the available evidence, identifies relevant uncertainty, acquires additional evidence, and
updates its internal state. Additional evidence may come from a new camera viewpoint, a different
sensing modality, an instrument measurement, or a controlled physical probe. The choice of obser-
vation should consider expected information gain, acquisition cost, execution risk, and potential
disturbance to the physical process.
For example, when observing unfamiliar storage furniture, a change in viewpoint may reveal
hinges or rails and help distinguish rotational from translational motion. If ambiguity remains,
a gentle probe with measured motion and force can provide further evidence about the underlying
mechanism. In a laboratory, an apparent liquid boundary may instead correspond to a reflection
or foam edge. A different viewpoint or illumination condition can test the visual hypothesis, while
a mass measurement may provide independent evidence. In both cases, active perception should
target the specific uncertainty rather than simply acquire more observations.
Feedback from execution provides another source of evidence. A failed grasp, unexpected resis-
tance, observed slip, or inconsistent measurement can revise the estimated object state, interaction
hypothesis, or process interpretation. Perception and cognition are therefore not restricted to a sin-
gle observation-decision sequence. They continuously update their representation of the physical
environment as new evidence becomes available.
Limitations, Multiple Time Scales, and Outlook
High-level semantic reasoning remains vul-
nerable when model outputs become detached from geometry, measurement, or physical history.
Plausible semantic predictions do not guarantee correct localization, physical feasibility, or accu-
rate state estimation. Evaluation should therefore extend beyond language quality to include en-
tity grounding, spatial relations, physical-property judgments, state estimation, affordance predic-
tion, and the appropriate use of new evidence. Occlusion, viewpoint changes, ambiguous mate-
rial boundaries, and conflicting instrument readings provide useful settings for testing whether a
system can recognize uncertainty and request additional evidence rather than produce an unsup-
ported conclusion.
Another challenge arises from the multiple time scales of physical perception. Contact and force
measurements may change rapidly, visual observations arrive at another rate, and material, ther-
mal, or experimental processes may evolve over much longer intervals. A shared physical state
should therefore preserve acquisition time, validity, uncertainty, and evidence provenance. High-
level semantic reasoning can query this state when needed without requiring every sensor update
to pass through a language model. This separation enables high-frequency physical sensing and
lower-frequency semantic reasoning to coexist within the same perception architecture.
Looking forward, a research direction is the development of persistent and grounded physical cog-
nition that combines multimodal memory, 3D spatial reasoning, quantitative measurements, and
active perception. Such systems should not only recognize objects and describe scenes, but also
maintain up-to-date estimates of physical states, identify missing evidence, and select informative
observations or interactions when uncertainty matters. For autonomous laboratories, this requires
connecting sample identity, material observations, instrument measurements, and experimental
history. For robotic manipulation, it requires linking semantic targets to geometry, physical prop-
erties, interaction states, and execution feedback.
Progress should ultimately be assessed by whether these capabilities improve the interpretation
and control of physical systems. The assessment should determine whether a system can correctly
identify relevant entities, maintain their evolving states, recognize when its evidence is insufficient,
acquire information that resolves the ambiguity, and revise its interpretation under real feedback.
From this perspective, VLMs provide a flexible semantic and reasoning interface within a broader
physical perception and cognition system, while grounded sensing, geometry, memory, and inter-
action provide the evidence that keeps such reasoning connected to the physical world.
65


4
Data for Physical AI
Perception and cognition are only passive to understand our physical world. Still, to build an active
embodiment, interaction data in the real world is critical, as it provides the empirical foundation
for AI systems to understand the actual physical dynamic environment and how to interact with it.
Since this data records how actions alter physical states under known operating conditions, one can
learn a control policy, calibrate a simulation pipeline, or build a validation benchmark. This chap-
ter focuses on how to build a robust data collection pipeline for these purposes. It first introduces
the data formats, curation pipelines, and real-world collection strategies spanning human teleop-
eration, autonomous exploration, and interactive feedback. It then examines how physics engines
and generative world simulators expand data coverage, and how sim-to-real transfer aligns syn-
thetic trajectories with physical hardware. Finally, it analyzes physical data scaling laws, the role of
heterogeneous cross-embodiment datasets, and closed-loop data flywheels driven by deployment
feedback.
4.1
Data Foundations for Physical AI
Physical data link observations, actions, and their consequences under specified operating condi-
tions. A drawer image may support recognition. Learning to open it also requires the applied com-
mands, contact events, and resulting motion. The same distinction applies to industrial processes,
traffic control, and automated experiments. This section defines the evidence and record structure
needed to interpret such data. Subsequent sections address its collection, generation, alignment,
and growth.
4.1.1
The Spectrum of Physical Data
Data sources differ in how directly they support physical execution. The Data Pyramid for Embodied
Manipulation organizes real-robot data, Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI)-style demonstra-
tions, egocentric and exocentric observations, simulation data, and general vision-language data
around the tension between scalability and robot alignment (Ye et al., 2026b). Here, the comple-
mentary question is what each record actually establishes. Video can reveal an object’s motion
without identifying the force or command that caused it. A simulated trajectory can include exact
action labels without establishing the corresponding real-world response.
Table 4.1 distinguishes these forms of evidence. They can coexist within one dataset and do not con-
stitute a ranking of quality. In particular, reconstructed poses and latent actions are action proxies.
Converting them into executable supervision requires a mapping to the target embodiment and
controller. Representative released datasets spanning robot execution, portable demonstrations,
and human observation are cataloged in Table 4.3 in Section 4.2.

4.1.2
Unified Representation
A common schema must preserve the meaning of its fields. In the RT-X experiments, Open X-
Embodiment converts actions into a common seven-dimensional end-effector representation, but

retains differences in coordinate frames and in absolute, relative, or velocity control. The same vec-
tor can therefore induce different motions on different robots (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration,
2024). Matching dimensions enables shared processing but does not establish physical equivalence.
Each record should retain the embodiment, tool geometry, control interface, and calibration needed
to interpret it. Coordinate transforms must specify their direction and reference frames. Sensor
acquisition, command issue, and physical response times must also remain distinguishable. Pairing
an image with a command issued before its exposure can change the supervision target. Sampling
rate, action duration, and controller update rate should be recorded separately.
Measured, estimated, and generated quantities require distinct provenance. A reconstructed wrist
pose is an estimate, and a simulator’s contact force is a model output. Neither should silently
replace a physical measurement. Derived fields should identify their source records, generating
method and version, and any available uncertainty or validity bounds. A shared coordinate frame
resolves geometric ambiguity but leaves embodiment-dependent limits and dynamics to be ac-
counted for.
Minimum Action Specification
An action field should identify its issuer and target, control
mode, reference frame and tool point, units, duration and effective time, applicable limits or satu-
ration, controller gains where relevant, and the associated execution feedback.
4.1.3
Data Organization
Physical records are organized into steps, transitions, segments, and episodes. These boundaries
carry learning semantics. Reinforcement Learning Datasets (RLDS), for example, distinguishes the
last recorded step from an environment terminal state. A truncated episode does not establish that
the task terminated, and its final observation need not have a valid outgoing action. Training views
must preserve these distinctions instead of treating every stored row as a complete transition.
Raw records, standardized records, and training views serve different purposes. Raw records pre-
serve the original signals and metadata. Standardized records make units, timestamps, coordinates,
and episode boundaries explicit. Training views specify selection, segmentation, annotation, and
augmentation. Keeping these stages traceable allows a calibration or labeling error to be corrected
without repeating collection.
Every episode should retain a stable identifier and links to its source, embodiment, operator or
policy version, calibration, and processing history. Segments and generated variants should retain
their parent identifiers. Dataset splits can then keep related records together and hold out the
task, scene, object, or embodiment relevant to the generalization claim. Splitting adjacent frames at
random cannot establish transfer to unseen physical conditions.
67


4.1.4
Annotation Framework and Workflow
A recording may show an object moving, a temperature rising, or a machine stopping. The sig-
nals are recorded, but what happened? Annotations identify the objects and materials involved,
the operating conditions, the actions taken, and their consequences. They may mark an object in
an image, contact during a motion, stages of a production process, or the outcome of an experi-
ment. The same record can then support different learning tasks, including recognizing a material,
predicting its response, choosing an action, or judging whether the outcome meets a goal.
Annotation starts with rules that different people and tools can apply consistently. A small trial
reveals unclear definitions and disputed boundaries before labeling expands. Automated tools
can propose labels, while reviewers examine uncertain cases and spot-check the rest against the
recordings. Each label keeps a link to its evidence and records whether it comes from measurement,
human judgment, inference, or simulation. Uncertainty remains visible, and corrections update the
labels without rewriting the underlying evidence.
4.1.5
Quality Governance
Quality checks should distinguish recording defects from difficult but valid experience. A force
spike may indicate contact. A stalled gripper may reveal an execution failure. Neither warrants
deletion solely because the signal is irregular. Checks should cover signal integrity, consistency
across timestamps and coordinate frames, correspondence between commands and responses, and
agreement between event annotations and outcomes.
Learning utility also depends on the learner and the intended supervision. The robomimic study
systematically varies demonstration quality, observations, and learning algorithms, showing that
these choices materially affect policy performance (Mandlekar et al., 2022). A valid failure trajectory
can support outcome prediction while providing unsuitable actions for nominal behavior cloning.
Data validity, task outcome, and suitability as an imitation target should therefore be recorded
separately.
Dataset documentation makes these judgments inspectable. Following Datasheets for Datasets, a
release should describe its composition, collection process, intended uses, and limitations (Gebru
et al., 2021). For physical data, this should include embodiment and control specifications, calibra-
tion history, missing modalities, outcome definitions, and known recording defects. A versioned
manifest should link released samples to their processing code and access or reuse conditions.
These records provide the basis for the collection procedures in Section 4.2 and the synthetic-data
validation developed in Section 4.3 and Section 4.4.
4.2
Data Collection and Interaction
Data collection and interaction proceed through collection design, human demonstrations, au-
tonomous collection, and interactive feedback in four linked steps. In this view, producing data
means actively sampling the physical world. The emphasis is on distributions, supervision, effi-
ciency, and safety. Implementation details of individual devices are addressed only where they
constrain the evidence that can be collected.
4.2.1
Collection Design
Collecting physical data is not indiscriminate recording of real-world processes. It is an active
sampling of the space of reachable states, possible actions, and actual outcomes. Initial states, task
goals, acting agents, control constraints, disturbances, and termination conditions all shape the
resulting distribution. The collection policy is therefore part of the data-generating mechanism. A
sound design first identifies the capability to be developed or the hypothesis to be tested, and then
determines what to collect.
Design typically starts with the intended deployment distribution and works backward to define
task families. A coverage matrix can span objects, scenes, initial states, goals, disturbances, embod-
68


iments, operators or policies, outcomes, and risks. Frequent states require sufficient density to es-
tablish basic competence. Rare but consequential states require targeted collection. Matched com-
parison cases can weaken spurious correlations with backgrounds, positions, or operator styles.
The number of task names is not a measure of coverage. “Tidy the desk” can probe very different
capabilities as object combinations, occlusion, starting poses, and time pressure change.
The variable specification should distinguish controlled factors, observable quantities, and poten-
tial confounders. In robotic manipulation, one can vary object positions and materials, container
states, illumination, and disturbances. Traffic and industrial systems also require records of topol-
ogy, load, shifts, operating rules, and decisions by multiple actors. Intelligent laboratory systems
should retain reagent batches, instrument states, step dependencies, and measurement uncertainty.
These conditions must be represented in task templates and metadata if performance differences
are to be attributed to plausible causes rather than described merely as isolated successes or fail-
ures.
Sensor configuration further bounds what can be observed. Measurement principles, mounting lo-
cations, and coverage determine which quantities can be measured directly. Range, noise, and cali-
bration determine how trustworthy those measurements are. An uninstalled or uncovered channel
should be marked as missing, rather than represented by a zero reading. Contact forces inferred
from images or a dynamics model must likewise be distinguished from directly measured forces.
Temporal resolution depends jointly on sensor bandwidth, sampling rate, filtering, and the trans-
mission path. A higher logging rate does not necessarily provide more usable information.
Force and tactile sensing illustrate these constraints. A six-axis wrist force/torque sensor measures
the net force and moment, not the distribution of fingertip contacts. A tactile array covers only
its sensitive surface. Some force sensors support sampling at kilohertz rates (ATI Industrial Au-
tomation, n.d.), whereas vision-based tactile sensors are limited by camera frame rate. The DIGIT
prototype, for example, operates at 60 frames/s (Lambeta et al., 2020). Directly reducing a high-rate
force stream to the video frame rate can hide collision peaks and transient slip. The raw time series
should therefore be retained, with a separately aligned stream generated after antialiasing. Col-
lection also requires calibration and zeroing, together with compensation of wrist readings for tool
weight and inertial effects. Quality checks are also required for thermal drift, hysteresis, saturation,
and dropped frames. Calibration versions, filter settings, and anomaly flags should accompany the
data. The confidence assigned to contact labels should account for both synchronization error and
measurement uncertainty.
Success criteria, failure categories, safety limits, and reset rules must be defined before collection.
Success should be expressed in verifiable object states, process conditions, or operational metrics
rather than left to an operator’s impression. Failures should distinguish perception errors, planning
errors, control deviations, unstable contact, timeouts, safety aborts, and external disturbances. An
incomplete reset, or physical traces left by a previous trial, can also compromise the independence
of subsequent data. When an outcome is difficult to determine automatically, sensor-based rules
can be combined with visual checks and human review in a staged assessment.
Temporal segmentation is likewise part of collection design. An episode should start at a verifiable
initialization or reset and end in success, failure, timeout, or an abort. Skill segments and action
chunks should have explicit temporal meanings. The acquisition system must distinguish the rates
of sensor sampling, model decisions, action updates, and low-level servo control. It should record
the issue, delivery, and actual effective time of each command. Source timestamps, coordinate-
frame calibration, latency measurement, and completeness monitoring are minimum requirements.
Detailed hardware and software implementation belongs in Chapter 9.
Recent large-scale real-world datasets illustrate different organizational approaches. DROID shows
how relatively uniform hardware and protocols can support distributed collection across sites.
RoboMIND brings multiple embodiments, task protocols, and demonstrations of failure with
recorded causes into one platform. AgiBot World scales trajectories through centralized facilities,
standard procedures, and human-in-the-loop verification. Humanoid Everyday further includes
whole-body locomotion, manipulation, and human-robot interaction (Khazatsky et al., 2024; Wu
69


et al., 2025b; AgiBot-World-Contributors et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). Together, these efforts show
that scaling requires reproducible task definitions, staffing procedures, equipment states, and qual-
ity judgments, as well as more devices.
Collection performance should be measured by effective data yield. Beyond raw hours and trajectory
counts, useful measures include minutes of meaningful interaction, the share of recordings that
pass training quality checks, incremental coverage after deduplication, the yield of rare events,
equipment availability, human and machine time, time spent resetting, and the final retention rate
from raw records to the training release. Consecutive stationary frames, repeated successes, and
multiple derived versions of the same behavior inflate volume without necessarily adding new ex-
perience. Efficient collection uses limited physical interaction to close identifiable capability gaps.
The output of collection design is thus an executable data-collection protocol, not merely a task list.
It specifies the target distribution, variable combinations, episode boundaries, success and failure
definitions, safety constraints, data schema, quality gates, and cost metrics. Human demonstra-
tions, autonomous execution, and interactive corrections are different ways of gathering evidence
under this plan.

Fig. 4.1 Human-demonstration data collection paradigms, arranged by their distance from executable
robot actions. (a) Teleoperation drives the target robot through leader-follower mechanisms and
records robot observations, actions, and outcomes directly (Mobile ALOHA, photo from Stanford
News). (b) Portable interfaces such as UMI record retargetable end-effector motion in natural envi-
ronments using a hand-held gripper, a wrist-mounted camera, and visual-inertial tracking (photo
from the UMI project). (c) Egocentric human data capture natural activity at scale with head-
mounted devices, providing broad behavioral priors without native robot states (photo from ABC
News)
Human demonstration converts human intent into behavioral evidence that a machine can learn
from and, ideally, execute on the target embodiment. Methods can be arranged by their distance
from executable robot actions (Figure 4.1). Teleoperation and kinesthetic teaching with the target
robot in the loop directly produce embodied actions. Portable tools, motion capture, and wearable
systems record motions that can be retargeted. Egocentric and Internet videos provide broad obser-
vations and behavioral priors. These sources complement one another in action fidelity, coverage
of natural settings, equipment occupancy, and processing cost.
Master-slave robot arms, spatial controllers, and immersive teleoperation operating on the target
embodiment can record robot observations, control commands, embodiment states, contacts, and
outcomes together. ALOHA uses matched leader and follower mechanisms for fine-grained bi-
manual demonstrations (Zhao et al., 2023). GELLO provides a low-cost, kinematically matched
70


interface that helps an operator perceive joint limits (Wu et al., 2024b). Open-TeleVision incorpo-
rates stereoscopic views and active head motion into the teleoperation loop (Cheng et al., 2025).
The collection interface is therefore not a neutral accessory. Its mapping, feedback delay, viewpoint
strategy, and operator burden systematically shape trajectories.
Portable, robot-independent interfaces bring demonstrations into natural environments.
UMI
records relative end-effector motion with a handheld gripper, wrist-mounted cameras, and visual-
inertial tracking, then accounts for target-robot reachability and latency at deployment (Chi et al.,
2024). DexWild uses a portable, human-centered system to extend dexterous demonstrations in
everyday settings (Tao et al., 2025b). FreeTacMan synchronizes visual and tactile collection, so that
contact feedback can support both the operator and supervision of contact phases (Wu et al., 2026a).
These methods reduce occupancy of the target robot and expand scene coverage, but still have to
address tracking errors, scale, action retargeting, and the target embodiment’s dynamics.
Humanoid and mobile manipulation extend demonstration beyond tabletop end-effector motion to
whole-body coordination. TWIST2 uses portable full-body teleoperation without external motion
capture to bring legged locomotion, torso, both arms, hands, and head-mounted views into one
loop (Ze et al., 2025). The central requirement is not simply more degrees of freedom. Navigation,
support, manipulation, and active vision must remain temporally consistent. A recording should
also distinguish actions supplied by the operator from compensation supplied by a stabilizer or
whole-body controller. Otherwise, high-level intent and low-level control corrections become con-
flated.
Egocentric human data offer natural behavior at greater scale. EgoDex synchronizes egocentric im-
ages with three-dimensional head, upper-body, and hand poses, turning video into a more calibrat-
able behavioral record (Hoque et al., 2026). AoE explores sustained collection of natural egocentric
experience and joint training with a smaller amount of robot teleoperation data (Yang et al., 2026a).
ActiveMimic jointly recovers camera and wrist trajectories from single-camera in-the-wild egocen-
tric video, emphasizing the relationship between active viewpoints and manipulation motion (Lin
et al., 2026). These approaches broaden the range of objects, scenes, behavioral phases, and view-
point priors. Human-video records themselves, however, do not natively supply robot joint states,
gripper signals, tactile measurements, or feedback from actual robot execution.
Turning human or Internet videos into robot supervision requires alignment of camera frames,
recovery of scale, mapping from hands or bodies to tools, correction for kinematic reachability,
temporal alignment, contact assumptions, and confidence assessment. Point tracks, wrist poses,
body poses, and latent actions are action proxies with different levels of reliability. They should
not all be labeled as ground-truth robot actions. Table 4.2 compares the supervision, executability,
and limitations of interaction data sources. More defensible training strategies include learning
visual and temporal representations first and then post-training on robot data, using separate loss
heads for human and robot data, weighting examples by confidence, or restricting explicit action
supervision to reliable channels.
Demonstration quality also depends on how people are organized. A collection plan should retain
anonymized operator identifiers, levels of training, interface configurations, and work periods.
Task rotation, fatigue monitoring, spot checks of replays, and coverage across operators can reduce
style bias. Expert demonstrations may not visit the error states encountered by novices, while
natural human movements may violate a robot’s safety constraints. The value of a demonstration
lies in how clearly it conveys intent, constraints, and an executable path.
Human data thus form a gradient from rich semantics to reliable executable actions. A sound
combination uses observational data to broaden tasks and scenes, wearable and tool-based data to
reduce the gap in action semantics, and interactions on the target embodiment to calibrate execu-
tion. Whether cross-domain data actually help must ultimately be established through closed-loop
evaluation on robots or other real systems. Section 9.6.4 follows these collection choices into a
dexterous-hand system, where wrist tracking, finger capture, and contact sensing supply different
parts of the demonstration.

4.2.3
Autonomous Data Collection
Autonomous data collection should be understood as an agent actively sampling the space of pos-
sible experiences, rather than a robot repeating its current policy indefinitely. Passive production
logs reflect the natural frequency of events but are often dominated by routine states. An active
system can instead select tasks and initial conditions according to novelty, uncertainty, prediction
error, failure density, gaps in coverage, or risk priority. If a collection policy repeatedly succeeds
only in familiar regions, the sample count may grow while behavioral diversity and the boundaries
of competence remain unchanged.
AutoRT illustrates an early use of foundation models to orchestrate collection. A vision-language
model describes the scene, a language model proposes and filters tasks, and the system schedules
their execution using existing policies or human operators (Ahn et al., 2024). Its contribution in this
context is not to replace physical control with a language model, but to bring scene understanding,
task discovery, safety rules, and available policy resources into a common orchestration process.
A high-level model may likewise identify gaps in coverage for factories, traffic systems, mines, or
laboratories, while concrete actions remain subject to control authority, real-time constraints, and
safety interlocks.
A systematic study of scaling autonomous robot data collection finds that environment instrumen-
tation, reliable object resets, success detection, and maintaining stable conditions remain major
costs. In some tasks, adding a small number of human demonstrations is more effective than
adding many autonomous episodes (Mirchandani et al., 2025).
These findings show how au-
tonomous collection shifts some labor from episode-by-episode teleoperation to environment in-
terfaces, online assessment, and risk control. If that infrastructure is unreliable, scaling up may
merely accumulate repetitive, mislabeled, or dangerous data.
74


The distinctive value of autonomous interaction is its access to states rarely covered by success-
ful human demonstrations. PlayWorld uses autonomous play to collect contact-rich and long-tail
robot-object interactions for learning action-conditioned changes in the world (Yin et al., 2026b).
The lesson for the present section concerns data production. Open-ended play can complement
demonstrations with failures, slips, precursors to collisions, and nonexpert trajectories. The use of
such data to train generative world models is discussed in Section 4.3 and Chapter 5.
Effective active sampling must balance information gain with representativeness. A collection bud-
get can be divided into three parts. One maintains a baseline density for states common in deploy-
ment, another targets regions where the current model is uncertain or incurs high loss, and the third
explores rare risks and new tasks. A task selector should also suppress near-duplicate trajectories
and avoid favoring short tasks merely because success is easy to detect. For high-risk states, con-
strained environments, low-speed operation, safe proxy tasks, or simulation-based prescreening
should take priority over deliberately inducing accidents.
A complete autonomous episode should retain the policy version, model inputs, raw outputs, com-
mands after safety filtering, actual execution, random seed, initial state, reset method, termination
reason, success-detector version, and any human involvement. In particular, a policy-initiated
abort, a safety-system intervention, a human emergency stop, and an equipment failure must be
distinguished because they carry different training semantics. Continuous operation also requires
monitoring for clock drift, frozen sensors, saturated actions, repeated tasks, degradation of the
scene, and failed resets, so that the pipeline does not continue blindly accumulating data after the
physical system has ceased to behave as intended.
Multiple robots can collect data in parallel, but the number of concurrent robots is not the only
measure of efficiency. As fleets grow, task scheduling, spare parts, networks, storage, calibration,
and on-site supervision become more complex. Drift and maintenance history across devices may
also introduce hidden domain differences. A more mature system coordinates equipment health,
task queues, risk levels, gains in coverage, and human workload, and admits each new data batch
into training only after it passes a quality gate rather than adding every operating log directly to
the model.
The scope of autonomous collection should be clear. This section concerns the selection and exe-
cution of interactions in the real world. Scaling simulated agents and generative scenes belongs to
Section 4.3, the simulation-reality gap to Section 4.4, and the longer-term deployment and retrain-
ing flywheel to Section 4.5. Autonomy is, first, a means of collecting informative experience and,
second, a means of reducing the human cost of each individual data point.
4.2.4
The Interactive Feedback Loop
The most valuable supervision often lies at the boundary of a policy’s competence. Complete,
successful demonstrations describe a manifold of nominal behavior, whereas autonomous deploy-
ment exposes the distribution of states induced by the current policy itself. Interactive supervision
connects the two. A failed episode, the warning signs before failure, the instant of human takeover,
corrective actions after takeover, and the recovery segment that returns the system to a feasible
state have different learning semantics. They should not be collapsed into a single “failure” label.
The collection system should retain the policy’s original actions, commands after safety filtering,
the human’s modifications, and the actual execution results, together with the reasons for inter-
vention, its start and end times, and the subsequent outcome. If only the smooth trajectory after
takeover is saved, a model may incorrectly attribute the human’s behavior to the policy. If only
the segment before failure is retained, it cannot learn how to recover. Linking warning, trigger,
takeover, correction, recovery, and outcome within one event chain supports risk prediction, cor-
rective policies, and recovery skills.
Human-in-the-Loop Sample-Efficient Robotic Reinforcement Learning (HIL-SERL) connects ini-
tial demonstrations and online human interventions with reinforcement learning on real robots,
showing that human-in-the-loop data can provide continued supervision on the policy’s execution
75


distribution, beyond offline imitation (Luo et al., 2025). Hi-ORS further combines online rejection
sampling with flexible human correction, exploiting recovery segments under comparatively stable
supervision targets (Lu et al., 2025). Together these works point to a shift from a single sequence of
“collect, then train” to a short-cycle loop among execution, evaluation, and updating.
HELP further organizes human-in-the-loop involvement as a scarce supervision resource. Dif-
ferent staff members undertake multi-robot monitoring, physical resets, and high-value remote
takeovers, while rollout segmentation distinguishes progress-making, idle, failure-inducing, and
recovery segments (Zhai et al., 2026). This exploration suggests that a scalable loop need not assign
one person to continuously control each robot. One person can monitor several robots, intervene
when risk warrants it, and concentrate limited human effort on states with the greatest learning
value. The results still depend on the platform and task. No particular ratio of people to robots
should be treated as a universal rule.
The quality gate is an intermediate layer of the loop. Before each round of data enters training,
it should undergo completeness checks, physical-consistency checks, event segmentation, review
of successes and failures, near-duplicate suppression, and provenance audits. After training, im-
provements must also be verified on held-out scenes, objects, operators, and embodiments. A new
version that improves only on the collection distribution, or raises average success at the cost of
safety and recovery, does not establish an effective feedback loop.
Safety is a system variable that determines what may be collected, when to intervene, and how
the resulting data may be used. Task rules, policy uncertainty, kinematic and dynamic constraints,
low-level monitoring, software and hardware interlocks, and human oversight should provide pro-
tection together. New policies should progress from offline checks through constrained environ-
ments and low-speed operation without a payload before normal operation. In settings involving
people, hazardous materials, public roads, or critical infrastructure, near misses, controlled pertur-
bations, and safe proxy tasks should take priority. Long-tail data should not be sought by causing
real accidents.
Interactive feedback loops also apply to Physical AI systems that do not have a single robot body.
Human takeover in a traffic system may mean reverting to a previous signal plan. Recovery in a
factory may mean degrading process parameters and isolating equipment. Correction in a labora-
tory may mean stopping a procedure, recalibrating, or changing experimental conditions. What-
ever the system, its recommendations, authorization decisions, issued commands, actual process,
alarms, human interventions, and final results should remain linked in the same event chain.
The efficiency of the loop should be measured by capability gains per human-hour or robot-hour,
alongside effective minutes of interaction, the fraction of usable episodes, rare-event yield, takeover
frequency, recovery success, gains in coverage, and safety incidents. Raw operating time is merely
a proxy for cost and cannot stand in for data value. The output of a short-cycle loop consists of
training batches that pass quality gates and traceable model versions. The longer-cycle flywheel of
deployment, failure discovery, renewed collection, and retraining is developed in Section 4.5.
4.3
Physics Engines and Generative Worlds
Section 4.1 defines physical data as records that link observations and actions to their consequences.
Among these records, failures and the recoveries that follow them are the most informative and also
the hardest to obtain (Section 4.2). A policy that must recover when a grasped object starts to slip
needs to experience many slips, and a legged robot that must get up after a fall needs to fall, yet
physical systems cannot be reset cheaply (Section 1.1). In simulation, a slip can be staged 1,000
times, and a simulated fall causes no physical damage to robot hardware. A model computes the
recorded consequences, so their physical consistency has to be tested before the data can be trusted.
Every synthetic trajectory depends on three choices. The world in which it unfolds may be au-
thored by hand, reconstructed from scans, or generated. The consequences of each action may
be computed by a physics engine or by a network trained on data. The actions may come from
planners, reinforcement-learning experts, or adapted human demonstrations. The section first con-

siders what simulation adds to a dataset and then takes the three choices in turn. Table 4.4 summa-
