of process plants, traffic systems, and laboratories.
4.3.1
What Simulation Adds to a Dataset
In the notation of Section 4.1, a simulator turns chosen actions into trajectories through two condi-
tional distributions,
st+1 ∼Ptr
ξsim(· | st, at),
ot ∼Oψrender(· | st),
(4.2)
where the physical and numerical parameters ξsim (masses, friction coefficients, time step, solver
tolerance) govern the dynamics and the observation parameters ψrender (camera models, lighting,
sensor noise) govern what is sensed. Delays in the real system, such as actuator response time or
sensor latency, have to be represented in st or in an explicit history buffer. Otherwise the simulator
assumes that commands act instantly and that sensors report the present. Two further ingredi-
ents complete a simulated dataset, namely the distribution of initial states and tasks from which
episodes start and the predicate that decides whether an episode meets the success criterion. The
dynamics, the observation model, the initial conditions, and the success predicate can each differ
from reality, and Section 4.4 classifies the reality gap along these four lines.
The most visible gain is access to the full state. Object poses, contact forces, and material parameters
can be recorded at every step, even though a deployed policy cannot observe them directly. This
privileged information is valuable for training teachers, critics, and state estimators (Section 7.2 and
Section 7.3), provided it never leaks into the deployed policy’s inputs. Each synthetic field should
therefore be tagged as simulator state, rendered observation, or inferred quantity.
77


A deeper gain is the exact and inexpensive reset, which physical systems lack. Episodes restart
from saved states, thousands of environments run in parallel, and the same initial state can be
replayed under different actions, friction coefficients, or disturbances to see what changes the out-
come. Counterfactual replay of this kind supports curricula, failure diagnosis, and targeted gen-
eration. Its findings concern the model, however. A policy’s sensitivity to a simulated friction
coefficient says something about a real material only after the simulator has been checked against
measurements.
Simulated episodes need the same conventions as real trajectories and the same care in task design.
An action vector means different things under torque, position, and Cartesian control, so the action
specification of Section 4.1 belongs with every episode. Favorable starting poses hide difficult ap-
proaches, and a reset triggered as soon as an object slips ends the episode before the recovery that
a deployed policy will need to learn. Success is best defined by the physical outcome of interest,
such as a plug that is fully seated or a lid that stays closed, instead of by whatever the simulator
makes easy to check.
4.3.2
Scenes from Scans and from Generators
Hand-built scenes are slow to author and tend to be few and tidy, so the training data available
to policies cover a narrow range of environments. Reconstruction from real scans and automatic
generation both widen that slice. Reconstruction has considerably reduced the appearance gap for
visual policies. Neural radiance fields and Gaussian splatting (Section 3.3) recover geometry and
appearance, although collision geometry, articulation, and physical parameters must still be added
before a scene can be simulated. With these additions, reconstructed scenes can largely stand in
for real ones. RGB manipulation policies trained entirely on data from SplatSim, which renders a
simulator’s scenes with Gaussian splats, achieve 86.25% average success in the reported SplatSim
experiments zero-shot on real hardware, against 97.5% for policies trained on real data (Qureshi
et al., 2025). RialTo fine-tunes policies with reinforcement learning inside a reconstructed replica
of the deployment scene itself, reporting an average improvement of 67% in success over baselines
under perturbed object poses, distractors, and disturbances (Villasevil et al., 2024).
Some pipelines use reconstruction without simulating dynamics at all. Real2Render2Real turns a
phone scan of an object and a single video of a person manipulating it into thousands of rendered
robot demonstrations (Yu et al., 2025a). The object’s motion is copied from the human and collision
modeling is switched off, so no model computes the consequences of the robot’s actions. Even so,
in the reported Real2Render2Real experiments, policies trained on data rendered from one human
video match policies trained on 150 teleoperated demonstrations. The approach works when the
object’s path alone defines the task, and it cannot handle tasks that depend on force.
Reconstruction also raises the question of how faithful a training scene needs to be. A digital twin
is tied to one physical site and kept up to date with it. A digital cousin, by contrast, is a generated
environment that preserves what matters for interaction in a real scene, such as where objects are
and how they can be grasped or opened, without copying it exactly. In the reported digital-cousin
experiments, policies trained across a set of cousins achieve 90% zero-shot success in the original
real scene, whereas policies trained on a single faithful twin achieve 25% (Dai et al., 2025).
Generating scenes at scale requires assets, and a training asset must be a physical specification
as well as a shape. It needs consistent scale, collision geometry, mass and inertia, joint axes and
limits, and material parameters. A photorealistic cabinet with a misplaced hinge axis adds visual
variety but nothing a policy can practice on. Articulation is particularly hard to produce automat-
ically. Articulate-Anything has a vision-language model write articulation code from text, images,
or video and revise it after inspecting the result. On the PartNet-Mobility benchmark, the reported
Articulate-Anything evaluation shows that this raises the success rate of reconstructed articulations
from 8.7 to 11.6% for earlier methods to 75% (Le et al., 2025).
Generative models can supply tasks as well as assets. GenSim and RoboGen prompt a language
model to generate tasks, write the code that builds their scenes, and produce the supervision
needed to learn them (Wang et al., 2024d;e). RoboCasa populates kitchens with assets from text-
78


to-3D and text-to-image models, and RoboCasa365 scales the approach to 365 tasks across 2,500
kitchen layouts (Nasiriany et al., 2024; 2026). A generated task is usable only if it resolves to identifi-
able objects, admissible actions, and a success predicate that can be checked, so generation pipelines
usually execute each proposed task and discard those that a solver cannot complete.
4.3.3
Agent-Built Scenes and Simulations
The methods above use a language model for one part of a scene at a time. Agents built on language
and vision-language models now assemble whole scenes, and increasingly whole simulations, by
writing code, running it, and inspecting the result. Early systems focus on layout. Holodeck asks
GPT-4 which objects a described room should contain and how they relate spatially, then places
Objaverse assets with a constraint solver (Yang et al., 2024c). Fine-tuning on Holodeck scenes raises
a navigation agent’s success in unfamiliar room types, such as music rooms and gyms, from 4.1%
to 20.4%, against 17.0% for scenes with the same assets in procedural layouts.
Later systems also supply physical properties. In SceneSmith, designer and critic agents build a
room in stages, from the floor plan to furniture to small objects, while a vision-language model
estimates each object’s mass and material from rendered views and articulated furniture is drawn
from a library (Pfaff et al., 2026). The generated rooms contain about 71 objects, against 11 to 23
for earlier generators, and 95.6% of the objects stay in place under simulation. SAGE uses a similar
generate-and-critique loop to build scenes for a given task (Xia et al., 2026). Parameters inferred
from appearance are enough to keep a scene standing, but contact-sensitive tasks still need them
calibrated.
General-purpose models released in 2026 can carry out the whole real-to-sim process. In its 2026
release materials, OpenAI presents 3D world and asset generation as a main capability of GPT-6
Astra (OpenAI, 2026), and reports published within weeks of release describe several groups using
it to build simulation scenes (Li et al., 2026d).3 In Agentic RSR, a Codex agent running GPT-6 Astra
turns an RGB video of a robot workspace into a MuJoCo scene with collision geometry and joints,
then develops a policy program by running it there (Li et al., 2026d). Across 18 tasks on 2 robot
arms, 10 succeed in simulation and 8 of those also succeed on the real robots. The authors find that
the agent behaves differently across interfaces and runs, so the model version belongs in the record
of any data it generates.
Benchmarks show where such agents still fall short. In Video2World, agents rebuild a simulated
world and the demonstrated behavior from a video of a robot or a person performing a task (Tang
et al., 2026). The best of 9 agent systems achieves 25.5% task success over 222 instances, against
58.8% for human-assisted reconstructions, and GPT-6 Astra achieves only 10.7% although it recov-
ers object shapes more accurately than any other agent. On indoor scans, the reported LiteReality-
Agent evaluation shows 24 interpenetrating furniture pairs for GPT-6 Astra and none for the spe-
cialized LiteReality-Agent pipeline (Huang et al., 2026b), and on 4DCodeBench good static recon-
struction does not carry over to deformation, fluids, or fracture (Shen et al., 2026). Accurate geom-
etry does not guarantee a scene in which the task can be performed.
Two recent systems close part of this gap by adding structure around the model. Text2Sim splits the
writing of a Genesis simulation among planner, writer, and critic agents, and the writers consult
Debug Cards, short notes distilled from 99 demonstrations in graphics papers on how simula-
tions of a given kind fail and how to repair them (Xiong et al., 2026). On 42 held-out prompts, its
automatic physical-quality score is 95.3, against 86.6 for direct use of its own underlying model
(GPT-5.6-Sol). Without the cards, the score falls to 91.3. WorldAgent instead verifies every con-
struction and simulation step in Blender, checking interpenetration, support, numerical stability,
and causal order against scene geometry and simulator states, so it also catches overlaps hidden
from the camera (Wang et al., 2026a). With GPT-6 Astra as the underlying model, WorldAgent
reduces the worst interpenetration during simulation to about 1/5 of that from direct prompting.
3Max Bickley and Ashley Goldstein, NVIDIA Technical Blog, How to Use AI Agents to Prepare 3D Scenes for
Simulation, September 16, 2026.
79


In these evaluations, neither system is checked against measured behavior, and both infer physical
parameters instead of measuring them.
World generators skip the agent altogether. Marble turns text, images, or video into Gaussian
splats with a collision mesh, and such worlds have been imported into MuJoCo and Isaac Sim.
The mesh is a single static surface, so the robot and the objects it manipulated were added from
asset libraries (World Labs Team, 2025a).4 Genie 3 generates an interactive environment from a
prompt in real time and keeps it consistent for several minutes, and DeepMind’s SIMA agent has
pursued goals inside such worlds.5 A world of this kind has no explicit state or parameters to
inspect, so, like the video world models discussed later in this section, it can be judged only by the
consequences it predicts.
4.3.4
Contact, Fidelity, and Throughput
Once a world is built, a model must compute what happens in it, and the accuracy required de-
pends on the task. Articulated rigid-body dynamics suffice for most legged locomotion and for
pick-and-place with rigid objects, whereas cloth, cables, food, and soft tissue need deformable or
continuum models. A useful test is whether the model reproduces the events that change the cor-
rect action, such as a grasp that slips, a peg that jams, or a support that gives way.
Most such events happen at contact. Section 2.1 describes contact through non-penetration and
Coulomb friction, and engines differ mainly in how they enforce these two conditions. Classi-
cal time-stepping schemes pose them as a complementarity problem, in which two bodies at a
contact either separate or push on each other, never both at once (Stewart and Trinkle, 1996). Mu-
JoCo relaxes them into soft constraints and solves a convex optimization problem at each step,
obtaining smooth, well-posed dynamics at the price of small interpenetrations and some compli-
ance (Todorov et al., 2012). For many tasks the relaxation does no harm, and a calibrated compli-
ance can even describe a rubber fingertip better than a perfectly rigid model. In tight-tolerance
insertion or stacking, however, a soft contact model can let a part slide into place where the corre-
sponding real part would bind.
Deformable objects make non-penetration harder to enforce. Incremental Potential Contact guar-
antees, under its algorithmic assumptions, that simulated deformable bodies never pass through
each other and that mesh elements never turn inside out (Li et al., 2020). Trajectories computed
with it are free of interpenetration artifacts, but the method says nothing about the stiffness, damp-
ing, or friction of a particular sponge or garment, and these values must be measured before the
recorded forces and deformations can be trusted.
Numerical artifacts are a separate hazard, because reinforcement learning can favor policies that
exploit them. A policy can learn to exploit interpenetration, spurious impulses from numerical
jitter, or contacts that stick when they should slide, and the time step, collision geometry, solver
tolerance, and constraint softness determine which of these artifacts the optimizer can find. A cheap
safeguard is to replay a sample of accepted trajectories with a smaller time step, tighter tolerances,
or perturbed contact parameters, and to discard behaviors whose success does not survive. The
check is best run before a large dataset is produced, since an artifact that goes unnoticed is copied
into thousands of examples.
Throughput determines how much variation can be explored.
Isaac Gym keeps physics sim-
ulation and policy training on the same graphics processing unit (GPU) and reports speedups
of two to three orders of magnitude over pipelines that simulate on the central processing unit
(CPU) (Makoviychuk et al., 2021), which makes it possible to train quadruped walking policies
in minutes (Rudin et al., 2022). For policies that use images, the bottleneck moves to rendering.
ManiSkill3 parallelizes rendering on the GPU along with physics and reports that, with rendering
enabled, it runs 10 to 1,000 times faster than other platforms on its benchmarks (Tao et al., 2025a).
4World Labs, Scaling Robotic Simulation with Marble, 2025.
5Jack Parker-Holder and Shlomi Fruchter, Google DeepMind, Genie 3: A New Frontier for World Models,
August 5, 2025.
80


Frame rates are nonetheless a poor guide to the cost of data. They vary with scene complexity and
contact density, and they leave out resets, policy inference, filtering, and storage. A better measure
is the simulated counterpart of the effective data yield of Section 4.2, which counts only trajectories
that pass the quality gates and weighs their cost against how much they improve the policy.
4.3.5
Learned Simulators and Video World Models
Hand-written engines are limited to what their authors can model. Learned models trade explicit
physical structure for coverage of phenomena that are hard to write down, and they can replace
the solver, the renderer, or both. The price is that their errors are harder to diagnose. An error in an
engine can usually be traced to a parameter, a missing mechanism, or a solver setting, whereas an
error in a learned model is spread across its weights. Measurements on the physical system then
become the main check on its physical consistency.
Learned simulators replace the solver but keep the state-based interface of Eq. (4.2).
Graph
Network-based Simulators and MeshGraphNets, for example, learn how particles and meshes
evolve for fluids, granular media, cloth, and deformable solids (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020;
Pfaff et al., 2021). In its evaluation, MeshGraphNets runs 1 to 2 orders of magnitude faster than
the solvers used to produce its training data. Such models are reliable mainly within their training
regime. Over long rollouts their errors accumulate, and conservation laws hold only approximately
unless they are built into the architecture (Section 2.4).
Observation generators leave the physics to an engine and replace only the renderer, changing the
lighting, textures, backgrounds, and clutter that the camera sees. Cosmos-Transfer, for instance,
generates realistic video conditioned on segmentation, depth, and edge maps rendered by a sim-
ulator (NVIDIA et al., 2025b). The risk is that the generator alters something the labels depend
on. If it shifts a handle by a few centimeters while restyling the scene, and the simulator keeps the
original pose, a correct grasp label becomes wrong. Agreement between image and simulator state
therefore needs checking near contacts, around thin structures, and under occlusion, where such
errors are most likely.
Video world models replace both, learning the consequences of actions directly from recordings
(Chapter 5) (Bruce et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b; NVIDIA et al., 2025a).
UniSim, an action-
conditioned video simulator, learns from image, robot, and navigation data and is used to train
policies that transfer to real robots. For generating data, the first question is which training data
the model has received. A model trained on demonstrations rarely observes failures or unusual
contact, so it tends to predict that actions succeed. Training on autonomous play, as in PlayWorld
(Section 4.2), exposes a world model to the slips, collisions, and near misses that demonstrations
omit (Yin et al., 2026b).
Because video models produce pixels, actions have to be recovered before their output can train a
policy. DreamGen fine-tunes an image-to-video model on the target embodiment and uses it to gen-
erate videos of familiar and new tasks (Jang et al., 2025). The videos are then labeled with actions,
either by an inverse-dynamics model, which infers the action taken between consecutive frames, or
by a latent-action model, which infers an abstract action code. Starting from teleoperation data for
a single pick-and-place task in one environment, a humanoid trained on these generated trajecto-
ries acquires 22 new behaviors in seen and unseen environments. The recovered actions are action
proxies in the sense of Section 4.1, and they can be screened by replaying them in a physics simu-
lator and keeping those whose simulated motion matches the generated video (Kim et al., 2026b).
A policy can also be fine-tuned inside a world model, on imagined successes or on rewards that a
vision-language model assigns to imagined rollouts (Guo et al., 2026b; Sharma et al., 2026a), at the
risk of learning to exploit the model’s errors (Section 5.4).
4.3.6
Synthetic Demonstrations and Pretraining Corpora
The third choice is the agent. Behavior can come from motion planners that use the simulator’s
exact state, from reinforcement-learning experts trained with privileged observations and then dis-
tilled into policies that use deployable sensors (Section 7.2), from programs written by language
81


models, or from a few human demonstrations adapted to new situations. Each source leaves its
mark on the data. Planners produce smoother and more direct motions than an operator would
produce, reinforcement learning may find strategies that a person would not demonstrate, and
adapted demonstrations carry human habits along with human skill.
MimicGen shows how far a few demonstrations can be stretched. It splits each demonstration into
segments defined relative to the objects involved, transforms the segments to new object poses,
stitches them together, and keeps the results that succeed when executed in simulation. In Mimic-
Gen, about 200 human demonstrations yield more than 50,000 demonstrations across 18 tasks with
varied scenes, objects, and robot arms. Policies trained on the synthesized demonstrations perform
comparably to policies trained on additional human demonstrations (Mandlekar et al., 2023). Later
systems extend the method to long-horizon skill sequences and to bimanual dexterous hands (Gar-
rett et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025). MimicGen’s output, however, recombines the strategies in the
seed demonstrations without adding new ones, and because failed executions are discarded, the
resulting training data provide few examples of failure or recovery.
Synthetic demonstrations should pass the same quality gates that Section 4.2 applies to real batches,
along with checks specific to synthesis. These checks cover action semantics that match the de-
ployed controller, privileged fields that are marked, and outcomes that survive the solver checks
described earlier. Rejected samples are worth keeping, sorted by the reason for rejection, because
different reasons call for different responses. Invalid geometry, a mismatch between the rendered
observation and the simulator state, and an infeasible task all point to defects in the generator. A
valid execution that ends in failure is ordinary failure data, unsuitable as an imitation target but
useful for learning to predict outcomes and to recover. If generator versions, parameter distribu-
tions, solver and renderer settings, and random seeds are kept on record, a problem found later can
be fixed at its source before more data are produced from it.
Synthetic data have also moved beyond narrow skills into pretraining. Simulated trajectories make
up a large part of the training mixture of the GR00T N1 humanoid model, and GraspVLA, pre-
trained on 1 billion frames of simulated grasping, transfers zero-shot to real objects (NVIDIA et al.,
2025c; Deng et al., 2025b). The most direct comparison comes from InternData-A1. In InternData-
A1, a model with the π0 architecture, pretrained only on its 630,000 simulated trajectories, matches
the official π0 on simulated, real, and long-horizon dexterous tasks. The official π0 had been pre-
trained largely on real robot data (Tian et al., 2025). Results of this kind are strongest where out-
comes depend mainly on geometry, as in grasping and pick-and-place. Where outcomes depend on
contact dynamics, a synthetic corpus is only as useful as the calibration of the engine that produced
it, and calibration requires real data.
4.4
Sim-to-Real Transfer and Real-World Alignment
A policy trained on synthetic data inherits the errors of its source, and how much those errors mat-
ter depends on the task. In legged locomotion, policies trained entirely in simulation with random-
ized dynamics and learned actuator models now routinely transfer without real-world fine-tuning.
Manipulation is harder. Contact, deformation, and vision all differ between simulation and reality,
and transfer there typically involves some real data. This section begins with what simulated and
real data each contribute. It then follows the order in which the reality gap is commonly addressed.
This sequence consists of finding where simulation and reality disagree, correcting the simulator
with measurements, training policies that are robust to the remaining error, and checking the result
in closed loop on the physical system.
4.4.1
What Simulated and Real Data Each Contribute
Choosing between simulated and real data means trading scale and label accuracy against the reli-
ability of the dynamics (Table 4.5). Simulation offers scale, exact perception labels, and free resets
(Section 4.3), but its dynamics, and therefore the consequences it computes, are only as accurate
as its contact, material, and actuator models. Real data have the reverse profile. They are limited
by robot time, operators, and the cost of resetting the world, and their observations are imperfect.

Cameras add noise and blur, depth sensors drop out on shiny surfaces, calibration drifts, and object
poses or contact forces must be estimated instead of read off. Their dynamics, on the other hand,
are the real ones. A real trajectory reflects the actual friction, compliance, backlash, and delay of
the system, including effects that no simulator models, even without direct measurements of those
effects. Neither source dominates. Simulation is most useful where exact labels and broad coverage
matter and the dynamics are easy to model, while real data are hard to replace where the outcome
depends on contact, deformation, or actuation that simulators approximate poorly.
Because real data are scarce, how they are spent matters as much as how much is collected. They
serve three purposes, namely training policies directly, calibrating the simulators and world models
that generate synthetic data, and validating both the generators and the policies trained on their
output. The three purposes compete for the same evidence, and evidence spent on one cannot serve
as an independent check on another. Trajectories used to fit a simulator cannot show that the fit is
accurate, and trials used to select a policy cannot certify it.
4.4.2
Where the Reality Gap Comes from
The four ingredients of a simulated dataset listed in Section 4.3 also give a natural way to classify
the reality gap (Table 4.6). A dynamics gap means that Ptr
ξsim in Eq. (4.2) is wrong, either because its
parameters are off or because it lacks a mechanism. Errors in mass, inertia, friction, and compliance
alter accelerations and contact outcomes, and actuators add discrepancies of their own through
gains, torque limits, backlash, and delay. An observation gap means that Oψrender misrepresents
what the sensors report, whether in appearance, camera calibration, depth dropouts on shiny or
transparent surfaces, proprioceptive bias, or timing. Touch is a particular weak point, since many
tactile sensors respond through elastomer deformation and internal optics that simulators capture
only roughly. The remaining two gaps are easier to miss. A distribution gap arises when training
does not cover the initial states, objects, and tasks the robot actually meets. An objective gap arises
when simulated success is not real success, as when a success predicate credits an insertion that
reaches the right depth but would not hold in a real fixture.
Each gap calls for a different remedy, so the gap has to be identified before anything is changed. A
delayed command is fixed by calibrating the interface, an unmodeled deformation needs a better
model, and an action that is executed correctly but is wrong for the task needs new supervision.
Telling these cases apart requires the commanded and executed actions, events, and outcomes in
the trajectory record (Section 4.1), which a binary success flag does not provide.

A gap of any kind is amplified in closed loop. An early mistake moves the robot into a state that no
demonstration covered, the policy’s next action there is worse, and errors snowball. For imitation
learning, this intuition has a precise form. With per-step task costs bounded in [0, 1], a cloned
policy with error probability ϵBC under the expert state distribution can incur an excess expected
cost of order T2ϵBC over T steps (Ross and Bagnell, 2010). Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) collects
expert labels on states visited during rollouts that may mix expert and learner policies. Under the
assumptions of its analysis and with sufficiently many iterations, some learned iterate has excess
expected task cost relative to the expert bounded by udevTϵDAgger,Niter + O(1). Here ϵDAgger,Niter is
the minimum average surrogate loss achievable within the policy class over the state distributions
induced by the rollout policies across Niter iterations, and udev bounds the increase in the expert’s
remaining cost after one deviating action (Ross et al., 2011). The constant udev is a measure of
recoverability, the property that Section 1.1 argues planning must take into account when resets are
not free.
The analysis assumes access to an expert policy that can label the states visited during data collec-
tion. A privileged teacher in simulation can supply such labels when its policy is defined on those
states, and teacher-student distillation usually labels the states that the student visits. Human op-
erators find it hard to say what the robot should have done in a state they are not controlling, which
is why intervention-based collection (Section 4.2) lets them take over when the policy goes wrong.
Either way, training data must include the states that the deployed policy actually reaches.
4.4.3
Calibrating Simulators and World Models with Real Data
Calibration adjusts a model’s parameters until it reproduces real measurements. With Dr denot-
ing a set of real trajectories, system identification can be written as Bayesian inference over the
simulator parameters,
p(ξsim | Dr) ∝p(Dr | ξsim) p(ξsim),
(4.3)
where the prior p(ξsim) encodes datasheet values and physical bounds and the likelihood measures
how well the simulator with parameters ξsim reproduces the recorded observations. When states
are only partially observed, the likelihood must also account for state and sensor uncertainty. A
point estimate is often enough in practice, but the full posterior keeps track of ambiguities that
matter later, for instance when randomization ranges are chosen.
The data used for identification must be informative. As Section 2.2 explains, accurate tracking
alone does not imply parameter convergence. Persistent excitation of the regressor supports pa-
84


rameter convergence under the assumptions of the specified adaptive law. Identification likewise
requires data that distinguish the relevant parameter directions. Slow motions in free space reveal
little about actuator bandwidth, grasps that never slip reveal little about sliding friction, and dif-
ferent combinations of motor strength, payload, and gain can produce nearly identical trajectories.
Calibration experiments should therefore excite the mechanisms the task depends on, for example
with fast reversals for actuator response, controlled pushes for friction, and loaded lifts for inertia,
while staying within safe limits.
Where first-principles models fall short, models learned from data often do better. Learned actuator
networks, which map commanded positions and recent history to delivered torque, are central in
the early legged-transfer study (Section 7.2) (Hwangbo et al., 2019). ASAP applies data-driven
correction to a whole humanoid. A motion-tracking policy trained in simulation is run on the real
robot, and the recorded rollouts train a delta-action model, a network that adds a correction to each
action inside the simulator so that simulated motion matches the recorded real-robot motion. The
policy is then fine-tuned in the corrected simulator. In tests of transfer between two simulators and
deployment on a real Unitree G1, the reported ASAP evaluation shows that the approach tracks
agile whole-body motions more accurately than system identification, domain randomization, or a
learned correction to the simulator’s dynamics (He et al., 2025a).
Learned corrections can, however, fit the data for the wrong reason. A correction trained on one
set of motions may absorb a calibration error elsewhere in the system, and testing at speeds, loads,
and contact points outside the fitting data exposes such errors. The same tests separate parameter
errors, which calibration can fix, from structural ones, which it cannot. No value of ξsim repairs a
model that omits cable twisting or a compliant gripper pad.
Nor is a single best-fit simulator always necessary. SimOpt instead calibrates a distribution over
parameters. It adjusts the distribution so that simulated rollouts of the current policy match real
ones, retrains the policy under the updated distribution, and repeats. Policies trained in this way
transfer to real swing-peg-in-hole and drawer-opening tasks (Chebotar et al., 2019). A simulator
fitted to one policy’s behavior can remain wrong in regions that policy never visits, so calibration
data should also cover the behaviors that later policies are likely to try.
Learned simulators can be calibrated more directly, because their parameters can be updated by
gradient descent on real data. NeRD replaces the dynamics and contact solvers of a conventional
simulator with a learned model that can be fine-tuned on real trajectories (Xu et al., 2025b). For
video world models, VLAW alternates between improving the model and improving the policy.
Real rollouts of a vision-language-action policy refine the world model, and the refined model
generates rollouts for training the policy (Guo et al., 2026a). On a real robot, the authors report
that the method raises success by 39.2 percentage points over the pretrained policy and by 11.6%
over fine-tuning on the same real rollouts filtered for success. In that evaluation, the refined world
model thus adds value beyond the real data used to build it. Establishing the accuracy of the model
would still require fresh trajectories from conditions outside the fitting data.
4.4.4
Randomization, Adaptation, and Co-Training
Calibration narrows the uncertainty that measurements can resolve, and the policy must tolerate
whatever remains. Domain randomization trains it to do so across a distribution pηsim(ξsim) over
simulator parameters, shaped by design parameters ηsim,
max

Eξsim∼pηsim

J(πθ; ξsim)


(4.4)
where J(πθ; ξsim) is the expected return of the policy in the world with parameters ξsim. Training
across varied models aims to reduce reliance on any one exact model, and randomizing appearance
and dynamics in this way underlies much of sim-to-real transfer in perception and control (Tobin
et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018b).
Choosing pηsim in Eq. (4.4) is a data-design problem.
Parameters should be resampled on the
timescale at which they actually vary. An object’s mass is fixed within an episode, sensor noise
85


changes with every reading, and actuator response drifts slowly with temperature and wear. De-
pendencies should be explicit, since appearance and friction are correlated for a given material.
Wide ranges are not enough by themselves. A range that contains the true value is of little use if the
distribution places almost no probability near it, and ranges that are too broad produce cautious
policies without fixing the failures seen in deployment. Moderate variation around a well-chosen
nominal value often helps more than pinning each parameter to a single estimate, as the digital-
cousin result of Section 4.3 suggests, and Section 4.5 reports a similar effect of diversity in real
data. The posterior in Eq. (4.3) is a natural source for both the nominal values and their spread,
and evaluation should report performance for groups of conditions as well as the average over the
distribution.
Automatic domain randomization automates part of this design by widening each range as the
policy meets the performance criterion within the current one, which turns randomization into a
curriculum. OpenAI uses it to train a Shadow Dexterous Hand to solve a Rubik’s cube. In ten
reported trials, the hand solves cubes needing 15 face rotations 6 times and solves the hardest
cubes (which need 26 face rotations) 2 times (OpenAI et al., 2019). The result also depends on a
cube instrumented with sensors, a classical solver that chooses the sequence of face rotations, and
months of large-scale training.
Adaptive policies deal with the remaining uncertainty differently. Instead of performing well un-
der every condition, they infer the current one from recent history and adjust to it, as in the teacher-
student and rapid motor adaptation methods of Section 7.2 (Kumar et al., 2021). Training them re-
quires data that contain changes and transients, such as a payload added in the middle of a task or
the onset of slip, as well as conditions that are unknown but fixed. When adaptive rollouts are later
reused for training, the inferred context should be stored with each example, because an action that
is correct for a heavy payload becomes a wrong label once the payload information is dropped.
In vision-based manipulation, where both the visual and the physical gap are large, a common al-
ternative is to train on simulated and real data at once and let each cover the other’s weaknesses
(Table 4.5). Co-training minimizes a weighted sum of losses over the two sources, the mixture ob-
jective of Eq. (9.1) with one simulated and one real component. Across tasks on a robot arm and a
humanoid, the reported co-training study shows that adding simulation data improves real-world
performance by an average of 38%, and the benefit persists when the real dataset grows to 400
demonstrations (Maddukuri et al., 2025). A controlled study of planar pushing from pixels exam-
ines when and why the benefit appears (Wei et al., 2025). In that study, simulation data raise success
two- to sevenfold when real data are scarce, but the gains plateau unless real data grow too. Nar-
rowing the physics gap matters more than improving visual fidelity. Unexpectedly, the best policies
can distinguish simulated inputs from real ones, and a modest visual difference between the do-
mains helps. A mechanistic analysis attributes this to a balance between aligning representations
across domains, so that knowledge transfers, and keeping the domains distinguishable, so that the
policy can apply the right dynamics to each (Lei et al., 2026).
The same pushing study finds that mixing the sources during training outperforms pretraining
in simulation and then fine-tuning on real data, and that fine-tuning a co-trained policy does not
consistently help. These comparisons involve single tasks and modest datasets. Whether broad
multi-task pretraining followed by fine-tuning helps is a separate question, taken up in Section 4.5.
4.4.5
Validating Transfer and Closing the Loop
Most of the evaluation that guides development happens away from hardware, yet the criterion
remains closed-loop performance on the physical system (Section 1.1), so every proxy evaluator
has to be checked against it. SIMPLER builds simulated counterparts of real manipulation setups,
matching camera views, appearance, and control. It compares policy rankings in simulation with
their rankings on real robots (Li et al., 2025b). Agreement is measured by the Pearson correla-
tion between simulated and real success rates and by the mean maximum rank violation (MMRV),
which penalizes the simulator for misordering two policies in proportion to the gap between their
real success rates. By these measures, simulated evaluation tracks real results far better than offline
86


metrics such as the error of predicted actions on held-out demonstrations. World models can serve
the same purpose. In WorldGym, success rates measured inside an action-conditioned video model
correlate with real success at r = 0.78 on tasks from the BridgeData V2 tabletop setup (Quevedo
et al., 2026).
Simulated and real trials can also be combined statistically instead of merely compared. SureSim
treats the problem as prediction-powered inference. A small number of paired real and simu-
lated trials estimate the simulator’s bias, and that estimate corrects a large number of simulated
trials (Badithela et al., 2025). The result is a valid confidence interval on real performance, which
raw simulated success rates cannot provide, and an interval of similar width needs 20 to 25% fewer
hardware trials than one estimated from hardware trials alone. Like any agreement between a
proxy and reality, the correction holds for the policies and conditions for which it is measured and
must be rechecked when either changes.
Consider a fleet of mobile manipulators that open drawers in office kitchens. At one site, pulls re-
peatedly stall after an approach and grasp that look correct in the logs. Engineers rebuild the scene
in simulation from the logs and a scan, and the simulated robot reproduces the approach but opens
the drawer without difficulty. Since the approach is reproduced and the stall is not, the discrep-
ancy most likely lies in the simulated drawer rather than in perception or in the grasp. Pulls with
a force-sensing gripper reveal a soft-close damper and a detent that the simulated drawer lacks.
Once the damper and detent are modeled and their parameters fitted (Eq. (4.3)), randomization is
restricted to damping and detent force around the identified values, and new scenes vary handle
position and pull direction near the failure. The retrained policy is screened in simulation and then
tested on held-out drawers at that site and at others, to confirm that the fix generalizes beyond the
cabinet where the failure occurs.
The example also shows the many points at which real data enter a pipeline nominally trained in
simulation, and claims of transfer should account for all of them. “Zero-shot” usually means that
the policy was not fine-tuned on the target embodiment, yet real data may still have been used to
identify parameters, reconstruct scenes, pretrain perception, or select checkpoints. Reporting these
uses makes the contribution of simulation measurable. It also sharpens a question that co-training
raises and that Section 4.5 takes up. The question concerns how many synthetic trajectories one
real trajectory is worth.
4.5
Scaling Laws and the Data Flywheel for Physical AI
Language-model scaling studies show predictable improvements as data, parameters, and com-
pute grow together, and progress in vision-language-action models now depends mainly on data
(Section 6.2). Whether physical data will yield equally predictable gains is far from clear. Every tra-
jectory comes from a particular body in a particular world and costs robot time and usually human
time. The practical question concerns allocation. It covers which data to collect or generate and
in what proportions. It also covers how to divide scarce physical interaction among training, cali-
bration, and validation. A further aspect is when a robot system can collect what it needs through
its own operation. Such a system, a data flywheel, is worth running only if the capability it adds
outweighs its cost. Throughout, value is measured by closed-loop performance on the physical
system, not by loss, frame counts, or simulated success.
4.5.1
The Data Pyramid
Section 4.2 describes human data as a gradient from rich semantics to executable actions. Figure 4.2
extends that gradient to all physically collected data and adds the dimension of scale, with layers
widening toward the base as cost per sample falls. The trajectory record of Section 4.1 gives a
way to judge relevance. Data are most relevant when they record the target embodiment issuing
executable commands under deployment conditions, together with the measured consequences of
those commands. Each layer below the apex gives up part of this record. Handheld and wearable
devices capture real contact and robot-like actions without a robot, human video captures real
physics without robot actions, and web data supply semantics without physical interaction. The

Fig. 4.2 The data pyramid for Physical AI. For physically collected data, relevance to the target em-
bodiment and cost per sample rise together toward the apex, where the target embodiment acts in
the physical world. Lower layers are cheaper, larger, and more diverse but supervise physical exe-
cution less directly. Simulated and generated data are drawn separately because they supply robot
actions at low cost while computing their consequences with a model, so their effective position
depends on calibration. Adapted from NVIDIA et al. (2025c) and Ye et al. (2026b). The order of the
layers reflects relevance and cost, not dataset quality
most relevant data are also the most expensive, since every hour of them needs a robot, an operator,
and resets, and they are correspondingly scarce. Goldberg estimates that the largest teleoperation
datasets amount to about a year of robot experience, whereas the text and images used to train
vision-language models would take a person some 100,000 years to read and view (Goldberg, 2025).
Simulation does not fit this ordering, which is why the figure draws it separately. It supplies ex-
ecutable actions on a model of the target embodiment at almost no marginal cost. The reported
GR00T N1 study produces 780,000 simulated trajectories, equivalent to about 6,500 hours of hu-
man demonstration, in 11 hours (NVIDIA et al., 2025c). Because its consequences are computed, its
relevance depends on calibration (Section 4.4), and simulated corpora have so far done best where
geometry decides the outcome (Section 4.3). Section 9.2 places simulation alongside handheld de-
vices in a related pyramid organized by the kind of evidence each source provides.
A capable system needs both ends of the pyramid. The apex provides executable actions and real
consequences on the system’s own body. The base provides diversity. Chen and colleagues argue
that diversity sets the ceiling on how far a model can generalize and that, for now, only internet-
scale data supply enough of it (Chen et al., 2026b). Much of this chapter concerns lowering the cost
of relevant data and raising the value of cheap data through calibration, retargeting, and filtering.
Within the physically collected layers, the collection method largely determines cost and yield.
Section 4.2 describes how each method works. The paragraphs below compare their economics,
including what an hour of collection costs, how much it yields, and what the resulting data lack.
Egocentric video is the cheapest to collect and the easiest to scale, since it needs only a head-
mounted camera or glasses. Its drawback is the embodiment gap, since human hands differ from
robot grippers and video records neither commands nor forces. The gap can be narrowed by de-
sign. If the robot is built to resemble the human and both are recorded with the same sensors,
human data can be worth more per hour than robot data. In EgoMimic, the reported evaluation
shows that an hour of egocentric recording yields about 1,400 demonstrations against 135 from tele-
88


operation, and adding an hour of human data improves the co-trained policy more than adding an
hour of robot data (Kareer et al., 2025).
A handheld gripper costs a few hundred dollars and needs no robot. Using UMI, 3 people collect
1,400 demonstrations across 30 locations in 12 person-hours, and on 1 task collection runs more
than 3 times faster than teleoperation with a 3D mouse (Chi et al., 2024). Because the fingers match
the robot’s, gripper-level actions transfer directly. The arm itself goes unrecorded, so its joint states
and dynamics are missing and reachability has to be checked at deployment. Forces are also absent
unless tactile sensors are added.
Teleoperation yields the most relevant data and the least of it. The hardware has become cheaper.
A kinematically matched leader arm costs under $300, and a complete bimanual system, robots
included, costs about $20,000 (Wu et al., 2024b; Zhao et al., 2023). A robot and an operator, however,
remain in the loop for every hour. The reported DROID data-collection effort involves 50 collectors
at 13 institutions gathering 76,000 trajectories over one year (Khazatsky et al., 2024). As Section 4.2
notes, the data also carry the imprint of the interface, since latency, limited haptic feedback, and
operator style shape the trajectories.
Exoskeletons and hand trackers fall between the handheld gripper and teleoperation, both in cost
and in how closely they match the robot. An exoskeleton with the same kinematics as the target
arm records joint-level motion directly. AirExo-2 costs about $600 for a dual-arm rig, and in the
reported user study its operators complete a task in 5.7 s on average against 17.3 s with joint-space
teleoperation (Fang et al., 2025). Gloves and motion-capture systems extend joint-level recording to
dexterous hands, and the DexCap study reports collection 3 times faster than teleoperation (Wang
et al., 2024a). In exchange, the operator has to wear the rig, the data must be retargeted whenever
the human and robot hands differ, and force feedback is limited.
Across the four methods, the cheaper the source, the further its data sit from the target embodiment.
How much each source is worth for a given task has to be measured. Scaling studies are the usual
instrument, but in their standard form they rest on assumptions that physical data do not meet.
4.5.2
Scaling Laws and What They Assume
Scaling laws come from language modeling. Kaplan et al. (2020) find that the test loss of language
models falls as a power law in model size, dataset size, and training compute, with some trends
spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. A common form separates the contributions of the
parameter count Npar and the amount of training data Ndata,
Lscale(Npar, Ndata) = Lfloor + ascaleN−αscale
par
+ bscaleN−βscale
data
,
ascale, bscale, αscale, βscale > 0,
(4.5)
where Lscale is a held-out loss and Lfloor an irreducible floor. With compute Ctrain ≈6NparNdata,
about six floating-point operations per parameter per training token, minimizing Eq. (4.5) at fixed
Ctrain makes the optimal Npar and Ndata grow as powers of Ctrain. The exponents prove harder to
pin down than the form. The original study concludes that most additional compute should go into
parameters, whereas Hoffmann et al. (2022) find that parameters and data should grow in equal
proportion as compute increases. Later work traces most of the difference to how parameters and
compute are counted and to optimizer settings (Pearce and Song, 2024; Porian et al., 2024). An
exponent, in other words, reflects the measurement protocol as well as the model family.
The allocation argument also rests on the three assumptions that every unit of data is equally infor-
mative, that compute is the only cost, and that lower loss means a better model. Physical data strain
all three. Robot trajectories are highly correlated, so much of a robot dataset behaves like repeated
data. Even in language modeling, repeating data for more than about 4 epochs yields rapidly di-
minishing returns (Muennighoff et al., 2023). Collecting robot data consumes robot time, operators,
and resets that never appear in Ctrain. Section 12.1 calls this resource physical interaction capacity
and argues that it must grow along with investment in compute. Held-out loss, finally, is a weak
guide to closed-loop success. In the robomimic study, the checkpoint with the lowest validation
loss performs significantly worse than the checkpoint with the highest rollout success (Mandlekar
et al., 2022).

4.5.3
What Robot-Learning Studies Show
Evidence for scaling in robot learning accumulates, but controlled studies remain rare. The cited
meta-analysis of 327 papers finds that robot performance generally improves as a power law
in data, model size, and compute, and that it improves faster than performance on language
tasks (Sartor and Thompson, 2025). Because meta-analyses average over very different tasks and
metrics, the clearest evidence comes from studies that vary one factor at a time, summarized in
Table 4.7. Some of these studies measure loss rather than success. Pretraining studies of imitation
policies and world models, for example, find language-like power laws in loss, with coefficients
that depend on the tokenizer, task, and architecture (Pearce et al., 2025).
The most consistent finding is that diversity matters more than volume. In a study of single-task
imitation with handheld grippers, generalization to new environments and objects follows a rough
power law in the number of environments and objects seen in training, while extra demonstrations
in environments already covered stop helping beyond a threshold (Lin et al., 2025). Guided by this
finding, the study reports that 4 people collect enough data in one afternoon to train policies that
succeed about 90% of the time on 2 tasks in new environments with unseen objects. Locomotion
shows the same pattern across bodies. Adding procedurally generated embodiments to training
improves generalization to unseen ones substantially more than adding data for a fixed set, and
the best policy transfers zero-shot to real Unitree Go2 and H1 robots (Ai et al., 2025).
Broad pretraining pays off chiefly by making new tasks cheaper to learn. In the Toyota Research
Institute’s study of large behavior models, evaluated in blind real and simulated trials, fine-tuning
90


a pretrained model matches single-task training with 3 to 5 times less task data, and the advantage
grows under distribution shift (Barreiros et al., 2026). Without fine-tuning, the pretrained model
gives mixed results. Pretraining may also extend what a model can handle. In the first training
phase of π0.5, 97.6% of the examples come from sources other than mobile manipulators working
in homes, such as other robots and web data, yet the reported model controls mobile manipulators
in homes that had not appeared in its training data (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025).
The split of additional compute between model size and data has been measured directly in at least
one physical domain. In motion forecasting and planning for driving, closed-loop metrics improve
along with the loss as compute increases, and the compute-optimal model size grows 1.5 times as
fast as the dataset (Baniodeh et al., 2025). Driving logs accumulate passively across a fleet and are
far cheaper than manipulation data, so the result does not carry over directly, but it shows that the
measurement can be made in a physical setting.
Industry now reports manipulation datasets far larger than academic ones. In a blog post, General-
ist AI describes pretraining on more than 270,000 hours of real-world manipulation data (Generalist
AI, 2025). It reports that the post-training validation error falls as a power law in the amount of
pretraining data, and that roughly billion-parameter models stop improving with more data while
seven-billion-parameter and larger models keep improving. These are prediction errors on the
company’s own tasks rather than closed-loop success rates, and they have not been peer reviewed.
Precision imposes a different kind of limit. In the cited simulation study, the demonstration count
Ndemo needed for a fixed success rate is modeled by the empirical fit log Ndemo = mfit/(Ptol −
clim) + nfit, with fitted coefficients mfit > 0 and nfit. Here Ptol is the length tolerance and clim the
fitted system limit. For Ptol > clim, this fit predicts that Ndemo diverges as Ptol approaches clim from
above (Xu et al., 2026). The limit depends on the whole system, and adding a wrist camera or using
a better expert moves it toward finer precision. For such tasks, better sensing can pay off more than
additional demonstrations.
All such curves are hard to measure precisely. Real-robot success rates are estimated from tens or
hundreds of trials, so each point carries a wide confidence interval (Section 9.5) and a fitted expo-
nent is loosely constrained. With that caveat, the evidence supports consistent gains from diversity
across environments, objects, embodiments, and data sources, and from pretraining followed by
fine-tuning. It does not yet establish universal exponents, compute-optimal model sizes for robot
policies, or a dependable link between loss and closed-loop success.
Better evidence requires purpose-built experiments that vary the quantity and the diversity of data
independently while keeping the training procedure fixed. Such experiments would report new
trajectories apart from extra passes over old ones, evaluate on held-out conditions that stay the
same between runs, and check predictions made from small runs against a larger run held in re-
serve. A plateau in such an experiment deserves attention in its own right, since it may point to
missing sensing, an inadequate model, or an unsuitable objective instead of a shortage of data.
4.5.4
Valuing and Curating Heterogeneous Data
Raw volume overstates what a dataset contains. Experience is nested, with frames inside trajec-
tories, trajectories inside tasks and scenes, and scenes inside embodiments and sites, so counts of
hours and frames treat many correlated samples as independent. This is why Section 4.2 measures
collection by effective data yield, and scaling studies should likewise report growth in independent
interactions and their spread over tasks, scenes, objects, and embodiments.
How many samples from one layer are worth one sample from another can be measured in spe-
cific settings. In the InternData-A1 study (Section 4.3), fewer than 1,600 simulated samples match
the performance of 200 real ones on 4 tasks with closely aligned simulated and real setups, a ratio
below 8:1 (Tian et al., 2025). EgoMimic’s hour-for-hour comparison, described above, gives a cor-
responding rate for human data. Both rates depend on how closely the source matches the task,
on how much contact is involved, and on how the sources are weighted in training, and neither
should be expected to hold elsewhere.

Curation can matter as much as collection. CUPID uses influence functions to estimate how a
trained policy’s closed-loop return would change if a given demonstration were removed, and
ranks every demonstration by its effect on performance (Agia et al., 2025a). On the simulated
robomimic benchmark, training on less than a third of the data, selected in this way, produces
diffusion policies that match the state of the art. Hardware experiments show similar gains. Related
methods weight whole datasets, as Re-Mix does for Open X-Embodiment by choosing mixture
weights that maximize worst-case performance across its constituent datasets (Hejna et al., 2025a),
or score demonstrations by the mutual information between states and actions (Hejna et al., 2025b).
A scaling curve plotted against raw demonstration counts can therefore partly reflect how much
harmful or redundant data a collection contains.
Knowing which kinds of diversity matter helps both collection and retrieval. A study using pro-
cedurally generated datasets with controlled composition identifies camera poses and the spatial
arrangement of objects as the dimensions most relevant in that study, both for diversifying new
collections and for retrieving relevant demonstrations from existing datasets. Retrieval guided by
these findings raises the real-world performance of policies trained with DROID data by up to
70% (Saxena et al., 2025).
Retrieval and curation presuppose that data can be found. A growing number of hubs collect robot
datasets, and Table 4.8 lists some of the largest. Aggregators such as the LeRobot hub, Open X-
Embodiment, and ARIO gather datasets in common formats, making cross-dataset training and
retrieval practical, while large single-source collections offer consistent protocols at scale. Licenses
and access conditions range from open to gated and non-commercial, and, as the documentation
practices of Section 4.1 require, they should travel with any dataset derived from these sources.
4.5.5
Building a Data Flywheel
Flywheels have worked best where success can be detected cheaply, because the robot can then
label its own experience. Large-scale autonomous collection on real robots therefore focuses on
grasping in early studies, where a robot can tell by itself whether it is holding the object. One early
study reports more than 800,000 grasp attempts on up to 14 robots (Levine et al., 2018), and the QT-
Opt study uses more than 580,000 attempts to train a vision-based Q-function that grasps unseen
objects with 96% success (Kalashnikov et al., 2018). Where success is harder to judge, people or
learned models have to supply the labels. Sirius-Fleet uses a visual world model to predict whether
a robot’s upcoming actions are likely to fail and asks a human to intervene when they are. As the
policy improves, the failure predictor adapts and requests for help become rarer (Liu et al., 2025a).
Post-training has since moved to the fleet level. RECAP, used to train π∗
0.6, combines demonstra-
tions, autonomous experience, and expert corrections in batched offline reinforcement learning
(Section 6.3) (Amin et al., 2026). SOP streams on-policy experience and intervention signals from
a fleet to a central learner that runs either interactive imitation, in which humans correct the robot
during execution, or RECAP (Pan et al., 2026). In its experiments, the wall-clock time needed to
reach 80% success falls from about 174 minutes with 1 robot to 127 with 2 and 72 with 4, a 2.4-
fold speedup from 4 times as many robots. The human-in-the-loop methods of Section 4.2 are the
short-cycle version of the same idea.

4.5.6
Choosing What to Collect Next
Section 4.2 discusses how active sampling selects tasks and states within a collection campaign. At
the level of the flywheel the choice is broader, because the next unit of effort may go to a new site, a
calibration experiment, corrective demonstrations, a batch of simulated scenarios, or held-out trials
for validation. A natural criterion is the expected improvement per unit cost,
x⋆= arg max

(4.7)
where ∆J is the resulting change in closed-loop performance on held-out conditions and cacq(x) is
the cost of collecting, curating, and learning from x. Physical options are expensive, since resets
take time and some trials carry risk. Synthetic options are cheaper but less certain to help. In prac-
tice, candidates are ranked with heuristic scores such as novelty, disagreement between models,
gaps in coverage, and predicted failure (Agia et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2025a). Each score can mis-
lead. An unfamiliar background may look novel without adding any physical information, and
persistent uncertainty may come from sensor noise instead of a gap the policy could learn to close
(Section 10.5).
Since Eq. (4.7) can at best be approximated before training, a collection strategy has to be judged
after the fact, by retraining on the selected data and testing the result. The comparison should be
made at a matched budget against reasonable alternatives, in particular stratified sampling over
known conditions. It should also include a frozen baseline evaluated under the same conditions
(Section 12.1), so that a better strategy is not confused with a larger investment. All costs belong
in the same account, from robot occupancy and resets to interventions, annotation, simulation, and
training. For repeatable tasks, total cost per accepted output is a convenient summary. Flywheels
complicate the comparison further, because each policy changes the data collected next and because
hardware, sites, and operators drift between iterations.
The measurements that would settle the central questions of this chapter are still largely missing.
Most published scaling curves for robot learning put demonstrations, hours, frames, or tokens
on the horizontal axis. Few relate closed-loop capability to the total amount of real interaction,
counting the simulation and human effort that come with it. Such curves would show whether the
next robot-hour is better spent on training data, on calibration, or on evaluation. They would also
show whether a flywheel is actually improving the system. Chapter 10 considers what it would
take for loops of this kind to sustain open-ended growth in capability.

World Models
Previous chapters discuss how perception captures physical scenes at the current moment, and
physical data record how it evolves over time (Chapter 4). With them, we can present a more
comprehensive account of world modeling, which studies how an environment evolves over time
and how external actions or interventions change that evolution. This is also an important step
for the physical agent that will be discussed in the later section, as it helps a physical agent to
predict, before acting, how the world will evolve and how its own action would change that evolu-
tion. Figure 5.1 illustrates this closed-loop interaction among the physical environment, the world
model, and the querying agent. Within the technical stack of this book, world models build on the
state-space formulations of Chapter 2, the perception of Chapter 3, and the data and simulation of
Chapter 4 to provide action-conditioned predictions for the manipulation and whole-body control
models in Chapters 6 to 7.

Based on this, this chapter frames physical world modeling in five parts. Section 5.1 establishes
the conceptual framework (state, belief, query, and evidence) and clarifies what a world model
is and is not. Section 5.2 surveys how the internal state is represented, ranging from generative
observation-space models to latent dynamics, 3D and object-centric structures, and unified mul-
timodal architectures. Section 5.3 develops training strategies, from self-supervised pretraining
to action-conditioned and interaction-driven learning. Section 5.4 addresses how predictions are
deployed and validated across forecast accuracy, physical consistency, and downstream decision
utility. Section 5.5 concludes with open challenges and the long-term role of world models in Phys-
ical AI.

finite-resource compression, local observation, asynchronous multimodal evidence, and the rela-

tionship between understanding and prediction (Chen et al., 2026b). This perspective organizes
the chapter’s discussion of current systems and future directions. The scope of the chapter in-
cludes robots, scientific instruments, and distributed physical processes rather than only visually
observed manipulation.
5.1
Concepts and Theoretical Frameworks of World Models
World models are compact, queryable descriptions of how an environment can change. They are
not required to reproduce every physical detail. Their purpose is to retain the distinctions needed
by the questions that an agent must answer, including what is present, what is hidden, what will
happen under an action, and which action is preferable. This section fixes the common vocabulary
of state, transition, query, and evidence used throughout the chapter. A model is useful when these
elements are connected and its claims can be checked against new observations.
5.1.1
Definition, Boundaries, and Basic Properties
Physical scenes contain objects, fields, energy, and interactions at many scales, while an agent has
finite sensors, memory, and time. A world model therefore compresses observations into an in-
ternal state from which future states and task-relevant outputs can be queried. The compression
is task-relative. A logo may be irrelevant when predicting whether a cup will spill, but essential
when identifying a reagent. A lower-dimensional representation is not automatically a better one.
It is better only when it preserves the distinctions needed by the intended queries.
The same visible image can correspond to different velocities, contact modes, temperatures, or
internal masses. A stationary drawer can be unlocked or held by a latch, and the same pull then has
different consequences. A world model must use history, interaction, and background conditions
to maintain these hidden alternatives. Operationally, its functions include inference from evidence,
conditional evolution over time, and readout of observations or physical and task quantities. These
functions may be modular or share parameters. A particular model can expose only a subset of
them, but its advertised interfaces should have testable meanings.
A Development Trajectory Organized by Underlying Problems
Three enduring questions ex-
plain the main technical lineages. First, how can an agent infer a sufficient state from incomplete
measurements? State-space estimation and filtering make a distinction between an evolving state
and its noisy observations. Kalman’s work provides a foundational linear formulation (Kalman,
1960a). Second, how can an internal model improve action rather than merely fit observations?
Dyna connects real experience, model learning, planning, and acting, so the learned model sup-
plies additional experience for decision learning (Sutton, 1991). Third, how can these functions
operate on high-dimensional sensory data? Learned encoders and recurrent dynamics replace
hand-specified state variables with representations shaped by prediction and control. The World
Models architecture separates visual compression, temporal memory, and a controller. PlaNet per-
forms planning through learned latent dynamics. Dreamer trains behavior using imagined latent
trajectories (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2019; 2020).
These developments do not form a sequence in which each new architecture makes its predecessors
obsolete. Explicit states remain useful when physical variables are measurable, generative models
retain information for rich observation queries, and decision-oriented latent models can avoid re-
constructing details that a task does not use. Recent multimodal and world-action models extend
the same underlying questions to the sharing of semantic, predictive, and behavioral information.
Their shared foundation is the connection among state inference, conditional prediction, and action
learning. The discussion below compares implementations of these functions rather than present-
ing successive product generations.
Predictive Sufficiency Rather than a Miniature Copy of the World
The central abstraction is a
state that preserves answers, not necessarily a state that reproduces every observation. Predictive
state representations make this idea explicit by representing a controlled system through predic-
96


tions of future observation tests rather than through a prescribed list of hidden variables (Littman
et al., 2002). Learned embeddings, object states, and physical fields are different ways of approxi-
mating such predictive sufficiency. A useful idealized criterion is

The criterion explains why compression and generality trade off. A representation sufficient to
decide whether a drawer opens can omit texture but must preserve the latch hypothesis. A repre-
sentation intended to answer new visual questions may need much more detail. A state sufficient
for ranking a particular policy’s actions need not be sufficient for estimating forces, synthesizing
views, or optimizing a different objective. Broader query coverage therefore requires richer tar-
gets, retained evidence, or a mechanism for refining the representation on demand. Changes of
latent coordinates do not change predictive capability when all interfaces transform consistently,
so physically meaningful readouts matter more than requiring every latent coordinate to have a
unique physical name.
Boundaries with Neighboring Systems
Several neighboring systems should be distinguished
by their interfaces. A video generator can reproduce motion without correctly responding to a
specified intervention. A physics engine advances a supplied state but need not infer that state
from open-ended observations. A digital twin is tied to a particular physical counterpart, whereas
a policy outputs actions without necessarily exposing conditional futures. Table 5.1 summarizes
the distinctions used here. These are functional distinctions. One implementation may combine
several rows, and a model’s name does not establish all the listed capabilities.
The state boundary must specify which variables are explicit, which are conditions, and which are
unknown disturbances. Precision and horizon are part of this choice. A temperature interval can
suffice for a safe-touch query but not for metrology. A short transport may treat material parame-
ters as fixed while a long heating process cannot. Local boundaries also require attention to external
inputs. A container can exchange heat and material with its surroundings. Missing measurements
should remain marked as missing and should not create unjustified certainty. Claims of generality
should state the tested state range, intervention interface, timescale, and query precision.
