5.1.2
Internal State and Belief Updating Under Partial Observation
A POMDP distinguishes the environmental state, the actions applied to it, and the measurements
available to an agent (Kaelbling et al., 1998). Let st be the physical state at discrete index t, ot a
possibly multimodal observation, and at the control input applied over the subsequent interval.
Let c denote the known embodiment, environment, and sensor conditions. Here a discrete index
orders updates. It need not imply equally spaced measurements. The history ht = (o0:t, a0:t−1)
contains observations and past inputs, with their timestamps and validity metadata understood.
The belief over the hidden physical state is the conditional distribution
bt(s) = p(st = s | ht, c).
(5.2)
The argument s is a possible state value. bt represents uncertainty about which value is current. A
learned internal representation zt is distinct from st. It may encode a point estimate, parameters of
a distribution, or information sufficient for selected future queries. Calling a vector a belief does
not by itself give it probabilistic semantics.
Belief maintenance alternates between prediction and correction. For a transition kernel T and an
observation likelihood O, the Bayesian filtering recursion is
ebt+1(s′) =
Z
T(s′ | s, at, c, ∆t) bt(s) ds,
bt+1(s′) =
O(ot+1 | s′, c)ebt+1(s′)
R
O(ot+1 | u, c)ebt+1(u) du
,
(5.3)
where s′ is a candidate next state, u a dummy integration variable, ∆t the elapsed physical time, and
ebt+1 the predictive prior before observing ot+1. The denominator normalizes the posterior when
the observation has nonzero probability. Integrals become sums for discrete states. The recursion
assumes a Markov state and an observation model conditionally independent of earlier history
given that state and c. Delays or actuator memory that violate these assumptions must be included
in the state or conditioning record. Learned filters approximate this recursion rather than inheriting
its correctness merely from architectural resemblance.
The distinction is concrete during grasping. If the gripper moves upward but the object remains on
the table, the observation should revise the attachment hypothesis. If the camera is occluded, lack
of visible motion need not mean a failed grasp. A delayed temperature reading belongs to its ac-
quisition time, not its arrival time. Using it may require correcting an earlier state and propagating
the correction through intervening actions. Asynchronous processing therefore requires temporal
bookkeeping, not compulsory resampling of every sensor to one frequency.
Keeping alternatives separate can be more meaningful than averaging them. The mean of two
possible object locations may lie inside an obstacle, and a mean of sticking and sliding contact is
not a realizable contact mode. Partial-observation uncertainty concerns the current hidden state.
Aleatoric uncertainty concerns variability unresolved at the chosen modeling level. Epistemic un-
certainty concerns limited knowledge of model parameters or mechanisms (Kendall and Gal, 2017).
These categories can interact, and their decomposition depends on the state and sensor specifi-
cation. Extra sensing may resolve a hidden contact, whereas collecting diverse interactions may
reduce model error. Simply increasing the number of sampled futures addresses neither problem
automatically.
5.1.3
Understanding-Oriented and Prediction-Oriented Objectives
Understanding is best stated as a set of testable abilities, including identifying entities and rela-
tions, recognizing operating modes, distinguishing variables that control subsequent change, and
identifying what present evidence cannot determine. A fluent explanation is not sufficient. For ex-
ample, a valve model must distinguish a command, the mechanical position, and the resulting flow.
A grasp model must distinguish a closed gripper from a stable attachment. The understanding-
prediction distinction in Chen et al. (2026b) provides a useful way to organize these requirements
without treating them as mutually exclusive capabilities.
98


Prediction supplies a complementary pressure. Given a history and conditions, the model should
produce a measurable future state, observation, or distribution. Copying a background and extrap-
olating smooth motion may solve short video prediction while ignoring contact. Longer horizons,
action perturbations, and event-level targets test whether the state retains the missing distinctions.
Distributional prediction matters when several qualitatively different outcomes remain possible. A
single mean trajectory can represent none of them.
Reconstruction is a useful information diagnostic but not proof of understanding. DIAMOND
demonstrates that visual detail can affect learned behavior in Atari, illustrating why discarding ap-
parently minor observations may be harmful (Alonso et al., 2024). Conversely, a model can render a
convincing container without connecting liquid level, acceleration, and spillage. Decision-oriented
abstractions are legitimate when they preserve distinctions needed to compare actions. MuZero
learns quantities needed for planning without requiring reconstruction of the original observation,
showing that control sufficiency and observation reconstruction are different targets (Schrittwieser
et al., 2020). Neither example establishes a universally preferred representation for physical mod-
eling.
Understanding also requires separating reusable relations from accidental correlations. If every
heavy training container is red, color may predict lifting success until the correlation changes. A
useful representation should allow mass hypotheses to be revised after force feedback without hav-
ing to change color identity. This example does not require every latent coordinate to have a human
name. It requires an intervention-relevant distinction to remain available to downstream queries.
Prediction and understanding can thus be mutual checks. An explanation proposes a testable con-
sequence, while a prediction error exposes a missing variable or an inadequate transition.
Representation Learning, Forecasting, and Identification
These goals differ in the evidence they
require. Representation learning can exploit correlations across regions or times. Forecasting must
respect the observations available at its issue time. Identifying an intervention response addition-
ally requires the action interface and relevant confounders to be accounted for. A passive video
predictor can learn that a human usually opens a drawer after reaching toward it, while still being
unable to distinguish a push from a pull applied by a robot. Likewise, fitting a trajectory does
not uniquely identify mass and friction when several parameter combinations produce the same
motion. An informative probe is one that makes these alternatives predict measurably different
outcomes. This connects world modeling to state estimation and system identification, rather than
treating physical knowledge as an automatic consequence of video scale.
Learning with a JEPA offers a complementary response to the information problem by predicting
selected representations of observations rather than all their low-level details. LeCun’s architec-
tural proposal places this idea within a larger system of perception, predictive modeling, memory,
and action selection (LeCun, 2022). The reusable principle is selective prediction. Whether the se-
lected information supports causal forecasting, planning, or physical explanation is determined by
the conditioning, training data, and readout tests developed below.
5.1.4
Functional Roles, Query Interfaces, and System Positioning
The role of a world model is determined by the questions it answers. An observation query pro-
duces a sensor-like output. A state query returns objects, relations, or physical quantities. A tran-
sition query predicts an action’s consequences. And a decision-related query estimates reward,
constraint violation, or task success. Figure 5.1 assembles these roles into a reference architecture.
A compact conceptual implementation is
zt = Eϕ(ht, c),
bzt+1 ∼Tθ(· | zt, at, c, ∆t),
bot+1 ∼Oωobs(· | bzt+1, c),
byt+1 = Qψ(bzt+1, g, c),
(5.4)
where Eϕ is a history encoder, Tθ a learned transition, Oωobs an observation decoder, and Qψ a task
readout. Their subscripts denote parameter sets, which may overlap in a shared network. The
goal or query specification is g, y is the requested task quantity, a hat denotes a prediction, and ∼
99


denotes sampling. Qψ is a generic query head, not necessarily an action-value function. Eq. (5.4) is
an interface-level synthesis of state-space and learned-model formulations, not a requirement that
these functions be separate networks (Kaelbling et al., 1998; Hafner et al., 2019).
In the figure, the history encoder Eϕ compresses the observation-action history ht and known con-
ditions c into the internal state zt, which approximates the belief bt(s) over the hidden physical
state. The prediction-correction update keeps hidden alternatives separate. The learned transition
Tθ then rolls out imagined latent states bzt+1, . . . , bzt+H under a candidate action sequence, and the
readouts Oωobs and Qψ answer observation, state, transition, and decision queries over the inferred
state and the imagined rollout. Figure 5.1 also makes two boundaries explicit. The first sepa-
rates inference from imagination. The internal state is updated from real observations only at the
correction step, whereas the rollout is advanced by the learned transition alone and accumulates
model error with horizon. The second separates the model from its consumer. Readouts answer
queries over the inferred state and the imagined futures, but the scoring of candidate actions and
the choice of the applied at belong to the agent or planner. A model may support transition and
decision queries without an observation decoder. Evaluation should follow the query interfaces it
exposes.
This decomposition helps localize failure. A wrong rendered texture with a correct measured tra-
jectory suggests a decoding problem. A wrong contact event suggests a state or dynamics problem.
A correct prediction that never influences action suggests a decision-interface problem. Such diag-
noses are hypotheses to test, since errors may also propagate across modules.
The world model can sit inside a model-predictive controller, provide training-time imagination to
a policy, supply predictive features to an action model, or expose a shared state service to several
agents. The surrounding loop remains perception, state inference, prediction, decision, execution,
and feedback. Actions change both the world and the observations available next. This connects the
chapter to physical data acquisition in Chapter 4 and to the foundation-model and motor-control
interfaces in Chapters 6 to 7. World modeling is one component of Physical AI. Sensing, actuation,
safety, and recovery do not follow automatically from a predictive network.
The remaining sections separate four questions concerning how information is represented, how
parameters are learned, how predictions are used and verified, and how the full loop can improve.
In particular, training with future observations, predicting future observations at runtime, and ex-
ecuting actions with real feedback are different operations. This chapter makes their information
boundaries explicit throughout.
5.2
Representations and Architectures of World Models
No single representation dominates all physical queries.
Observation generators retain visible
detail, latent dynamics can reduce imagination cost, and structured three-dimensional or object-
centric states make entities and relations explicit. These are composable design routes rather than
disjoint model classes. Following the distinction between functional and architectural taxonomies
in Chen et al. (2026b), it is useful to ask separately what is predicted, how dynamics are represented,
which functions share computation, and which modules run at deployment. A diffusion model can oper-
ate over pixels, compressed video latents, or object states. A geometric representation can support
both rendering and planning. And any of these can be coupled to a policy.
Figure 5.2 organizes representative world models along two complementary dimensions of func-
tional role and architectural representation. The functional axis distinguishes rendering observa-
tions, simulating state evolution, and generating actions for decision making. The architectural axis
distinguishes observation-level generation, structured world representations, and latent-space dy-
namics. These categories are not mutually exclusive. A model family may span several functions,
and a system may combine multiple representational choices.

5.2.1
Generative Architectures in Observation Space
An observation-oriented model predicts images, video, audio, or other sensor streams. For an
externally specified action sequence, a causal autoregressive factorization is
pθ(o1:Nstep | o0, a0:Nstep−1, c) =
Nstep−1
∏
t=0
pθ(ot+1 | o0:t, a0:t, c),
(5.5)
where Nstep is the final sequence index, θ the model parameters, and i:j an inclusive sequence of in-
dices. The elapsed times are included in c for this expression. Each action is aligned to the interval
in which it acts. The equation assumes that future prescribed actions do not affect earlier observa-
tions. With actions selected in response to future measurements, conditioning retrospectively on
the entire executed action sequence can reveal additional information. Such observational condi-
tioning is not automatically equivalent to an intervention.
Tokenization and Generative Mechanism
Autoregressive models predict a sequence of discrete
or continuous tokens from preceding context. Their ordering makes causal rollout natural, but
generating many spatial and temporal tokens can require substantial sequential computation. Dif-
fusion and flow-based models instead generate a frame or chunk through iterative denoising or
transport, enabling parallel updates within the chunk while requiring multiple network evalua-
tions. Chunkwise generation combines these choices. Chunks advance causally in physical time,
while tokens within each chunk can interact bidirectionally. Physical rollout time and the artificial
denoising time are different axes. Section 5.3.1 defines the corresponding training objectives.
101


An observation-oriented generator need not perform all computation in pixel coordinates. A vari-
ational autoencoder (VAE) can compress observations, a generative model can predict the com-
pressed variables, and a decoder can reconstruct the output. Latent diffusion demonstrates this
division between perceptual compression and generative computation (Rombach et al., 2022). It
reduces the number of generated elements but does not, by itself, turn video latents into a suffi-
cient physical state. The architectural distinction from an abstract latent-dynamics model concerns
the representation’s role and supervision, not whether a tensor is called a latent.
Conditioning and Interaction
Genie learns latent controls from videos and uses them for inter-
active generation, whereas UniSim learns conditional real-world video simulation from heteroge-
neous data (Bruce et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b). These examples illustrate different intervention
interfaces. A latent action inferred from visual changes is not automatically a robot command.
Camera motion, actor motion, and object motion can be confounded. Executable control requires
a mapping to an embodiment and verification of the resulting response. Language can specify
desired behavior, but the same sentence may leave force, speed, contact, and timing unspecified.
Observation generation is useful when detail matters for perception, when imagined data will train
a visual policy, or when a person must inspect a predicted future. Its limitations include high
spatial cost, temporal drift, and the possibility of replacing a wrong state with a plausible texture.
A video of a drawer opening should be checked for the commanded displacement, latch state,
object identity, and occluded contents, not only visual sharpness. Multiple rendered views are
valuable only when they describe a compatible underlying scene. These requirements motivate
persistent latent states, geometric structure, and action-grounded supervision rather than ruling
out generative prediction.
Broad Video Priors and Spatially Indexed Memory
Cosmos illustrates how pretrained video
models, tokenizers, and data processing can form a reusable platform for physical-AI adapta-
tion (NVIDIA et al., 2025a). Such a prior can supply appearance and motion regularities before
task-specific action data are available. Its contribution is different from learning the calibrated re-
sponse of a particular actuator. Downstream conditioning and validation must establish that inter-
face. This separation between broad pretraining and local grounding remains useful as individual
video backbones change.
Persistent visual context can also be organized spatially rather than only as a recent temporal win-
dow. World Labs’ RTFM uses an autoregressive diffusion frame model with camera poses and
retrieval of relevant posed frames as spatial memory (World Labs Team, 2025b). It illustrates a
learned rendering route that need not construct an explicit mesh at every update. Revisiting a place
queries stored evidence about that place rather than forcing an ever-growing sequence through a
fixed context window. Camera-conditioned view generation, however, primarily specifies how
observation changes with viewpoint. Controlling a camera and predicting an object’s response to
force are distinct interfaces. This distinction is important when a navigable generated world is later
used for interaction.
5.2.2
Latent-Space Dynamics Architectures
Latent models encode observation history and propagate a compact state. A generic form is
zt = Eϕ(ht, c),
bzt = zt,
bzt+k+1 ∼Tθ(· | bzt+k, at+k, c, ∆tk),
byt+k+1 = Qψ(bzt+k+1, g, c),
k = 0, . . . , H −1,
(5.6)
where H is the rollout horizon, ∆tk the duration of its kth interval, Eϕ the history encoder, and Qψ
the query readout. The symbols z and bz distinguish inferred and imagined states. y may be an
observation, reward, physical variable, or event. The readout can be omitted during intermediate
rollout steps. A useful state preserves the conditional distribution of the intended queries. Histories
merged into one representation should not demand incompatible answers after the same future
102


input. A recently heated vessel and a long-cooled one may look alike while requiring different
temperature forecasts.
Generative State-Space Models
PlaNet combines deterministic recurrent memory with stochas-
tic latent variables, while Dreamer uses learned latent dynamics to train an actor and critic through
imagination (Hafner et al., 2019; 2020). A recurrent component can retain predictable history, and
stochastic variables can represent outcomes that remain uncertain. Training distinguishes a prior
predicted without the next observation from an approximate posterior corrected by that observa-
tion. Reconstruction and auxiliary targets encourage informative states. Prior-posterior regulariza-
tion makes them predictable. Overly strong regularization can suppress observation information,
whereas a weakly trained prior can fail when real frames are absent. The loss and its multi-step
extensions are developed in Section 5.3.
JEPA: Predicting in a Learned Target Space
A JEPA relates a context representation to a target
representation through a predictor. Its defining choice is the prediction target, not a particular re-
current layer, transformer size, or policy head. I-JEPA learns image representations by predicting
target-region embeddings from visible context. It is a spatial representation learner, not by itself
an action-conditioned temporal simulator (Assran et al., 2023). V-JEPA extends feature prediction
to masked spatiotemporal regions of video, using a predictor and a slowly updated target encoder
rather than a pixel-reconstruction objective (Bardes et al., 2024). In both cases, what is hidden and
what remains visible determine whether the task teaches spatial completion, temporal interpola-
tion, or future anticipation.
V-JEPA 2 connects large-scale action-free representation learning to a separately post-trained
action-conditioned latent predictor. Its planning variant uses robot observations, proprioception,
and recorded actions to predict future features, then evaluates candidate actions against an image
goal in representation space (Assran et al., 2025). Recorded interactions ground the predictor in
robot actions. Self-supervision constructs targets from these records without task-success annota-
tions or a hand-designed reward for each training example.
The architectural advantage is that a predictor can avoid synthesizing every unpredictable texture
while retaining information useful for recognition or control. The corresponding obligation is to
show that contacts, relative motion, object identity, and material cues have survived the target
representation. A deterministic embedding forecast need not describe the distribution of possible
futures, and its distance to a goal need not be a calibrated measure of physical reachability. Obser-
vation reconstruction and predictive embeddings are therefore complementary choices. A model
can learn from both, or attach an optional decoder without making rendering a prerequisite for
each decision. Section 5.3.1 develops the target update and loss, while Section 5.4.3 discusses tests
that do not privilege models with a visual decoder.
Decision-Oriented Abstraction and State Maintenance
MuZero and TD-MPC-style systems em-
phasize reward, value, or latent consistency sufficient for decision making rather than unrestricted
observation queries (Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2024). DreamerV3 retains a generative
latent model while improving robustness of model and behavior learning across different domains
through normalization and loss balancing (Hafner et al., 2025). These examples distinguish the
choice of representation from the numerical techniques needed to train it reliably. A small state is
efficient only if it preserves the distinctions required by the objective. Changing the goal or down-
stream query can expose previously harmless information loss.
Latent coordinates need not correspond one-to-one to physical quantities. A feature from which
mass can be decoded may still entangle mass with shape, and an arbitrary coordinate edit need not
realize a meaningful mass intervention. A history encoder should also distinguish an observation-
corrected state from one propagated without new evidence.
Its memory may be recurrent,
attention-based, spatially retrieved, or hierarchically summarized. What matters is whether the
representation preserves consequential hidden alternatives through occlusion and updates them
when new evidence arrives. Tests should compare posterior updates, pure open-loop prediction,
and feedback-interleaved prediction at the same physical horizons.
103


5.2.3
3D, 4D, and Object-Centric Architectures
Structured states make geometry, entities, and relations directly queryable. They can use occu-
pancy or bird’s-eye grids, object slots, scene graphs, particles, meshes, or continuous fields. Their
relation to world modeling depends on the associated transition. A static 3D reconstruction sup-
ports novel views but does not specify what a push will do. A 4D reconstruction describes temporal
observations but may not predict a new intervention. The spatial perception methods in Chapter 3
become a world-model substrate when they are connected to evolving attributes, interactions, and
conditional prediction.
Object-centric methods allocate separate representations to entities and model their interactions.
Slot Attention provides a mechanism for learning object-centric representations from observa-
tions (Locatello et al., 2020). Graph-network simulators and MeshGraphNets illustrate dynamics
expressed through local interactions among particles or mesh elements (Sanchez-Gonzalez et al.,
2020; Pfaff et al., 2021). These structures can make interaction locality and changes in object count
easier to express than an undifferentiated global vector. However, the structure is an inductive bias,
not a guarantee. Learned slots may exchange identities, an object may split or merge, and contact
can change the interaction graph discontinuously.
Geometry and physical attributes should be distinguished. Shape alone does not identify mass,
friction, stiffness, temperature, or internal contents. A deformable state may need both configura-
tion and a constitutive description. A liquid requires boundary conditions and appropriate conser-
vation accounting. PhysGaussian couples Gaussian-based rendering with continuum-mechanics
simulation, illustrating how visual representation and physical evolution can share a substrate
within a specified regime (Xie et al., 2024). The same representation must still be supplied with
suitable physical parameters and verified against the intended materials and interactions.
Hybrid representations can assign different resolutions to different objects or processes. A rigid
container may be represented as an object, while its contents are a field or a small set of effective
variables. A coarse query could ask whether spilling is likely. A fine query might require the flow
near an outlet. Expanding the representation only where the query requires it is a plausible way to
balance cost and detail. The levels must share coordinate frames, identity, units, boundary fluxes,
and physical time so that a coarse state is compatible with a refined prediction.
The structured route is attractive for metric queries, contact reasoning, and compositional changes.
It introduces costs in reconstruction, correspondence, annotation, and numerical integration, and
it may inherit a simulator’s modeling assumptions. A representation built around rigid objects can
fail on cloth or fragmentation. A fixed field resolution can miss thin contacts. Validation should
test identity through occlusion, changed topology, altered parameters, and action-dependent re-
sponse. Structured models can be combined with learned latent residuals and generative observa-
tion heads, rather than being treated as alternatives to neural representation learning.
Hierarchies, Fields, and Physical-Prediction Structure
The Hierarchical Relation Network
(HRN), developed by Mrowca and colleagues, represents bodies with hierarchies of particles and
learns their interactions through graph-based computation (Mrowca et al., 2018). Its lasting con-
tribution is the separation of local interactions from larger-scale object structure, allowing rigid
and deformable dynamics to share a representation without pretending that all objects are single
rigid slots. Hierarchical modeling can reduce the distance over which information must propagate,
but the useful grouping and coupling still depend on the physical process. The related Physion
evaluation program tests future object contact across varied physical scenarios and distinguishes
learning from images from prediction with privileged state (Bear et al., 2021). It provides an empir-
ical counterpart to the architectural question of which state distinctions are needed to forecast an
event.
Continuous-field models broaden the scope beyond articulated robots and discrete objects. Fourier
neural operators learn mappings between parameter or input fields and solution fields for families
of partial differential equations (Li et al., 2021). They can serve as components for fluid, thermal,
or other distributed-process predictions. A field-to-solution surrogate need not include perception,
104


uncertainty, or an action policy. It supplies one transition or query component of a larger world
model. Generalization across spatial resolution also differs from generalization across boundary
conditions or physical regimes. Coupling a learned field solver to objects requires consistent inter-
faces for forces, fluxes, time, and units.
Persistent Spatial Generation and Multimodal Reconstruction
The spatial-intelligence route as-
sociated with World Labs should be distinguished from, rather than conflated with, the physical-
dynamics work above. Marble generates persistent, editable 3D environments from multimodal
prompts and supports explicit scene outputs (World Labs Team, 2025a). It illustrates the value of
a scene that can be revisited and queried from different viewpoints, instead of a sequence whose
geometry is reconstructed anew at every frame. The public Atlas description further combines text,
posed images, and depth within a shared spatial context using an autoregressive diffusion architec-
ture, with reconstruction and space-time generation interfaces (World Labs Team, 2026). These are
developer-described systems. Their available interfaces should not be expanded into unsupported
claims about arbitrary contact dynamics or physical precision.
The underlying distinction is between reconstructing evidence, completing unobserved regions,
and evolving a state under interventions. A model may do all three, but their outputs carry dif-
ferent evidential status. Adding real views can constrain a previously imagined region. Creating
a visually plausible hidden room does not measure that room. An explicit 3D scene can supply
geometry for a simulator while leaving collision properties, mass, and material parameters to be
assigned or identified. Conversely, an implicit renderer can maintain useful spatial consistency
without exposing a simulation-ready mesh. The choice of explicit or implicit representation should
therefore follow the required queries, not a blanket identification of 3D output with physical un-
derstanding.
5.2.4
Unified Multimodal and Cross-Paradigm Architectures
Unification concerns several different design decisions, including sharing an input interface, shar-
ing a representation, learning multiple objectives together, and executing multiple functions in one
runtime. A system may unify one level while retaining separate modules at another. Describing
the level of unification is more informative than calling the entire architecture unified.
Multimodal Evidence and Representation Sharing
Vision, touch, proprioception, sound, tem-
perature, and process readings can update a common state while retaining modality-specific noise
and timing. Fusion can occur at the input, in intermediate state representations, or at query time.
Early fusion preserves rich interactions but couples token budgets and preprocessing. Separate en-
coders with state-level exchange preserve sensor-specific processing while introducing alignment
interfaces. Query-time fusion is modular but can lose information already discarded by each en-
coder. In a lifting task, disagreement between vision and torque may indicate an incorrect mass
hypothesis, a grasp failure, or a sensor fault. Averaging the signals into an unexplained scalar is
not a solution.
Understanding and generation also have different representational needs. Show-o combines au-
toregressive and diffusion-based modeling within a unified transformer. BAGEL studies shared
multimodal understanding and generation with specialized representational pathways (Xie et al.,
2025; Deng et al., 2025a). These attempts show that shared processing need not require identical
tokenizers or identical prediction targets. They motivate joint semantic and generative learning,
but successful image understanding and synthesis do not independently verify a model’s response
to physical interventions.
Coupling Future Prediction and Action Generation

where Θ denotes the model’s parameters. The action and observation horizons must refer to com-

tion proposal followed by consequence prediction. The second suggests a future subgoal followed
by inverse-dynamics action generation. An observed conditional distribution is not automatically
an interventional model, and an attractive generated goal is not necessarily reachable.
Unified World Models (UWM) couples video and action diffusion with independent modality-
specific noise levels, using the conditioning pattern to obtain policy, forward-dynamics, inverse-
dynamics, and video-generation interfaces (Zhu et al., 2025). This illustrates how the same pa-
rameter set can support different queries when the training distribution and masks explicitly cover
those queries. It does not imply that every joint generator reliably supports every conditional query.
A cascaded design is easier to inspect but can compound errors and latency. A jointly sampled de-
sign enables stronger coupling but must control incompatible objectives and future-information
leakage.
DreamZero supplies another representative use of a pretrained video prior for joint future-video
and action modeling (Ye et al., 2026a). Together with UWM, it illustrates a broad design axis in
which action supervision can shape a model of anticipated observations instead of being added
only to a static visual encoder. The systems need not share the same architecture, sampling proce-
dure, or adaptation protocol. OpenWAM’s composable framework makes this distinction explicit
by separating prediction, action generation, their interaction structure, and inference choices for
controlled comparison (Wang et al., 2026c). Its methodological lesson is to compare one interface
choice at a time, rather than attributing every difference between complete systems to “world mod-
eling.”
A third route uses future supervision to shape a representation available from present evidence,
without generating future observations during deployment. InternVLA-A1.5 trains foresight to-
kens through a frozen video model and removes the video branch at inference (Ma et al., 2026a).
InternW0-∆combines a video expert, an action expert, frozen VLM semantics, and training-only
4D distillation. Causal Imprint connects future-derived supervision to observation-conditioned
action features (Miao et al., 2026). Such systems unify predictive learning with action generation
without requiring a full future rollout for every policy call.
Expert Specialization and Runtime Organization
A mixture-of-transformers can retain separate
parameters and token streams while allowing masked attention between experts. The mask spec-
ifies which observations, predicted variables, and action tokens can influence one another. Shared
attention does not imply unrestricted bidirectional access. A cache can be reused across action-
denoising steps only if its inputs and all upstream dependencies remain unchanged. Architectural
independence, gradient isolation during training, and asynchronous execution are three distinct
properties.
InternW0 illustrates a complementary runtime design in which slower video prediction supplies
cached context, and a faster action expert adapts that context to recent observations through an
observation-conditioned routing interface (Cai et al., 2026b). This differs from training away the
future generator. In InternW0-∆, future-video tokens are omitted at inference, but the video expert
still processes observed context and Causal Imprint once before action-only denoising (Miao et al.,
2026). Neither arrangement should be summarized simply as “the video module is free.” Their
evidence boundaries are taken up again when decision utility is evaluated in Section 5.4.4.

A design can therefore combine an object-centric state, latent stochastic transitions, an optional
video decoder, and a policy trained from future supervision. The right combination is determined
by the required queries and evidence. Cross-query consistency is useful. Rendering a state and re-

their agreement is not independent physical validation. Section 5.5 returns to hierarchical, multi-

fully shared backbone as inevitable.
Reading Representative Work Through Common Design Questions
Table 5.3 summarizes rep-
resentative implementations of the preceding principles. It is a map of mechanisms, not an exhaus-
tive catalog or a ranking. A new model can be located by its retained state, supervisory target,
intervention interface, and deployed computation without adding a new supposedly disjoint cate-
gory for every paper.
The table also exposes missing interfaces. An image representation learner still needs a temporal,
action-conditioned predictor to support control queries. A persistent scene generator still needs
dynamics for manipulation. And a successful policy still needs separate tests before being used as
a general predictive simulator. These are opportunities for composition, not reasons to exclude the
corresponding lines of research from world modeling.
5.3
Training World Models
Training must make the internal state useful for future queries rather than merely reconstruct fa-
miliar observations. A complete account specifies the data available to each objective, the variables
predicted, the parameters updated, the rollout horizon, and the information excluded from de-
ployment. Representation learning, dynamics learning, policy learning, physical constraints, and
uncertainty estimation solve related but different problems. Their combination is a design choice,
not one mandatory loss shared by all world models.
A practical training program can start from scratch, adapt pretrained components in stages, or
connect frozen specialists through learned interfaces.
Broad observation pretraining supplies
reusable visual and temporal structure. Action-conditioned training grounds intervention seman-
tics. Downstream post-training adapts the model to a task or embodiment. Interaction-driven
updates address the states reached by the deployed system. Some systems combine these stages,
and some do not require all of them. PlaNet illustrates joint latent-model learning, V-JEPA 2 sep-
arates broad representation learning from action-conditioned post-training, and UWM combines

fed by the data sources of Chapter 4 (left). Interaction-driven updates retrain on the states reached

The data foundations are developed in Chapter 4. Their training consequences differ. Action-free
videos can supervise observation or representation prediction. Recorded controls can supervise
action-conditioned transitions. Demonstrations can supervise a policy. And simulator states, force
readings, or teacher features provide additional targets with distinct provenance. A valid failed tra-
jectory can teach dynamics and outcomes without being an appropriate nominal imitation target.
Missing channels must be masked rather than treated as measured zeros.
The four stages in the center of Figure 5.3 carry different objectives. Broad observation pretraining
applies masked reconstruction, autoregressive likelihood, diffusion or flow, and feature-prediction
targets, with an exponential-moving-average teacher where the target representation must stay sta-
ble. World-action learning adds forward, inverse, and behavioral targets on recorded interaction.
Downstream post-training adapts the model to a task and embodiment. And interaction-driven
updates retrain on the states the deployed system actually reaches. That last stage closes the loop
only through new data, which is what distinguishes continual improvement from repeated fitting
of a fixed corpus. In the right panel, the forward mode predicts bF from C and A, the inverse mode
predicts bA from C and F, and the policy mode predicts bA from C only, with the future-to-action
path masked out as a leakage route (red cross). In all three modes the context rows are barred
from reading F, so the context representation remains a pure function of observed evidence even
when the action query may consult the future. These interfaces are reading modes over the same
token groups, selected by attention masks, rather than three separate models. One network can be
trained to serve all of them provided the masks are enforced exactly, as Section 5.3.2 discusses. The
deployment-ready model is then an inference pass with all training-only branches absent.
5.3.1
Self-Supervised and Generative Representation Learning
Self-supervised objectives extract structure from observations without requiring every physical
variable to be annotated. Temporal prediction, masked reconstruction, contrastive discrimination,
and target-representation prediction impose different information bottlenecks. A reconstruction
target retains observable detail. A feature target retains distinctions present in its encoder. A tem-
poral target encourages information predictive over its selected horizon. None automatically iden-
tifies mass, contact, or causality when the observations do not distinguish them.
Autoregressive Likelihood and Masked Reconstruction
Let x = (x1, . . . , xNtok) be a target se-
quence of Ntok tokens, κ the available conditioning information, and D the training distribution. A
maximum-likelihood objective is
LAR = −E(x,κ)∼D

The index i orders tokens, x<i contains preceding target tokens, and θ denotes trainable parame-

the advertised query. Discrete tokens yield cross-entropy training. Continuous outputs require
an explicit conditional density. During teacher-forced training, preceding targets are real tokens,
whereas free generation conditions on the model’s own outputs. Thus a low teacher-forced loss
does not establish stable recursive prediction.
Masked reconstruction instead withholds selected spatial or temporal observations and predicts
them from visible context. A mask that reveals observations on both sides of a hidden frame trains
interpolation or smoothing, not causal future prediction. Such supervision can still be valuable
for representation pretraining, but a causal predictor needs a corresponding future-blind training
or adaptation stage. The mask pattern, temporal window, and conditioning availability should be
recorded alongside the loss.

The variational sequence distribution is the product of its filtering factors. DKL is Kullback-Leibler

The reconstruction term trains the encoder and decoder to retain evidence. The divergence trains
the prior to match the observation-informed posterior while limiting information that the prior
cannot predict. Reparameterized sampling allows gradients through continuous latent variables.
In practice, balancing or stopping selected gradient paths, protecting a minimum latent information

budget, and adding reward or event targets can stabilize learning. Their details should be reported,
because identical symbolic losses can optimize different parameters under different gradient rules.
A deterministic recurrent memory may be included alongside the stochastic state, provided its
dependencies are included in the model definition.
Predicting Target Representations
For a context encoder Eϕ, predictor Pθ, and target encoder E ¯ϕ,

different spatial and temporal scales (Assran et al., 2023; 2025).
The predictor and context encoder learn to make retained target information predictable. Stop-
gradient alone is not a universal proof against collapse. The target update, masking, architecture,
and representation statistics must work together. A collapsed representation can achieve a trivial
small distance, and a semantic target can discard fine motion. Comparing downstream readouts,
representation variation, and controlled physical predictions is therefore necessary. The main trade-
off concerns which information is retained, how expensive the target is to produce, and which later
queries the representation supports.
From Masked JEPA Pretraining to Causal Latent Dynamics
A typical training iteration first se-
lects a clip and its visible and target regions. The context encoder receives only the visible content.
The target encoder processes the target evidence, possibly with the wider context specified by the
method, and produces the features to be matched. The predictor is conditioned on the target po-
sitions and, when the task requires them, actions and elapsed time. After the student update, an
exponential-moving-average teacher can be updated as
¯ϕ ←mEMA ¯ϕ + (1 −mEMA)ϕ,
0 ≤mEMA < 1,
(5.13)
where ϕ is the updated student-encoder parameter vector, ¯ϕ the teacher vector, and mEMA the
momentum coefficient. The teacher is not updated by the predictive-loss gradient. A larger mEMA
changes targets more slowly but can leave them behind a rapidly adapting student. This target-
update mechanism is used in the JEPA lineage (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024). Freezing an
independent pretrained teacher is a different design.
For causal dynamics learning, the visible context must stop at the forecast origin, and the pre-
dictor must associate a proposed control sequence with later target features. V-JEPA 2’s action-
conditioned post-training illustrates this additional step (Assran et al., 2025). Bidirectional pre-
training remains useful, but its masked-completion score should not be relabeled as open-loop
prediction accuracy. A goal-conditioned planner also needs a meaningful discrepancy between
predicted and goal features and a valid action-search procedure. Representation quality, transition
quality, and search quality are separately testable.
Feature regression has a statistical limit worth making explicit. With a fixed target representation
and squared error, the population-optimal deterministic prediction is its conditional mean. With
scalar absolute error, it is a conditional median. Neither objective by itself recovers multiple modes
or assigns probabilities to them. A scene with two plausible future contact states can therefore
require a stochastic latent predictor, multiple hypotheses, or a probabilistic event head. The appro-
priate objective depends on whether the downstream consumer needs a reusable feature, a most
likely outcome, or a calibrated distribution. This applies to JEPA-style targets and to predictive-
feature distillation in world-action models alike.
111


5.3.2
Action-Conditioned Dynamics and World-Action Learning
Actions connect prediction to intervention, but an action record must have a precise meaning. Dis-
tinguish a proposed command, the command actually applied after clipping or safety filtering, and
the subsequent measured physical response. A deployable forward model can condition on the
applied input or model the actuator transformation from a proposed command. It must not re-
quire the future measured response as an input to predict that same response. Controller mode,
reference frame, units, duration, delays, and saturation belong in the record. The notation at refers
to the declared input interface, not an unspecified mixture of command and consequence.
Forward, Inverse, and Behavioral Targets
A forward model predicts the next observation or state
from current evidence and an input. An inverse model predicts an input compatible with two states
or observations. A policy predicts an input from current evidence and a goal. These targets are
related by the joint distribution in Eq. (5.7), but they are not equivalent. Several actions can reach
the same endpoint, and matching endpoints can hide different contact forces or unsafe intermediate
states. Inverse-dynamics training therefore needs a multimodal output distribution or an explicit
criterion for selecting among compatible actions.
The three targets correspond to the three world-action interfaces in the right panel of Figure 5.3, de-
fined as attention masks over observed-context tokens C, action tokens A, and future-observation
tokens F. A forward dynamics model (FDM) predicts bF from C and A. Given what is observed and a
candidate input, it forecasts the consequence, which is exactly the transition query of Figure 5.1 and
the rollout mechanism used in planning and imagination. An inverse dynamics model (IDM) predicts
bA from C and F. It reads how the scene actually changed and infers a compatible input. An IDM
that requires the realized future observation cannot use that observation to choose the preceding
action online. In the training interface considered here, it labels recorded interaction with action
estimates, recovers latent actions from action-free video, and shapes representations that encode
how actions change the world. Even here, only the action query may read the future. The context
rows of the inverse mask bar C from attending to F, so context features, which may be cached or
shared with the policy mode, remain deployable summaries of observed evidence rather than car-
riers of future information. A policy mode predicts bA from C alone, possibly with a goal encoded
in the context. The future-to-action attention path is therefore masked out entirely (the crossed-out
cell in Figure 5.3). A single leaky edge would let action tokens read future observations at training
time and silently lose that input at test time.
Sharing one network across the three modes is attractive because the modes provide complemen-
tary supervision. The FDM grounds what actions do, the IDM grounds which actions produce
observed change, and the policy converts both into executable behavior. The cost is discipline in
the masks and in gradient routing. A stop-gradient blocks a parameter update but not a forward
information path, so frozen and detached components must be distinguished from masked ones,
and a deployment-mode forward pass with all training-only branches absent is the decisive test
that the policy mode’s inputs are exactly those available at runtime.
Behavior cloning learns demonstrated actions, using a likelihood, regression, diffusion, or flow ob-
jective. Diffusion Policy exemplifies a conditional distribution over action sequences rather than
a single independent action at each step (Chi et al., 2023). A failed action can remain useful for a
forward model and an outcome predictor while being excluded from a nominal imitation objec-
tive. Reward, termination, contact-event, and task-progress heads can make a state more useful for
decisions, but they supervise different quantities. A progress label is not a value target unless its
connection to future return has been established.

The distinction between sampling weights and loss weights matters. Increasing a robot source’s
sampling rate increases all of its enabled objectives, whereas increasing an action-loss coefficient
changes the balance within sampled records. Loss scales also depend on token counts and units.
A long video target can dominate a short action chunk unless normalization is deliberate. Joint
training can share useful structure but can also let appearance gradients erase precise control in-
formation or let narrow action data degrade broad semantics. Freezing pretrained modules, staged
unfreezing, separate experts, restricted gradient paths, and alternating updates offer different com-
promises between preservation and adaptation.
Future Supervision Without Future-Input Leakage
Future observations are legitimate training
targets. The restriction is on the forward information available to the deployed policy. A pre-
dictive feature branch can map present history to future-relevant features and align them with a
detached future teacher. Alternatively, a frozen generative model can receive learned conditioning
and send a loss gradient back through that conditioning while its own weights remain fixed. Freez-
ing weights is not the same as disabling the gradient with respect to the model’s input. InternVLA-
A1.5 uses this latter mechanism to train foresight conditioning (Ma et al., 2026a).
InternW0-∆uses latent-change supervision and detached future-feature alignment for Causal Im-
print, alongside training-only 4D teacher targets (Miao et al., 2026). The general lesson is to doc-
ument every route by which future information could reach action activations, including shared
attention, side conditioning, cached features, and preprocessing. A direct mask between future
and action tokens is insufficient if an intermediate token first reads the future and then passes it
onward. A detached target blocks a gradient path. A causal attention restriction blocks a forward
information path. Both can be required, but they solve different problems. Temporal “causality” of
a mask also does not by itself establish causal identification of the physical system.

video branch sees supplied actions, generated actions, or neither. The behavioral benefit of future
supervision and the correctness of action-conditioned physical prediction are different claims.

One minibatch update proceeds as follows. Construct a time-consistent observed context, action
chunk, future targets, and validity masks. Encode frozen inputs and retrieve any valid cached
teacher descriptors. Noise the video and action targets according to their declared schedules, while
keeping the observed conditioning and clean change targets separate. Run the experts with the
intended directed dependencies, compute only the supported losses, normalize them by valid en-
tries, and update the trainable parameter groups. If a moving-average teacher is used, update it
after the student step. Finally, test an inference-mode forward pass with all training-only future
and teacher branches absent. The policy must still have every input it requires.
This last test should inspect indirect as well as direct paths. An observed token that reads a future
token at one layer can leak that future to the policy at a later layer even when future-to-action
attention is masked. Temporal preprocessing can leak in the same way. Encoding an observed
frame together with future frames through a noncausal video encoder can contaminate its latent.
Cache reuse additionally requires independence from the evolving action and artificial-time inputs,
not merely independence from future observations. These checks turn a verbal claim of “training-
only supervision” into an auditable computation graph.
Learning a World Model Versus Learning Within One
Model-based reinforcement learning
adds a second optimization problem in which a policy is improved using transitions generated
by a learned model. In Dreamer, imagined trajectories train behavior while the learned dynamics
provide the rollout mechanism (Hafner et al., 2020). Model parameters can be held fixed during
policy optimization even when derivatives through the model are used to update policy parame-
ters. Conversely, updating the model to maximize its own predicted reward would not necessarily
improve its physical accuracy.
Dyna-style alternation uses real experience to improve the model and model-generated experi-
ence to improve decisions (Sutton, 1991). MBPO highlights a useful compromise by using short
model rollouts branched from real states, limiting reliance on distant model predictions (Janner
115


et al., 2019). Longer imagination expands possible credit assignment but exposes the policy to
compounding errors and model exploitation. Offline data create an additional support problem.
A proposed policy may select actions absent from the training distribution. Policy improvement
should therefore be coupled to rollout-length selection, conservative use of uncertain predictions,
renewed real data, and independent physical evaluation rather than judged only by imagined re-
turn.
5.3.3
Physical Constraints, Counterfactuals, and Uncertainty Modeling
Physical structure can enter through loss penalties, architectural restrictions, or a hybrid of known
dynamics and learned corrections.
Physics-informed neural networks demonstrate the use of
governing-equation residuals as learning signals (Raissi et al., 2019).
Structured simulators il-
lustrate complementary restrictions arising from a representation and its update rules (Sanchez-
Gonzalez et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2024). The appropriate choice depends on which laws, parameters,
and boundary conditions are actually known.

Examples include joint limits, nonpenetration, contact consistency, and energy or mass balance un-
der known boundary fluxes. A system exchanging heat or liquid with its surroundings should obey
a balance equation, not an inappropriate constant-energy or constant-mass penalty. Tolerances
should reflect measurement precision and modeling assumptions. A strong incorrect constraint
biases the model. A weak penalty may leave violations large. Enforcing symmetries or integrating
known mechanics can reduce violation by construction, but only for the constrained property and
under the numerical method’s assumptions. It cannot identify an unmeasured friction coefficient
or certify all downstream behavior.
Counterfactual and Intervention Supervision
Paired rollouts can compare different actions from
matched initial conditions. A resettable simulator can hold state and external inputs fixed while
varying an intervention. In a physical experiment, the same comparison requires reproducible ini-
tial conditions, controlled confounders, or a justified statistical design. Outcome diversity from an
unconditioned video generator is not evidence that it learned how a particular action changes the
outcome. Synthetic counterfactuals supervise the simulator’s mechanisms. Independent measure-
ments are needed before transferring those conclusions to reality.
A useful training contrast varies the commanded magnitude, direction, or duration while keeping
nonintervened conditions comparable. It can supervise the sign and scale of the response as well
as which objects should remain unchanged. Care is required near discontinuities. A slightly larger
force may change sticking to sliding rather than yield a slightly larger displacement. A smooth
penalty that averages these modes can suppress the event the model is supposed to predict.

Deterministic regression is cheap but cannot
express multiple plausible outcomes. A conditional Gaussian supplies a mean and variance. Mix-

but they should not be presented as calibrated probabilistic simulators. Section 5.4.3 explains how
uncertainty is evaluated rather than inferred from the mere presence of stochastic layers.

actions without incorporating intermediate real observations. The target yt+k is a later measure-
ment or explicitly identified teacher target. wk weights horizon k, H is the maximum horizon, and
ℓis a suitable regression or probabilistic loss. A probabilistic by denotes a distribution, not necessar-
ily one sampled value. Supervision should score that distribution appropriately rather than force
every sample to match one realized future.
Teacher Forcing, Free Rollout, and Curriculum
Teacher forcing provides stable local supervision
but exposes the model mainly to data states. Free rollout trains on its own evolving predictions and
addresses the deployment distribution more directly, at the cost of unstable early trajectories and
longer gradient paths. Scheduled sampling mixes real and generated preceding inputs (Bengio
et al., 2015). It is a training heuristic, not generally the original sequence-likelihood objective. A
sensible comparison therefore includes teacher-forced error, open-loop error, and task behavior
rather than assuming that mixed inputs always improve all three.
Latent overshooting in PlaNet extends consistency pressure beyond one transition by matching
multi-step predictive distributions to observation-informed states (Hafner et al., 2019). Related
multi-step objectives can supervise physical readouts or future embeddings. Longer windows
117


improve exposure to delayed effects, but require more memory and can overweight a particu-
lar target encoder’s errors. A curriculum can begin with short horizons and then include longer
windows and contact-centered segments, while preserving enough ordinary motion to avoid a dis-
torted training distribution. Truncating backpropagation lowers cost but changes which temporal
dependencies receive direct gradient signals.
Multiple Timescales and Temporal Consistency
Different sensors and physical variables evolve
at different rates. Training should include elapsed-time conditioning, modality-validity masks,
and action durations rather than assuming one frame equals one control interval. Slow semantic
context, faster visual dynamics, and high-rate force feedback can share state through explicit timing
interfaces. Interpolation is appropriate only when its assumptions hold. Interpolating across an
impact can erase the discontinuity.
For a Markov transition kernel under the same constant control input a and conditions c, time
consistency takes the form
Tθ(z′′ | z, a, c, ∆1 + ∆2) ≈
Z
Tθ(z′′ | u, a, c, ∆2)Tθ(u | z, a, c, ∆1) du,
(5.23)
where z, z′′ are initial and final latent states, u is an intermediate latent state, and ∆1, ∆2 > 0 are
physical durations. This is a distribution-level Chapman-Kolmogorov consistency condition under
the stated Markov and fixed-input assumptions. It is not generally valid to replace the intermediate
distribution by its mean in nonlinear dynamics. If actions or external conditions change, both sides
must use the same time-varying input schedule. If the compressed state is not Markov, residual
inconsistency may reveal missing memory rather than numerical error.
Post-Training, Distillation, and Continued Interaction
Task-specific post-training can refine ac-
tion interfaces, contact targets, or selected dynamics. InternW0 adds available force and tactile his-
tories and predicts future contact channels during contact-aware post-training (Cai et al., 2026b).
Such adaptation requires valid contact supervision. Missing physical channels cannot be recovered
simply by adding a new output head. Distillation can transfer an expensive teacher’s features or
predictions to a smaller or less frequently executed branch, but the teacher’s uncertainty and errors
should remain distinguishable from measured truth.
Local adaptation should separate belief correction, physical-parameter identification, and updates
to learned network weights. A failed grasp may revise a contact hypothesis without changing the
model. Repeated measured slip may justify identifying friction. Systematic errors across condi-
tions may require a new training round. Replay, regularization, and selective parameter updates
address the trade-off between new learning and retention. Elastic weight consolidation is one ex-
ample of limiting changes to parameters important for previous tasks (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), not
a guarantee against forgetting in an arbitrary world model. New versions should be accepted only
after tests of both new and retained capabilities.
Staging Auxiliary Supervision and Adapting the Deployed Interface
A multi-objective recipe
can be organized around a stable behavioral and predictive baseline rather than enabling every
target from the first update. InternW0-∆first performs joint pretraining and subsequently adds
cached 4D supervision during continued pretraining, before task- and embodiment-specific post-
training (Miao et al., 2026). The general choice is between early joint shaping and later auxiliary
refinement. Early auxiliary losses can guide representation formation, but noisy or mismatched
teachers can interfere before the action interface becomes useful. Later introduction reduces that
early interference but may require a smaller learning rate or replay to avoid disturbing established
behavior. Neither schedule is a universal optimum.
Post-training should match the actual deployment contract. A target robot may change valid ac-
tion dimensions, normalization, camera configuration, actuation delay, or the relation between pre-
dicted and executed chunk lengths. Adapt the relevant input/output mappings and condition the
model on these differences. Do not reinterpret an identical numerical vector as an identical physical
action. If successive chunks overlap or part of a chunk has already been committed to execution,
118


the training condition should identify that prefix and the loss should target the remaining control-
lable portion. Where online feedback is used to choose future actions, it must be separated from
the fixed action sequence assumed by an open-loop dynamics objective.
Frozen-encoder and teacher caches can reduce repeated training work, but only while their depen-
dencies remain fixed. Changing an encoder checkpoint, a crop, a view layout, an instruction, or the
temporal window can invalidate a cached feature. Offline geometric descriptors should retain their
source clip, teacher version, confidence, and normalization. Activation checkpointing trades extra
computation for memory. Mixed precision reduces storage and arithmetic cost but needs checks
for unstable losses and gradients. Report these implementation choices separately from reductions
in the amount of training data or the number of optimization steps. A faster experiment pipeline is
valuable, but it is not itself evidence of better learned dynamics.
For model selection, monitor the component losses alongside open-loop predictions and closed-
loop behavior. A lower teacher-feature error can coexist with worse action accuracy if the repre-
sentation discards contact detail. Likewise, a lower action loss on demonstration states can conceal
failure on states visited by the policy. Compare a frozen baseline, a joint-training variant, and
an auxiliary-supervision variant on fixed held-out conditions, with unchanged target preprocess-
ing and comparable budgets. This distinguishes the contribution of predictive supervision from a
larger backbone, a different data mixture, or additional optimization.
Training Trade-Offs and Reproducible Reporting
Table 5.5 summarizes choices that should be
reported together rather than hidden inside a total loss. At minimum, an experiment should state
its data mixture and splits, temporal sampling, target normalization, trainable and frozen modules,
gradient paths, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, effective batch size, sequence length, number
of updates, numerical precision, and training and inference budgets. No fixed recipe is optimal
across video generation, latent planning, and multimodal control.
The common criterion is whether the resulting model answers the intended queries on evidence it
could actually receive. Training losses are useful diagnostics, but the relationships among recon-
struction, dynamics, uncertainty, and behavior must be established through the validation proto-
cols below.

5.4
Using and Validating World Models
Using a world model means making a query under a declared information boundary and, when
appropriate, using its answer to choose an intervention. Validation should separate the quality of
a forecast from its physical consistency and from the utility of the decision it supports. A model
119


can produce physically possible but inaccurate futures, accurate short-term forecasts that do not
improve a policy, or useful actions without exposing a general-purpose predictive interface. This
section develops protocols that make these distinctions measurable.
5.4.1
Interactive Simulation and Conditional Queries
An interactive call starts from an inferred state, belief, or observation history and returns one or
more conditional futures. A query may request an image, object trajectory, contact event, temper-
ature, boundary crossing, or task outcome. It should specify the available evidence, intervention
interface, physical horizon, environment conditions, and required precision. For a partially known
scene, the returned uncertainty should include unresolved state alternatives, not only randomness
introduced during decoding.
State Posterior, Future Prediction, and Retrospective Checking
The state posterior summarizes
evidence available up to the prediction time. A future forecast propagates that posterior without
using the future measurements to be predicted. For an observation-generating latent model, a
representative factorization is

The integration marginalizes the current and future latent states zt:t+H. ∆tk specifies each physical

prediction with respect to the current latent state, not necessarily a Bayesian average over uncer-

tion 5.1.2. A model with additional dependencies must include them explicitly (Kaelbling et al.,
1998; Hafner et al., 2019).
After real execution, the withheld observations can be used to check the forecast and then update
the state. This retrospective validation of an earlier prediction is different from reconstructing a future
frame after that frame has already entered an inference network. Likewise, smoothing a past state
using later evidence can be useful for diagnosis but cannot be reported as an online forecast made
with less information. Evaluation logs should retain the prediction, model version, conditioning
evidence, and issue time before the target outcome is revealed.
Eq. (5.24) describes a query interface, not a requirement that every architecture evaluate an explicit
density. Sample-based models can approximate the predictive distribution. Deterministic mod-
els return a restricted point prediction. A latent-only model can answer a physical or task query
through a readout rather than an observation decoder. In all cases, a goal specifies what is desired
and should not be treated as evidence that the goal will occur. Scenario assumptions, such as a
proposed payload or a fixed external temperature, must remain distinguishable from measured
conditions.
Interactive Correction and Information Acquisition
Real feedback should update the inferred
state before the next query. A prediction made before a grasp slips may no longer be a valid context
for later actions even if its video remains visually coherent. Asynchronous systems should therefore
expose the age and observation support of cached predictions, together with the conditions that
trigger correction, regeneration, or rejection.
Predictions can also help choose what to observe next. If two action rankings differ mainly because
contact is uncertain, an additional tactile measurement may be more useful than another distant
camera frame. This is an information-acquisition decision within the partially observable control
problem (Kaelbling et al., 1998). Its value depends on an observation model, the cost of sensing,
120


and whether the proposed measurement can actually resolve the ambiguity. Querying the same
model repeatedly does not create independent evidence about the physical state.

Planning proposes candidate actions, predicts their consequences, and ranks them using task ob-
jectives and constraints. An imagined collection of branches can be written as

A planner may optimize actions by sampling, tree expansion, or differentiating through a learned
transition. PlaNet uses latent-space planning, while probabilistic ensemble methods such as PETS
propagate alternative dynamics and state outcomes during action evaluation (Hafner et al., 2019;
Chua et al., 2018). A separately trained actor may instead amortize this computation into direct ac-
tion generation. The actor can be trained using imagined trajectories without running a planner at
deployment, as in Dreamer (Hafner et al., 2020). Planning at inference and policy learning through
imagination therefore have different runtime costs and failure modes.
Receding-horizon execution applies only an initial portion of the selected sequence and replans
from new real evidence. Without this correction, action optimization may deliberately enter re-
gions where prediction errors create unrealistically high reward. Longer imagined rollouts are not
automatically better. They can change action ranking for the wrong reason. Model-based policy
optimization addresses this issue by controlling the use and length of imagined experience (Janner
et al., 2019). Uncertainty-sensitive ranking can compare candidate outcomes across hidden-state
hypotheses, but agreement among several copies of a biased model is not independent confirma-
tion.
Hierarchical imagination can compare coarse routes or process phases before refining a selected
interval. Candidates should terminate at a common physical horizon or comparable completion
event, with appropriate terminal-value treatment. Otherwise a shorter trajectory can appear prefer-
able merely because its later costs are omitted. Efficient execution can also reuse observation fea-
tures or invoke detailed prediction only near consequential events. These savings must be eval-
uated together with the error introduced by stale context, reduced branching, or omitted detail,
rather than by model throughput alone.

5.4.3
Prediction Quality and Physical-Consistency Tests
Prediction quality asks whether a forecast agrees with the subsequently observed outcome or its
conditional distribution. Physical consistency asks whether the predicted trajectory respects rel-
evant identities, mechanisms, and constraints. These are separate axes. Several trajectories may
be physically possible, while only one occurs per trial. A visually similar output may still violate
contact or respond incorrectly to an action. Table 5.6 organizes the evidence needed for each claim.
Prediction Quality at a Fixed Information Boundary
Report one-step prediction from newly
observed context, open-loop multi-step prediction without future measurements, and feedback-
interleaved prediction with explicitly scheduled observations separately. Also specify whether
future controls were fixed before the forecast or recorded from a feedback policy. Conditioning
retrospectively on a policy’s later actions can reveal information about later states. It is not equiva-
lent to forecasting an independently supplied intervention sequence.
Observation forecasts can be compared using pixel errors, perceptual feature distances such as
learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and distribution-level video measures such as
Fréchet video distance (FVD) (Zhang et al., 2018; Unterthiner et al., 2018). These answer different
questions. Pixel error is sensitive to small spatial misalignment. Perceptual metrics inherit the
features of their evaluator. A good aggregate distribution score does not establish that each sample
follows its supplied action. Multimodal futures further complicate paired image error. A legitimate
but unobserved outcome can be penalized even when the predicted distribution is appropriate.
Report the sample budget and avoid presenting best-of-many selection as the performance of a
single unselected prediction.
State and event queries require measurements matched to their meaning. Object positions and
velocities can be evaluated in physical units. Orientations need an appropriate rotational distance.
Contact or phase-change events require detection and timing errors. For a scalar physical quantity,
a horizon-specific summary is

temperatures without scaling. Plotting or tabulating the error against elapsed time exposes drift
hidden by an average over horizons. A probabilistic forecast also needs a distributional score, not
only error of its mean.
Physical Consistency and Intervention Response
Evaluate persistence of object identity and hid-
den attributes through occlusion, compatibility of geometry across views, non-penetration within
measurement tolerance, contact creation and release, and agreement between predicted motion
and known control changes. When forces, boundary fluxes, and physical parameters are avail-
able, check momentum, energy, or material balances under the corresponding assumptions. Con-
servation of an isolated system must not be imposed on an open or externally actuated process.
These tests should use the physical quantities underlying the constraints of Section 5.3.3, not merely
whether an auxiliary loss is small during training.
Contact and other mechanism changes deserve event-centered reporting. Most recorded frames
may show easy steady motion, so an aggregate average can conceal incorrect impact timing, slip
onset, or release. Partition errors into free motion, contact formation, sustained contact, release,
and relevant process transitions. Controlled changes in action direction, magnitude, duration, or
timing test whether the model predicts the right change, rather than merely any change. Where
possible, paired trials should hold the initial conditions and non-intervened factors fixed. Simula-
tion supports precise resets. Physical repeats require reporting reset variability and measurement
uncertainty.
Physics judged only from rendered images remains an indirect test. A perception model used to ex-
tract trajectories can introduce correlated errors, and a language-model judge can prefer plausible-
looking motion. Such evaluators should be validated against independent labels or measurements
for the claimed quantity. A state predictor without a visual decoder can instead be assessed through
its native physical outputs or a readout fitted only on training data. Requiring every architecture
to produce a video would conflate query availability with dynamics quality.
Benchmark Tasks and Information Parity
Physion illustrates evaluation of a physical event by
asking a model to predict, from an initial visible segment, whether specified objects will contact
during the unseen continuation, rather than requiring every model to generate a video (Bear et al.,
2021). The task permits comparisons among learned visual features, explicit states, and dynamical
predictions, provided that their input privileges and readout training are reported. A model given
simulator particle states has a different information budget from one given RGB observations. Their
gap can help diagnose perception versus dynamics, but cannot be interpreted as a matched-input
architectural ranking.
The same principle applies across model families. Spatial generators need held-out-view and re-
visit consistency tests with measured regions distinguished from completed regions. JEPA-style
models need fixed, independently trained readouts or action-conditioned rollout tests, not only
similarity to their own changing teacher. Joint world-action models need both policy evaluation
and any separately claimed forecast evaluation. No single rendering metric, contact classifier, or
robot success rate covers all these interfaces. A useful benchmark suite therefore combines common
physical questions with native-interface tests and publishes what information each model receives.
Probability, Calibration, and Sharpness
A forecast distribution should place probability on out-
comes in a way that is both accurate and informative. Proper scoring rules reward the predictive
distribution rather than a conveniently selected sample (Gneiting and Raftery, 2007). For a binary
event, a scalar observation, and its predictive distribution, two representative scores are
