Calibration asks whether probabilities or intervals agree with empirical frequencies. For example,
cases assigned a contact probability near a specified value should exhibit contact at approximately
that frequency. A nominal prediction interval should be assessed by empirical coverage and width,
since an excessively broad interval can cover almost every outcome while being unhelpful. Cal-
ibration curves and post-hoc calibration techniques are useful diagnostics, but calibration on one
distribution need not persist after a shift (Guo et al., 2017). Marginal coverage alone does not es-
tablish correctness within each task, contact mode, horizon, or material group. Sample diversity
and ensemble disagreement should therefore be tested against realized outcomes rather than inter-
preted as uncertainty quality by construction.
Splits, Aggregation, and Reproducibility
Separate model fitting, calibration or threshold selec-
tion, and final testing. Group related frames and derived samples by trajectory, scene, object com-
bination, and collection session as appropriate to the generalization claim. Report results by phys-
ical horizon, event type, and change of conditions before aggregating them. Confidence intervals
should account for trajectory-level dependence. Treating adjacent frames as independent trials
substantially overstates the amount of evidence. Include failure cases and invalid predictions in a
declared accounting scheme rather than silently removing them from the denominator.
The rows in Table 5.6 are complementary, not interchangeable levels of one score. A model may
pass state-persistence tests while failing intervention tests, or yield useful decisions while offering
no calibrated probability interface. The evaluation report should identify supported claims and
missing evidence separately. Decision-level evaluation is developed next.
5.4.4
Decision Utility and Applicability Boundaries
The operational question is whether model calls improve real outcomes. Compare systems with
and without the relevant world-model function while matching the policy proposal mechanism,
observation history, action interface, training data, and inference budget as closely as possible. For
a specified real-task score Jreal, define
∆J = Jreal(πwith model) −Jreal(πreference),
(5.29)
where πwith model is the policy or complete decision procedure using the tested model function,
πreference the comparison procedure, and ∆J their difference under the same outcome definition
and evaluation distribution. The score may be success rate, measured task quality, or another
explicitly specified objective. It is not the model’s own predicted reward. Report initial conditions,
repetitions, uncertainty intervals, failures, interventions, and resource costs. A positive average
gain can conceal systematic failure on the very candidates the model ranks most confidently.
Ablations should replace one function at a time. A persistence predictor tests the value of temporal
evolution beyond current state. An action-shuffled predictor tests sensitivity to the supplied con-
trol. Removing future supervision tests its contribution to the learned representation. Matched his-
tory and parameter budgets help separate predictive learning from a larger encoder or additional
context. These controls diagnose mechanisms but do not individually prove a causal explanation
for an entire system’s improvement.
Efficiency has several boundaries, including observation acquisition and transfer, encoding, predic-
tive prefill, action or video sampling, communication, and physical execution. Report model-side
action-update time separately from sensor-to-command latency, full query latency, and successful
task throughput. Asynchronous prediction moves work off a critical path but does not remove its
computation or the risk of stale predictions. Hardware, precision, batch size, context length, action
124


horizon, denoising steps, and update rates should accompany timings. Neither the inverse of av-
erage inference time nor a high low-level servo rate establishes closed-loop responsiveness under
all conditions.
Applicability boundaries should cover objects, materials, actions, temporal horizons, modalities,
and embodiments. A model may generalize to new appearance while failing under new friction, or
predict free motion while failing after a contact switch. Test combinations of mechanism changes as
well as isolated shifts. Distinguish recovery through fresh observation, belief correction, physical-
parameter identification, and network retraining. These require different resources and support
different transfer claims. Uncertainty, modality disagreement, and residuals can trigger shorter
horizons, additional sensing, or fallback, but their thresholds need validation against actual errors.
Independent execution constraints and safety mechanisms remain system responsibilities.
Deployment validation should establish whether a world model improves outcomes under
matched comparisons, within stated boundaries, and at a cost the system can afford. Its query
interfaces must specify the limits of those claims.
5.5
Current Challenges and Future Outlook
The preceding sections suggest that progress should be described through capabilities and their
evidence rather than a single architecture label. Broad pretrained priors, explicit physical struc-
ture, and efficient action interfaces contribute different strengths. Their integration raises questions
about what can be learned from existing observations, what requires new intervention, and how a
model can remain useful while its environment and operating conditions change.
5.5.1
Acquiring Physical Knowledge from Observation to Intervention
Videos provide rich evidence about appearance and motion but usually omit commanded forces,
contact states, and other variables that determine the response to an intervention. Different mech-
anisms can explain the same observed trajectory. Larger observational datasets can improve cov-
erage without resolving this ambiguity when the distinguishing variable is never measured or ex-
cited. The relevant challenge is to connect reusable visual and semantic priors with evidence that
identifies executable action consequences.
Action-free pretraining followed by grounded interaction learning offers one division of labor, as
illustrated by the separate representation and action-conditioned stages of V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al.,
2025). Other systems can jointly train on several evidence types or transfer a prior through distil-
lation. The choice should follow the gap to be closed. Unfamiliar object semantics, an unobserved
material property, a new control interface, and a missing deformation mode are different problems.
Transferring a representation does not remove the need to calibrate units, timing, and embodiment-
dependent dynamics.
Multimodal measurements and targeted probes can expose distinctions that passive video leaves
unresolved. A controlled lift with load measurements constrains mass. A slide under measured
force constrains friction within a contact model. A thermal observation distinguishes visually iden-
tical process states. Such experiments should be chosen for their ability to separate plausible expla-
nations, not merely to maximize visual novelty. Their cost and risk must be included in learning
efficiency. For instruments and infrastructure, the intervention may be a process-setting change
rather than a robot motion, but the same requirement holds. Predicted effects must be checked
against the measurements relevant to the mechanism.
A further challenge is preserving uncertainty where evidence remains insufficient. A model should
represent several compatible explanations instead of inventing a unique physical parameter from
appearance. Uncertainty reduction through new sensing, identification through repeated interac-
tion, and correction of structural model error should remain distinct. This distinction gives the
closed loop a scientific role. Action tests an explanation, and the resulting discrepancy determines
what knowledge should be revised.
125


5.5.2
Reliable Consequence Prediction in Complex and Long-Horizon Processes
Contact switches, non-rigid deformation, and coupled physical processes can turn small local er-
rors into qualitatively different futures. Long-horizon prediction therefore requires more than a
longer context window. It needs persistent state, representations of consequential events, appro-
priate time resolution, and uncertainty that remains useful as the forecast extends. A model may
need to predict a phase boundary accurately without reproducing every intermediate texture.
The architectural routes in Table 5.2 are likely to be combined in several ways, but no single com-
bination is established as universally preferable. One design direction connects compact predictive
states to detailed generative readouts on demand. Another combines object- or field-based physical
structure with learned residual dynamics. A third coordinates slower semantic and process mod-
els with faster contact or motion models. Each requires an interface that preserves identity, units,
physical time, and uncertainty. A hierarchy is not useful when its levels describe incompatible
worlds.
Combining routes along any of these directions raises a representation question. A shared substrate
can support understanding, prediction, and action, while specialized encoders and heads preserve
the information each function needs. Shared parameters are only one implementation. Aligned
representations, directed cross-expert communication, and training-only predictive supervision of-
fer alternatives, as discussed in Section 5.2.4. The roadmap’s distinction between functional roles
and architectural choices is useful here. A common physical description should support compatible
queries without forcing all modalities into one update frequency or every task into one decoding
objective (Chen et al., 2026b).
Future comparisons should therefore test composition rather than only larger monolithic models.
Does adding structure improve held-out contact response? Does a generative head retain informa-
tion needed by a new query? Does selective prediction save computation without making action
ranking less reliable? Longer horizons and richer modalities should be assessed at matched re-
source budgets, with prediction errors decomposed by mechanism. These tests can reveal when
an interface is missing information, when a transition is wrong, and when extra detail simply does
not help the task.
A persistent challenge is deciding what must remain explicit across abstraction levels. A coarse
state may encode that liquid will spill, while a fine field predicts where it flows. The two outputs
should refer to the same container, contents, and boundary conditions. Learned refinement must
recover detail compatible with the coarse state, not silently revise the initial condition until a pre-
ferred prediction becomes possible. The model may retain raw evidence or an external memory
so that a new query can request information omitted from its current compact state. This makes
memory retrieval and adaptive resolution part of world modeling, rather than equating longer
token context with a sufficient physical state.
A second challenge is modular identification. If a prediction fails, the system should distinguish
a wrong observation interpretation, an incorrect physical parameter, a missing interaction mecha-
nism, and an inadequate decision objective. Composable models make these distinctions easier to
test when their interfaces have clear semantics. A monolithic model can offer the same diagnos-
tic access through controlled readouts and interventions. The long-term comparison is therefore
not simply modular versus end-to-end. It is how reliably a system can localize error, acquire the
evidence needed to correct it, and preserve previously valid knowledge at an acceptable cost.
5.5.3
Closing the Real-World Loop: Real-Time Operation, Transfer, and Continual Improvement
A deployed world model participates in a continuing loop among observation, understanding,
prediction, action, and external feedback. It may help identify an uncertain state, propose infor-
mative experiments, screen candidate actions, or supply imagined experience for policy learning.
The physical process then produces evidence that the model did not choose. This separation be-
tween internal imagination and external verification is essential. Repeated agreement between a
126


generator and an evaluator sharing its assumptions does not establish improved knowledge of the
world.
Real-time operation requires allocating computation while the environment continues to change.
Cached context, asynchronous experts, selective decoding, and short action chunks can reduce
particular costs, but each creates a responsibility for freshness and correction. Transfer adds another
problem. A new body, tool, sensor, or process can change what an action means. Reusable physical
knowledge should be separated from the local parameters and interfaces that require new evidence.
Systems such as InternW0 and InternW0-∆show concrete ways to separate training and runtime
work, not a guarantee that one update schedule transfers unchanged to every physical system.
Continual improvement should use diagnosis to choose the scale of an update. Fresh evidence may
be enough to correct the current belief. Repeated discrepancies may justify identifying a small set of
physical parameters. A persistent missing mechanism may require new data and network retrain-
ing. These responses should be recorded separately, together with the amount of real interaction,
human intervention, and computation required. Updating every model after every observation can
be wasteful, while never updating parameters can leave systematic errors unresolved.
A practical improvement cycle retains real failures and corrections, selects data that target identi-
fied gaps, updates the relevant model or policy components, and evaluates the candidate version
on both new conditions and a retained regression suite. Synthetic rollouts can broaden practice
near a known weakness, but acceptance must include evidence not produced by the same model.
Replay and parameter regularization can help retain previous skills. They must still be checked for
interference and loss of adaptability. Chapter 4 treats the data-side loop, while the present chapter
specifies the predictive interfaces whose validity must survive each update.
The long-term aim extends beyond more elaborate imagined worlds. It is a system in which bet-
ter representations produce more informative forecasts, forecasts support better real interventions,
and the resulting evidence produces measurable correction. Progress should be reported through
predictive accuracy, physical consistency, calibrated uncertainty, and improved physical outcomes,
together with the costs of training, adaptation, operation, and recovery. This closes the chapter’s
organizing chain from state and transition to query and evidence.
These challenges converge on a single claim about priorities. Perception models tell an agent what
is present. Policy models tell it what to do. A world model has the potential to help an agent un-
derstand what will happen, what would have happened instead, and why. In this sense the world
model is one of the most important foundation models of Physical AI, providing a substrate on
which perception, decision, and control can all stand. Its importance lies in the potential to connect
testable predictions of the world with better decisions. More accurate predictions of task-relevant
dynamics can support safer exploration, cheaper learning, and more reliable decisions across tasks
and embodiments. For a world model to support decisions, its predictions need sufficient accuracy
at the relevant resolution. Building machines that act in the world therefore depends, to a large
extent, on building models of it and on making the limits of their evidence and predictions explicit.
127


6
Foundation Models for Robot Manipulation
Physical AI not only discusses how to perceive the world dynamics, but also instructs robots to
actually interact with it. In robotics, manipulation is one of the important forms of physical action,
which includes grasping, moving, assembling, and transforming objects through controlled con-
tact, and beyond. This chapter examines foundation models for robot manipulation, which are the
core of an embodied system that maps multimodal observations and task instructions to behavioral
goals or low-level motor actions. Because open-ended environments present an unbounded vari-
ety of objects and tasks, engineering each manipulation skill individually is impractical. Instead,
foundation models learn web-scale multimodal priors from physical robot trajectories, enabling a
single pretrained model to be reused across tasks, environments and embodiments.
The chapter begins with the evolution of manipulation foundation models, focusing on the vision-
language-action (VLA) architectures that dominate current practice.
It then examines the pre-
training and post-training that shape the model’s capabilities, the model’s adaptation across em-
bodiments, and its deployment under real-time and resource constraints. It closes by applying
these ideas to multi-fingered hands, where high-dimensional actuation, intricate contact transi-
tions, and scarce demonstration data push every stage of the pipeline to its limits.

6.1
Emergence and Taxonomy
An embodied agent should transform an instruction into a sequence of physically meaningful de-
cisions. Recognizing a bottle is only one part of opening it. The agent must identify the requested
outcome, choose a grasp and an opening strategy, interpret resistance during contact, and deter-
mine whether the cap has actually been released. Foundation models for robot manipulation aim
to make these capabilities reusable across tasks, objects, environments and sometimes even bodies.
They bring together multimodal representation learning, generalist robot policies and models of ac-
tion consequences. Figure 6.1 provides an overview of foundation models for robot manipulation.
The key question is how broadly acquired knowledge can guide ongoing physical interactions.
128


6.1.1
Conceptual Scope and Enabling Conditions
In this chapter, a foundation model for robot manipulation is a pretrained model that can adapt to
new tasks. It draws on multimodal evidence and task context to make task-relevant decisions, set
behavioral goals, or generate robot actions. The foundation model property concerns the reuse of
learned structure. A single model should provide a useful starting point for many downstream
tasks or operating conditions. Neither a large parameter count nor a natural-language interface
establishes this property on its own.
Let ot denote exteroceptive observations, qt denote proprioceptive measurements, at denote an
action at the model’s declared control interface, ℓlang denote a task instruction, and e describe the
embodiment. The interaction history is defined as follows.

output a subgoal gt, a skill identifier, a program, or a constraint on the desired interaction. These
outputs are different interfaces to physical behavior, and should not be treated as interchangeable.
An instruction to “grasp the bottle” leaves substantially more work to downstream modules than
a sequence of end-effector poses or joint targets.
Four developments have made this reuse practical. Vision-language pretraining supplies broad
semantic representations. Increasingly diverse robot datasets provide action-grounded supervi-
sion. Sequence and generative models capture temporal and multimodal behavior. Training infras-
tructure and simulation make repeated optimization and controlled data variation feasible. These
conditions are complementary. Additional computation cannot recover action semantics that were
never recorded, and simulated diversity is useful only to the extent that learned behavior transfers
to the target physical conditions.
The distinction from adjacent chapters follows these interfaces. The perception models of Chapter 3
extract task-relevant evidence from observations, while Chapter 4 addresses the data that support
learning. The world models of Chapter 5 represent conditional evolution and answer questions
about possible consequences. Foundation models for robot manipulation use evidence and predic-
tive knowledge to decide what behavior to pursue. The foundation models for whole-body motor
control discussed in Chapter 7 regulate the realization of that behavior under body dynamics and
contact constraints. One network may implement several of these functions, and a VLA model
may extend into motion generation. The distinction concerns the responsibility of an output, not
the size, name, or location of a network. Chapter 8 then considers how these capabilities are assem-
bled into agents that manage memory, tools, and extended activities.
For example, during cap opening, task reasoning first identifies which bottle to open and what the
desired open state is. Prediction then estimates what will happen if the agent grasps and rotates
it. Action generation proposes a motion, and local control adjusts that motion based on contact
feedback. The same tactile event may cause either a local correction, such as reducing grip force, or
a task-level revision, such as regrasping. Effective coordination therefore requires feedback in both
directions.

A second development is the transfer of semantic knowledge from language and vision-language
pretraining. In modular systems, a language model can select grounded skills or generate programs
that invoke perception and control functions. SayCan and Code as Policies illustrate these two
approaches (Ichter et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2023a). In direct action models, Zitkovich et al. (2023)
incorporate robot action prediction into vision-language training with RT-2, and Kim et al. (2025b)
release OpenVLA as a pretrained VLM-based policy available for adaptation. This kind of transfer
can broaden object and instruction understanding, but it does not supply the missing dynamics or
contact experience of an unfamiliar robot.
A third development focuses on temporal structure and continuous behavior. Diffusion Policy
demonstrates multimodal action-sequence generation for visuomotor control, Octo combines a
generalist policy with adaptable observation and action interfaces, and π0 connects a pretrained
VLM to a flow-based action expert (Chi et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025a). These
designs make a useful distinction between the representation needed to understand a scene and
the computation needed to generate a coherent trajectory. They also show that a foundation model
for robotics need not be an autoregressive language model throughout.
Finally, broad pretraining is increasingly connected with heterogeneous supervision and deploy-
ment experience. π0.5 studies open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training, while
the RECAP approach underlying π∗
0.6 uses experience and corrections to improve a pretrained pol-
icy (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025; Amin et al., 2026). The progression is consequently not a
simple replacement of control by larger language models. It is the integration of semantic pri-
ors, physical action interfaces, predictive representations, and feedback-driven improvement. Each
component addresses a different limitation of demonstration-only learning.
6.1.3
Major Model Lineages and Architectural Evolution
The main model lineages can be compared along the three axes of primary knowledge source,
learning objective, and decision interface. Generalist policies emphasize reusable behavior learned
from robot trajectories. VLAs introduce broad vision-language knowledge into action generation.
And world-action models couple behavior with predictions of environmental change. Table 6.1
summarizes these emphases. The categories overlap. A generalist policy can be a VLA, and a VLA
can contain a world model. Direct, hierarchical, and prediction-assisted execution are architectural
choices that cut across all three lineages.

Unified World Models
Generalist Robot Policies
These policies learn primarily from collections of robot trajectories,
usually conditioned on language, goal images, or task identifiers. Shared training allows reaching,
grasping, placing, and other recurring structures to contribute to multiple tasks. RT-X explores such
sharing across embodiments, and Octo provides a policy initialization that can be adapted to new
observation and action spaces (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024; Ghosh et al., 2024). Gen-
erality here comes from how broadly the behavior covers and transfers, not from conversational
ability. Language may serve as a conditioning representation without making the policy itself a
pretrained language model. The main limitation is coverage. Robot trajectories provide physically
grounded actions but are costly to collect and can be concentrated in a few environments or control
interfaces.
Vision-Language-Action Models
These models connect visual observations and linguistic goals
with a declared action space. A prominent route initializes the policy from a pretrained VLM so
that the policy does not have to learn object knowledge and instruction semantics entirely from
robot demonstrations. Action supervision then grounds that knowledge in the robot’s control in-
terface. The phrase VLA specifies a multimodal policy interface more clearly than it specifies a
single architecture. Discrete autoregression, deterministic regression, diffusion, and flow matching
are alternative ways of producing actions within this broad class. Their differences concern pre-
cision, multimodality, learning signals, and execution cost, as developed in Section 6.2. Semantic
transfer is especially useful for interpreting an unfamiliar instruction, but successful interpretation
still requires a motor repertoire capable of realizing it.
Predictive and Joint World-Action Models
A world model can choose actions in several ways,
including evaluating proposed actions, generating subgoal observations, or sharing a represen-
tation with a policy. Joint video-action modeling, illustrated by Unified World Models, couples
predictive and behavioral learning (Zhu et al., 2025). These couplings should be distinguished.
A model that predicts a future image that appears to satisfy the task goal does not thereby show
that the robot can reach that image. Likewise, predicting a future and an action together does
not automatically provide a calibrated answer to every counterfactual action query. The benefit of
prediction must be demonstrated through better decisions or more transferable representations.

can supervise the predictive component while action-labeled robot data ground executable deci-
sions. This is a potential advantage of joint learning, but the missing robot actions in human video
cannot be recovered merely by renaming visual motion as an action. Viewpoint, embodiment, and
unobserved forces still constrain transfer.

Architectures for Organizing Decisions
A direct policy maps the current task context straight
to actions. A hierarchical system exposes subgoals or skills between task reasoning and motion
generation. A prediction-assisted system brings anticipated outcomes into learning or action se-
lection. Language and program-mediated planners can compose existing behaviors, provided that
their calls are grounded in perception, skill preconditions, and execution feedback. A higher-level
process can also maintain context while a faster process updates motion using recent observations.
GR00T N1 provides an example of tightly coupled vision-language and action-generation mod-
ules (NVIDIA et al., 2025c). Gemini Robotics 1.5 illustrates the coordination of embodied reasoning
with action capabilities (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025). Architectural separation does not mean
asynchronous execution. Whether modules run independently, share cached features, or wait at
synchronization points is a deployment property that must be specified separately.
Connecting Policy, Prediction, and Evaluation
The relationships among these arrangements can
be expressed with the following shared task representation and three possible output interfaces

Here zt summarizes available evidence, the policy proposes behavior, the transition model predicts
its consequences, and the evaluator estimates a task-related quantity. Not every system contains all
three heads, and the equations do not require shared parameters. They distinguish functions that
are often conflated in discussion of unified models.
There are several ways to connect them. A policy may use a predicted subgoal as conditioning,
a planner may score sampled action chunks through a world model, or predictive training may
improve an encoder that is used without online rollout. In a joint generative model, what the model
samples (an action, a future observation, or both) depends on how it is conditioned and masked.
Each choice changes which questions can be asked at inference time and which computational costs
lie on the control path.
Evaluation also requires precise semantics. A progress score estimates how far an observed process
has advanced. A success classifier estimates whether a terminal criterion holds. A value function
estimates future return under a specified policy and reward. A model trained for one of these
tasks is not automatically a substitute for the others. During cap opening, observing rotation may
indicate motion without demonstrating release. Outcome feedback must therefore be grounded in
the property the task actually requires.
Interpreting Generalization Claims
Embodied generalization has several independent dimen-
sions. A model may transfer to new object appearances while still relying on the same workspace
and robot. It might understand a new composition of familiar instructions while lacking the cor-
responding motor skill. Or it might adapt to a new embodiment only after target demonstrations.
Claims should specify which factors change and which remain fixed. In particular, zero-shot exe-
cution, few-shot adaptation, and large-scale fine-tuning are distinct capabilities.
Closed-loop evaluation should test the decisions that make reuse valuable, including selecting the
intended object among distractors, completing unfamiliar combinations of known stages, revising
behavior after a disturbance, and transferring with a stated amount of new data. A useful experi-
mental design varies task, environment, and embodiment separately before testing their combina-
tion. Retaining performance on previously supported conditions matters as much as improvement
on the new condition. Offline action prediction error alone cannot establish these properties be-
cause it does not measure the states visited by the executing policy.
The remainder of this chapter follows the resulting development path. Section 6.2 examines ac-
tion representations and multimodal architectures. Section 6.3 explains how different supervision
132


sources shape capabilities. Section 6.4 addresses the physical meaning of transfer between bod-
ies. Section 6.5 then asks how these capabilities can be delivered within the timing and resource
constraints of an actual robot.
6.2
Vision-Language-Action Model
Many current VLA models start from a pretrained VLM and extend it to output actions, a modality
its pretraining never covered. This section begins with how actions are represented and generated,
then turns to how they are combined with visual and linguistic inputs in a single sequence model,
and closes with how this model is extended to sensory inputs beyond images and language.
6.2.1
Action Representation and Generation
Within a VLA, action is treated as a third modality alongside images and language, although it
behaves quite differently from both. Actions are continuous rather than symbolic, their dimen-
sionality and control rate vary with the embodiment, and consecutive actions are sampled at high
frequency and are strongly correlated. Since action is also the model’s output, how it is represented
decides both how demonstrations are encoded during training and how commands are decoded at
run time. Writing at ∈Rd for the action at step t and Aseq

= [a⊤

motion, and spreads the cost of one forward pass over H control steps. Existing methods fall into
two families according to how Aseq

efficiency, inference speed and the preservation of the pre-trained VLM in opposite ways, which is
why recent hybrid schemes combine discrete training with continuous execution.

This requires no change to the VLM architecture, and since robot data and web data are trained with
the same loss, the backbone remains a language model shaped by both. The methods differ mainly
in the tokenizer that produces zact
1:Nacttok. The simplest, per-dimension binning, splits each action di-
mension into a fixed number of uniform bins (256 in RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2023), RT-2 (Zitkovich et al.,
2023) and OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2025b)). RT-2 writes the bin indices as text, so the VLM outputs an
action as a string of integers, while OpenVLA reassigns the least-used tokens of the Llama vocab-
ulary to action bins. Binning is easy to implement but scales poorly, because a chunk becomes
H · d tokens that must be decoded one after another, neighboring tokens at high control rates
are nearly identical and therefore carry little learning signal, and precision can never exceed the
bin width. Compression-based tokenization turns this redundancy into an advantage. FAST (Pertsch
et al., 2025) applies a discrete cosine transform to each action dimension, quantizes the coefficients
so that most high-frequency ones become zero, and compresses the result with byte-pair encod-
ing. The resulting sequences are much shorter than those produced by binning, the same tokenizer
transfers across embodiments, and π0-FAST reaches the performance of the flow-matching π0 with
less training compute. Learned quantizers take a different approach and train a vector-quantized
autoencoder (van den Oord et al., 2017) whose codebook entries act as short motion primitives.
Residual vector quantization (RVQ) increases resolution by quantizing the remaining error over
several stages, and VQ-VLA (Wang et al., 2025b) shows that training the tokenizer on more real
and simulated trajectories improves both long-horizon success and smoothness. The price is an
embodiment-specific decoder that has to be deployed together with the policy. Sequential autore-
gressive decoding of long action-token chunks through a billion-parameter backbone can incur
133


substantial inference latency. Parallel decoding in OpenVLA-OFT (Kim et al., 2025a) predicts all
action tokens in a single pass and thus raises throughput, but it no longer models the joint distri-
bution over tokens explicitly.

avoid action-bin quantization and can represent multimodal action distributions. Compact action
expert modules and a small number of sampling steps can make inference efficient. However, in
the cited VLA comparisons, training with a continuous action expert converges more slowly than
autoregressive action-token training, and gradients from a randomly initialized expert can inter-
fere with the pretrained backbone. Gradient control and co-training with VLM data mitigate this
interference in the reported settings (Driess et al., 2025). Co-training with web data, or interleaving
actions with language reasoning, also requires additional machinery. It is therefore natural to use
tokens for learning and continuous generation for execution, and several recent systems combine
the two in this way. π0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) pre-trains the whole model autoregres-
sively on FAST tokens and adds a flow-matching expert only during post-training, where it opti-
mizes L = LAR + αmixLFM with the two action representations masked from each other. At run
time the model first decodes text and then runs a few denoising steps of the expert. Knowledge in-
sulation (Driess et al., 2025) merges the two stages into one. The backbone is trained on FAST tokens
and vision-language data while a stop-gradient prevents the flow-matching loss from reaching it.
The reported model trains faster, runs faster, and generalizes better than either pure route. These
systems point toward a division of labor in which discrete tokens shape the backbone’s representa-
tion and a lightweight continuous generator handles control. Which tokenizer shapes the backbone
best, and how the two representations should be scheduled across pre-training, post-training and
continual learning, are still open questions.

Components
Both structures in Figure 6.3 share three components. The first is a vision encoder,
usually the SigLIP or DINOv2 vision transformer (ViT) inherited from the VLM, which maps each
camera image to a few hundred patch tokens. When there are several views, each is encoded
separately and the tokens are concatenated. The second is a vision-language backbone, typically
a decoder-only transformer with 2 to 7 billion parameters in open models (Llama 2, Qwen-VL,
PaliGemma) and a frontier-scale model in closed systems, which processes the image tokens to-
gether with the tokenized instruction and produces the representation from which actions are read
out. The third is an action output module, one of the heads described in Section 6.2.1, which turns this
representation into an action chunk. Discrete action tokens need nothing beyond the backbone’s
own language-model head, as in RT-2 and OpenVLA, whereas current generalist VLAs mostly fol-
low the continuous route and add a smaller action expert trained with flow matching or diffusion.
Proprioceptive state qt enters alongside them, either as discretized tokens in the prefix or through a
small embodiment-specific multilayer perceptron (MLP), and other sensing modalities are deferred
to Section 6.2.3.
Two Mainstream Structures
With a continuous expert in place, the key architectural question be-
comes how the expert reads from the backbone, and current VLAs answer it in one of two ways
(Figure 6.3). In a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) design (π0 (Black et al., 2025a), π0.5 (Physical Intelli-
gence et al., 2025), LingBot-VLA (Wu et al., 2026b), InternVLA-A1 (Cai et al., 2026a)), the expert is
a narrower transformer with the same depth as the backbone. The two keep separate weights but
share a single self-attention operation in every layer, so the action tokens simply form another block
of the same sequence and read the backbone’s keys and values layer by layer (Figure 6.3a). This
gives the tightest possible coupling, since the expert can draw on every level of the backbone’s
representation and the backbone’s language-model head remains available for reasoning text or
FAST tokens in the same sequence. The downside is that the expert is bound to the backbone’s
depth and clock, and its gradients reach every backbone layer, which is what knowledge insula-
135


tion (Driess et al., 2025) is designed to stop. In a cross-attention design (GR00T N1 (NVIDIA et al.,
2025c), SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025), InternVLA-M1 (Chen et al., 2025b)), the expert is a separate
diffusion transformer (DiT) over state and action tokens that reads backbone token-feature ma-
trix HVLM
t
through cross-attention layers interleaved with self-attention (Figure 6.3b). The position
and width of this interface are then free design choices, and published systems make them differ-
ently. GR00T N1 conditions its DiT on middle-layer rather than final-layer features of the VLM, and
SmolVLA keeps only the lower half of a small VLM’s layers so that the whole model has just 0.45B
parameters. InternVLA-M1 inserts a querying transformer whose learnable queries cross-attend to
intermediate layers of a 3B VLM, passes the resulting fixed set of tokens to an 86M diffusion action
expert, and attenuates the expert’s gradients before they reach the backbone. Decoupling allows
the expert to be sized and clocked independently of the VLM, which dual-system layouts exploit
by running a slow VLM above a fast expert, as GR00T N1 does. The price is a narrower channel,
because the expert sees the backbone only through the features or queries it is given and does not
take part in the backbone’s own attention. In practice, MoT is preferred when the expert and the
backbone are trained jointly on one sequence, and cross-attention when the expert has to be small,
fast or run at its own rate.

before it and bidirectionally within itself, since all H actions are produced together, but no earlier
block attends to the suffix. This keeps the prefix key-value cache independent of the actions, so
that it can be reused across denoising steps. A cross-attention design arrives at the same structure
by construction, because the backbone processes only the prefix and the reasoning block while the
expert processes the suffix and reads the backbone through cross-attention. Here too the backbone
features are computed once per observation and reused across denoising steps. When discrete
and continuous representations coexist in training, as in π0.5 (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) and
knowledge insulation (Driess et al., 2025), the two suffixes are additionally masked from each other
so that the flow expert cannot copy the FAST tokens.
Development
The template described above takes shape over several years. RT-1 (Brohan et al.,
2023) predates the use of VLMs but sets conventions that later work retains. A transformer with
35 million parameters, trained on about 130,000 teleoperated episodes from 13 robots, learns to
follow several hundred instructions. Its actions are discretized into 256 bins per dimension and
emitted as tokens. Its generalization grows with the breadth of tasks and robots rather than with
model size. RT-2 (Zitkovich et al., 2023) then co-fine-tunes internet-scale VLMs (PaLI-X 55B, PaLM-
E 12B (Driess et al., 2023)) on web data together with robot episodes whose actions are written
as integer strings, and the resulting policy generalizes semantically in ways that no robot dataset
could have taught it, for instance picking up the object “that could be used as a hammer”. RT-2,
however, is neither open nor backed by shared data. Open X-Embodiment (Open X-Embodiment
Collaboration, 2024) addresses the data gap by pooling 60 datasets from 22 embodiments into more
than a million episodes and showing positive transfer across robots, and OpenVLA (Kim et al.,
2025b) addresses openness by releasing a 7B open-weight policy trained on this corpus.
The current generation keeps this foundation but adopts continuous action experts and trains on
data far beyond public collections, and its progress has come on three fronts. The first front is scale,
136


starting with π0 (Black et al., 2025a), which pairs a 3B PaliGemma backbone with a 300M flow-
matching expert and trains it on roughly 10k hours of data from 7 robot configurations. π0.5 (Phys-
ical Intelligence et al., 2025) adds heterogeneous co-training and subtask prediction, which allows
the same policy to work in homes that had not appeared in its training data, GR-3 (Cheang et al.,
2025) reproduces the template on a Qwen2.5-VL backbone, and LingBot-VLA (Wu et al., 2026b)
reports steady gains as its bimanual data grow from 3k to 20k hours, with no sign of saturation.
The second front is hierarchical control, motivated by whole-body and long-horizon tasks for which
a single synchronous model is too slow. GR00T N1 (NVIDIA et al., 2025c) establishes the open
dual-system template for humanoids, with a 2B VLM feeding a diffusion transformer that runs at
120 Hz, and the Gemini Robotics series (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025) pairs a frontier VLA
with a separate embodied-reasoning model that plans in natural language and orchestrates the
VLA.
On the third front, supervision has moved beyond imitation. π∗
0.6 (Amin et al., 2026) learns from
its own deployment experience through reinforcement learning, while π0.7 (Physical Intelligence
et al., 2026) conditions on subgoal images generated by a world model and shows early signs of
compositional generalization to tasks that have no demonstrations in its training data. InternVLA-
A1 (Cai et al., 2026a) unifies understanding, future-frame generation and action in one mixture-
of-transformers, and its successor InternVLA-A1.5 (Ma et al., 2026a) replaces explicit future-frame
generation with a small set of learnable foresight tokens supervised by a frozen pre-trained video
generator, so that the policy inherits the generator’s dynamics priors while the video branch is dis-
carded at inference. X-VLA (Zheng et al., 2026a) shows that a 0.9B transformer with embodiment-
specific soft prompts can match far larger models. Overall, the field has settled on the template
and the two structures described above, and the main axis of scaling has moved from parameters,
with open-weight VLAs still at 1 to 7B, to data, which now amounts to tens of thousands of hours
supplemented by human video, synthetic trajectories and autonomous experience.
6.2.3
Extending Multimodal Inputs
Images and language are the default inputs of a VLA because they are the modalities used for VLM
pretraining, but they leave out much of what manipulation depends on, such as events preceding
the current frame, how far away objects are, and what happens at the moment of contact. An
additional input can enter the sequence of Section 6.2.2 in one of two places. It can be added to the
prefix as extra tokens that the backbone attends to together with images and text, or it can be given to
the suffix and the action module as a conditioning input that bypasses the backbone. Writing mmulti
t
and mmulti′
t

Multiple camera views, including the wrist camera, are already handled by the vision encoder as
described in Section 6.2.2, and proprioceptive state qt usually takes the second route, so the rest of
this section reviews three further extensions, namely temporal history, 3D geometry and contact.
Temporal History and Memory
Most VLAs condition only on the current frame, even though
many tasks depend on the past, for example when the arm hides the target, when an object has
been placed under a container, or when the robot must keep track of which stages of a task are
already done. Concatenating past frames into the prefix, as Octo (Ghosh et al., 2024) does, brings
sharply diminishing returns beyond one extra frame while adding hundreds of tokens per frame
and view, and it also invites causal confusion (de Haan et al., 2019), in which the policy copies
the behavior implied by past observations instead of reacting to the current one. Longer mem-
ory therefore comes down to compression, and two recent systems approach it in different ways.
137


MEM (Torne et al., 2026), which underlies π0.6 (Amin et al., 2026) and π0.7 (Physical Intelligence
et al., 2026), keeps memory inside the sequence at two time scales. Over the short term, a video
encoder compresses recent frames, packing six of them into the token budget of a single frame
in π0.7. Over the long term, a high-level policy rewrites a natural-language summary at every
step and places it in the reasoning slot rreason
t
, which supports tasks that require up to 15 minutes
of memory. RoboTTT (Jiang et al., 2026) instead moves memory out of the sequence and into the
weights. Its test-time training layers update a small fast-weight network with one gradient step per
timestep, so history is stored in these weights and inference cost stays constant however long the
context becomes. With this design the context reaches 8K timesteps, or about 5 minutes, and pre-
training with an 8K-timestep context outperforms pre-training with 1K timesteps, which suggests
that context length may be a scaling axis for robot policies just as it is for language models.
3D Information
An RGB image projects the scene onto a plane, so grasp height, clearance and
relative depth must be inferred, whereas depth sensors and point clouds supply this geometry
directly. The most direct way to use this geometry is to feed it into the model. SpatialVLA (Qu
et al., 2025) turns depth from a monocular estimator into 3D positional encodings for the image
tokens, while PointVLA (Li et al., 2026a) converts point clouds into native 3D tokens that only the
action module consumes. Explicit geometry improves precision on spatially demanding tasks, but
the 3D encoder lacks web-scale pre-training, and commodity depth sensors fail on transparent and
reflective objects. Spatial Forcing (Li et al., 2026b) takes a second route and uses geometry only as a
training signal. Having found that the visual tokens of an RGB-trained VLA carry little recoverable
depth structure, it aligns an intermediate layer of these tokens with the features that the geometry
foundation model VGGT (Wang et al., 2025a) extracts from the same images. Since VGGT is needed
only during training, inference is unchanged, and training nevertheless becomes faster and more
data-efficient, which shows that an input can shape the backbone’s representation without ever
entering its sequence.
Force and Tactile Sensing
Contact-rich tasks such as insertion, screwing and handling fragile
objects depend on forces that vision cannot observe, and the wrist camera is usually occluded at
exactly the moment of contact. Contact information can enter a VLA in three ways. Images from
vision-based tactile sensors such as GelSight (Yuan et al., 2017) can be fed to the vision encoder
as an additional view, albeit across a domain gap. Force-torque readings (Cao et al., 2021) can
be treated like proprioception and placed in the suffix. And dedicated tactile encoders that cover
several sensor types, such as Sparsh (Higuera et al., 2025), can produce tokens for the backbone.
Tactile-VLA (Huang et al., 2025a) follows the token route, fusing tactile tokens with vision and
language inside the VLM and outputting target positions and forces for a hybrid position-force
controller, whereas ForceVLA (Yu et al., 2025b) follows the conditioning route, fusing force-torque
tokens with VLM features in a mixture-of-experts module on the action path. TA-VLA (Zhang
et al., 2025d), a systematic study of torque inputs, comes out in favor of the conditioning route for
such signals, finding that torque helps more in the action decoder than in the encoder and that a
torque history summarized into a single token works best.
6.3
Pre-Training, Post-Training, and Capability Shaping
Figure 6.4 summarizes the overall training pipeline for embodied VLA models, which proceeds
through three stages. Pre-training uses multi-source data to learn general representations and be-
havioral priors. Supervised post-training, including SFT, turns these priors into executable policies.
Reinforcement learning-based post-training, including RFT, improves the policy through action
outcomes. The remainder of this section discusses each stage in turn and then addresses continual
learning, which converts deployment experience into lasting capabilities (Figure 6.5).

Fig. 6.4 Overview of the embodied VLA training pipeline. Pre-training combines multi-source data
under multi-task objectives to produce a VLA base model. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) during

ulation. Embodied pretraining must integrate language, visual inputs, robot proprioceptive states,
actions, and task outcomes within a common temporal framework, enabling the model to learn
relationships among instructions, states, actions, and outcomes. Conditioned on observation histo-
ries, previous actions, task instructions, and embodiment characteristics, the model learns how to
select actions in the current state. Observations may include not only RGB images but also depth,
tactile measurements, force and torque readings, joint states, and equipment telemetry.
Embodiment characteristics include degrees of freedom, end-effector type, control frequency,
workspace, and action limits. Explicitly incorporating these conditions helps distinguish shared
task structure from embodiment-specific execution mechanisms, providing a basis for transfer
across tasks and robot platforms.
Different data sources offer complementary supervision. Internet image-text data provide seman-
tic knowledge about objects, scenes, and tasks. Videos of human activity reveal action sequences,
tool use, and state transitions. Robot demonstrations supply action labels associated with spe-
cific control interfaces. And simulated interactions provide relatively inexpensive data on contact,
forces, collisions, and failures that are difficult to collect at scale. Mixing these sources is intended
to combine semantic, temporal, and physical information, rather than merely increase the number
of training examples.
This complementarity also offers a way to address the scarcity of labeled robot actions. Video pre-
diction, inverse dynamics, and latent action models can extract task-relevant behavioral representa-
tions from human videos, which an embodiment adaptation module can subsequently decode into
executable actions. Studies such as UniVLA (Bu et al., 2025) show that task-centered latent action
representations can exploit video data spanning different embodiments and viewpoints. Never-
theless, their physical executability still requires calibration through robot interaction. Acquiring
behavioral knowledge from human video therefore also requires aligning that knowledge with
robot control interfaces, sensor feedback, and physical outcomes.
139


To support this alignment, embodied pretraining commonly combines action prediction, language
understanding, state recognition, task progress estimation, and outcome prediction. These objec-
tives correspond to different forms of supervision available in embodied data. Consider a bottle-
opening task as an example. Action supervision specifies the robot actions needed to approach,
grasp, and rotate the cap, and is typically obtained from teleoperated or scripted demonstrations
recorded in the robot’s own action space. State supervision describes the relevant object and contact
conditions, such as the poses of the bottle and cap and whether the end effector is in contact with
the cap. In simulation these labels come from ground-truth physics, while on real robots they are
estimated by the perception stack or annotated offline. Progress supervision identifies the current
stage of the task, such as approach, grasp, rotation, release, or completion. This supervision can
be supplied by scripted stage detectors, human annotators, or a vision-language evaluator of the
kind used in reinforcement learning-based post-training. Outcome supervision indicates whether
the bottle has ultimately been opened, which can be determined from a terminal physical observa-
tion or task-specific success criterion. Language supervision associates the visual and behavioral
sequence with the task instruction, such as “open the bottle”, and is available whenever trajecto-
ries are paired with instructions or narrations. These five objectives train distinct, complementary
capabilities.
These objectives can be summarized by a weighted multi-task loss of the form
Lpre = λaLaction + λsLstate + λpLprogress + λoLoutcome + λℓlangLlanguage,
(6.7)
where the coefficients balance action learning, state understanding, progress estimation, outcome
prediction, and language supervision. This schematic loss combines objectives whose labels may
be available on different samples. Each loss is evaluated only where its supervision is available,
with missing labels handled by masking the corresponding objective.
Table 6.2 summarizes how this masking scheme applies to each data source, which objectives in
Eq. (6.7) it can support, and which model components the resulting gradients primarily update.
Because available supervision varies by data source, the same foundation model is trained by ap-
plying different subsets of the objectives to different data sources. The resulting training process
aligns semantic, temporal, state, and action representations without requiring a homogeneous label
space across the entire dataset.

How such multi-task, multi-embodiment data are curated, balanced, and mixture-weighted is a
data engineering question treated in Chapter 4. This section examines how the composition of the
mixture enters optimization. On the training side, a curriculum may progress from short-horizon
skills with limited contact to multistage tasks, perturbed states, and failure recovery, and it should
specify success and failure boundaries so that the model learns when to continue execution, acquire
new observations, or terminate safely. As action learning progresses, retaining existing multimodal
knowledge becomes an additional concern. When an action expert is connected to a pretrained
vision-language backbone, gradient updates from action learning may interfere with established
semantic representations. Staged unfreezing, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, gradient isolation,
and knowledge distillation can help preserve language understanding and visual knowledge while
new action capabilities are acquired. The heterogeneous joint training used in π0.5 and the Knowl-
edge Insulation approach illustrate this principle. Training across diverse data sources expands
task and environmental coverage while limiting interference with existing multimodal knowledge.
Pretraining should consequently be evaluated using more than training loss or offline action pre-
diction error. Evaluation should also examine closed-loop performance on unseen objects, novel
combinations of instructions, and mildly perturbed conditions. These tests assess whether shared
representations support perception, decision-making, and action under the new conditions. Pre-
training supplies an initialization for the task- and embodiment-specific adaptation discussed next.
Where the prior does not yet support the target task or embodiment, supervised post-training is
one route to consistent execution. Outcome-based adaptation provides another, as developed be-
low. Some pipelines also introduce an explicit alignment stage between broad pretraining and task
adaptation. Section 6.6.2 examines these choices for dexterous hands through EgoScale on Sharpa
Wave.
6.3.2
Supervised Post-Training: From General Priors to Executable Policies
Supervised post-training uses expert demonstrations, teleoperation trajectories, task procedures,
and high-quality simulated data to adapt general behavioral priors to specific tasks, embodiments,
and environments. Behavioral cloning increases the likelihood of expert actions conditioned on ob-
servations, task instructions, and embodiment characteristics, bringing the policy closer to the be-
havioral distribution represented in the demonstrations. Its effectiveness depends first on whether
demonstrations cover the complete task. Training examples should include task initiation, critical
contacts, transitions between stages, completion verification, and safe termination, rather than be-
ing restricted to locally standardized actions extracted from successful trajectories. For multistep
tasks, stage labels, subgoals, and outcome criteria should also be recorded to support learning of
temporal relationships among actions.
Adaptation to a new task or embodiment may then use full-parameter fine-tuning, updates
to selected modules, or parameter-efficient methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA). Full-
parameter fine-tuning offers greater scope for parameter adjustment but requires more data and
computation. Parameter-efficient methods facilitate rapid iteration, although their effectiveness
may be limited by discrepancies between the new task and existing representations. For a VLA ini-
tialized from a pretrained vision-language model, parameter-efficient adaptation has a further ben-
efit. The backbone can be kept frozen so that the semantic priors built during pre-training are pre-
served, while a small number of action-side parameters are learned. Gradient isolation during pre-
training addresses the same interference concern. Results reported for OpenVLA and Octo (Kim
et al., 2025b; Ghosh et al., 2024) indicate that large-scale multitask pretraining can substantially
reduce the data required for downstream adaptation. Performance after adaptation nevertheless
depends on appropriate treatment of sensors, action spaces, and embodiment characteristics.
Even with high-quality demonstrations, behavioral cloning faces a discrepancy between training
and deployment state distributions. Training typically uses states visited by an expert, whereas
deployment states are determined by the model’s own actions. A small localization error can cause
subsequent observations to depart from the demonstration distribution, allowing errors to com-
pound over time. Interactive dataset aggregation addresses this problem by executing the cur-
rent policy, requesting expert actions or corrections at the off-distribution states it encounters, and
141


adding these examples to the training set. DAgger exemplifies this approach to distribution shift in
sequential decision-making. For a fine-tuned VLA, the expert is typically a teleoperator who shares
the policy’s action interface, so corrective labels can be appended to the training set without retar-
geting, and interactive aggregation becomes a natural extension of demonstration collection rather
than a separate pipeline. Demonstration collection thus extends beyond recording ideal execution
to include difficult states and recovery behaviors encountered by the model itself.
Human intervention data should be differentiated according to their training function. Valid ac-
tions preceding a takeover can serve as positive demonstrations. Human corrections can provide
supervised labels for off-distribution states. And failure outcomes can support the training of suc-
cess classifiers or value models. Erroneous actions, however, should not automatically become
imitation targets. This treatment preserves both the conditions under which errors arise and the
corresponding recovery strategies, enabling supervised post-training to learn normal execution as
well as recovery to feasible states. Nevertheless, supervised post-training primarily learns condi-
tional relationships between states and actions in demonstration data. It does not directly opti-
mize completion time, energy consumption, precision, or long-term success rate. It is well suited
to establishing a stable initial policy, particularly when operating procedures are clearly defined
and expert demonstrations are of high quality, but reductions in training loss cannot substitute for
closed-loop validation on the physical system.
Validation should therefore cover instruction following, action executability, critical state transi-
tions, outcome assessment, and termination under abnormal conditions. For tasks such as liquid
transfer and precision assembly, success criteria should also incorporate mass, flow rate, applied
forces, leakage, and instrument readings, explicitly distinguishing the execution of action com-
mands from the achievement of task objectives. When a model can reliably follow procedures but
remains limited in efficiency, contact precision, or recovery from complex disturbances, feedback
from action outcomes is needed to support policy improvement beyond imitation.
6.3.3
Reinforcement Learning-Based Post-Training: Improving Policies Through Action
Outcomes
Behavioral cloning can reproduce demonstrator behavior, but its objective does not directly ad-
dress efficiency gains subject to success-rate requirements, action adjustment under changing con-
tact conditions, recovery from states outside the demonstration distribution, or improvements in
action sequences discovered through autonomous interaction. Reinforcement learning evaluates
the long-term consequences of actions through environmental feedback, enabling continued policy
improvement toward task objectives. For Physical AI, it is particularly relevant to precise contact
interactions, long-horizon tasks, disturbance recovery, and efficiency optimization. Reinforcement
learning is not, however, necessary for every task. When procedures are stable, demonstrations
provide sufficient coverage, and performance already meets requirements, supervised training and
deterministic control may be more appropriate. The decision to introduce reinforcement learning-
based post-training should depend on the limitations of the existing policy and whether environ-
mental feedback provides an effective signal for addressing them.
Compared with virtual environments, reinforcement learning on physical robots involves slow
interactions, costly resets, equipment wear, delayed rewards, and safety risks. States are often
partially observable, contact and friction exhibit discontinuities, and outcomes may also depend on
material batches, temperature, and tool condition. Large-scale random exploration in the physical
world is therefore generally impractical. Under these constraints, policy optimization typically
seeks to maximize expected cumulative return while accounting for task rewards, safety costs, and
energy consumption, with discounting controlling the relative weight of returns over different time
horizons. For physical robot tasks, this objective can be written as

where the terms represent task achievement, progress, safety cost, and energy consumption, respec-
tively. Task rewards, progress, safety constraints, and resource consumption should be recorded
142


separately to determine whether apparent gains reflect improved task performance or exploitation
of a particular metric. Safety penalties can help a policy learn risk boundaries, but they cannot
replace independent limit enforcement, collision detection, emergency stops, or human takeover
mechanisms.
Reward design must likewise guide learning while remaining verifiable against
physical outcomes. Terminal success signals are simple and reliable but too sparse for many long-
horizon tasks. Intermediate rewards can capture distance to the goal, contact quality, trajectory
error, completion time, and stage progress, yet may be exploited in ways that diverge from the
actual objective. Reward design should therefore prioritize observable, independently verifiable
physical quantities, such as changes in mass, position error, peak force, leakage status, and instru-
ment readings, and validate them against independently assessed final outcomes.
Alongside rewards, value functions estimate how current states and actions contribute to future
task outcomes, helping the policy identify behaviors with long-term benefits. Vision-language
evaluators can infer progress, completion, and stagnation from successive observations, provid-
ing denser feedback for physical robots. Such evaluators may nevertheless misclassify outcomes,
and policies may exploit evaluation biases through reward hacking. Calibration against physical
outcomes is therefore necessary. VLAC (Zhai et al., 2025) illustrates an approach that uses vision-
language models for progress estimation and asynchronous reinforcement learning on real robots.
These methods broaden the sources of feedback while reinforcing the need to cross-check interme-
diate evaluations against final outcomes.
For a fine-tuned VLA, a practical pipeline begins offline. The demonstrations, successful and failed
trajectories, and human corrections already accumulated during supervised post-training form the
dataset from which values are estimated and a policy is derived, reducing the risks of physical
exploration. A subsequent online stage can collect a limited amount of autonomous execution
data, focusing on states associated with model uncertainty, repeated failures, or high informational
value. Training should constrain the policy from deviating excessively from behaviors supported
by the data, thereby limiting overly optimistic value estimates for actions absent from the dataset.
Human intervention can also be adjusted as the policy improves. Takeovers can prevent hazardous
exploration early in training, corrective actions can address difficult states at intermediate stages,
and later interventions can be confined to infrequent anomalies. HIL-SERL (Luo et al., 2025) com-
bines demonstrations, reward classifiers, and progressively reduced human intervention to im-
prove the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning on physical robots, illustrating the comple-
mentary roles of demonstrations, autonomous interaction, and human correction.
For large VLA models, conventional online policy-gradient methods such as PPO (Schulman et al.,
2017) often entail substantial sample requirements and challenges in training stability. An alter-
native is to collect experience in batches and update the policy between collection rounds. The
RECAP method used in π∗
0.6 (Amin et al., 2026) integrates autonomous execution outcomes, hu-
man corrections, and existing demonstrations within iterative offline reinforcement learning. It
estimates advantages using a value function and then derives an improved policy through advan-
tage conditioning. This approach illustrates how reinforcement learning on physical robots can
alternate between batch data collection, offline policy updates, and validation on the robot, with-
out modifying model parameters after every action. The same workflow supports independent
validation between updates to determine whether policy improvements persist during physical
execution.
To further reduce physical interaction costs, world models can compare the short-term conse-
quences of candidate actions before execution, helping to screen out behaviors likely to cause colli-
sions, slippage, leakage, or task failure. They can also generate supplementary experience in simu-
lation or latent space. However, world models are subject to modeling errors, which a policy may
exploit to obtain inflated estimates of return. They are therefore useful for candidate evaluation,
risk prediction, and data augmentation, but cannot replace physical outcome measurements, low-
level controllers, or independent safety mechanisms. Regardless of the training approach, evalu-
ation should report success rate, completion time, precision, failure recovery rate, the number of
physical interactions, human intervention rate, and the number of safety incidents. Improvements
beyond demonstration performance can be established only when gains persist on independent
143


test tasks and under physical disturbances. Retaining and extending those gains during long-term
deployment additionally requires continual learning.
6.3.4
Continual Learning: Turning Deployment Experience into Lasting Capabilities
Long-term deployment exposes embodied agents to situations that cannot be fully anticipated dur-
ing pretraining or post-training. The resulting need for continued adaptation can be understood
in light of Sutton’s Big World Hypothesis. As Javed and Sutton (2024) articulate, many decision-
making environments are far larger and more complex than an agent’s perceptual, representational,
and computational resources can accommodate. An agent must therefore act on an incomplete un-
derstanding of its environment, learning and revising the knowledge most relevant to its current
decisions rather than relying on an exhaustive representation of all possible states and optimal ac-
tions. For embodied systems, this perspective provides a rationale for continual learning. Capabil-
ities acquired before deployment provide an initial basis for action, but must be evaluated and re-
fined as interaction reveals unfamiliar states, changing task demands, and limitations of the current
policy. Such refinement must also preserve previously acquired skills that remain relevant. Sup-
porting this process requires experience records that retain the temporal, spatial, and embodiment
context of each interaction, including the model version, task instruction, sensor state, commanded
action, observed outcome, and any anomaly or human intervention. Distinguishing successful
execution, failure, warnings, takeovers, and recovery within these records allows deployment ex-
perience to inform subsequent supervised training, value estimation, and policy improvement.
As experience accumulates, the central challenge in continual learning shifts from increasing data
volume to identifying the learning value of individual experiences. Samples can be selected accord-
ing to failure frequency, model confidence, state novelty, intervention points, and environmental
changes, while balancing task value, information gain, collection cost, and risk. Recurrent grasp
slippage, for example, calls for additional data on contact states and recovery actions. Occasional
instrument anomalies require complete telemetry and procedural context, rather than a final fail-
ure label alone. Active sampling should also help identify capability boundaries, allowing the
system to distinguish tasks already mastered under current conditions from changes addressable
through context updates and changes requiring parameter updates or retraining. This distinction
links newly collected data to specific capability gaps and prevents local adaptation from being
conflated with improvements in general competence.
Clarifying the form of adaptation is also essential to managing the relationship between new and
existing capabilities. Immediate adaptation through context or memory, and runtime calibration
through updates to state estimates or embodiment parameters, do not necessarily modify the foun-
dation model. Long-term learning that changes model parameters, by contrast, requires model ver-
sion control and regression testing. As new tasks arrive and parameters are updated, catastrophic
forgetting, interference across tasks, and policy drift may occur. Continual learning therefore needs
to optimize new-task adaptation while retaining previously acquired capabilities (Kirkpatrick et al.,
2017; Dohare et al., 2024), using an objective of the form
LCL = Lnew + λretainLretain + λregLreg,
(6.9)
where Lnew measures adaptation to new tasks, Lretain preserves previous capabilities, and Lreg
limits undesirable parameter changes. Replay of representative experiences can preserve cover-
age of previous task distributions. Knowledge distillation can constrain the new model’s behavior
on earlier tasks. Parameter regularization can limit changes to parameters important for retained
knowledge. And modular architectures can isolate new skills within specific components. Meth-
ods such as elastic weight consolidation (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) mitigate forgetting by restricting
changes to important parameters, although their effectiveness in embodied tasks must still be val-
idated through physical interaction. Continual learning should therefore be evaluated in terms of
both gains on new tasks and retention of existing skills.
As illustrated in Figure 6.5, continual learning should follow a controlled iterative process to
make capability gains verifiable.

experience, update the model offline, jointly validate performance on new and existing tasks to-
gether with compliance with safety constraints, and deploy only after predefined performance and

retained, how much data and human effort adaptation required, and whether failure recovery has
become more reliable. Deployment experience can be regarded as a source of established system
capabilities only when these results are reproduced across independent tasks, different batches of
objects, and sustained operation. It can then provide a reliable basis for subsequent task adaptation
and policy optimization.
As summarized in Figure 6.4, capability development in foundation models for robot manipula-
tion thus proceeds through a feedback loop of prior acquisition, task adaptation, outcome-based
optimization, and experience accumulation, rather than a direct transition from large-scale pre-
training to autonomous operation. Pretraining supports shared semantic and behavioral structure.
Supervised post-training enables execution of procedures on specific embodiments. Reinforcement
learning-based post-training uses physical outcomes to improve precision, efficiency, and recovery.
And continual learning supports the long-term retention of these gains and their transfer to new
tasks and environments. Each stage has a distinct training emphasis, while demonstrations, inter-
action feedback, and deployment experience connect them. Together, they support the progression
from demonstration-driven behavioral learning toward continual policy optimization grounded in
physical feedback.
6.4
Multi-Embodiment Modeling and Model Adaptation
The action interfaces in Section 6.2 specify how a model generates behavior, while the pre-training
and post-training procedures in Section 6.3 establish reusable behavioral priors. Realizing these
priors on a different physical system requires compatible observation and action interfaces, to-
gether with adaptation to its morphology and interaction dynamics. Here, an embodiment denotes
the robot platform together with its end-effectors, sensing and actuation systems, and control in-
terfaces. Replacing a parallel gripper with a dexterous hand therefore changes the embodiment
even if the manipulator remains unchanged. The substitution alters the available contact modes,
action dimensionality, sensing geometry, and feasible manipulation strategies. Multi-embodiment
modeling seeks to transfer task-relevant knowledge across these configurations while preserving
the physical distinctions that determine executable behavior.
Cross-robot training in Open X-
145


Embodiment provides empirical evidence that heterogeneous interaction data can support such
transfer, although its reported evaluations do not establish generalization to arbitrary unseen
robots (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024).
