6.4.1
Embodiment-Aware Data Representation and Alignment
Pooling trajectories across robots requires compatibility of physical meaning, not merely compat-
ibility of tensor shapes. Let De denote the collection of trajectories associated with embodiment
e. Each trajectory retains its instruction, ordered observations and actions, outcome annotations,
and acquisition metadata. Let mmeta
t
denote acquisition metadata. Metadata should identify the
robot and end-effector configuration, sensor calibration, coordinate frames, units, control mode,
timestamps, command duration, latency, and the data-collection policy or operator. These fields
determine how a recorded command relates to an observed physical consequence.
Semantic, Geometric, and Dynamic Alignment
Semantic alignment concerns task goals, object
roles, and stages of behavior. Two robots can share the goal of opening a container while requir-
ing different grasps and motion sequences. Geometric alignment concerns reference frames, pose
conventions, kinematics, and correspondences between observation and action representations. A
command expressed in a camera frame, tool frame, or joint space requires an explicit interpretation
before it can be transferred. Dynamic alignment concerns the embodiment-dependent transition
kernel Ptr
e , including actuator response, payload, friction, compliance, and execution delay. Geo-
metric correspondence alone does not establish equivalent contact behavior.
These distinctions also delimit what data standardization achieves. The RT-X experiments use a
canonical camera view and a coarsely aligned end-effector action interface, with dataset-specific
action normalization. The original control conventions are retained, and action coordinate frames
are not fully aligned across datasets (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024). Thus, numeri-
cal normalization facilitates joint training without making identical action vectors physically inter-
changeable. UMI illustrates a complementary interface-level approach in which relative trajectories
146


and inference-time latency matching support transfer of demonstrations collected with handheld
grippers to compatible robot systems (Chi et al., 2024). Neither approach removes the need to verify
reachability, tracking, and contact behavior on the receiving embodiment.
Heterogeneous Sensing and Action Interfaces
Observation interfaces may differ in camera
count, viewpoint, and calibration. They may also differ in whether proprioceptive, force, or tactile
measurements are available. Modality-specific tokenizers, sensor identity encodings, and validity
masks can expose these differences to a shared model. Octo supports adding or removing observa-
tion tokenizers and adapting to new sensory inputs. HPT uses embodiment-specific input stems to
map heterogeneous visual and proprioceptive inputs into a common token interface (Ghosh et al.,
2024; Wang et al., 2024c). Missing measurements should remain distinguishable from valid zero-
valued measurements. For high-rate contact signals, timestamps and observation windows must
also preserve the temporal relationship between commands and measured interaction.
Action interfaces require comparable care. A Cartesian displacement, joint target, velocity com-
mand, and force target define different interventions even when their numerical dimensions coin-
cide. Padding and normalization can accommodate dimensional heterogeneity, but do not resolve
differences in units, control mode, or effective duration. The original π0 implementation pads state
and action vectors to a common dimensionality and masks unused image slots (Black et al., 2025a).
Such implementation choices should be specified for the particular model rather than treated as
universal conventions of cross-embodiment learning. Likewise, resampling a trajectory does not
establish dynamic equivalence between robots operating at different control rates.
Complementary Supervision Sources
Human video provides evidence about task structure, ob-
ject transformations, and behavioral stages, but usually lacks robot-executable action labels. Robot
demonstrations and teleoperation provide action-grounded supervision under a specified inter-
face. Simulation supports controlled variation of morphology and dynamics, whereas autonomous
rollouts expose the state distribution induced by the executing policy. These sources therefore su-
pervise different aspects of transfer, as discussed in Section 6.3.1 and Chapter 4. HPT combines data
from robot teleoperation, deployed robots, simulation, and human video through heterogeneous
input and output interfaces (Wang et al., 2024c). For human video without robot action labels, it
uses estimated poses and two-dimensional positions as surrogate supervision rather than treating
visual motion as a robot command. Failures, interventions, corrections, and recovery segments
should remain identifiable because they represent different supervision signals and operating con-
ditions.
Embodiment-aware representation consequently establishes the conditions under which data can
be combined or transformed. The desired internal representation zt should suppress irrelevant
variation while preserving information about physical differences that affect the next decision. It
is a learned summary of available evidence, following Chapter 5, rather than a physical state or a
calibrated belief distribution by definition.

The descriptor ηe may comprise measured calibration quantities, a learned embedding, a struc-
tured prompt, or an estimate inferred from interaction history. Explicit identity conditioning and
148


inferred physical parameters serve different purposes. An identity token can index a known con-
figuration, whereas adaptation to unobserved payload or compliance requires evidence about the
changed dynamics. Shared features need not be strictly embodiment-invariant. For example, a
representation of a feasible grasp should depend on hand geometry even when the object and task
are unchanged.
Embodiment Representations and Adaptation Mechanisms
The descriptor and interface mod-
ules in Eq. (6.12) can be implemented through tokens, prompts, adapters, dedicated action heads,
or latent action decoders. These mechanisms differ in where embodiment information enters the
model and which components are adapted. They are complementary rather than mutually exclu-
sive. A soft prompt can itself consist of tokens, and a dedicated action head can incorporate a latent
decoder.
Embodiment information can be introduced as learned identity embeddings or structured tokens
encoding morphology and control properties. Structured tokens expose joint attributes and kine-
matic relationships to the shared transformer, providing a representation of physical configuration
beyond a categorical robot label. Suzuki et al. combine joint-wise kinematic action tokens with
topology-aware attention and joint-attribute conditioning (Suzuki et al., 2026). Their kinematic
tokens organize action trajectories, while topology and joint descriptors introduce morphologi-
cal information. The latter instantiate embodiment context associated with ηe. The action tokens
themselves should be distinguished from an identity descriptor. An identity embedding indexes a
known configuration, whereas generalization to an unseen configuration requires a representation
of its relevant physical properties.
An embodiment-specific prompt supplies contextual information that modulates shared computa-
tion. A structured textual prompt may describe available sensors or the action interface, while a soft
prompt represents such context through trainable continuous embeddings. X-VLA introduces sep-
arate learnable soft prompts for heterogeneous data sources, together with domain-specific projec-
tions for action-related inputs and outputs (Zheng et al., 2026a). This illustrates how embodiment-
dependent context can be incorporated without duplicating the shared backbone. Prompt condi-
tioning should be distinguished from the task instruction ℓlang. The former describes the execution
configuration, while the latter specifies the desired behavior.
Parameter-efficient adapters introduce a restricted set of trainable parameters within a pretrained
model, allowing the shared computation to be adjusted for a target configuration. LoRA parame-
terizes weight updates through low-rank factors, and OpenVLA evaluates this approach for data-
efficient robot-policy fine-tuning (Hu et al., 2022a; Kim et al., 2025b). In Eq. (6.13), the adapter
parameters can constitute Θupd while the remaining pretrained weights are fixed. The resulting
update changes the model’s internal computation. It does not by itself define a compatible obser-
vation or action interface.
An embodiment-specific head maps shared features to the dimensionality, units, and control se-
mantics required by the target robot, implementing πψe or its deterministic counterpart gψe. HPT
explicitly combines a shared transformer trunk with embodiment-specific input stems and pol-
icy heads, reinitializing the head for transfer to a new embodiment (Wang et al., 2024c). Octo
similarly permits new observation tokenizers and action readouts when sensory inputs or action
spaces change (Ghosh et al., 2024). Interface modularity does not prescribe a head-only update. In-
put modules, readouts, and shared features can be adapted jointly rather than restricting learning
to the action head.
A shared latent action space permits policy learning over a common behavioral representation
while an embodiment-specific decoder reconstructs executable actions. Unlike the context rep-
resentation zt, which summarizes evidence for decision-making, the latent action represents the
behavior proposed by the policy. Latent Action Diffusion learns aligned end-effector action rep-
resentations using contrastive encoders, trains a diffusion policy in that latent space, and selects
the corresponding embodiment-specific decoder during execution (Bauer et al., 2026). The action-
generation interface is thereby factorized into shared latent prediction and embodiment-dependent
149


reconstruction. Its transfer capacity depends on the learned alignment and the target decoder’s
ability to realize feasible actions.
These mechanisms instantiate different parts of the shared-execution decomposition. Tokens and
prompts principally supply embodiment context, adapters modify selected internal computations,
and action heads or latent decoders determine how shared information becomes an executable
output. The appropriate combination depends on whether the mismatch concerns sensing, mor-
phology, action semantics, or interaction dynamics.
Adaptation Targets and Learning Regimes
For a target configuration e⋆, adaptation should ad-
dress the source of mismatch. A change in camera mounting position or orientation, even with
the same number of cameras, primarily affects observation encoding and calibration. A change
in end-effector degrees of freedom, such as replacing a parallel gripper with a dexterous hand,
affects action dimensionality, kinematic retargeting, feasible contact configurations, and action de-
coding. Changed payload, friction, or actuator response affects dynamics estimation and feedback-
dependent execution. Several components may require joint adaptation, but the update scope
should follow the identified mismatch rather than being determined solely by a generic fine-tuning
recipe.
Zero-shot transfer uses the pretrained policy and a declared target interface without target-specific
learning data. Any calibration or robot description available at inference should be reported sepa-
rately. Few-shot adaptation uses a stated, limited target-data budget. Offline and online adaptation
describe when the adaptation evidence is collected and used, and are independent of the number
of demonstrations. Moreover, adaptation through context, state estimation, or calibration need not
change model weights, whereas fine-tuning does. RoboCat explicitly studies adaptation to new
tasks and embodiments using target demonstrations (Bousmalis et al., 2024).
Target Performance and Capability Retention
The complete parameter set Θ includes the rep-
resentation parameters, relevant input and action-interface parameters, and any trainable embodi-
ment descriptors. Let Θ0 denote their values before target adaptation, including the initialization of
newly introduced interface modules, and let Θupd denote the selected trainable subset. Following
Eq. (6.9), parameter adaptation can be formulated as

All parameters outside Θupd remain fixed. The target loss Lnew uses the action-generation objective

supervision or behavioral distillation. The nonnegative coefficients control the relative weighting
of these objectives. Consistent with Section 6.3, Lreg constrains undesirable parameter changes.
Data and computational budgets are reported separately rather than identified with this regular-
izer. Elastic weight consolidation exemplifies parameter-based protection of previously acquired
knowledge (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), but such a regularizer does not guarantee retained closed-loop
manipulation performance.
Negative transfer can result from incompatible action semantics, an imbalanced training mixture,
or shared features that omit information essential to one embodiment. Embodiment-aware sam-
pling, modular interfaces, replay, and targeted regression evaluation can reduce these sources of
interference. Physical feasibility and interaction limits must additionally be enforced and validated
at the relevant execution interface. Minimizing Eq. (6.13) alone does not establish them.
6.4.3
Adaptation Validation and Deployment Handoff
Claims of successful embodiment adaptation require evaluation on independently collected target-
embodiment trials. Offline action agreement does not measure the state distribution visited by the
150


executing policy or its response to contact disturbances. Evaluation should distinguish supported
embodiments from held-out embodiments and separately control changes in task, object, scene,
operator, and acquisition period. Splits should be made at the trajectory or collection-session level,
with paired or retargeted versions of one demonstration grouped together, to prevent correlated
samples from inflating generalization estimates.

Adaptation time, computational resources, and the number of updated parameters provide com-
plementary cost measures. These evaluation quantities assess distinct aspects of adaptation. They
are not in one-to-one correspondence with the three optimization terms in Eq. (6.13).
Physical Validation and Deployment Interface
Target trials should include the failure modes
that motivated adaptation, such as grasp loss after an end-effector change, tracking error after a
control-interface change, or unstable contact under altered compliance. Alongside task success,
relevant measurements include executable-command rate, trajectory deviation, contact stability,
recovery success, and intervention frequency. Proposed model outputs and applied controller com-
mands should be recorded separately, so that success obtained through controller corrections can
be distinguished from intrinsic policy performance.
The deployment handoff comprises more than a neural checkpoint. It should specify the em-
bodiment and controller configuration, observation and action contracts, normalization statistics,
calibration and timing information, descriptor and adapter versions, validated operating condi-
tions, and behavior when required inputs or model outputs are unavailable. Unsupported con-
ditions should remain identifiable, and updates must preserve compatibility among these com-
ponents. Multi-embodiment modeling thus connects reusable task representations with verified,
embodiment-specific physical behavior.
6.5
Model Deployment and Efficiency Optimization
A trained policy becomes a useful embodied capability only when its decisions arrive in time to
influence the physical process.
Deployment therefore concerns more than fitting a checkpoint
into accelerator memory. It connects sensor acquisition, preprocessing, model execution, action
interpretation, and feedback control into an operating system with finite computation and variable
delay. A policy with higher offline accuracy can perform worse on a robot if it acts on older ob-
servations, pauses between action chunks, or loses contact information during preprocessing. The
objective is to improve task performance under a specified resource and timing budget.
6.5.1
Deployment Architectures and the Execution Pipeline
Where the Model Runs
Onboard deployment keeps sensing and inference close to the robot and
avoids dependence on a network for every policy update. Its limits are accelerator capacity, mem-
ory bandwidth, power, and heat dissipation. A nearby workstation or local server can support a
larger model and several robots, but introduces transmission and scheduling delays. Cloud deploy-
ment provides elastic computation and centralized model management, while adding a wider-area
communication path whose delay and availability may be difficult to bound. These are engineering
trade-offs rather than a hierarchy in which a more remote or larger computer is necessarily better.
The computation can also be split. A remote process may interpret instructions or generate task
context, while an onboard policy produces actions and a local controller regulates motion. The
partition should follow decision time scales and communication dependencies. A task goal can
remain useful for seconds, while contact feedback may lose value within a small fraction of that
interval. Sending every force sample through a remote language model can consequently increase
bandwidth and delay without improving the decision that requires the sample. Conversely, split-
ting a transformer across machines can create repeated inter-device dependencies and be slower
than moving the whole policy to one machine.
Table 6.3 compares the deployment choices. The appropriate configuration depends on the task’s
tolerance for delayed decisions, the expected concurrency, and the behavior available when an
inference request is late. For a manipulation system, task reasoning and learning can often be
remote even when action validation, control, and timeout handling must remain local.
The Online Data Contract
Every inference request needs a reference time, an instruction, an
embodiment identifier, the observations it requires, and a clear record of what is missing or delayed.

The preprocessing pipeline must reproduce the training convention for image crops, color channels,
camera ordering, state normalization, action scaling, and coordinate frames. A model trained on
relative tool-frame displacement cannot be deployed by interpreting its output as an absolute base-
frame pose. Likewise, reversing the sign of a gripper command or applying normalization statistics
from another embodiment can invalidate an otherwise correct prediction.
To align modalities sampled at different times, retain each modality’s acquisition time and validity
mask and construct the input history according to the model’s convention. Interpolation can work
well for smoothly varying joint positions, but averaging across a contact onset may erase the very
event the policy needs. Training augmentations such as random cropping should also be distin-
guished from the deterministic preprocessing used for evaluation. These details link deployment
directly to the data representation of Section 6.4.
For a sequential execution path, a useful latency decomposition is
Le2e = Lacq + Lpre + Lnet + Lqueue + Lmodel + Ldecode + Ldispatch,
(6.17)
where the terms describe acquisition, preprocessing, communication, queueing, model execution,
action conversion, and dispatch to the control interface. Overlapped implementations should in-
stead measure the critical path without double counting concurrent work. The interval ends once
a command is available to the controller. When measuring response to a disturbance, the physical
actuator response adds further delay. Even with fast accelerator kernels, waiting for camera frames,
host-device copies, and server queues can account for substantial delay.
The deployed controller should retain both the requested and the applied command. Saturation,
rate limiting, inverse kinematics, or a lower-level safety filter can alter an action after model infer-
ence. Subsequent history and learned dynamics should reflect what actually took effect. Recording
only the unmodified output makes later failures appear to be modeling errors even when their
cause lies in the execution interface.
6.5.2
Model Compression and Inference Acceleration
Optimization begins with profiling the actual execution path. A large VLM backbone may be bot-
tlenecked by weight movement and visual-token processing. An autoregressive policy may be
slowed by repeated sequential decoding. A generative action expert may spend most of its time
on repeated denoising evaluations. For a small policy, preprocessing, device transfers, and Python-
level dispatch can become the dominant cost. The benefit of the same optimization therefore varies
across architectures and hardware.
Compression of Parameters and Activations
Quantization stores selected weights or activations
at reduced numerical precision. It can lower memory use and data movement, but speed gains
require supported kernels and favorable tensor shapes. OpenVLA studies quantized deployment
as part of its efficiency analysis (Kim et al., 2025b). Calibration for a robot policy should include
the states where precision matters, such as small displacements near contact, rare sensor values,
153


and transitions between action modes. Keeping sensitive output projections or normalization op-
erations at higher precision may be preferable to applying the same precision everywhere.
Structured pruning removes channels, heads, layers, or entire processing branches. Unstructured
sparsity does not necessarily accelerate dense hardware kernels, and removing a rarely used fea-
ture can damage a rare but important recovery behavior. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller
student to reproduce useful teacher behavior or representations (Hinton et al., 2015). The student
can be trained on actions, subgoals, intermediate features, or generated trajectories. For closed-loop
control, training should cover perturbed states and the teacher’s corrections, and recovery should
be tested after the student’s own errors.
A lightweight action expert provides another form of computation allocation. The expensive back-
bone constructs semantic context, while a smaller module performs repeated action-generation
steps. This division is exemplified by π0 and studied through knowledge insulation (Black et al.,
2025a; Driess et al., 2025). Parameter-efficient methods like LoRA mainly cut the cost of adapting a
model. They do not, however, make the original backbone any cheaper to run. An adapter merged
into supported weights can avoid extra adapter operations, but the main model still runs.
Reducing Work Per Decision
For autoregressive policies, action tokenization determines the
number of sequential backbone evaluations.
FAST compresses temporal action structure and
thereby changes this trade-off (Pertsch et al., 2025). Parallel prediction can remove token-by-token
dependencies, but must be supported by the training objective and attention structure. OpenVLA-
OFT combines parallel decoding, action chunking, and continuous regression (Kim et al., 2025a).
Its result should not be described as merely running the original autoregressive policy faster.
For diffusion and flow-based policies, fewer sampling steps reduce the number of action-expert
evaluations. An excessively coarse solver can change action quality, especially at sharp transitions
or for narrow contact tolerances. Few-step distillation, combined with suitable training objectives,
can improve this trade-off. Reducing the number of inference steps requires a new closed-loop
evaluation. The number of steps generated, how many are actually executed, and how often new
observations arrive should all be tuned together.
Visual token reduction can lower the cost of processing several camera views. Cropping, token
pooling, selective view use, and compact history encoders are possible choices, but the retained
information must match the task. A small contact region can occupy few pixels while determining
success. Compression that works for reaching may therefore fail during insertion or when distin-
guishing two similar tools.
Execution-Level Optimization and Cache Validity
Operator fusion, compilation, fixed-shape
execution, preallocated buffers, and reduced host-device synchronization can remove overhead
without intentionally changing the policy function. IO-aware attention implementations such as
FlashAttention reduce attention memory traffic (Dao et al., 2022). Their end-to-end benefit still
depends on whether attention dominates the deployment workload. Warm-up and compilation
cost should be separated from steady-state inference, while occasional recompilation and shape
changes should remain visible in tail-latency measurements.
Caching is useful only when the dependency being cached is unchanged. Within a flow or dif-
fusion solve, the observation-language prefix can be reused if it cannot attend to changing action
tokens. Across different robot observations, cached visual features generally become stale. Even
an unchanged instruction does not imply that every text hidden state can be reused if the backbone
mixes text and images bidirectionally. A deployment should distinguish reusable tokenization or
independent encodings from context-dependent transformer states. This distinction prevents ap-
parent speed from silently reducing responsiveness.
Efficiency should be reported at a consistent boundary. If the policy generates H actions in Lmodel
seconds, its nominal action-generation throughput is
Rgen =

This quantity describes generated commands. It does not count independent decisions made from
fresh measurements. Comparisons must hold the action duration, prediction horizon, execution
horizon, input views, sampling settings, and hardware conditions sufficiently explicit to interpret
the number.
6.5.3
Asynchronous Inference and Real-Time Closed-Loop Control
Four Distinct Frequencies
The sensor frequency determines how often measurements become
available. The policy frequency determines how often a new observation-conditioned prediction
is produced. The command frequency determines how often targets are delivered to the lower-
level controller. The servo frequency determines how often that controller updates actuator in-
puts. These frequencies can differ by orders of magnitude. Interpolating a predicted trajectory or
streaming a long action chunk raises the command frequency without raising the policy’s feedback
frequency.
Let ∆t be the interval between action targets, H the predicted chunk length, and Nexec ≤H the
number of actions selected for execution before replacing the remaining plan. The prediction hori-
zon is H∆t, whereas the nominal replanning interval is Nexec∆t. Action chunking captures tempo-
ral correlations and amortizes inference. Receding-horizon execution retains only a prefix and uses
new evidence to reconsider the rest. Longer Nexec reduces inference demand but delays responses
to unexpected changes. The appropriate value depends on the physical event, not only on available
compute.
Observation age gives a more direct measure of responsiveness. If a command applied at physical
time tapply is based on a reference observation acquired at tobs, define
∆age = tapply −tobs.
(6.19)
For multimodal policies, ages may also be reported separately by modality. A small model runtime
does not guarantee small observation age when old frames are queued or a long action prefix is
committed. Dropping obsolete requests can improve feedback freshness even when it reduces the
total number of processed frames.
Overlapping Prediction and Execution
In synchronous execution, a robot may finish a chunk
and wait for the next inference. Naively removing this pause creates a different problem. The next
chunk was generated from a state that no longer coincides with the state at which it will begin. The
remaining trajectory must account for commands executed during inference. Real-time chunking
addresses this issue for flow and diffusion policies by conditioning the new chunk on a committed
prefix while regenerating the uncommitted future (Black et al., 2025b).
If a request requires Lreq seconds from input availability to usable output, the approximate number
of command intervals that elapse during the request is

at a command rate of 50 Hz, a 100 ms request spans five action intervals. A 50-action chunk has
a one-second prediction horizon, but neither that horizon nor the command rate implies 50 fresh
policy decisions per second. This is an illustrative timing calculation, not a benchmark result.

buffer also commits the robot further into an old plan. Responsiveness requires replacing the un-

Chunk transitions require semantic as well as numerical consistency. Averaging two trajectories
may smooth a position jump while mixing incompatible modes, such as opening and closing a
gripper or maintaining and releasing contact. Continuity should be checked for the commanded
quantity and its physical role, including pose, velocity, force targets, and discrete events. A late
result associated with an earlier instruction or aborted task should be rejected rather than appended
to the current action stream.
Slow Context and Fast Correction
A multi-rate system can update task context or predictive
features less frequently than local action decisions through the following decomposition

where k(t) selects the latest valid context. The fast module uses recent evidence, including contact
history when available, while the slow module revises task interpretation or predicted futures. For
this separation to work, the action module must be trained to operate in context of varying age and
must receive enough current information to correct behavior. Merely caching an old full-policy
output does not create such a capability.
Replanning can combine periodic updates with event triggers. Target motion, grasp loss, unex-
pected force, a completed subtask, or a change in instruction may invalidate the current context.
Thresholds and hysteresis can prevent excessive switching around noisy events. The event path
itself needs a delay bound. Also, a task-level replan should not interrupt a local stabilization re-
sponse that is physically necessary. The control principles for this fast feedback layer are developed
further in Chapter 7.
6.5.4
Deployment Evaluation and Operational Maintenance
Deployment evaluation should compare complete operating configurations.
Alongside model
weights, record numerical precision, input resolution and views, action horizon, execution hori-
zon, sampling steps, device, concurrent workload, and communication conditions. Otherwise, a
higher throughput may reflect a larger chunk or a less responsive execution schedule rather than
an improvement in the same task interface.
The evaluation should connect computation to behavior. Table 6.4 links deployment measurements
to their interpretations and test conditions. Relevant computational quantities include end-to-end
latency, latency percentiles and variability, observation age, missed deadlines, peak memory, and
power. Relevant physical quantities include task success, completion time, trajectory and contact
accuracy, recovery after disturbances, and human intervention. Energy per completed task is often
more informative than accelerator power alone. A faster inference configuration may consume
more instantaneous power but finish the task sooner, while a slower configuration may increase
robot holding time.
A staged evaluation can first compare numerical outputs on recorded observations. Next, test
timing under replay or hardware-in-the-loop execution, and finally measure closed-loop behavior.
Recorded-data agreement is a diagnostic rather than a substitute for robot trials. Dynamic-target
tasks expose delayed feedback, contact tasks expose precision loss, and long-horizon tasks expose
accumulation of small errors. Comparisons should use matched task conditions and report trial
counts and uncertainty. A speedup measured on one accelerator does not establish a hardware-
independent property.
Operational logs should connect each input snapshot to its model version, preprocessing version,
inference timestamps, proposed action, applied command, and observed outcome. This makes
it possible to distinguish recognition errors from stale observations, action conversion errors, or
controller overrides. Model weights, tokenizer or action decoder, normalization statistics, embod-

while retaining incompatible normalization or action decoding is not a complete rollback.
Timeout behavior must be appropriate to the task. Holding position may be reasonable in free
space but undesirable during a forceful contact. Stopping a pouring motion can require a controlled
change in orientation. Such responses should be implemented and validated at the execution layer,
with a clear path to human takeover where needed. After compression, compiler changes, or hard-
ware migration, a fixed regression suite should test both nominal skills and the disturbances that
previously caused failures.
Deployment is where this chapter’s modeling loop closes.
Training creates behavioral priors.
Adaptation makes them an embodiment-specific interpretation. The execution system then de-
cides when those priors can actually affect the world.
Efficiency is established when reduced
computation or communication produces timely, accurate behavior under the intended operating
conditions. The resulting execution traces then supply the evidence needed for the next round of
capability improvement.
6.6
Dexterous Manipulation Foundation Models
Most of the models discussed in this chapter act through a parallel gripper, whose action is a wrist
pose and a single opening width. A multi-fingered hand breaks three assumptions behind that de-
sign. The action space grows to 20 or more finger joints, and whether an object stays under control
depends on how those joints move together. Many decisive events, such as a finger beginning to
slide or load shifting onto the palm, happen at contacts the cameras cannot see. Robot data are
scarcer still. Teleoperating 20 joints is much harder than teleoperating one, and every hand defines
its own action space. Human hands, meanwhile, manipulate objects constantly and on camera,
which makes human data the obvious place to look for scale.
The subsections examine how to represent finger actions (Section 6.6.1) and how to learn from
human hands, with EgoScale as the worked example of the stages in Section 6.3 (Section 6.6.2).
They then examine how much of a policy can be shared across hands, extending Section 6.4 (Sec-
tion 6.6.3), where touch helps (Section 6.6.4), and what current results establish (Section 6.6.5). The
hands themselves are described in Section 9.6, and the low-level hand controllers that sit beneath
these models in Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5.
6.6.1
Action Representations for Multi-Fingered Hands
A dexterous policy has to fix the meaning of its action vector before data collection begins. Current
systems use one of three options. Joint targets for a specific hand are directly executable but bind the
model to that mechanism. Fingertip or keypoint targets are closer to what human data measure, but
157


need a solver to turn them into joint commands. Functional coordinates give each entry a meaning
shared across hands, such as index flexion or thumb opposition, and keep a separate map from
those entries to each hand’s joints. Most systems also command the wrist separately, as a relative
change in hand pose. The choice decides which data can supervise the model and how much of it
can be shared between hands.
Human data enter through retargeting, the geometric alignment of Section 6.4.1, which for hands
can be written as
min

where q is the robot hand configuration, T aligns the wrist frames, pi is a fingertip position, and
wi weights its importance. The second term penalizes abrupt changes. The objective is illustrative,
not the loss of a particular study, and practical versions add collision and contact constraints. As
Figure 9.15 shows, a MANO pose vector and a robot joint vector do not correspond one to one. Re-
targeted human motion is useful supervision only insofar as the mapped action keeps the relevant
interaction. More data widen coverage but do not remove a systematic geometric mismatch.
6.6.2
Learning from Human Hands: Pretraining, Alignment, and Post-Training
EgoScale is the clearest evaluated example of the training stages of Section 6.3 applied to a dex-
terous hand. It is evaluated on a Galaxea R1Pro with two 22-DoF Sharpa Wave hands and three
RGB cameras (Zheng et al., 2026b). The hands are described in Section 9.6.3. Figure 6.7 lays out the
stages.
Pretraining: Learning Reusable Wrist-Finger Coordination
EgoScale represents human-video
motion as relative wrist displacement plus retargeted hand actions (NVIDIA, 2026). Predicting
articulated actions pushes the model to encode how the wrist and fingers move together. Carrying
a bottle without losing the grasp is a different coordination pattern from twisting its cap. Patterns
like these recur across tasks and can be learned before any target-robot data are collected. The
representation also commits early to an execution interface. Relative wrist motion transfers easily,
but the finger component has to be realizable in the target hand’s joint space, so the retargeting of
Eq. (6.23) is already present during pretraining.
Alignment:
Connecting Human Observations to Robot Actions
EgoScale’s aligned mid-
training uses about 50 hours of human and 4 hours of robot play data. The human capture matches
the robot’s camera viewpoints and intrinsics, with Vive wrist tracking and MANUS hand capture
synchronized to video (Zheng et al., 2026b). The question at this stage is which differences in ap-
pearance and motion come from the embodiment and which signal a different task state. A human
finger and a robot link may occupy different parts of the image while doing the same job of sup-
porting a cup, and similar silhouettes may hide different reachable contact surfaces. In the terms
of Section 6.4.1, matched viewpoints and retargeting reduce observation and geometric mismatch,
while robot play exposes dynamic mismatch under load. The capture hardware and its calibration
are described in Section 9.6.4.
Post-Training: Specializing the Prior to a Physical Task
Task-specific robot data then tie the
prior to the actual arm, hand, objects, and cameras. For a handle grasp, the prior may already orga-
nize approach, closure, and transport, but only the target setup determines how far the fingers must
close to engage the handle and which wrist path leaves room for the next step. In EgoScale’s scaling
experiment, direct post-training without aligned mid-training raises the average task-completion
score from 0.30 to 0.71 as human pretraining grows from 1,000 to 20,000 hours (Zheng et al., 2026b).
This experiment varies the amount of human data, unlike the comparison with and without pre-
training summarized in Section 2.3. A separate one-shot protocol uses 1 robot demonstration plus
100 aligned human demonstrations per object, after the earlier stages (NVIDIA, 2026). The two
experiments answer different questions concerning whether more prior experience helps, and how
158


little robot data is then needed to select a behavior the model already supports. Section 4.5 dis-
cusses what such scaling variables can and cannot establish.
Two other studies on Sharpa hands use human data in narrower roles.
CAIP aligns images
with hand-action proxies to pretrain a visual encoder and evaluates policies without tactile in-
put (Sharma et al., 2026b). Do as I Do reconstructs and retargets human hand-object motion into
robot trajectories on a dual-UR3e Sharpa system (Paliwal et al., 2026). Each improves one ingre-
dient, the representation or the execution data. EgoScale shows how the ingredients fit into one
training sequence.
6.6.3
Sharing Actions Across Hands
UniDex asks which finger-level action roles can be shared when joint structures differ. Its dataset
spans eight hand types and is built by retargeting human demonstrations, with interactive cor-
rection and visual alignment. Its Function-Actuator-Aligned Space (FAAS) assigns joints with the
same function to common coordinates, the functional-coordinate option of Section 6.6.1, and keeps
a map to each hand. A policy conditioned on point clouds, language, and proprioception predicts
action chunks (UniDex Team, 2026).
A spray bottle shows what such a mapping has to preserve. The thumb must reach the trigger while
the other fingers resist its reaction force. Moving the wrist for better trigger access can weaken the

The Wuji experiments in UniDex use the 20-DoF hand on a Franka arm with RGB-D sensing, on

outcome measures. Pretraining improves intermediate progress and final success, but because the
aggregate pools Wuji and Inspire tasks, it does not isolate the contribution of the Wuji hardware.
Without further training, an Inspire-trained policy transferred to Wuji reaches 40% average task
progress over 10 trials (Zhang et al., 2026a). A shared flexion coordinate lets the parameters be
shared, but the resulting fingertip motion still depends on link lengths, couplings, and joint ranges,
so task structure transfers while contact execution is only partly preserved. SimToolReal (Sec-
tion 7.4.4) takes the opposite approach. It places the shared interface at the object and leaves finger
coordination to the controller.
6.6.4
Where Tactile Input Helps a Dexterous Policy
Section 6.2.3 describes three ways contact information can enter a VLA. For dexterous hands the
narrower question is at which decision a tactile signal changes the outcome. Two XHAND studies
give opposite answers.
DexUMI collects demonstrations with an exoskeleton fitted to the target hand and replaces the
human hand in the images with the robot hand (Section 9.6.4). Its policy predicts wrist and finger
actions from visual and tactile input (Xu et al., 2025c). In an XHAND kitchen task of turning a knob,
moving a pan, and adding salt, touch matters in the salt step because the fingers are hidden from
view, and closing the hand to a plausible posture does not show that they reached the salt.6 With
relative actions and visual adaptation fixed, accumulated success through the salt stage is 75% with
tactile input and 15% without, over 20 episodes per task (Xu et al., 2025c).
In the shared-autonomy system of Cui et al. (2025), DexGrasp-VLA controls the 12-DoF hand from
vision and touch during data collection, and the resulting trajectories, supplemented by corrective
demonstrations, train an arm-hand VLA with separate arm and hand feature branches. The full
system reaches 88.7% pick-and-place success across 50 objects with 3 trials each. In an ablation,
adding tactile features directly to the arm-hand policy lowers success from 95% to 82%, although
the same features help the hand-only controller (Cui et al., 2025).
The difference lies in the decision the signal feeds. Touch helps where the next action depends on
a contact that vision cannot resolve, and hurts where it becomes one more input to a policy that
primarily selects where to reach and place. A third option keeps touch out of the foundation model
and uses it in a faster refinement loop beneath it, as T-Rex does (Section 7.4.5).
6DexUMI Team, DexUMI: Using Human Hand as the Universal Manipulation Interface for Dexterous Manipula-
tion, project page and demonstrations, 2025.
160


6.6.5
Evaluating Dexterous Foundation Models
The studies above report different endpoints (task-completion score, stage-wise progress, final suc-
cess, and accumulated success through a sequence) on different hands, arms, cameras, objects, and
trial counts, and some pool results over several hands. They cannot be ranked against each other.
Each supports a narrower claim. EgoScale shows that a larger human prior improves post-trained
performance under a fixed protocol. UniDex, that a functional action space allows pretraining
across hands and some zero-shot transfer. DexUMI and DexGrasp-VLA, that tactile input pays off
only at decisions it can change.
Three questions remain open. Does human pretraining keep scaling once tasks require sustained
force, not just reaching the right configuration? Can a shared action space carry contact strategies
across hands, or only task structure? And how should a model with slow visual updates hand
authority to faster contact-driven control, the interface studied in Chapter 7? Answering them
requires the closed-loop protocols of Chapter 11, applied to whole tasks from grasping through
recovery on declared hardware.
161


7
Foundation Models for Whole-Body Motor Control
Humanoid and other whole-body robots are an important class of physical embodiments. With im-
provements in hardware, more recent work focuses on controlling the entire body as a coordinated
system. This chapter discusses how to extend current foundation-model algorithms to whole-body
motor control. The whole-body control connects task-level decisions to coordinated physical ac-
tion: it uses control interfaces to regulate motion and contact within the robot’s dynamic limits,
while adjusting in real time to external forces, terrain changes, and contact transitions. Each of
them is discussed in detail as follows.
7.1
Scope, Taxonomy, and Control Interfaces
Task-level objectives specify what a robot should accomplish, but generally leave open how its
joints and contacts should be coordinated under the body’s dynamics and actuation limits. Motor
control addresses these execution requirements through feedback from the body and its environ-
ment, as Figure 7.1 illustrates. This section defines the role of whole-body motor control in this
process, traces the control principles underlying it, and identifies the interfaces needed to reuse
motor capabilities across tasks. In humanoid tasks that combine locomotion and manipulation,
body support must be coordinated with arm motion and hand-object contacts.

7.1.1
Functional Scope and Foundation Models
In this chapter, a whole-body motor controller is a goal-conditioned sensorimotor model that coordi-
nates robot motion and physical interaction through closed-loop control. It uses available observa-
tions of the body, contacts, and task-relevant environment to select and revise actions at high fre-
quency as forces and contact conditions change. Building on this feedback capability, a foundation
model for whole-body motor control acquires reusable motor capabilities through broad pretraining
and exposes them to multiple downstream objectives or control modes (Zeng et al., 2025; 2026).
162


This role complements task-level planning. Task-level models interpret instructions, select objec-
tives, and organize activities. Motion or behavior generators express those objectives as body ve-
locities, end-effector poses, contact requirements, or reference trajectories. The motor controller
executes these targets using the available state information. A specified hand position, for instance,
may admit different arm configurations, trunk postures, and support arrangements. Selecting a
realization requires accounting for its effects on the rest of the body (Khatib, 1987).
A motor objective remains subject to execution feedback after it is issued. Small disturbances may
be corrected locally. Persistent tracking errors, unexpected contacts, or sustained actuator satura-
tion from torque demands beyond hardware limits may require the upstream planner to revise the
target or its timing. Information must therefore flow in both directions. Goals guide execution,
while measured execution constrains subsequent planning. A planner must account for estimates
of the state reached during execution, including deviations from the preceding reference.
Realizing this feedback loop also requires observation processing, state estimation, target interpre-
tation, actuator interfaces, and mechanisms for enforcing execution limits. Some components may
be learned jointly. Others remain explicit. A pretrained tracking policy can provide the core motor
capability while relying on external estimation and low-level servos. Such architectures combine
explicit control components with learned motor capabilities, drawing on complementary develop-
ments in model-based control and reinforcement learning.
7.1.2
From Control Principles to Reusable Motor Capabilities
For articulated robots, the main difficulty is that control objectives are coupled through mechan-
ics. Operational-space control expresses motion and force objectives in task coordinates and re-
lates them to joint actuation, making end-effector behavior an explicit object of control (Khatib,
1987). Impedance control further regulates the dynamic relationship between motion and interac-
tion force, rather than requiring exact position tracking in all circumstances (Hogan, 1985). Classical
work on robot hands similarly analyzes grasping through fingertip geometry, force transmission,
and frictional interaction (Mason and Salisbury Jr, 1985). Together, these methods establish that an
appropriate motor interface can specify a physical interaction rather than a complete sequence of
joint configurations. In legged robots, the same mechanical coupling must be coordinated across
repeated contact transitions. Raibert et al. (1984) decompose hopping into regulation of forward
velocity, body attitude, and hopping height.
To account for future motion and support requirements, MPC makes the consequences of candidate
actions explicit over a finite horizon. At each update, it optimizes a control sequence from the
current state estimate, applies the initial input, and repeats the optimization after receiving new
feedback. State and input constraints can be included directly, although feasibility and stability
depend on the model, formulation, and assumptions (Mayne et al., 2000). In 2003, zero-moment-
point preview control provides a related predictive formulation for biped walking, using future
support references to shape the current motion through optimal linear feedback (Kajita et al., 2003).
By 2018, the MIT Cheetah 3 controller uses convex MPC to optimize ground-reaction forces over a
finite horizon, while a gait state machine and swing controller supply contact timing and swing-leg
motion (Di Carlo et al., 2018).
In the late 2010s, deep reinforcement learning (RL) expands the use of simulated interaction to
acquire feedback policies. DeepMimic combines reference-motion imitation with task rewards to
learn coordinated skills for physics-based characters (Peng et al., 2018a). Hwangbo et al. (2019)
train policies for ANYmal using a simulator that combines rigid-body dynamics with an actuator
model learned from robot data, then deploy those policies on the physical robot. Lee et al. (2020)
extend locomotion to challenging terrain by training a privileged teacher and distilling its behavior
into a student that uses proprioceptive history. History-conditioned adaptation further uses re-
cent observations and actions to infer information about unobserved dynamics, including changes
in load or ground interaction. Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) makes this inference a dedicated
learned module that conditions a locomotion policy (Kumar et al., 2021). The estimation methods
supporting such adjustment are developed in Section 7.2.
163


A parallel line develops motor knowledge that downstream tasks can reuse. Neural probabilistic
motor primitives (NPMP) compress expert skills into a shared latent representation (Merel et al.,
2019). An adversarial motion prior (AMP) learns a distributional motion prior that shapes policy
optimization (Peng et al., 2021). Adversarial Skill Embeddings (ASE) learns a skill-conditioned pol-
icy whose latent space can serve as the action space of a downstream controller (Peng et al., 2022).
A distributional prior shapes policy learning, while a skill-conditioned policy generates executable
actions. Their shared contribution is to separate the acquisition of coordinated movement from the
specification of a particular downstream task.
Modern systems develop both hybrid execution architectures and more reusable command inter-
faces. Deep Tracking Control combines an online trajectory-optimizing planner with a learned
tracking policy that executes its references under model mismatch and disturbances (Jenelten et al.,
2024). This combination retains explicit predictive structure while learning the feedback needed
during execution. More recent humanoid controllers extend reuse to the control interface. HOVER
distills motion-tracking capability into a policy supporting multiple command modes (He et al.,
2025b). A behavior foundation model (BFM) uses motion imitation and masked online distillation
to pretrain a shared behavioral repertoire, while ScaleBFM studies direct goal-conditioned RL pre-
training with varied motion data and model capacity (Zeng et al., 2025; 2026). These humanoid
approaches allow downstream applications to invoke learned movement through different target
specifications, as developed in Section 7.4.
These approaches reflect two complementary design choices concerning the execution mechanism
and how motor knowledge is acquired and reused. Table 7.1 shows representative combinations.

Figure’s Helix 02 provides a concrete example through its publicly described System 2-System 1-
System 0 hierarchy.7 System 2 interprets scenes and language, sequences behaviors, and supplies
latent goals to System 1. Conditioned on these latents, System 1 combines head-camera and palm-
camera images, fingertip tactile sensing, and full-body proprioception to generate full-body joint
targets at 200 Hz. System 0 is a learned whole-body controller that tracks these targets, using full-
body joint state and base motion to produce joint-level actuator commands at 1 kHz. This division
connects semantic goals to visuomotor targets and then to feedback execution that handles balance,
contact, and whole-body coordination. The additional sensing also serves specific feedback needs.
Palm cameras provide in-hand visual feedback when an object is occluded from the head camera,
and fingertip tactile sensors detect contact forces.
Throughout this chapter, st denotes the physical state at control step t, including the robot and any
environment variables needed to describe its evolution. The observation ot contains information
available during execution. An explicit state estimate is denoted by ˆst. Neither is assumed to equal
the full state. A finite observation-action history is
ht = (ot−L+1, at−L+1, . . . , ot−1, at−1, ot),
at ∼πθ(· | ht, gt),
(7.1)
where L ≥1 is the history length, θ denotes policy parameters, and gt is the command representa-
tion. The policy πθ(· | ht, gt) is a conditional action distribution, and ∼denotes sampling from it.
For L = 1, ht = ot. A recurrent state or learned history encoding can summarize longer histories.
Privileged observations provide training-time access to variables that can be read directly in sim-
ulation but are difficult to obtain reliably from the robot’s sensors. HUGWBC uses base linear
velocity, ground friction, and foot contact forces as such variables (Xue et al., 2025). In its asymmet-
ric actor-critic training, the critic combines these quantities with proprioception and commands
to predict returns. Its value estimates then enter the advantage estimates used to update the ac-
tor with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017; HugWBC Authors, 2025). This allows the simulator’s richer
information to contribute to policy optimization through the critic. The actor’s execution inputs

include recent proprioceptive history, commands, and estimates of selected hidden quantities ob-
tained from that history (Xue et al., 2025; HugWBC Authors, 2025).
Command granularity determines how much of the movement the controller must choose. A de-
sired body velocity leaves freedom in foothold placement and posture, as in the locomotion com-
mands of Section 7.3. A full reference motion constrains the coordinated body trajectory more
closely, while targets for only selected body links leave the remaining movement free to accom-
modate support and interaction constraints. Desired reference quantities are denoted by sref
t , with
the hat reserved for estimates. The policy receives their command representation gt, which can
encode a velocity request, a reference horizon, or selected body targets. For partial targets, a mask
identifies the specified components and distinguishes an unspecified target from a specified value
of zero, as in the masked-target representation of Section 7.4.
Executing these goals requires translating the policy’s action at into physical joint actuation. When
at contains joint-position targets, a low-level servo converts position error and joint feedback into
torque commands. Actuator dynamics then determine the actual joint torque τt, including the
effects of saturation and delay (Hwangbo et al., 2019). Policies may instead output joint-velocity
targets, direct torque commands, or a residual added to an existing controller, changing what the
downstream control interface must realize. For a stochastic training policy, µθ(ht, gt) denotes its
action mean, which can also be used for deterministic execution.
Consider a hand target fixed in the world while the humanoid turns or takes a step. The target
stays fixed, but its pose relative to the body changes, so a body-frame encoding must be updated
using the current body pose. An object-relative target instead follows the object’s motion. Timing
matters for the same physical reason. A reference computed for one support configuration may
need revision after touchdown or lift-off. When perception, goal generation, and actuation update
at different rates, a controller can receive observations or references describing an earlier body
or contact state. Feedback correction between target updates must therefore relate these inputs
to the current motion. A measurement timestamp indicates the time of the observed state, and
a reference’s validity interval indicates when it is intended to apply. Delayed information can
increase tracking error, motivating the latency analysis in Section 7.5.
For a humanoid traversing uneven ground through a low passage, successful motion requires both
placing the feet and keeping the torso clear of overhead obstacles. Proprioceptive history reflects
body motion and the response to contact, supporting correction of ongoing execution. Extero-
ceptive observations supply the geometry ahead of the robot so that motion can be adapted before
contact. Visual servoing uses the discrepancy between current and desired visual features to correct
robot motion (Chaumette and Hutchinson, 2006). For perceptive locomotion, Miki et al. combine
proprioception with terrain-height observations from a robot-centric elevation map, allowing the
controller to adapt its motion before contact while retaining feedback from body motion (Miki et al.,
2022). A ground-height map, however, does not preserve all geometry relevant to a humanoid’s
whole body. Gallant instead uses LiDAR-derived voxel grids together with proprioception to rep-
resent lateral obstacles and overhead constraints as well as ground-level terrain (Ben et al., 2026).
These examples illustrate control-oriented perception, in which the system retains the information
needed to select a physical action and correct it as the body interacts with its surroundings.
7.1.4
Generality, Dexterity, and Evaluation
Generality concerns reuse under changes in objectives and physical conditions. Reproducing many
training motions establishes behavioral coverage. A more demanding test is whether the controller
can combine familiar capabilities to meet new task requirements. Goal flexibility allows an existing
capability to be invoked through different target representations, while task transfer asks whether it
remains useful in a new activity. A controller may track new references yet need substantial retrain-
ing for new interaction dynamics. Reuse therefore involves both executing new goal combinations
and adapting coordinated behavior to changes in load, terrain, or contact.
These demands become tightly coupled when locomotion and manipulation share the same body.
Maintaining an object pose during locomotion imposes constraints that are absent from either un-
166


constrained walking or stationary manipulation (Fu et al., 2023). For a humanoid carrying an ob-
ject with both hands, body acceleration changes the forces required to support the object, while
arm configuration affects both reach and whole-body balance. Dexterous execution additionally
requires finger configurations that maintain the grasp. An end-effector pose specifies a hand’s po-
sition and orientation but leaves its internal contact configuration unresolved. In bimanual manip-
ulation, the two hands interact through the shared object. Their contact forces jointly determine ob-
ject motion, but different force distributions can produce the same resultant wrench while imposing
different grasping loads. Coordinated execution must therefore account for support, object motion,
and contact maintenance together, especially during load transfer or changes in the grasp (Bicchi,
1994). The learned hand-control and force-adaptive balance examples in Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5
provide concrete examples of contact execution and load-dependent body support.
Extending this reuse to another embodiment introduces changes in the body itself. Robots differ
in topology, geometry, actuation, and sensing, so a shared controller must represent these differ-
ences or accommodate them through embodiment-specific components. Morphology-conditioned
transformers provide one approach to sharing control representations across bodies (Gupta et al.,
2022). Task-space and contact-based goals can reduce dependence on a particular joint layout, but
the mapping from those goals to actions remains constrained by each robot’s capabilities. Transfer
to a physical platform additionally depends on its actuator and sensor characteristics, beyond the
morphological variation represented in simulation.
The carrying example makes these forms of generality directly testable. Changing walking speed
and object-pose targets tests the composition of movement requirements. Varying the carried load
tests adaptation. Using a robot with a different morphology tests embodiment transfer. Tracking
error, object slip, and loss of balance assess target execution, grasp maintenance, and body support,
respectively. For goals or conditions that require further learning, the benefit of pretraining can be
measured by the data and optimization needed to reach a given task performance, compared with
learning from scratch (Merel et al., 2019; Zeng et al., 2025).
7.2
Body Dynamics and State Estimation
The motor-execution layer is a high-frequency control loop around a physical system. Figure 7.3
depicts floating-base dynamics, contact constraints, and the actuation interface. It receives task
commands from the planning layer, reads proprioceptive measurements (joint encoders and an in-
ertial measurement unit, IMU) together with exteroceptive ones such as depth cameras and LiDAR,
and issues control commands realized through the actuator interface. Three questions organize this
loop, asking how the body moves, where it is now and what it touches, and what the model is get-
ting wrong. This section develops the three answers in turn. Throughout, st denotes the actual
state, ˆst its estimate, and sref
t
a commanded reference.

expose the central structural fact of legged robotics. The first six rows contain no joint torque, so
no actuator acts directly on the base. Joint torque moves the base through inertial coupling (an
airborne robot can pitch its trunk by swinging its legs) and through contact with the environment.
Internal joint forces cancel in the center-of-mass (CoM) balance, so changing limb or trunk posture
cannot create horizontal CoM acceleration when the net external horizontal force is zero. Foot
friction, hand contacts, and other external interactions supply such forces. This underactuation
makes contact forces central to movement (Wensing et al., 2024).
168


Contacts enter the equations both as forces and as constraints on admissible motion. A foot in
sticking contact with stationary ground satisfies Ji(q)v = 0. Each contact is unilateral. The ground
pushes but does not pull, and friction bounds the tangential force. In world coordinates, let ni be
the unit surface normal and µi the friction coefficient, and split fi into a normal part fi,n = fi · ni
and a tangential part fi,t = fi −fi,nni. Unilateral contact and Coulomb friction require

(7.6)
The pinned foot turns the stance leg into a reconfigurable strut that couples the base to the ground,
and the same coupling is what lets the base state be inferred from joint encoders and an IMU,
as the next subsection shows. Contact forces must also be compatible with the available joint
torques. Contacts are ultimately hybrid. A contact is open, sticking, or sliding, and impact is
discontinuous. Time-stepping complementarity formulations capture this without pre-specifying
a mode sequence (Stewart and Trinkle, 1996; Posa et al., 2014), while deployed controllers often
fix a contact sequence from a gait or footstep plan and optimize the force distribution within each
mode (Di Carlo et al., 2018).
Two further properties of the dynamics recur throughout control and identification. The Coriolis
matrix can be chosen with an energy property that underlies passivity-based control arguments,
and the dynamics are linear in the inertial parameters, with ten parameters per rigid link. This
linearity forms the basis of classical identification (Khalil and Dombre, 2004; Featherstone, 2008).
Standard recursive algorithms evaluate inverse dynamics and unconstrained forward dynamics in
time linear in the number of joints. Forming a dense mass matrix, resolving contacts, and solving
control optimizations have additional costs (Featherstone, 2008). Any gap between the simulated
body and the real one is a model error the deployed controller must absorb.
So far the joint torque is a free input. On hardware it is not. The actuator sits between the com-
manded torque and the torque that reaches the joint. Three common designs illustrate different
trade-offs. Hydraulic actuation provides high force density, as on HyQ (Semini et al., 2011). Series
elastic actuation introduces compliance that protects the drivetrain and makes torque measurable
from spring deflection at the cost of bandwidth (Pratt and Williamson, 1995). And quasi-direct
drive uses high-torque motors behind a low-ratio gearbox, as on the MIT Cheetah and Mini Chee-
tah (Seok et al., 2015; Katz et al., 2019). A simplified torque-interface model uses a first-order lag
with saturation,

and policies trained with this model transfer to hardware (Hwangbo et al., 2019).
7.2.2
Explicit State Estimation: Attitude, Velocity, Contact, and Local Terrain
In an explicit state-estimation architecture, the controller acts on physical quantities reconstructed
from sensor measurements. Figure 7.4 contrasts explicit estimation with implicit estimation from
observation history. On a legged robot the fused body state includes the base pose and velocity
and the joint states, while the estimation pipeline additionally determines the contact set and, on
perceptive platforms, maps the local terrain. Joint encoders observe joint configuration, with ve-
locity obtained through sensor processing. An IMU provides angular velocity and specific force.
Neither directly measures base position or translational velocity. The estimator must account for
sensor orientation, lever arms, timestamps, and coordinate transforms.
A torso-mounted IMU, taken to sit at the base origin, provides two high-rate signals. The gyroscope
measures angular velocity up to a slowly drifting bias. Integrating it gives short-term attitude that
accumulates drift. The accelerometer measures specific force, physical acceleration minus gravity
expressed in the sensor frame. At rest it reads not zero but a vector opposite gravity. Aligning the

Fig. 7.4 Explicit and implicit state estimation on a legged robot. Explicit estimation fuses inertial
and kinematic measurements, joint encoders, and an estimated contact set into a body state esti-
mate through a propagate-correct loop. Implicit estimation maps recent observation-action history
to a task-relevant latent. Deployed systems combine the two routes
predicted gravity direction with the measured one corrects roll and pitch when other accelerations
are modeled or sufficiently small, while yaw requires an external reference such as vision or a
magnetometer. Complementary fusion trusts gyro integration at high frequency and the gravity
reference at low frequency, implemented on the HRP-4 humanoid as an extended Kalman filter
(EKF) (Caron, n.d). The EKF loop propagates the state and its covariance with the model and
then corrects both with each measurement. On the rotation manifold, the error-state Kalman filter
(ESKF) propagates a nominal orientation and estimates a small rotation-vector error (Solà, 2017).
The contact-aided invariant extended Kalman filter (InEKF) has log-linear, estimate-independent
error dynamics under its idealized deterministic model and improves convergence and consistency
in the reported Cassie comparisons. IMU-bias augmentation weakens some theoretical guarantees,
and covariance accuracy still depends on the model and noise assumptions (Hartley et al., 2020).
The contact set is itself an estimate. Simple detectors threshold contact-force estimates obtained
from joint-torque measurements using the leg Jacobian and a dynamics model.
Classification
is particularly sensitive during touchdown and lift-off transients. Probabilistic estimators main-
tain a per-foot contact probability from proprioceptive signals, with explicit impact detection, on
HyQ (Camurri et al., 2017), and filter-based estimators fold contact uncertainty into the measure-
ment update (Bloesch et al., 2012). A false stance introduces an incorrect constraint, while a false
swing discards a useful update. With the contact set decided, a foot in firm stance on stationary
ground provides a velocity constraint. Its world-frame velocity is zero, so the base velocity follows
from the gyroscope, the encoders, and the leg Jacobian. This inference is the legged analog of wheel
odometry. Bloesch et al. carry the foothold positions and IMU biases in the filter state and fuse these
measurements with IMU propagation in one EKF (Bloesch et al., 2012). Leg odometry is only as
good as its premise. Slipping feet and misclassified swings bias the estimate. During flight phases,
the estimator propagates inertially without contact corrections, and uncertainty grows according
to sensor quality and the assumed dynamics.
Even perfect fusion leaves global translation and rotation about gravity unobservable when only
inertial and relative kinematic measurements are available (Bloesch et al., 2012; Hartley et al., 2020).
Anchor schemes reduce accumulated drift by assuming that a selected stance-foot point occupies its
planned world location and combining this with orientation and encoder-based forward kinemat-

foot flexibility (Caron, n.d).
In addition to the body state, locomotion over unstructured ground needs a local terrain model,
commonly an elevation map that fuses depth measurements under an uncertain robot pose and
retains a height estimate and variance for each cell, as illustrated in Figure 7.5 (Fankhauser et al.,
2018). Because the map is anchored to the estimated state, pose drift affects the geometry supplied
to control. The perceptive internal model (PIM), for example, uses an elevation map produced
from point clouds and odometry and sampled around the robot in a gravity-aligned frame (Long
et al., 2025a). Miki et al. show on ANYmal that a policy trained over corrupted maps can learn to
discount unreliable perception (Miki et al., 2022). Maps are computed in an estimated pose and
updated at lower rates than the control loop, so they must be aligned to the current estimate before
use. Occlusion and outdated geometry further motivate control that tolerates imperfect perception.
7.2.3
Implicit Estimation from Observation History
Explicit estimators rely on nominal dynamics, measurement models, and uncertainty assumptions.
Real deployments introduce effects outside these models. Scree is slipperier than the simulated fric-
tion coefficient assumes, a carried payload changes the inertial parameters, actuators wear, and en-
coders are miscalibrated. Classical identification estimates such parameters offline from designed
excitation, while a deployed robot can also infer its current response from recent observation-action
history ht. In implicit estimation, a learned encoder recovers a compact, task-relevant representation
zt without naming every hidden physical parameter. The history must be temporally aligned and
sufficiently informative. Actuator saturation, for example, can make the requested action differ
from the input actually experienced by the body.
Training-time randomization varies the physics (masses, friction, and actuation) so that deploy-
ment conditions appear as further variations (Tobin et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2018b). Random-
ization alone does not require a dedicated estimate of the current dynamics, although a history-
conditioned policy may learn adaptation. A complementary line trains with a targeted adversary
171


in which a learnable disturber selects destabilizing pushes, with an H-infinity-style constraint relat-
ing control cost to disturbance intensity (Long et al., 2025b). Privileged teacher-student distillation
explicitly trains a student to reproduce a privileged teacher’s behavior from proprioceptive his-
tory (Lee et al., 2020). The history thereby supplies information about hidden conditions that the
teacher observes directly.
RMA makes the estimator a dedicated module (Kumar et al., 2021). A base policy acts on the cur-
rent observation and a latent vector, and an adaptation module produces the latent from 50 recent
observation-action steps, corresponding to 0.5 s in the reported implementation. During training
the latent is supervised to match a privileged encoder. At deployment the module updates it with
no gradient computation. The latent encodes how behavior should change without requiring ac-
curate recovery of friction or payload parameters. The hybrid internal model (HIM) combines an
explicitly estimated velocity with an implicit response representation trained against successor ob-
servations (Long et al., 2024). Its humanoid extension, the PIM, adds terrain sampled from the
robot-centered elevation map described above (Long et al., 2025a). Learned estimation can there-
fore expose physical state, latent response information, or both. The pattern spans platforms. A
history-conditioned humanoid transformer combines sequence-model pretraining with reinforce-
ment learning (Radosavovic et al., 2024). Deep whole-body control unifies manipulation and lo-
comotion on a quadruped with an arm through regularized online adaptation (Fu et al., 2023).
And Deep Tracking Control (DTC) pairs a trajectory-optimizing planner with a learned tracking
controller (Jenelten et al., 2024).
Generalized momentum, the product of the mass matrix and velocity, provides a dynamics residual
through a momentum observer (De Luca and Mattone, 2003). This residual can indicate unmodeled
interaction, but also contains torque or model mismatch, so it cannot uniquely separate a push
from a payload change. It complements learned response representations with a physics-derived
diagnostic.
Several limits shape the division of labor. Distinct physical conditions can produce indistinguish-
able histories, and conditions outside the training distribution can invalidate a learned latent. A
conventional latent vector carries no calibrated confidence measure. An EKF covariance also re-
mains conditional on its model and noise assumptions. History can recover local motion and dy-
namic response, but inertial and relative kinematic inputs cannot supply a missing absolute posi-
tion or yaw reference. Implicit representations cover model-resistant effects such as friction varia-
tion, actuator response, and soft-ground compliance, while explicit tools provide named physical
estimates and external references. Deployed systems combine the two (Miki et al., 2022; Jenelten
et al., 2024). A learned policy can consume the latent directly, while a model-based controller uses
physical estimates, parameter corrections, or a momentum residual.
Table 7.2 summarizes sensor inputs, estimated quantities, controller uses, and characteristic failure
modes. The control interface specifies the components supplying ˆst, ht, and zt, together with their
frames and timestamps. Persistent estimation or tracking errors may require a slower command, a
different contact plan, or upstream replanning, connecting local estimation to the task-level feed-
back in Section 7.1.
7.3
Command-Conditioned Motor Control
A motion controller converts an abstract request such as “walk forward at a given speed” into a
time sequence of coordinated joint actions. For a humanoid, this conversion is difficult because the
request is multi-dimensional, the body is underactuated during foot contact, and the same joint
motion simultaneously affects translation, turning, balance, foot clearance, and upper-body pos-
ture. A useful controller must therefore expose commands at a semantic level while learning (or
solving) the coordination needed at the joint level. A velocity command leaves joint configurations
and foot placement largely unspecified, while posture and phase commands specify body config-
uration and support timing. Reference-conditioned tracking, developed in Section 7.4, supplies
more detailed time-varying motion targets.

7.3.1
Command Interfaces and Controller Families
Framework and Modules
A model-based controller separates prediction over a future horizon
from instantaneous enforcement of whole-body dynamics. A reference generator converts velocity,
posture, and gait commands into trajectories and a contact schedule. Nonlinear model predic-
tive control (NMPC) plans the motion and support wrenches. And a faster whole-body controller
(WBC) realizes them through joint commands. State estimation combines IMU and encoder mea-
surements with contact kinematics, while a robot-model module supplies the dynamics and Jaco-
bians. Figure 7.6 adapts this organization to a humanoid robot.

7.3.3
From Commands to Coordinated Actions
The policy observes a history of joint positions and velocities, base angular velocity and gravity di-
