During training, exploration uses a stochastic policy around this mean. A history encoder and state
estimator supply estimated translational velocity, body height, and foot clearance. The privileged
critic additionally sees linear velocity, body-height error, foot clearance, contact forces, friction,
terrain samples, and collision indicators during training. The history allows the policy to infer
quantities that are not directly measured or are delayed, a practical form of implicit state estimation.
The action is interpreted as a joint target (or a residual around a nominal posture) and passed
through the robot’s low-level actuator loop. Consequently, a velocity command is not converted
to a fixed stride table. The policy coordinates stance-leg actuation, swing-leg trajectories, trunk
inclination, and arm motion to reduce the velocity error. Contact forces are controlled indirectly
through body motion and joint actuation.

7.3.5
Environment Rewards and Mirror Regularization
The environment reward contains task tracking, behavior tracking, and regularization terms, com-
bined as
rt = rtask
t
+ rbehavior
t
+ rreg
t
.
(7.24)
Task terms track the three velocity components with dense exponential errors. Behavior terms
track height, pitch, and waist yaw, and include the contact and swing terms above. Regularization
penalizes torque, joint-speed limit violations, joint acceleration, and action increments. Collision-
based termination discourages failed execution. In particular, an action-rate term −∥at −at−1∥2
discourages frame-to-frame jitter. These rewards define the rollout return and advantages used by
PPO.
Mirror consistency is a separate training loss. Let Fh mirror body observations and past actions
at each history step, Fg mirror the associated commands, and Fa mirror actions across the robot’s
sagittal plane. The intervention indicator is unchanged. For rollout minibatches Droll, the released
implementation uses

the state-estimation loss when jointly trained. The mirror loss does not enter each-step reward,
discounted return, or advantage. An independent foot-position symmetry reward used for non-
walking gaits can enter the environment return. It is distinct from policy mirror consistency (Hug-

7.3.6
Couplings Between Commands
The learned controller exposes several useful couplings. At approximately steady forward speed,
the pair (vx, f gait) controls displacement per cycle. At fixed speed, raising frequency shortens each
cycle’s displacement. At fixed frequency, raising speed requires greater displacement. The pair
( f gait, ℓclear) trades clearance against swing speed and work. Lateral velocity and turning interact
with foot placement, phase offset, and waist orientation. Body height zcmd changes leg configura-
tion and effective workspace, while pitch βpitch changes body geometry and the relation between
base-frame and world-frame velocity. Finally, phase offset ψphase and duty factor dstance specify
the intended contact rhythm. A unified policy can learn these trade-offs from the return, while
coordinated actuation and contact still limit the command combinations it can realize.
The reward weights also interact with these commands. For example, a high-frequency, high-
clearance target increases the acceleration required by the swing trajectory, so an action-rate penalty
suitable for walking may over-damp hopping. Curriculum sampling gradually expands command
ranges and intervention magnitude.
Massive parallel simulation makes such coverage practi-
cal (Rudin et al., 2022). Periodic reward composition and multiplicity of behavior provide related
examples of diverse gait learning through explicit command spaces (Siekmann et al., 2021; Margolis
and Agrawal, 2023).
A useful diagnostic is therefore a command-interaction map rather than a list of single-command
errors. Evaluate tracking error and smoothness on a grid of (vx, vy, ωz, f gait, ℓclear, zcmd, βpitch, χ),
then inspect where one command degrades another. Such tests assess behavior between command
combinations as well as at isolated settings. They also expose saturation. If increasing f gait no
longer changes measured cadence, actuator or contact limits may be responsible, but further tests
are needed to distinguish these limits from inadequate command conditioning.
7.3.7
Disturbance Rejection and External Control
Robustness is trained as part of motion generation. Upper-body intervention replaces the pol-
icy’s arm actions with sampled joint targets or bounded noise, while the lower-body command
remains active. The intervention indicator tells the policy which control mode is present, and the
intervention is interpolated over a finite interval rather than switched instantaneously. Regular-
ization rewards for the intervened joints are masked, while velocity tracking, contact objectives,
collision-based termination, and lower-body regularization remain active. A curriculum gradually
increases the contribution of external actions once baseline velocity tracking is reliable. This trains
trunk and leg compensation for arm motion while preserving the commanded gait, supporting
loco-manipulation.
The resulting architecture closes the feedback loop at each control step. A semantic command is
encoded as velocity, posture, and phase variables. Temporal proprioception supports state estima-
tion. A command-conditioned policy maps the combined input to joint targets. And contact and
motion-quality objectives shape the solution. Low-level torque limits and deployment checks com-
plement this learned control. For deployment, the most important tests jointly assess command
tracking under phase changes, recovery after external impulses, action-rate and contact behavior,
and retention of lower-body stability during upper-body intervention. Maintaining this coordina-
tion on hardware also depends on the delays and actuator limitations examined in Section 7.5.
7.4
Motor Pretraining and Dexterous Whole-Body Control
Command-conditioned control exposes a specified behavior domain. Motor pretraining seeks ca-
pabilities that can be reused across downstream objectives. Three approaches serve different roles.
Reference tracking learns to execute supplied motions. Learned priors and skill representations
support downstream policy learning. And multi-mode pretraining or distillation exposes a shared
repertoire through varied commands (Peng et al., 2018a; 2021; 2022; He et al., 2025b; Zeng et al.,
2025). These approaches can be combined. This section first develops tracking as a common learn-
178


ing objective, then examines behavior foundation models, and finally shows that the same dynam-
ics, estimation, tracking objectives, and command interfaces carry over to the multi-fingered hand,
where the held object rather than the robot’s base is the unactuated body.
7.4.1
Motion Tracking
Motion tracking formulates humanoid whole-body control as the reproduction of a reference mo-
tion under the robot’s dynamics. Reference trajectories provide a time-varying description of the
desired behavior, capturing the coordinated movement of the body across different skills. Deep-
Mimic (Peng et al., 2018a) establishes a reinforcement-learning formulation of this approach in
physics-based character animation. Recent humanoid systems, including BeyondMimic (Liao et al.,
2026) and SONIC (Luo et al., 2026), build on this principle to acquire physically executable skills
and broad behavior repertoires. The reference specifies how the robot should move, while re-
inforcement learning discovers the feedback control needed to reproduce that movement under
physical dynamics.

Several practical strategies support effective learning. Reference state initialization starts episodes
from sampled reference configurations and velocities, exposing the policy to later phases of a mo-
tion before it can reliably reach them from the beginning. Early termination ends episodes when
predefined failure conditions are met, such as excessive tracking errors, avoiding prolonged roll-
outs in unsuccessful states. Adaptive sampling further directs training effort toward challenging
motions or segments. For example, BeyondMimic (Liao et al., 2026) prioritizes temporal regions
with high estimated failure rates while retaining a uniform sampling component to preserve cover-
age. Together, these strategies determine where rollouts begin, when they end, and how experience
is distributed across the reference corpus.
7.4.2
Behavior Foundation Model
Motion tracking provides a shared learning objective, but a general-purpose controller must also
accommodate the diverse commands used in downstream applications. A complete reference se-
quence may be suitable for motion replay, whereas interactive control may specify targets for only
a few body links. This motivates behavior foundation models, humanoid controllers pretrained on
large-scale motion data to acquire a broad repertoire of reusable whole-body behaviors and execute
them in response to diverse behavioral specifications (Zeng et al., 2025; 2026). By combining broad
behavioral coverage with a versatile control interface, BFMs enable learned motor capabilities to be
shared across multiple control modes and downstream tasks.
In this formulation, a behavior is defined as a trajectory of body states and actions, where sp
t denotes
the proprioceptive body variables selected from st. The trajectory is written as
Bseq ≜(sp
0, a0, sp
1, a1, . . . , sp
T−1, aT−1, sp
T).
(7.31)
Goal specifications are treated as external conditions that guide or constrain the execution of a
behavior. A single behavior may satisfy different specifications, while a given specification may
admit multiple physically valid behaviors. For example, specifying a hand target leaves consider-
able freedom in the robot’s stance and the movement of its other arm. Separating goals from the
definition of Bseq therefore distinguishes the executed behavior from the conditions used to specify
it.
From this perspective, BFM pretraining requires both a shared objective for acquiring diverse be-
haviors and a versatile interface for specifying their execution. Motion tracking provides the former
through coordinated demonstrations and dense tracking rewards. The control interface provides
the latter by allowing downstream applications to specify only the aspects of movement relevant
to their objectives. Motion tracking thus serves as a proxy task for learning reusable motor capa-
bilities, which can subsequently be invoked through commands that need not describe a complete
whole-body trajectory.
One practical realization of this interface uses masked Cartesian body targets. Let xtarget

target from a valid target whose encoded value is zero. Sampling different masks during pretrain-

specified targets, root-relative encoding uses the robot pose relative to the target.

The original BFM implementation trains a motion-imitation policy and transfers its behavior

It also evaluates learning new behaviors through a resid-
ual decoder with the BFM frozen (Zeng et al., 2025). ScaleBFM studies direct goal-conditioned
reinforcement-learning pretraining, examining the joint effects of training data and model capac-
ity (Zeng et al., 2026). Its findings highlight the complementary roles of reference-motion diversity
and on-policy experience. Diverse references expand the range of behaviors available for learning,
while rollouts supply the interaction experience needed to acquire them. Effective scaling there-
fore calls for coordinating these two resources with an architecture capable of translating diverse
behavioral specifications into coordinated actions.
As its model backbone, ScaleBFM introduces the Humanoid Transformer, which combines tempo-
ral context with goal-conditioned control, as illustrated in Figure 7.7. Proprioceptive states and
past actions are encoded as interleaved tokens and processed through self-attention to capture the
recent execution history. A learnable query token aggregates this information for action or value
prediction. Future goal states, together with their temporal offsets, are encoded into goal tokens
and incorporated through cross-attention. This design allows the controller to interpret the re-
quested movement in the context of its ongoing behavior, directly accommodating the history and
commands in Eq. (7.32).
ScaleBFM also studies the representations learned through goal conditioning. It applies root mean
square normalization (RMSNorm) (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019) to goal embeddings and analyzes
181


their normalized directions. For the selected motion sequences, neighboring targets yield nearby
representations, while behaviors such as forward and backward walking occupy distinguishable
regions. Perturbation experiments test how changes in embedding direction affect control perfor-
mance. These findings provide evidence of local organization and robustness in the learned goal
representation.
Together, these components illustrate how the general BFM framework can be instantiated in prac-
tice. Motion tracking supplies a shared learning objective, masked targets provide a versatile con-
trol interface, and the Humanoid Transformer relates behavioral specifications to the robot’s exe-
cution history. ScaleBFM thus offers a concrete example of learning coordinated motor skills and
structured goal representations within a single pretrained controller, supporting the reuse of its
behavioral repertoire across multiple control modes.
7.4.3
Evaluation Metrics
Evaluating a BFM requires measuring how reliably and accurately it realizes the behavioral spec-
ifications supplied through its control interface. Motion tracking provides a direct setting for this
assessment because the executed behavior can be compared with a time-aligned reference. Using
the tracking metrics reported by ScaleBFM (Zeng et al., 2026), this chapter considers sequence-level
success rate together with mean per-keypoint position and rotation errors in global and local coor-
dinates. These metrics describe complementary aspects of control, including persistent compliance
with the command, accuracy in the world frame, and fidelity of the body configuration after hori-
zontal root displacement and heading differences are removed.

of a reference, mean errors should be interpreted together with success rate and rollout duration.
Applying the same protocol to held-out motions from familiar sources and motions from unseen
sources further distinguishes tracking accuracy from cross-source generalization. These measures
characterize the realization of behavioral specifications. Downstream scene-interaction tasks addi-
tionally require evaluation of their own task outcomes.
7.4.4
Dexterous Hands: Motor Control at the Finger Level
A Cartesian hand target in a body controller specifies where the hand should move, but leaves
its finger configuration and object contacts unresolved. Extending motor pretraining to dexterity
therefore requires examples of contact transitions, together with an interface that can request useful
movement without prescribing every contact.
The Held Object as a Floating Base
A multi-fingered hand needs the same layers of low-level
control as the humanoid body, because its control problem has the same structure. Recall from
Eq. (7.5) that the first six rows of a legged robot’s dynamics contain no joint torque. The base
moves only through inertial coupling and contact. In in-hand manipulation the unactuated body is
the held object. With the wrist pose given by the arm, the object twist νo ∈R6 and the finger joints
qh evolve as
Mo ˙νo + bo = G(qh, xo) fKhand + wext,
Mh(qh) ¨qh + bh = τ −J⊤
h,KhandfKhand,
(7.41)
where Khand is the set of active finger-object contacts, xo is the object pose, Mo and bo its spatial
inertia and bias wrench, fKhand stacks the forces that the fingers apply at the active contacts, and
the grasp matrix G maps them to the resultant wrench on the object (Lynch and Park, 2017). Each
contact force must lie in the friction cone of Eq. (7.6). As for the floating base, no actuator acts
on the object directly. Joint torque τ reaches it only through Jh,Khand and G, and only while the
corresponding contacts are closed. Contact forces in the null space of G squeeze the object without
moving it. They set the friction margins that keep the grasp stable (Bicchi, 1994).

ment changes the stance Jacobian, so the contact mode is part of the state to be estimated. Second,
the hand differs in scale and instrumentation. Finger actuators are small, often heavily geared, and
work close to their force limits, so the gap between commanded and realized torque in Eq. (7.7)
matters more than it does for a leg. Available sensing ranges from motor current to fingertip tactile
images (Section 9.6.3). And the hand’s “floating base” has a different mass and shape in every task.
The three routes to reusable motor skills named at the start of this section, namely reference track-
ing, learned priors, and goal-conditioned interfaces, carry over to the hand with the object in place
of the base.
Tracking Human Hand References
TeleDexter makes the desired object motion explicit (Li et al.,
2026c). The operator specifies fingertip positions and object pose in the wrist frame. A recurrent
hand policy maps these goals and the observed hand-object state to residual joint-position com-
mands, while independent inverse kinematics tracks the operator’s wrist with a fixed-base Franka
FR3 arm. Training uses consecutive hand-object subgoals, with sparse goal-reaching rewards sup-
plemented by dense tracking rewards. The hand can discover contact strategies between subgoals
rather than reproduce every reference frame. Deployment runs at 30 Hz. Reaching and initial
grasping use kinematic retargeting before the operator switches to the learned in-hand controller.
Its training signal follows Eq. (7.28), but the reference covers the object and fingertips instead of
every joint, much like the sparse masked targets of Eq. (7.32).
On a SharpaWave hand, TeleDexter achieves 75.2% mean success over seven reorientation and tool-
use tasks, with 15 trials per task. Reusing the human reference data after retargeting and training
a separate LeapHand controller yields 60% and 73.3% success on two reorientation tasks. This is
reuse of data and a training procedure across hand morphologies. The current controller remains
object-specific. A new object requires reference collection and policy training.
A Learned Motion Prior for Fingers
DexterityGen gives a concrete pretraining implementa-
tion (Yin et al., 2025). Simulation reinforcement learning generates transitions between nearby
sampled grasps, supplemented by free-finger and precision-manipulation behaviors. Varying ob-
ject geometry, wrist motion, and physical parameters broadens the resulting dataset. A diffusion
model then learns a distribution of future finger-keypoint motion conditioned on proprioceptive
history and a mode indicator. An inverse dynamics model maps sampled motion to joint-position
targets. At deployment, an external motion command guides diffusion sampling toward the re-
quested finger movement while the learned prior favors motions represented in the training data.
Thus, the command enters through sampling guidance. It is not simply copied to the joints. As in a
behavior foundation model, a prior learned from broad simulated experience supplies coordinated
motion, and a sparse command selects among behaviors it already supports.
The experiments demonstrate reuse on an Allegro hand attached to a separately controlled Franka
Panda arm, with human teleoperation supplying motion commands. Test objects are absent from
the pretraining dataset. Assisted teleoperation improves object retention and completes reorienta-
tion and regrasping tasks, but complete screwdriver and syringe tasks succeed in only 3/20 and
4/20 trials, respectively. These results support a reusable hand-motion prior while identifying the
difficulty of composing skills into long tasks. The low-level controller uses proprioception rather
than visual or tactile input. Control errors provide only an indirect contact cue.
Object-Goal Control Learned in Simulation
SimToolReal asks whether simulated experience
can produce a controller that follows object goals taken from a human demonstration. It uses a 22-
DoF Sharpa hand on a KUKA iiwa arm and trains a recurrent goal-reaching policy on procedurally
generated tool-like objects. At deployment, a human RGB-D demonstration supplies a sequence of
object poses. The policy observes proprioception, the current object pose, a grasp-region bounding
box, and the current goal, and commands arm and hand joint targets (Kedia et al., 2026). A demon-
stration can thus specify how a brush should be oriented without saying which finger releases first,
and the controller is free to rotate the brush in the hand when moving the whole arm would hit the
table. This is the object-centered goal representation of Section 8.3.1. The study evaluates 120 real
rollouts over 24 trajectories, 12 tool instances, and six categories. Its Task Progress metric counts
185


the fraction of demonstrated poses reached within a distance threshold and does not measure each
tool’s effect (Kedia et al., 2026). Reaching the intended hammer trajectory is not the same as driving
a nail to depth. In the terms of Table 7.3, SimToolReal tracks a reference for the unactuated body it-
self and leaves the contact schedule to the policy, as a velocity command leaves footstep placement
to a locomotion controller.
Adapting a Prior to Tight Contact
Play2Perfect, also on a Sharpa hand and KUKA arm, pretrains
object manipulation in free space and then fine-tunes in CAD-derived assembly environments with
sparse goal rewards. In 10 real trials at 0.5 mm insertion clearance, the fine-tuned policy succeeds
6 times and the play-only policy never (Lum et al., 2026). The deployment is zero-shot sim-to-real,
but the policy for the assembly task itself was trained in simulation. Free-space reorientation can
reach the right pose through many contact arrangements. Insertion cannot, since a small angular
error produces an edge contact that jams the part, and the grasp must still allow corrective motion.
This is the hand counterpart of adapting a pretrained body controller to a new behavior, as the
residual decoder of the original BFM does. The prior makes the approach reachable, and task-
specific training concentrates on the final contact.
The interfaces exposed by the four controllers to the layer above are fingertip and object goals
(TeleDexter), guided finger-keypoint motion (DexterityGen), object-pose sequences (SimToolReal),
and a task reward in simulation (Play2Perfect). Any of them could be where a manipulation foun-
dation model (Section 6.6) hands a goal to a hand controller, as a semantic planner hands targets
to a humanoid controller (Section 7.1.3). None yet combines broad object coverage with contact
sensing, the subject of the next subsection.
7.4.5
Contact Feedback and Force-Adaptive Body-Hand Coordination
Contact execution requires feedback that distinguishes mechanically different states. Similar finger
positions can occur during pressing, sliding, or a failed regrasp. TeleDexter excludes contact-force
and tactile observations. Its failure analysis links tracking stalls to the inability to distinguish press-
ing against an object from sliding past it. Tool impacts also perturb grasps beyond its free-space
hand-object training distribution. Motion targets specify intended interaction, while contact feed-
back helps determine whether it is being realized.
One response is to give the controller a state that keeps evidence the current image has lost. WM-
Craftnet combines wrist depth, binary tactile contact, proprioception, and previous actions in a
recurrent World Synesthesia Model, whose state conditions a PPO policy that outputs relative tar-
gets for the 22 joints of a Sharpa Wave hand. Simulation supplies clean-depth reconstruction targets
during training. At deployment the state is updated from noisy sensor data (Yin et al., 2026a). The
model gives the policy context and does not generate imagined rollouts, so it is a history-based state
estimator in the sense of Section 5.1.2, serving as the hand counterpart of the RMA-style estimators
of Section 7.2.3, with the object and its contacts as the hidden state. On an unseen double-notched
block, WM-Craftnet meets the rotation criterion (more than half a revolution within 20 seconds) in 8
of 10 real trials, while a policy using WSM-denoised depth succeeds in none (Yin et al., 2026a). This
favors recurrent interaction context over image denoising alone, although matched comparisons of
history, capacity, and objectives would be needed to pin down the source of the gain.
Touch can also correct execution between visual updates. T-Rex, evaluated on a fixed-base dual-
arm system with two Sharpa Wave hands, refines actions asynchronously from recent fingertip
deformation and force history, reusing the visual-language context instead of recomputing it for
every refinement (Niu et al., 2026a). A separate 300 Hz thread tracks the updated targets. Recent
contact evidence can therefore change finger motion while the action chunk remains valid at the
task level, the multirate interface of Section 7.1.3. In a six-task ablation, the average score is 65 for
the full system, 42 without touch, and 60 without asynchronous refinement, under the paper’s task-
specific scoring (Niu et al., 2026a). Both the tactile signal and the way it is integrated contribute.
The split between slow refinement and a fast servo is the hand version of the latency budget of
Section 7.5. The tactile rates that make it necessary are given in Section 9.6.3.
186


Body-hand coordination introduces a further mechanical constraint. When a held object acceler-
ates with the body, its required net contact force changes. Arm configuration can also change the
moment transmitted to the base. With both hands on one object, their forces jointly determine its
resultant wrench. Force components that cancel at the object can still change internal grasp loading
and friction margins (Bicchi, 1994). Coordinating a feasible object trajectory therefore also requires
maintaining contacts and body support.
FAME provides direct evidence for force-adaptive standing (Pudasaini et al., 2026). An encoder
jointly maps 15 torso-and-arm joint positions and the two three-dimensional hand forces to an
eight-dimensional latent, which conditions a lower-body policy. Training combines an upper-body
pose curriculum with sampled hand loads. Deployment estimates each hand force from measured
joint torques τt, rigid-body inverse dynamics, and the hand Jacobian, without wrist force/torque
sensors. The policy outputs 12 leg-joint position offsets at 50 Hz. Upper-body motion remains
externally specified. This force estimate describes the load transmitted through an arm.
In simulation, FAME is evaluated on 100 upper-body configurations sampled from the training
pose distribution, with 25 load draws per configuration. Success requires remaining upright, pre-
serving the stance, and limiting force-induced hand displacement. At a 150 mm tolerance, success
is 38.9%, compared with 16.6% when the same force information is supplied without jointly encod-
ing force and upper-body configuration. On a Unitree H1-2, FAME maintains stance in all three
asymmetric single-arm and all three symmetric bimanual loading trials. The pose-only baseline
falls in all corresponding trials. These limited hardware tests establish load-dependent leg com-
pensation. Together, the cases identify complementary interfaces. Object-and-finger goals request
contact execution, tactile observations refine local actions, and hand-load estimates inform body
support. An integrated system would need to be evaluated on simultaneous grasp maintenance,
object motion, and balance.
7.5
Real-Time Execution, Recovery, and Safety Control
Deploying learned control policies from simulation to real humanoid robots involves challenges
that extend beyond the performance of the policy itself. In practice, the system must operate under
limited computational resources, perception and communication delays, actuator dynamics, and
unexpected external disturbances while maintaining stable, continuous, and safe control. This is
particularly challenging for humanoid robots due to their high-dimensional, strongly coupled, and
partially underactuated dynamics, where local errors can propagate into whole-body deviations
or even loss of balance. Therefore, real-world deployment requires jointly addressing real-time
inference, motion smoothing, sim-to-real adaptation, anomaly monitoring, disturbance rejection,
and recovery, ultimately forming a closed-loop safety framework from normal execution to failure
handling and task recovery. Standing up from a fallen, seated, or leaning posture brings several of
these requirements together. The robot must reorganize its contacts, control the resulting motion,
and settle into stable support. HoST, introduced in Learning Humanoid Standing-up Control across
Diverse Postures, provides a concrete example of learning this recovery capability (Huang et al.,
2025b).
7.5.1
Real-Time Execution and the Sim-to-Real Gap
Deploying learned control policies on physical humanoid robots requires bridging a substantial
gap between simulation and the real world. This gap arises from multiple mismatches between the
simulated and physical systems across dynamics, actuation, sensing, computation, and environ-
mental interaction. An implementation with explicit state estimation can be summarized as
ot −→ˆst −→πθ(· | ˆst, gt) −→at −→actuator and physical system −→ot+1,
(7.42)
where ot denotes the observation at time t, ˆst is the estimated robot state, πθ is the learned pol-
icy, gt is the command, and at is the resulting action. The schematic suppresses the estimator’s
memory and any additional policy history. A history-conditioned policy can instead use ht directly
or combine it with explicit estimates. In practice, the discrepancy between the simulated and real
187


execution of this loop can progressively degrade motion tracking, stability, and task performance.
The major sources of the sim-to-real gap are discussed below.
Dynamics and Physical Parameter Mismatch
The physical dynamics of a humanoid robot are
difficult to reproduce exactly in simulation. Differences in mass distribution, center of mass, in-
ertia, joint friction, damping, actuator strength, gear transmission, and joint limits can cause the
simulated robot to respond differently from its physical counterpart under the same control com-
mand. Contact-related parameters, such as ground friction, restitution, and collision geometry,
further introduce discrepancies during locomotion, jumping, and other highly dynamic motions.
Although system identification and domain randomization can reduce these differences, the real
robot inevitably exhibits unmodeled dynamics and parameter variations that are difficult to cap-
ture completely during training.
Actuation and Low-Level Control Mismatch
The action produced by a learned policy is not
directly realized as an idealized control input on a physical robot. Instead, it is typically con-
verted through a low-level controller, actuator dynamics, communication interfaces, and hardware-
specific constraints. Differences between simulated and real actuator response, including torque
tracking errors, motor bandwidth, saturation, dead zones, and control frequency, can therefore
introduce discrepancies between the commanded and realized motion. These errors become par-
ticularly significant for fast motions, where accurate timing and high-frequency torque responses
are essential.
Perception and State-Estimation Errors
In simulation, the policy can often access accurate robot
states, object positions, or environment information, whereas real systems must estimate these
quantities from noisy and delayed sensor measurements. Camera noise, depth errors, occlusions,
motion blur, imperfect calibration, and tracking failures can lead to discrepancies between the true
physical state and the state provided to the policy. Such errors can alter both the magnitude and
timing of the resulting control actions, especially for tasks involving fast-moving objects or rapidly
changing contacts.
Control Latency and Asynchronous Execution
Real-time execution also introduces computa-
tional and communication delays across perception, state estimation, policy inference, commu-
nication, and actuation. For a sequential processing path, the total latency can be approximated
as
dtotal = dperception + destimation + dpolicy + dcommunication + dactuation,
(7.43)
where each d is a time duration. In asynchronous or overlapping pipelines, the observation times-
tamp and actual execution time determine information age. The sum alone is insufficient. Given
a control period ∆t, a large dtotal means that the action is effectively computed from an outdated
state, introducing a phase lag into the control loop. This effect is particularly detrimental to fast dy-
namic motions and balance control, where even a small temporal mismatch can result in noticeable
tracking errors. In addition, asynchronous execution between perception, policy inference, and
low-level control can introduce variable delays, making the effective control dynamics different
from those assumed during simulation.
HoST illustrates how policy updates and joint feedback operate at different rates. On the 23-DoF
Unitree G1, a three-layer MLP uses a short proprioceptive history, including body roll and pitch,
angular velocity, and joint states, together with the previous action and action scale. The policy
updates joint-position targets at 50 Hz, while the physical robot’s proportional-derivative (PD) ser-
vos run at 500 Hz (Huang et al., 2025b). Joint feedback thus continues between policy updates.
The simulation uses a 200 Hz PD loop, illustrating why transfer depends on the response of the
complete policy-servo system as well as the policy update rate.
Contact and Environmental Mismatch
Physical interaction with the environment is another im-
portant source of discrepancy. Contact locations, collision geometry, ground compliance, friction
conditions, and external disturbances are often simplified in simulation but can vary substantially
188


in the real world. For humanoid robots, small differences in foot-ground contact or object interac-
tion can change the resulting contact forces and consequently alter the entire-body motion. Such
discrepancies are particularly challenging for behaviors involving impacts, rapid changes of sup-
port, or interaction with non-rigid or unstructured environments.
Reference-Tracking Error
For systems that generate reference motions and subsequently track
them with a learned controller, the sim-to-real gap can be further amplified by tracking errors.
Even if a kinematic trajectory generated by a planner is physically plausible, the real robot may
not reproduce it exactly due to actuator limitations, modeling errors, latency, and state-estimation
noise. The resulting deviation between the reference trajectory and the executed motion can ac-
cumulate over time, causing the robot to gradually drift away from the intended state. This issue
is especially important in hierarchical architectures, where the output of one module becomes the
input or conditioning signal of another.
Error Accumulation in Hierarchical and Autoregressive Systems
The effect becomes more pro-
nounced when motion generation and control are coupled through multiple sequential modules.
Consider a hierarchical system consisting of a high-level motion planner and a low-level tracking
controller. If the planner generates a reference trajectory qref
t:t+H spanning the current step and H
future control steps and the tracker executes it with tracking error, the actual state can deviate from
the planned trajectory. When subsequent planning decisions use execution feedback, this deviation
can propagate to future references. Errors in previously generated references can also propagate
through the history used by an autoregressive planner.
This problem is particularly evident in autoregressive kinematic planners. Instead of generating an
entire trajectory independently, an autoregressive planner predicts future motion conditioned on
previously generated reference states and a planning condition cplan
t
according to
qref

(7.44)
where Fplan is the motion generator. Consequently, an error in an earlier prediction can become
part of the input to subsequent predictions, resulting in accumulated prediction error over a long
horizon. In a hierarchical planner-tracker architecture, tracking errors introduce another source of
deviation between the planned and physically executed states. When execution feedback enters
cplan
t
or another planning input, these state deviations can change future references. This coupling
is particularly important for long-horizon and highly dynamic behaviors, where small local dis-
crepancies can progressively amplify over time. Deep Tracking Control combines an optimization-
based planner with a learned tracker (Jenelten et al., 2024). AdaPT conditions a tennis planner on
robot and ball information and adapts the reference execution speed (Huang et al., 2026a). These
examples illustrate how planner-tracker interfaces connect motion generation with physical exe-
cution. Figure 7.8 summarizes sources of sim-to-real mismatch and their propagation through a
planner-tracker system.
7.5.2
Motion Smoothing and Continuous Execution
In addition to inference speed, the temporal continuity of policy outputs is critical for stable real-
world execution. Directly executing the actions produced by a learned policy at each timestep
may result in high-frequency oscillations, particularly under observation noise, out-of-distribution
states, or discrepancies between simulated and real dynamics. Such oscillations can introduce un-
necessary joint acceleration, actuator load, and mechanical wear.
Locally Lipschitz Continuous Constraint (L2C2) regularization encourages local smoothness of policy
and value functions during training (Kobayashi, 2022). It penalizes changes under nearby input
perturbations, helping reduce sensitivity to small observation changes. For highly dynamic behav-
iors, the resulting action continuity must be considered together with the responsiveness needed
to preserve task-relevant motion components.

HoST applies L2C2 to the actor and each critic, constructing nearby inputs from differences be-
tween successive observed states. This training objective encourages smoother actor and value
outputs. In hardware experiments with 5 trials in each of 4 settings (ground, platform, wall, and
slope), HoST succeeds in 20/20 trials, compared with 11/20 after removing L2C2 (Huang et al.,
2025b). These results connect local function smoothness to the reliability of physical execution
under the tested conditions.
Motion amplitude introduces a complementary trade-off. Large actions aid exploration but can
produce violent transitions. HoST bounds the policy output and constructs each joint target relative
to the current joint position according to

where qj,t and qd

target increment in radians. Meeting an episode-end head-height criterion advances an action-scale

displacement at each update and indirectly moderates motion through the PD response. Gradual
tightening retains early exploration while encouraging less abrupt execution as the skill develops.
For tracking a reference motion with specified timing, smoothing must also preserve the required
movement speed. The objective is to suppress high-frequency noise while preserving the temporal
structure and key dynamic characteristics of the original motion. Excessive smoothing may, for
example, reduce the speed of a tennis swing or alter the timing of a dynamic motion. Therefore,
motion smoothing should be designed jointly with motion phase, robot dynamic capabilities, and
task constraints. The planner-tracker decomposition in AdaPT converts generated motions into
executable commands through a dedicated tracking controller.
7.5.3
Sim-to-Real Adaptation
The deployment mismatches described above motivate training and adaptation across variations
in dynamics, sensing, and latency.
A widely used approach is domain randomization, where physical and environmental parameters
are randomized during training by sampling from a distribution
ξsim ∼p(ξsim),
(7.46)
where ξsim may include robot mass, friction coefficients, joint damping, actuator strength, obser-
vation noise, control latency, and external disturbances. By exposing the policy to a distribution of
possible environments, the learned controller can become less sensitive to modeling errors.
Another approach is to calibrate the simulation using real-robot data through system identification,
thereby reducing the discrepancy between simulated and physical dynamics. In practice, these
approaches can be combined. Real-robot data are first used to estimate the dominant physical
parameters, while domain randomization is then applied to cover the remaining uncertainty.
HoST combines coverage of initial support conditions with randomization of physical parameters.
Ground, platform, wall, and slope settings expose training to different starting postures and con-
tacts. Within these settings, randomization includes base center-of-mass offsets of up to ±3 cm and
control delays from 0 to 100 ms, alongside friction, actuator strength, and PD gains (Huang et al.,
2025b). Hardware deployment also adjusts hip and knee PD stiffness to compensate for differences
in torque response. The example shows how broad simulation coverage and servo-gain adjustment
contribute jointly to transfer.
For humanoid motion control, an important observation is that a motion that is kinematically fea-
sible in simulation is not necessarily dynamically executable on the real robot. Consequently, the
training pipeline should account not only for task-level objectives but also for the actual controller,
state estimation process, and execution constraints used during deployment. For systems that gen-
erate high-level motion references, the generated motion must ultimately be converted into exe-
cutable behavior by a tracking controller that accounts for these constraints.
7.5.4
Balance Protection and Fall Recovery
For humanoid robots, a particularly important aspect of safety control is the possibility of losing
balance and falling. A complete safety framework should therefore not assume that the robot never
falls, but should also provide mechanisms for controlled falling, post-fall recovery, and subsequent
task resumption.
Balance protection can be organized into several stages according to the severity of the instability.
The first stage is rapid disturbance rejection, such as adjusting foot placement, torso orientation,
and motion speed. If the robot can no longer recover its standing state and a validated protective
controller is available, the system can enter a controlled fall mode and modify the body configura-
191


tion to reduce impact. After falling, a dedicated, trained and validated get-up controller can bring
the robot back to a stable standing configuration.
Learning such a controller requires objectives that guide the robot through changing support
configurations.
HoST learns standing-up motion without reference trajectories, using height-
dependent reward activation to organize righting, rising, and stable standing (Huang et al., 2025b).
Its four reward groups (task, style, regularization, and post-task) describe progress, motion quality,
and the stability of the achieved posture. Each group has a separate critic. Its generalized ad-
vantage estimates are normalized within the training batch, then combined in a weighted sum to
update a shared actor with PPO. This separates return estimation for signals with different scales
and temporal structure while learning a policy that coordinates their requirements.
Exploration is especially difficult before the robot discovers how to raise its body into a supported
posture. HoST therefore applies an upward force to the base during training when the trunk is
nearly vertical. As the episode-end head-height criterion is met, the assistance decreases from 200 N
in 20 N steps until it reaches zero. Together with the action-scale curriculum, this lets training first
discover the recovery motion and then refine its execution with reduced assistance and smaller tar-
get increments. Post-task rewards favor low base linear and angular velocities and the maintenance
of body height and posture. Consistently, simulation success requires the base to reach the target
height and remain above it for the rest of the episode (Huang et al., 2025b). Recovery thus includes
stabilizing the terminal posture.
Executing a learned recovery skill also depends on the available space around the body.
HoST reports collisions with the surroundings in some seated-start trials using proprioception
alone (Huang et al., 2025b). Such cases motivate environmental checks when selecting and ini-
tiating a recovery motion. Incorporating the skill into an autonomous system further requires fall
detection, controller handover, and task resumption. The HoST study leaves this integration for
future work.
Task recovery should go beyond simply returning the robot to a standing posture. The system
should also restore the task context. For example, if the robot loses balance during a long-horizon
motion imitation task, the recovery module should determine the current task phase and decide
whether to restart the current motion, resume from an intermediate state, or replan a new exe-
cutable trajectory. Integrating these decisions with balance protection makes recovery part of the
task-level control process.
Future humanoid control systems should account for dynamic feasibility while integrating mo-
tion generation, real-time control, failure detection, risk mitigation, recovery, and task resumption.
These functions need validation within the intended operating conditions.
192


8
Physical Agents
For a long time, research on the interaction between AI and the physical world has focused primar-
ily on short-term actions and isolated skills, such as executing a single grasp or traversing a short
stretch of terrain. Yet a true embodied agent must be able to operate continuously in real envi-
ronments over extended periods of time. Achieving this requires more than low-level perception,
motor skills, and future prediction. Instead, it demands a capable cognitive core that can perform
long-horizon planning and adapt as conditions change.
This chapter discusses how to build such an integrated system, which is a physical agent, that
can interact with the physical world continuously in a closed loop. To this end, the chapter first
defines the scope of physical agents and clarifies how they differ from purely digital agents and
conventional robots. It then discusses how physical agents scale to adapt to entity-level, composite,
and system-level constraints. Building on this foundation, it explains how physical goals become
assessable task specifications, how available skills are organized into feasible behavior, and how
execution feedback supports verification and recovery. Finally, it examines collaboration among
heterogeneous agents and the emergence of distributed capabilities.
8.1
Definition of Physical Agent
As artificial intelligence extends from digital information spaces into the physical world, the no-
tion of an intelligent agent acquires additional requirements. A digital agent may pursue goals,
maintain memory, reason over observations, and invoke software tools, while its actions primarily
alter informational states. A physical agent must additionally operate through an embodied sys-
tem whose actions are constrained by geometry, dynamics, contact, sensing limitations, actuation
uncertainty, time, energy, and safety (Russell and Norvig, 2020; Pfeifer and Bongard, 2006; Siciliano
and Khatib, 2016). Its decisions can change not only the state of the task, but also its own phys-
ical configuration, the surrounding environment, and the observations and actions that become
available afterward.
A physical agent should therefore not be understood simply as a robot equipped with an artificial
intelligence model. The relevant distinction lies in how the system organizes perception and action
around an objective under physical constraints. In this chapter, the term refers to systems that are
physically situated, possess some degree of autonomy in selecting their behavior, and continuously
use the consequences of physical interaction to guide subsequent decisions. This perspective pro-
vides a common basis for discussing agents implemented as mobile robots, manipulators, legged
systems, aerial vehicles, autonomous machines, or more distributed physical systems (Brooks,
1991; Liu et al., 2025d).
8.1.1
Concept and Boundary of Physical Agent
A Working Definition
In this chapter, a physical agent is defined as a goal-directed, relatively au-
tonomous unit that perceives physical conditions, selects and executes feasible actions through its embod-
iment, and uses feedback from their physical effects to adjust subsequent behavior. Its embodiment de-
termines what it can sense and how it can act, while environmental conditions, resource limits,
and assigned authority constrain admissible behavior. Feedback connects intended outcomes to
observed changes in the agent and its surroundings, enabling it to continue execution, correct its
actions, or revise its plan.
This definition treats physical agency as a relationship among objective, embodiment, environment,
action, and feedback. The agent is situated because its behavior takes place in an environment
governed by spatial and physical relationships rather than solely by symbolic or computational
rules. It is goal-directed because its behavior is organized around a desired outcome rather than a
fully prescribed sequence of actions. It is autonomous or semi-autonomous because at least part of
the mapping from a task objective to concrete actions is determined during operation rather than
completely specified in advance.

Physical embodiment is essential to this definition. The embodiment includes the system’s mechan-
ical structure together with its sensors, actuators, onboard computation, and the interfaces through
which it exchanges information and physical influence with the environment. It determines what
the agent can observe, which actions are feasible, and what physical consequences those actions
may produce. The embodiment is therefore not merely a carrier on which an intelligent algorithm
is deployed. It constitutes part of the agent’s sensing and action capabilities and thereby defines
part of its operational boundary (Pfeifer and Bongard, 2006; Siciliano and Khatib, 2016).
The definition also requires closed-loop interaction (Brooks, 1991; Åström and Murray, 2008). An
action produces a physical consequence, that consequence gives rise to new observations, and those
observations may alter subsequent behavior. This interaction is illustrated in Figure 8.1.
Perception and action are coupled in this loop. Actions change the world from which future obser-
vations are obtained, and new observations change which actions are subsequently selected.
Physical Agents and Digital Agents
A physical agent and a digital agent share several funda-
mental properties. Both may be goal-directed, maintain internal state, use memory, reason over
uncertain information, invoke tools, and revise their behavior according to feedback. The distinc-
tion therefore does not lie in whether the system performs reasoning or planning.
The more consequential difference concerns the domain in which actions take effect. A digital agent
primarily changes informational states, for example by generating text, editing files, querying a
194


database, executing code, or invoking a software service. These actions may indirectly lead to
physical consequences when mediated by an external system, but the agent’s immediate action
space is digital.
A physical agent acts through a physical embodiment. Its actions may change its position, orien-
tation, velocity, configuration, contact state, or energy state, as well as the location, configuration,
or physical condition of external objects. Such actions are subject to feasibility constraints and may
produce delayed, uncertain, or irreversible consequences. A manipulator cannot instantaneously
move its end effector to an arbitrary pose. An aerial vehicle cannot change velocity without satis-
fying its dynamics. A mobile robot cannot traverse an occupied region merely because a planner
identifies it as geometrically desirable.
The distinction can therefore be expressed in terms of the state directly affected by action. Digital
agents act primarily on informational states, whereas a physical agent directly participates in the
evolution of physical states. This difference introduces requirements that are less prominent in
purely digital settings, including dynamic feasibility, physical safety, execution uncertainty, limited
sensing, resource constraints, and the need to verify the actual outcome of an action rather than
only whether a command was issued.
Physical Agents and Robots
The terms robot and physical agent also overlap without being syn-
onymous. A robot primarily identifies a class of embodied machines capable of sensing, com-
putation, and actuation. The concept of a physical agent places greater emphasis on how such
capabilities are organized around an objective and how much of the resulting behavior is selected
during interaction with the environment.
Consider an industrial manipulator that repeatedly follows a predetermined welding trajectory.
The system is clearly a robot, and it may employ sophisticated feedback control to achieve high
precision. Nevertheless, if the task, sequence, and responses to relevant situations are almost en-
tirely specified in advance, its behavior exhibits relatively little agent-level autonomy. By contrast,
a manipulation system that is given a desired outcome, selects an appropriate grasp and motion
strategy from the observed scene, detects unsuccessful execution, and chooses an alternative course
of action has stronger agentic properties even if the underlying physical platform is similar.
The distinction is therefore one of emphasis rather than a strict separation of system categories. A
robot characterizes the physical means through which sensing and action are realized, whereas a
physical agent characterizes a mode of operation in which perception, decision-making, physical
action, and feedback are organized in pursuit of a goal. Many modern robotic systems satisfy both
descriptions, while some robots remain primarily automated machines with narrowly prescribed
behavior.
8.1.2
Functional Organization and Interaction Loop
Building on the four elements in Chapter 1 (Section 1.3), this section distinguishes five functional
roles by discussing world representation and physical prediction separately. These roles comprise
physical state perception and estimation; physical representation and world models; physical pre-
diction and simulation; physical decision-making, planning, control, and execution; and closed-
loop feedback and multiscale adaptation. A physical agent realizes this same loop within an identi-
fiable operational boundary. The following account applies those elements to agent-level behavior,
without prescribing separate software modules. Their functions may be explicitly implemented,
learned jointly, or distributed across computational and physical subsystems (Siciliano and Khatib,
2016; Liu et al., 2025d).
Embodiment, objectives, and operating constraints provide the conditions under which all five
functional roles function. The embodiment includes mechanical structure, sensors, actuators, com-
putation, and environment interfaces. It determines which observations and physical actions are
available. A wheeled platform, manipulator, and aerial robot may therefore use different strategies
for the same objective. Goals specify desired outcomes, while kinematic and dynamic limits, col-
lision avoidance, energy, time, permissions, and safety requirements delimit acceptable behavior.
195


These conditions guide the entire loop. Memory supports continuity across its elements, and safety
mechanisms constrain and monitor their operation.
Physical State Perception and Estimation
A physical agent generally lacks direct access to the
complete state of the world. Cameras, depth sensors, LiDAR, tactile and force sensors, inertial
units, encoders, and other instruments provide incomplete measurements affected by noise, oc-
clusion, calibration errors, and latency (Siciliano and Khatib, 2016). Perception and estimation
construct task-relevant descriptions of the body’s state and surroundings, including pose, motion,
object configurations, contact, free space, or process quantities such as temperature. The required
information and its accuracy depend on the decisions and control actions that follow.
Physical Representation and World Models
Representations organize estimated information
into spatial, semantic, relational, or physical descriptions that support action. Memory retains ear-
lier observations, explored regions, attempted actions, and outcomes, enabling the physical agent
to reason beyond its current view. A world model may encode object relationships, affordances,
and transition regularities. Such information can be explicit, implicit in a learned policy, or dis-
tributed across components. A comprehensive internal simulator is therefore unnecessary. The
relevant requirement is a representation adequate for the task and operating conditions.
Physical Prediction and Simulation
Prediction uses available representations to anticipate how
candidate actions, disturbances, or other participants may change physical conditions. Scenario
simulation can compare alternative sequences before committing to execution, using analytical dy-
namics, learned models, or other approximations. Its usefulness depends on the prediction hori-
zon, uncertainty, and computational cost. This element need not be a separate predictive module.
A reactive controller or learned policy may incorporate local expectations implicitly, while explicit
prediction supports longer horizons and more complex dependencies. Forecasts remain condi-
tional on their assumptions and must be checked against interaction outcomes.
Physical Decision-Making, Planning, Control, and Execution
This element connects estimated
conditions and the objective to feasible physical intervention (Russell and Norvig, 2020; Kober
et al., 2013). A complex objective can be decomposed into intermediate goals and realized through
reusable skills, such as approaching, grasping, transporting, or inspecting. Planning coordinates
these skills and their dependencies. Control converts the selected behavior into trajectories, veloc-
ities, forces, torques, or actuator commands compatible with the embodiment. An instruction to
grasp a container may thus require approach motion, alignment, contact establishment, closure,
and force regulation. Modular architectures may expose these stages individually, while learned
policies may combine them. In either case, action selection remains conditioned on the task, current
information, and admissible operating conditions.
Closed-Loop Feedback and Multiscale Adaptation
Execution changes the physical state and
produces new evidence. Feedback compares intended and observed outcomes and informs cor-
rections at different scales (Åström and Murray, 2008). A controller can regulate contact force, a
skill can adjust its motion, and a task planner can replace an unsuccessful operation. Over re-
peated operation, calibration and retained experience can support adaptation to equipment drift or
changing conditions. Adaptation may update estimates, representations, predictions, or behavior
without necessarily changing learned parameters online. Safety mechanisms operate throughout
the loop by restricting candidate actions, monitoring execution, and triggering recovery, fallback,
or intervention when limits are approached. Feedback therefore connects local regulation, task-
level revision, and longer-term adaptation, sustaining the closed-loop organization described in
Chapter 1 and its application loop (Section 1.5.1).

8.1.3
Autonomy and the Transition from Automation to Agency
Autonomy as a Continuum
The distinction between a physical agent and a conventional auto-
mated system is not binary. Physical systems exhibit different degrees of autonomy, and many use-
ful machines occupy intermediate positions between fixed automation and general goal-directed
agency (Parasuraman et al., 2000).
In fixed automation, task structure and action sequences are largely specified before deployment.
A production system may repeatedly execute the same sequence with high precision, while con-
ventional feedback control compensates for deviations in variables such as position, velocity, force,
or temperature. Such feedback is essential to reliable physical operation, but local error correction
alone does not imply that the system selects its behavior at the task level.
As sensing, computation, and adaptive control become more capable, physical systems can respond
to a wider range of environmental variations. A mobile robot may choose a different route when
an aisle is blocked, and a manipulator may adjust its motion when an object is displaced. In such
cases, some aspects of behavior are determined online, although the range of possible tasks and
responses may remain strongly bounded by predefined representations and skills.
A more agentic system shifts the specification from actions toward outcomes. Rather than being
provided with a complete trajectory or procedure, it may receive a target state or higher-level objec-
tive and determine an appropriate sequence of actions from the current situation. The progression
can be represented schematically as
Fixed Automation →Feedback Control →Adaptive Robotics →Goal-Directed Agency.
(8.6)
197


This sequence should be interpreted as an organizing continuum rather than a strict taxonomy.
Real systems may combine characteristics from several stages and may exhibit different levels of
autonomy in different parts of the same task.
Goal-Conditioned Action Selection
A central feature of agency is that the same objective can
lead to different actions depending on the current physical situation. If a direct route becomes
obstructed, a mobile agent may select an alternative path. If an intended grasp is infeasible, a ma-
nipulation system may choose another grasp configuration or reposition itself before trying again.
The objective remains unchanged while the means of achieving it are revised.
This distinguishes goal-conditioned action selection from a fixed input-output response.
The
agent’s action depends jointly on the current state, the desired outcome, the available capabilities,
and the constraints under which it operates.
Adaptation Under Uncertainty
Physical environments are only partially observable and are
rarely perfectly predictable. Objects may move, materials may behave differently from expected
models, sensing may degrade, and the effect of an action may differ from its nominal prediction.
A physical agent must therefore operate despite uncertainty about both the current state and the
consequences of its own actions (Kober et al., 2013; Brunke et al., 2022).
Adaptation in this context does not necessarily imply online learning of model parameters. It
more generally refers to the ability to revise behavior as new evidence becomes available. The
agent may update a state estimate, change a planned path, select another skill, reduce speed, re-
quest additional observations, or transfer control to a human operator. These mechanisms differ
in implementation but serve the same role by preventing execution from being tied irreversibly to
assumptions made before interaction.
Outcome-Driven Correction and Recovery
An important consequence of closed-loop autonomy
is that issuing an action is not equivalent to completing it. Physical execution must be assessed in
terms of outcomes. A command to close a door is not successful merely because the corresponding
motor command was sent. The agent must establish, to the extent required by the task, that the
resulting physical state satisfies the intended condition.
When execution does not produce the intended outcome, an agent may need to distinguish among
transient error, action failure, environmental change, or an infeasible objective. Recovery can then
involve repeating the action, selecting an alternative action, revising the plan, modifying the ob-
jective within permitted limits, or requesting external intervention. The ability to make such dis-
tinctions becomes increasingly important as tasks extend over longer horizons and involve larger
numbers of dependent actions.
Autonomy Does Not Imply Unrestricted Operation
Autonomy should not be equated with
the absence of human control. In practical physical systems, autonomous behavior is typically
bounded by authority, safety, and operational constraints. A robot may plan its own route while
requiring authorization for a safety-critical manipulation, or it may execute a task independently
while requesting human assistance when uncertainty exceeds an acceptable threshold.
For this reason, a physical agent is more appropriately described as an autonomous or semi-
autonomous system than as a necessarily fully autonomous machine. Its autonomy concerns the
degree to which action selection and adaptation are delegated to the system within a specified
operating envelope.
Autonomy should also not be treated as synonymous with intelligence. A narrowly specialized
machine may operate with little human intervention while possessing limited ability to generalize
beyond a predefined task. Conversely, a system with sophisticated perception, reasoning, or learn-
ing capabilities may intentionally operate under substantial human supervision. The development
of Physical AI should therefore be considered along multiple dimensions, including autonomy, task
198


diversity, environmental openness, uncertainty, temporal horizon, and the complexity of adaptive
behavior.
From this perspective, the transition from automation to physical agency is characterized less by the
addition of any single algorithm than by a change in how behavior is organized. The system moves
from executing actions specified in advance toward selecting and revising actions in response to
goals, physical constraints, and interaction outcomes. This concept provides the foundation for
the subsequent discussion of goal representation, perception, world modeling, planning, learning,
control, and other capabilities required for a physical agent.
8.2
Physical Forms of Physical Agent
A physical agent can take different forms, distinguished by how its body provides access to the
world. A manipulator changes an object’s pose through contact, a mobile robot changes position
and viewpoint, and a laboratory installation transforms and measures samples. These differences
arise from both bodily morphology and the arrangement of sensing, actuation, computation, and
resources. Accordingly, physical form denotes the organization through which an agent acts, includ-
ing systems whose action interfaces are distributed across several devices. Situated robotics and
embodied intelligence provide the conceptual foundations for relating behavior to the coupling of
controller, body, and environment (Brooks, 1991; Pfeifer et al., 2007).
Under the working definition adopted in this chapter, a physical agent is a relatively autonomous,
goal-directed unit that perceives physical conditions, selects feasible actions, changes those condi-
tions, and adapts through feedback. A robot is one possible realization of its body. Agency is a
property of the complete operational loop, including the executive and its authority over physical
interfaces. Software that recommends an action remains a digital agent at that boundary. Attribut-
ing physical agency to a software-equipment installation requires including the equipment that
executes the action and the measurements used to evaluate it.
Figure 8.2 introduces three complementary views. An entity-level view treats a coherent acting body
as one unit. A composite view resolves functionally separable action subsystems that fulfill a joint
mission. A system-level view encompasses distributed resources coordinated across an operational
domain. This is the chapter’s analytical framework, rather than a standardized taxonomy or an
autonomy ranking. For example, a mobile manipulator can be one entity in a transport study, a

Three criteria make that choice explicit, namely command authority, observable outcomes, and the
allocation of responsibility to people or other systems. They distinguish an operational boundary
from a building perimeter or a network membership list. Task objects usually remain part of the
environment, even while grasped. Materials and mechanisms can themselves support adaptive
behavior, as emphasized in physical intelligence research (Sitti, 2021). The working definition here
additionally requires a goal-directed action loop. With this boundary established, physical forms
can be examined through the interfaces and constraints that make particular actions possible.
8.2.1
Entity-Level and Composite Forms of Physical Agent
Entity-Level Forms and Their Action Interfaces
An entity-level physical agent has a coherent
body and an identifiable action interface. Mobility, contact geometry, compliance, workspace, pay-
load, and sensing arrangement describe how that body interacts with its surroundings. Figure 8.3
pairs representative morphologies with the physical variables through which they act.

Fixed Manipulators
An arm controls end-effector pose and interaction forces within a bounded
workspace. Operational-space control formalizes the relationship between joint actuation and end-
effector motion or force (Khatib, 1987). Geometric reach is only one requirement. Tool shape,
friction, collision clearance, and admissible contact loads also determine whether an operation is
feasible. Pairing two arms adds complementary contact roles, such as stabilizing and inserting.
ALOHA demonstrates learned fine manipulation using such a bimanual arrangement and human
demonstrations (Zhao et al., 2023). At the installation scale the pair can be treated as one manipu-
lation unit. A composite view makes its coordination requirements explicit.
Ground-Mobile Robots
Wheeled bodies provide efficient transport where supporting surfaces
are traversable. Legged bodies can select footholds across uneven terrain, with balance and contact
transitions forming part of the action problem. Miki et al. (2022) integrate terrain information with
proprioception for quadrupedal locomotion under unreliable perception. Terrain estimates support
action through the footholds and dynamics available to the body. Humanoids extend this family
200


with human-like proportions and manipulation interfaces. Resemblance to people is not a criterion
for physical agency.
Aerial Robots
Flight provides three-dimensional access and changes the sensor’s viewpoint
without continuous ground support. This capability couples navigation to lift, attitude stabiliza-
tion, obstacle clearance, and energy availability. Loquercio et al. (2021) demonstrate high-speed
autonomous flight using onboard sensing and computation. Inspection and delivery build on
aerial access but additionally depend on task-specific sensors, payload interfaces, and operating
conditions.
Process Equipment and Compliant Bodies
Stationary equipment can change geometry, temper-
ature, pressure, or composition through tools and process inputs. Cyber-physical manufactur-
ing architectures connect such equipment to state assessment and adaptive responses (Lee et al.,
2015). Soft structures, meanwhile, support conformal interaction by distributing deformation over
a body (Rus and Tolley, 2015). Passive dynamic walking offers a complementary demonstration of
mechanics contributing to organized motion (McGeer, 1990).
Composite Forms: Coordinated Action Across Modules
A composite physical agent combines
functionally separable action subsystems under one mission and outcome criterion. Typical combi-
nations join locomotion with manipulation, ground transport with flight, or sample handling with
experimental processing. The analytical emphasis lies on the interfaces between these capabilities.
Mechanical attachment is one coupling mechanism. Shared timing, resources, and responsibility
can also bind modules that separate in space.

Mobile Manipulation
Base motion extends access beyond a fixed arm’s workspace while chang-
ing its reference frame, sensing viewpoint, and collision envelope. The pose relation in Figure 8.4(a)
expresses this geometric dependence. Contact forces and stability introduce additional dynamic
constraints. Mobile ALOHA combines a mobile base, two arms, and whole-body demonstration
collection to learn coordinated tasks, including cabinet operation and use of a kitchen faucet (Fu
et al., 2025). Locomotion establishes access to a work location, while manipulation determines
where the base can operate. The cited study evaluates learned execution after demonstration col-
lection, so its teleoperation apparatus and its autonomous policy serve distinct roles.
Vehicle-Drone Systems
A carrier can move a drone between launch sites while the drone serves
locations through complementary aerial routes. The flying sidekick traveling salesman problem
models the resulting route, endurance, and rendezvous dependencies (Murray and Chu, 2015).
Figure 8.4(b) makes one consequence visible. Arrival at the recovery site must be synchronized,
potentially through waiting. This is an optimization formulation, with human driving of the truck
retained in the original problem setting. A composite interpretation becomes useful when one mis-
sion executive is responsible for both delivery and recovery. Separate vehicles with independently
assigned goals invite a multi-agent interpretation.
Multi-Device Experimental Platforms
Dispensing, processing, transfer, and measurement mod-
ules can form a composite when they execute a bounded protocol. Burger et al. (2020) connect
laboratory stations through a dexterous mobile robot in a photocatalyst search. Transporting one
vial can be attributed to the robot, whereas conducting the experimental search also requires the
stations and experiment-selection software. The example shows how changing the attributed out-
come changes the necessary physical boundary.
Composite form can itself be variable. Modular self-reconfigurable robots alter the connectivity
and arrangement of their modules (Yim et al., 2007). Self-modeling robots can revise their behavior
after bodily damage (Bongard et al., 2006). Capability consequently depends on current connec-
tivity, calibration, module condition, and coordinated skills. This dependence becomes still more
prominent when the acting resources form a persistent, distributed installation.
8.2.2
System-Level Physical Agents
A Distributed Body with an Operational Boundary
A system-level physical agent acts through
distributed sensors, robots, process equipment, computing nodes, and control networks. Its opera-
tional unity comes from an objective and the coordinated use of resources across a domain. Physical
distribution and controller organization are separate design choices. A distributed body may use
centralized, distributed, or hybrid coordination. Holonic manufacturing provides an early account
of autonomous units participating in a larger production organization (Van Brussel et al., 1998).
Cyber-physical production connects computational coordination with physical processes (Monos-
tori et al., 2016).
Two related graphs clarify the organization of such a body:
Gphys = (Vphys, Ephys),
Ginfo = (Vphys ∪Vcomp, Einfo),
(8.7)
where Gphys and Ginfo are the physical-dependency and information-exchange graphs. The resource
vertex sets Vphys and Vcomp contain sensing/acting and logical computation resources, respectively.
Computation may be hosted on the same devices. The edge set Ephys encodes mechanical, material-
transfer, or process dependencies. The edge set Einfo encodes sensing, coordination, or command
exchange. The union Vphys ∪Vcomp comprises both resource types. Figure 8.5 illustrates the orga-
nization of a system-level physical agent. This descriptive model distinguishes the existence of a
communication path from the existence of an executable physical operation. For example, rerout-
ing a part requires a compatible transport path as well as a revised assignment.
