Attribution of agency at this scale requires an actionable system objective, authority over the nec-
essary equipment, and measured outcomes that change subsequent interventions. A production
objective, for example, becomes operational through coordinated transformation, transport, and
quality evaluation. Sensor aggregation alone supplies only part of that loop. Similarly, a fixed
command sequence can automate execution while leaving adaptation to an operator. The relevant
distinction concerns who selects and revises physical actions when conditions change.
The operational boundary also spans different timescales. Fast contact and motion loops coexist
with slower production and experiment cycles. Local stabilization and protective responses must
remain effective within the coordination architecture. Human supervisors can set objectives, re-
plenish resources, and authorize exceptional operations, provided these responsibilities are stated.
A system-level physical agent can therefore contain local agents and depend on specified human
support. What justifies the higher-level description is the additional feedback loop that coordi-
nates resources to achieve an installation-wide outcome. Smart factories, intelligent mines, and
autonomous laboratories are representative realizations of a system-level physical agent.
Protocols and Standards for a Physical Agent
For a system-level physical agent, interoperability
determines whether independently developed resources can participate in a common course of ac-
tion. Robots, instruments, and process equipment need shared ways to describe their capabilities,
accept delegated work, and report what occurred. Protocols specify these exchanges, while stan-
dards establish common information models and requirements against which implementations can
be checked. Together, they make the relationships between reasoning, coordination, and physical
execution explicit enough to support integration across manufacturers and applications.
A useful organization separates objective formation and revision, task coordination, and local ex-
ecution. Protocols connect these responsibilities by carrying capability descriptions, task requests,
and execution feedback. This separation allows planning methods and equipment implementa-
tions to evolve while preserving agreed interfaces. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), for ex-
ample, specifies how AI applications discover and invoke tools with structured input and output
descriptions (Model Context Protocol, 2025). Applying such interfaces to physical resources re-
203


quires their descriptions and results to carry the operational meaning needed by the task, includ-
ing which objects are affected, which conditions permit execution, and what observations establish
completion. Anthropic’s Model Hardware Standard (MHS), introduced as a research preview in
collaboration with HHMI Janelia Research Campus in 2026, addresses the discovery and opera-
tion of programmable physical devices.8 MHS combines standardized drivers with descriptions
of device characteristics and operating limits, and supports access through MCP, command-line
interfaces, and code. It thus provides a concrete example of connecting general agent interfaces to
laboratory and manufacturing equipment.
The central abstraction is the capability that a resource makes available to the wider system. This
may be a measurement, a material-processing operation, a robotic skill, or an established procedure
involving several devices. A common description helps an agent determine what can be requested
and what information it can expect in return. The Web of Things Thing Description provides one
foundation for describing interactions with heterogeneous devices (W3C, 2023). At the system
level, this suggests a way to organize access around useful functions while retaining the specialized
knowledge and control methods within each resource. The same planning system could then work
with different combinations of equipment through compatible descriptions.
An autonomous laboratory illustrates how this organization connects reasoning with diverse phys-
ical capabilities. In an illustrative materials study, a scientific agent might propose candidate com-
positions and the properties to be measured. A laboratory coordination system would relate this
plan to available preparation, processing, and characterization capabilities. Dedicated instruments
would perform established procedures, while robots could contribute manipulation or transport
where needed. The protocol would connect these contributions to the same experimental objective
and return their results in an interpretable form. The OPC UA Laboratory and Analytical Device
Standard supports this kind of integration through common models for device functions, program
execution, and results (OPC Foundation, 2023). Here OPC UA denotes OPC Unified Architecture.
The significance of this connection extends to what the agent can learn from an intervention. In the
laboratory example, measurements become useful feedback when they remain associated with the
candidate material, preparation history, and conditions under which they were obtained. The agent
can then compare outcomes, revise an explanation, or select a subsequent experiment. Similar re-
lationships arise when a production system uses inspection results to adjust processing conditions,
or an environmental monitoring system directs further measurements toward an uncertain region.
Across these settings, a protocol should preserve the context that makes returned observations rel-
evant to the objective. This connects access to physical resources with the continuing development
of the agent’s understanding.
Shared descriptions also create opportunities for reuse across tasks and facilities. A preparation-
and-measurement procedure could be offered as a composite capability for later studies, while its
constituent functions remain available for other combinations. Another facility could contribute
a complementary measurement or a compatible processing operation. Industrial asset represen-
tations such as the Asset Administration Shell provide standardized structures for accessing asset
information and services (IEC, 2023). Research linking these representations with capability mod-
els and OPC UA communication explores how such descriptions can support reconfigurable sys-
tems (Justmann et al., 2024). Reuse still depends on whether the available methods, materials, and
operating conditions fit the new task.
From this perspective, protocols and standards provide shared infrastructure through which phys-
ical capabilities can accumulate and be used by different agents. A common core can organize
capability discovery, task interaction, and contextualized feedback, while domain-specific descrip-
tions express the knowledge needed in manufacturing, laboratories, or other settings. As models,
instruments, and procedures improve, compatible interfaces could allow those advances to benefit
multiple workflows. The broader opportunity is to connect independently developed intelligence
and physical resources into systems that can pursue objectives, evaluate their interventions, and
8Anthropic, Previewing the Model Hardware Standard, research preview, August 27, 2026.
204


draw on a growing range of capabilities. Autonomous laboratories offer a concrete setting in which
to examine these relationships.
8.2.3
Correspondence Between Form, Capability, and Application
Reaching an object, exerting a controlled force, and checking the result require different physical
provisions. A long reach does not establish that an operation can be performed at every reachable
position. A large payload does not establish precise control of contact. Connecting form to applica-
tion therefore requires examining how the body produces the actions a task needs, and under what
conditions it can produce them reliably.
Geometry and Motion
Link lengths, joint arrangements, and movement limits determine which
positions and orientations a mechanism can reach. Its current posture also matters. Joint motion
can produce end-effector motion more readily in some directions than in others, and this relation-
ship changes as the mechanism moves. This posture dependence is captured by manipulability
measures (Yoshikawa, 1985). For capability assessment, the implication is that access to a posi-
tion and freedom to act there should be examined separately. The relevant description includes
the required working posture and motion direction, alongside collision clearance and load condi-
tions. Manipulability supplies one local kinematic measure. The other requirements need their
own checks.
Contact and Material Response
Surface geometry, friction, and compliance affect how a body
establishes contact and transmits force. Compliance allows a body to deform under contact, some-
times accommodating differences in object shape through its mechanics. A deformable gripping
interface, for instance, can conform to an object before stiffening to hold it. Its effectiveness still
depends on obtaining suitable contact (Brown et al., 2010). Changing the object or contact condi-
tions can therefore change the result even when the controller remains the same. Thus, describing
a body as compliant or adaptable should be accompanied by the object properties and loads for
which that behavior is useful.
Sensing Geometry
The placement and mobility of sensors determine which information the body
can acquire. A camera may have adequate resolution while lacking a useful view of the interaction.
Moving the sensor or the body can expose an occluded region. Active perception explicitly connects
sensing to such purposeful actions (Bajcsy et al., 2018). Physical form consequently affects both the
execution of an action and the possibility of obtaining the feedback needed to guide it. Relevant
capabilities include reaching an informative viewpoint, maintaining visibility during movement,
and accessing the measurements required to verify the result.
Relating Task Requirements to Physical Arrangements
These mechanisms give the form-
capability-task-constraint relationship a practical meaning. Form specifies the available physical
means, capability describes the actions and performance those means support, task specifies the
required effect, and constraints establish the conditions that must hold during execution. A use-
ful comparison starts with requirements such as a working region, permissible contact force, po-
sitional tolerance, or completion time, and then examines whether a proposed arrangement can
satisfy them together.
Table 8.1 organizes this comparison into five dimensions. It is an analytical synthesis of the mech-
anisms and performance-assessment approaches discussed here, rather than a standardized classi-
fication. The task determines which dimensions and criteria need evaluation.
The requirements interact. Extending a mechanism’s reach can alter the actuator effort needed for
a motion. Adding mobility changes the relationship between the working tool, its support, and
the surrounding space. This interaction motivates the joint design of morphology and control. Re-
search on morphology-control co-design makes this relationship explicit by optimizing mechanical
dimensions and actuator placement together with motion trajectories and forces, subject to phys-
ical and task constraints (Ha et al., 2018). This connects design choices to the behavior needed

For a composite or system-level physical agent, the same reasoning extends to the physical connec-
tions between resources. Cyber-physical production research situates computational coordination
within ongoing physical processes (Monostori et al., 2016). Applying that perspective here, com-
patible connections between local operations are a prerequisite for system-level capability. A trans-
fer must deliver an object in a state and location that the receiving resource can accept, and shared
equipment must be available when required. These conditions must be combined with effective co-
ordination and feedback to achieve the overall task. Communication enables coordination, while
physical interfaces and material routes determine which coordinated operations can actually oc-
cur. The relevant scale of embodiment follows these dependencies and may take the form of one
coherent body, several coupled modules, or a distributed arrangement of resources.
Comparing Forms Through Demonstrated Performance
Capability descriptions should distin-
guish the physical means available, the performance of the implemented agent, and the consis-
tency of that performance. End-effector benchmarking, for example, measures grasp strength, cy-
cle time, and repeatability separately because they answer different questions about application
suitability (Falco et al., 2020). At the task level, the relevant evidence may include success rate,
completion time, error, and required human intervention. Hardware specifications and task results
consequently provide complementary evidence when comparing forms.
The conditions of comparison must also be explicit. The YCB benchmarking framework records the
task, environment and object states, hardware, prior information, procedure, and execution con-
straints (Calli et al., 2015). Following this approach, alternative embodiments should be compared
against stated outcome criteria and documented conditions, while allowing each an appropriate
means of execution. Repeated trials establish how consistently the implemented system meets
those criteria. They also make clear the operating range within which a capability has been demon-
strated, rather than assuming that one successful demonstration establishes performance across
settings.
The correspondence between form and application is therefore established through a traceable
connection. Task requirements identify the necessary physical interactions, bodily organization
makes those interactions possible, and evaluation establishes the conditions under which they
are achieved. This provides a basis for selecting among entity-level, composite, and system-level
forms, and for expressing the physical goals developed in the next section.
206


8.3
Physical Goal Representation and Task Grounding
A physical agent realizes intended changes in the world through actions constrained by its embod-
iment and environment. A request such as “store the sample safely” must therefore identify an
acceptable outcome, admissible interactions, and evidence of completion. This connection applies
both to individual robots and to system-level implementations of a physical agent acting through
machines, instruments, and control interfaces.
Task realization involves specifying the required outcome, organizing available capabilities to
achieve it, and using feedback to assess and revise execution.
These functions are examined
through the instruction “Place the sealed sample container in cabinet B, keep it upright, and close
the cabinet.” The example connects goal semantics and task-relevant state representations to feasi-
ble behavior and observed results.
8.3.1
Physical Goal Representation and Semantic Grounding
From an Instruction to a Physical Specification
A goal specifies a desired outcome. A plan de-
scribes how available actions may achieve it. The container-storage goal should remain meaningful
whether executed by a mobile manipulator or by a fixed manipulator supplied through a conveyor.
Separating outcomes from procedures supports alternative plans and transfer across embodiments.
For exposition, a physical task can be summarized as
Ttask =

Ggoal, Cexec, Ppref, Vverify

,
(8.8)
where Ttask is the task specification. Here Ggoal specifies acceptable outcomes, Cexec constrains exe-
cution, Ppref expresses preferences among acceptable solutions, and Vverify specifies how outcomes
and constraints are assessed. This is an organizing abstraction rather than a prescribed data struc-
ture. Reaching the storage region is an outcome. Preserving the seal is a constraint. Minimizing
travel time is a preference. Checking placement and closure belongs to verification. Timing and
resource requirements may be constraints or preferences, depending on the application.
Let xt denote the joint physical state of the physical agent and environment at decision index t. In
this example, ccont labels the container and Bcab the cabinet. An illustrative Boolean terminal-goal
predicate g is
g(xT) = Inside(ccont, Bcab) ∧Supported(ccont) ∧Released(ccont)
∧Upright(ccont) ∧Closed(Bcab),
(8.9)
where T is the terminal decision index, xT the corresponding physical state, and ∧logical conjunc-
tion. Evaluated on xT, the predicates require the container to be inside the intended storage region,
physically supported, released by the manipulator, and upright. They also require the cabinet to be
closed. Keeping the container upright throughout transport additionally constrains the interven-
ing trajectory. Operational definitions must specify tolerances and evidence appropriate to the task
and sensing capabilities. Support and release distinguish completed placement from holding the
container at the target.
Complementary Representations and Task Abstractions
Goals may originate from language,
images, demonstrations, geometric designs, or numerical process specifications. They may require
a terminal state, sustained conditions, or repeated service. Symbolic descriptions express objects,
relations, and logical requirements. Geometric representations specify poses, regions, and clear-
ances. Physical variables describe forces, temperatures, or velocities. Temporal specifications dis-
tinguish eventual achievement from requirements that must persist throughout execution (Kress-
Gazit et al., 2009). These descriptions serve different decisions within the same task. A target
image communicates arrangement but may omit hidden contact conditions. A learning reward
guides optimization but need not fully specify acceptable behavior.
Task-relevant abstractions connect these descriptions to observations. Object properties and rela-
tions indicate which conditions currently hold, while action models describe how those conditions
207


may change. Such abstractions can be designed or proposed from language, video, and interaction
records, then checked for consistency and against available data. A learned detector may assess
whether a cabinet is open, while an action model associates opening with access to its interior. The
representation provides an adjustable interface for reasoning, learning, and verification. It need
not impose a fixed symbolic vocabulary or a particular architecture. Learning this interface must
preserve the task’s specified requirements.
Grounding Entities and Conditions in the Current Scene
Semantic grounding identifies the in-
tended container and cabinet and estimates their task-relevant properties and relations. Recogni-
tion alone does not establish that the cabinet is accessible or has sufficient storage space. Even a
small observational difference, such as an open versus closed door, changes the conditions from
which action must begin. Grounding therefore relates instruction semantics to the current scene
and the agent’s capabilities.
Language and vision-language models can supply useful priors. SayCan combines language-based
skill relevance with skill value estimates grounded in the robot’s situation (Ichter et al., 2023). Vox-
Poser constructs observation-linked spatial value maps to guide motion generation (Huang et al.,
2023a). They illustrate different interfaces between semantic interpretation and physical behav-
ior, each relying on appropriate perception and capability estimates. Figure 8.6 summarizes the
grounding process. Action organization is developed in the next subsection.

Uncertainty and Evidence Requirements
Physical states are partially observed. The belief state
bt(x) = p(xt = x | o0:t, u0:t−1) represents the conditional probability mass or density of a candi-
date physical state x at decision index t. Here p is the conditional state distribution, o0:t denotes
observations from indices 0 through t, and u0:t−1 denotes the executed control inputs over pre-
ceding transitions. ut is the control input implementing the selected action at. This representation
distinguishes measured information from inferred conditions and supports information-seeking
actions (Kaelbling et al., 1998). Implementations may instead use confidence-tagged records, alter-
native hypotheses, or other uncertainty estimates.
If two containers match the instruction, further evidence may be needed to resolve their identity.
An occluded cabinet interior may require inspection before placement. Clarification is appropriate
when ambiguity materially changes the intended outcome or acceptable risk. Observation should
resolve the uncertainty relevant to the next decision.
208


Verification requirements must reflect what can be established from evidence. A visually closed
door does not establish latching without suitable observations. Conditions should therefore admit
an “unknown” assessment when evidence is insufficient. The specification must identify both the
required conditions and the evidence that would justify claiming their satisfaction.
8.3.2
Task Decomposition and Action Organization
A Functional Hierarchy from Goals to Control
Task realization connects decisions at different
abstractions and timescales. A useful functional hierarchy is
goal specification −→subgoals and dependencies −→skills
−→motion or process references −→control inputs.
(8.10)
Upper levels determine desired outcomes and their dependencies. Intermediate levels select skills
and parameters. Lower levels generate movement or process evolution. These are functional re-
sponsibilities. A learned policy may combine several levels, while a system-level physical agent
may refine tasks into instrument commands rather than joint trajectories.
For the storage example, decomposition includes preparing access, acquiring and transporting the
container, placing it, and closing the cabinet. The order depends on capability and resource avail-
ability. A single-gripper robot may need to open the cabinet before acquiring the container or
use an intermediate support surface. An additional manipulator permits other arrangements. De-
composition therefore accounts for resources occupied by each action and conditions needed by
subsequent actions.
Task Planning and Dependency Structure
Task planning uses action conditions and predicted
effects to identify dependencies and construct plans, as exemplified by the Stanford Research In-
stitute Problem Solver (STRIPS) (Fikes and Nilsson, 1971). Hierarchical decomposition organizes
recurring procedures into reusable task structures. The planning model should reflect the agent’s
available skills and the current environment, so that task steps correspond to capabilities the agent
can invoke.
A plan need not impose a total order. Access must precede insertion, and the manipulator must
leave the door’s swept region before closure, whereas independent operations may be reordered
or run concurrently when resources permit. Logically independent steps may still compete for the
same manipulator or instrument. Conditional branches accommodate initially unknown states,
such as whether the cabinet is open. The resulting structure separates persistent dependencies
from ordering choices that vary with initial conditions and resources.
Coupling Task Planning with Physical Feasibility
Grasp choice, approach configuration, and
placement pose affect which task sequences are feasible. A grasp may obstruct passage through
the opening, or a placement may leave insufficient room for withdrawal. Task and motion plan-
ning (TAMP) addresses these interactions by coupling discrete action and contact choices with
continuous configurations, grasps, and trajectories (Garrett et al., 2021).
The coupling is bidirectional. A task planner proposes actions and required conditions, while geo-
metric and physical reasoning supplies feasible parameters or revises those choices. PDDLStream
connects symbolic planning to black-box procedures that generate values satisfying continuous
constraints (Garrett et al., 2020). Failure to find suitable parameters can prompt a different grasp,
approach, or task sequence. These parameters must support the entire relevant interaction, includ-
ing approach, contact, transport, and release, rather than merely reaching an isolated pose.
Relevant constraints extend beyond collision avoidance. Container transport requires stability and
acceleration limits. Door manipulation involves contact and changing geometry. Manufacturing
and laboratory workflows similarly couple operation ordering to machine availability, instrument
access, and admissible process or sample states. These conditions must be represented where they
affect planning. Geometric feasibility alone cannot capture them all. Figure 8.7 summarizes this
organization.

Skills as Reusable Units of Interaction
Skills such as grasping, opening, docking, and measur-
ing encapsulate temporally extended interactions. In the options framework, a skill comprises an
initiation set, an internal policy, and a termination rule (Sutton et al., 1999):

its state-dependent termination probability in [0, 1]. Practical inter-

Such interfaces support composition independently of whether a skill is programmed or learned.
Composition requires compatible boundary conditions. Grasping must leave the container suitable
for transport. Placement must preserve access for withdrawal and closure. Skill quality includes
its contribution to subsequent actions. Behavior trees organize conditions, skills, and alternative
branches into a modular execution structure (Colledanchise and Ögren, 2018), providing one way
to assemble reusable capabilities into longer tasks.
Learning, Adaptation, and Hybrid Organization
Learning can acquire skills from demonstra-
tions or interaction, estimate skill parameters, and support action selection. It can also be used to
adapt a planner to a particular task domain and skill library. Learning a planner concerns the selec-
tion and organization of actions, whereas learning a skill concerns how an interaction is executed.
The two can share experience while retaining distinct objectives. Such adaptation should preserve
the relationship between proposed steps, available capabilities, and task constraints.
Generative policies offer expressive representations for skill execution. Diffusion Policy produces
observation-conditioned action sequences with receding-horizon updates (Chi et al., 2023). Open-
VLA connects visual observations and language instructions to learned robotic actions (Kim et al.,
2025b). Their use in new settings depends on data coverage and compatibility with the agent’s
embodiment and operating conditions. Adaptation may therefore involve updating selected com-
ponents rather than redesigning the entire hierarchy.
Hybrid organization assigns complementary functions to planning and learned behavior. A plan-
ner can select subgoals and skills, while a learned policy handles contact-rich interaction. Code as
Policies illustrates another interface by generating programs that compose perception and control
210


functions (Liang et al., 2023a). The allocation of functions should follow task demands and the
evidence available for validating each component.
8.3.3
Closed-Loop Execution and Failure Recovery
Execution as Repeated State-Dependent Commitment
Execution tests a plan’s predictions
against a changing world. At each decision point, the physical agent updates its state estimate
and task context, then decides whether to continue, obtain information, adjust behavior, or replan.
A compact representation is
bt+1 = Update(bt, ut, ot+1),
dskill
t+1 = Supervise(bt+1, Ttask, ζexec
t

(8.12)
where t indexes decision steps, bt is the task-relevant belief state, ut is the control applied dur-
ing step t, and ot+1 is the resulting observation. The function Update revises that belief, while
Supervise selects the next supervisory decision dskill
t+1 using the task specification Ttask and execu-
tion context ζexec
t
. This context records the active skill, verified subgoals, and relevant constraint
history. The decision may authorize continuation, information gathering, recovery, replanning, or
termination. History matters because terminal observations cannot reveal every earlier constraint
violation. If another actor closes the cabinet during transport, the remaining plan must accommo-
date the changed access condition.
Feedback operates at several timescales.
Controllers regulate physical variables, skills assess
progress and termination, and task-level supervision revises dependencies. Model predictive con-
trol repeatedly solves a finite-horizon problem and executes an initial portion before updating
it (Mayne et al., 2000). Inner Monologue uses success feedback, scene descriptions, and human
feedback to inform language-based task planning (Huang et al., 2023b). These levels provide com-
plementary corrections. Timely control feedback regulates execution, while task supervision as-
sesses its relevance to the goal.
Monitoring Effects and Diagnosing Discrepancies
Monitoring tests whether prerequisites re-
main valid, expected changes occur, constraints hold, and goals are achieved. Evidence may in-
clude images, joint states, contact measurements, instrument readouts, and elapsed time. Gripper
closure does not establish acquisition, a placement pose does not establish support, and a door-
close command does not establish closure. The relevant checks concern physical effects.
Diagnosis distinguishes semantic mistakes, state-estimation errors, infeasible plans, skill failures,
and external changes. A small alignment error may be corrected locally. Persistent lack of progress
may indicate a blocked mechanism or an incorrect condition estimate. Repeated discrepancies also
warrant checking the state abstractions and action models used for planning. Execution records can
support revisions to initiation conditions or effect predictions, which should be validated before
reuse.
Monitoring itself is uncertain. Confirmation over time, complementary sensors, and explicit “un-
known” assessments can reduce false alarms and missed detections. Confirmation must neverthe-
less remain compatible with timely protective action. Figure 8.8 relates these checks to subsequent
decisions.
Recovery as Constrained Continuation
Recovery addresses the diagnosed cause while preserv-
ing progress that remains valid. Responses range from local correction and renewed observation
to another grasp, repositioning, or task-level replanning. Each response starts from the current
physical state. A failed placement may leave the container tilted or partially supported, so the con-
ditions for retrying must be reassessed. Previously verified subgoals must also be rechecked when
subsequent actions may have disturbed them.
Physical actions can consume resources or cause irreversible changes. Retries should therefore
depend on remaining resources, acceptable risk, and evidence that another attempt can address

Safety and Bounded Autonomy
Protective mechanisms constrain commands and monitor oper-
ating limits independently of unrestricted task-level decisions. Control barrier functions provide
one approach to enforcing safety-related state constraints under modeling and feasibility assump-
tions (Ames et al., 2019). Their guarantees depend on those assumptions, including valid state
estimates and available corrective control. Safety requirements therefore need explicit physical
conditions and appropriate protection.
Fallback behavior must suit the embodiment and situation. A loaded manipulator may need to
maintain support. A moving platform may require controlled deceleration. The scope of autonomy
should specify when task execution yields to protective control or an operator, as well as which
actions may be initiated.
Execution Evidence and Broader Evaluation
Recorded observations, verified subgoals, con-
straint violations, and interventions preserve the evidence behind execution decisions. Chapter 11
develops their use in systematic task evaluation, capability comparison, and benchmarking. Here,
verification supplies the evidence needed to continue, recover, or terminate the current task.
The connection between task specifications, capability-dependent plans, and execution evidence
also underpins the coordination among multiple locally autonomous participants discussed next.
8.4
Multi-Agent Collaboration and Distributed Physical AI
Section 8.2.2 describes a system-level physical agent through its operational boundary. Distributed
sensors, robots, equipment, and computing resources act toward a system objective, with mea-
sured outcomes informing subsequent interventions. This section examines the collaboration among
multiple physical agent instances that retain local sensing, decision-making, and action capabilities.
The distinction concerns the level at which agency and coordination are analyzed. System-level
agency does not require every component to be autonomous, whereas multi-agent collaboration
concerns the relationships among locally autonomous participants. A laboratory or production
212


installation may therefore be a system-level physical agent as a whole and a multi-agent organiza-
tion internally. Centralized task allocation is compatible with local agency. An instrument accessi-
ble through an application programming interface (API) that only executes commands can instead
remain a supporting resource.
Distributed Physical AI denotes the collective ability of agents to combine observations, complemen-
tary capabilities, and coordinated actions across a shared physical environment (Parker, 2007; Rizk
et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2025a). Coordination must reconcile local autonomy with collective commit-
ments when decisions are coupled through space, time, resources, and the effects of physical ac-
tion. Communication supports the exchange of observations and coordination information (Zhou
et al., 2023). Shared infrastructure and observed actions also inform coordination. Humans may
contribute objectives, expertise, supervision, and intervention. Building on the individual-agent
mechanisms in Sections 8.1 and 8.3, the following discussion focuses on the distribution of decision
authority, inter-agent coordination, and the capabilities and limitations of the resulting teams.
8.4.1
Organizational Architectures for Distributed Physical AI
Consider a partially collapsed tunnel in which a heterogeneous robot team searches for trapped
workers and delivers supplies. An aerial vehicle surveys accessible openings. A quadruped tra-
verses rubble and carries relay equipment. A mobile manipulator transports supplies and removes
small obstacles where feasible. Their tasks depend on shared access routes, communication cover-
age, and complementary capabilities. Organizing the team requires specifying where coordination
state, computation, and decision authority reside (Yan et al., 2013). Four representative architec-
tures are centralized, hierarchical, decentralized, and hybrid.
Centralized Organization
A central node aggregates reported state and performs team-level allo-
cation, resource coordination, or joint planning. It may combine automated planning with human
supervision. In the tunnel example, it assigns search, relay, and delivery responsibilities using the
available map and robot status. Agents retain local execution authority within these assignments.
The center’s decisions depend on the coverage and freshness of the information it receives.
Hierarchical Organization
Coordination responsibilities are divided across mission, team, and
agent levels. A mission coordinator sets rescue priorities. Team coordinators organize operations
within assigned regions. Agents execute their responsibilities locally. Decisions that affect several
teams are escalated, while regional details remain within the relevant team. Effective hierarchy
requires explicit interfaces between levels and sufficient information to recognize cross-team de-
pendencies.
Decentralized Organization
Agents coordinate without a single team-level decision center, us-
ing local observations and information from other agents. After discovering a trapped worker, an
explorer can request assistance. Candidates exchange capabilities and costs and agree on respon-
sibility. Coordination may use negotiation, consensus, or distributed optimization. Agents must
track the validity of agreements and revise or suspend them when information or connectivity
changes.
Hybrid Organization
Different functions or operating conditions use different arrangements. A
team may build maps cooperatively while a mission center assigns priorities, or negotiate passage
access locally while following centralized scheduling. If communication is interrupted, agents may
continue within agreed limits. Such changes require rules for transferring authority and reconciling
outstanding commitments when coordination is restored. Figure 8.9 summarizes the four forms.
Table 8.2 compares their typical tradeoffs. Actual performance depends on task coupling, network
conditions, and the implementation of coordination protocols.

8.4.2

Organizational architecture determines where coordination decisions are made.
Coordination
mechanisms determine how agents align their objectives, information, and actions. The central
issue is how decisions made by different agents remain compatible when they depend on shared
resources or on one another’s behavior.
Eight interdependent mechanisms organize this discussion, namely establishing shared goals, ca-
pability and role modeling, task allocation, collaborative perception, shared state, joint planning,
conflict resolution, and execution and reallocation (Rizk et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2025a). They operate
concurrently and revise one another as conditions change. Their ordering in the figure is schematic.

Capability and Role Modeling
Coordination requires descriptions of what each agent can cur-
rently contribute. These combine configuration-dependent capabilities, such as locomotion, sens-
ing range, and payload, with changing conditions, including battery energy, communication con-
nectivity, equipment, and health (Chen et al., 2025a). Roles express how those capabilities serve the
mission. A quadruped carrying relay equipment may maintain communication rather than search,
while another takes over exploration. Distinguishing capability from role allows responsibilities to
change without assuming that robots of the same category are interchangeable.
Task Allocation
Allocation assigns tasks to agents or temporary groups, accounting for capability
matching, dependencies, energy, risk, and completion time (Gerkey and Matari´c, 2004). A delivery
task may require both a carrier and a relay, making the assignment a joint choice rather than two
independent selections. Centralized optimization, auctions, negotiation, and distributed optimiza-
tion offer different ways to establish these assignments. Allocation also determines which agents
remain available for subsequent demands. Minimizing the immediate travel distance can therefore
conflict with preserving scarce capabilities for later tasks.
Collaborative Perception
Collaborative perception combines complementary observations and
coordinates sensing effort (Xu et al., 2024). An aerial vehicle can survey the tunnel structure, while
ground robots inspect occluded regions and assess traversability. Agents can divide observation
responsibilities according to uncertainty and information value, reducing unnecessary duplication.
Time synchronization, coordinate transformations, and target association support observation fu-
sion across viewpoints (Hu et al., 2022b). Fusion should preserve relevant uncertainty and identify
conflicting observations.
Shared State
Shared state maintains information needed for joint decisions, including maps,
targets, agent locations, resource occupancy, and task progress. Unlike collaborative perception,
which concerns acquiring and combining observations, this mechanism concerns distributing and
updating the resulting operational information.
State may reside centrally or in local copies.
Limited bandwidth favors task-relevant abstractions over continuous transmission of raw sensor
data (Chang et al., 2023). Agents need sufficiently current and consistent information about the
resources and dependencies on which their decisions rely. Identical knowledge of the entire envi-
ronment is unnecessary. The required consistency depends on how tightly the agents’ actions are
coupled.
Joint Planning
Joint planning addresses dependencies among agents’ actions in space, time, and
resource use. Two robots sharing a narrow passage must coordinate traversal order. A delivery
robot may depend on a relay reaching its coverage position first. Plans can be generated centrally
or reconciled through iterative negotiation (Mandi et al., 2024). Coordination can concentrate on
strongly coupled near-term actions while leaving independent actions locally planned. This limits
the need to fix every agent’s full trajectory while retaining explicit commitments where another
agent’s progress depends on them.
Conflict Resolution
Conflicts concern spatial occupancy, schedules, power, bandwidth, or in-
compatible task assignments. They may arise from competing objectives, outdated information, or
deviations from agreed plans. Priorities, reservations, negotiation, and replanning can resolve re-
source contention. Protective intervention may be required for imminent physical conflicts (Zhang
et al., 2025c; Lee et al., 2025). Resolution must propagate changes to affected commitments so that
other agents can revise their dependent actions.
Execution and Reallocation
Execution reports reveal whether assignments and inter-agent com-
mitments remain viable. Agents share progress, exceptions, and remaining resources when these
216


affect collaborators. A blocked route, lost connection, or unavailable executor may require transfer-
ring a task or reorganizing a group (Liu et al., 2025b). Reallocation should account for work already
completed, current resource reservations, and dependencies on other agents. Updating roles and
shared state alongside the assignment prevents a replacement agent from duplicating completed
work or continuing under obsolete assumptions.
8.4.3
Open Problems and Trends in Distributed Physical AI
Coordination can extend the coverage, throughput, and range of tasks achievable by a team. These
gains depend on how sensing, task dependencies, resources, and failures are managed across its
members.
Collective Capabilities
Complementary sensing and coordinated revisits extend spatial coverage
and the frequency of environmental updates (Francos and Bruckstein, 2023). Independent subtasks
can proceed concurrently, while ordered operations can be pipelined. Under the idealized assump-
tion of equal per-participant execution rates, let Wwork denote total workload measured as the time
required by one physical agent, Nagent ≥1 the number of participating instances, Lcrit the duration
of the critical path induced by task dependencies, and T the team’s completion duration. In this
bound, Wwork, Lcrit, and T use the same time unit, and

This lower bound exposes the limits of parallelism (Brent, 1974). Physical contention and coordi-
nation overhead can further restrict the benefit of additional agents. Heterogeneous capabilities
also expand the feasible task set. Aerial reconnaissance, ground access, manipulation, and infras-
tructure support can form task chains unavailable to any member alone. Alternative executors and
routes can preserve service after failures (Bossens et al., 2022), but resilience requires substitutes
for critical tools, capabilities, and communication links. Realizing these gains raises the following
open problems.
Communication, Information Freshness, and Consistency
Communication range changes with
robot motion and environmental conditions, while bandwidth, delay, and packet loss constrain in-
formation exchange (Gielis et al., 2022). Collaboration requires deciding which observations, task
commitments, and resource states to share, and when their expected benefit justifies transmission.
Agents must also track whether information remains valid when making coupled decisions. A
delayed passage-occupancy update can be more consequential than an incomplete distant map.
Maintaining sufficient consistency requires task-specific priorities and rules for conflicting or out-
dated updates. Because motion changes network topology, communication and physical planning
may need to be optimized jointly.
Cross-Embodiment Knowledge and Semantic Interfaces
Different observation spaces, action
spaces, and dynamics prevent direct transfer of many policies between embodiments.
Cross-
embodiment learning provides useful experience (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024), but
collaboration additionally requires alignment of object identities, task states, capability descrip-
tions, and expected skill outcomes. An aerial vehicle and a mobile manipulator may interpret the
same destination while requiring different access conditions and control policies. Shared interfaces
should expose these differences so that task assignment and composition remain meaningful. Com-
patible task semantics must therefore support coordination while preserving embodiment-specific
actions and requirements.
Collaborative Safety and Runtime Assurance
Individually acceptable actions can conflict
through shared space, resource occupancy, or coupled task dependencies. Updating one learned
policy can also change the operating conditions encountered by other agents (Garg et al., 2024). As-
surance must therefore address joint behavior, including the validity of reservations and commit-
ments when communication is delayed or an agent fails. Local protective responses need to respect
217


team interactions. Stopping one robot may obstruct another or interrupt a jointly supported load.
Coordination protocols should specify how such responses are communicated and how affected
commitments are revised, including the respective authority of agents, coordinators, and human
supervisors.
System-Level Evaluation
Embodied multi-agent benchmarks provide a basis for assessing col-
laborative task performance (Chang et al., 2025). Evaluation should also measure the benefit and
cost of coordination, including team completion time, duplicated work, workload distribution,
communication demand, inter-agent conflicts, and recovery after member failures. Tests should
vary team size, embodiment combinations, connectivity, and capability availability. Comparisons
with suitable single-agent or independently operating baselines help identify gains attributable
to coordination. Recovery results should distinguish loss of a replaceable member from loss of a
unique capability. These protocols reveal whether performance reflects effective distributed collab-
oration and whether it persists as the team changes.
The following directions seek to address these limitations.
Shared World Models
Shared world models extend exchanged state records toward predictions
of how one agent’s actions affect other agents and the environment (Zhang et al., 2025a). For ex-
ample, moving a relay robot changes the communication conditions under which other agents can
proceed. The challenge is to coordinate local models with different spatial resolutions and predic-
tion horizons without requiring a single central model. Their predictions should expose coupled
constraints and support comparison of alternative joint actions. Learning these interactions from
team experience could improve planning when capability, resource, and communication depen-
dencies cannot be handled independently.
Multi-Agent Foundation Models
Learned coordination components, including collaborative
perception (Blumenkamp et al., 2025), suggest a route toward broader models of team behav-
ior. Models trained across tasks and team configurations could acquire priors about capability
differences, task dependencies, and other agents’ likely actions. Transfer to new teams would
require representations that accommodate variable membership and embodiment-specific capa-
bilities. Such models should provide reusable coordination knowledge for allocation and joint
planning, assessed through physical team performance.
Self-Organizing Collaboration in Open Environments
Long-running teams must accommodate
agents joining or leaving, newly arising tasks, changing connectivity, and human intervention. Self-
organization can form temporary teams, select coordinators, and revise roles according to available
capabilities (Zhu et al., 2024). Such changes must preserve task ownership and outstanding com-
mitments across organizational transitions. The resulting direction is adaptive coordination that
maintains core services while membership and architecture evolve, extending distributed Physical
AI beyond fixed teams and predefined operating conditions.
218


9
Hardware and Systems
At last, every Physical AI program ultimately depends on an actual machine to execute proposed
actions in the real world. Therefore, this chapter discusses the actual hardware and system through
five questions: what physical interactions a body’s morphology can support (Section 9.1), how
sensing and actuation close the feedback loop (Section 9.2), where computation can run without
missing the time to act (Section 9.3), how software organizes these capabilities (Section 9.4), and
how they remain reliable through repeated use and updates (Section 9.5). For the ease of under-
standing, there are several case studies: a simple component case in Section 9.2, a dexterous-hand
case study in Section 9.6 to illustrate how hardware shapes interaction, and a more complex hu-
manoid case that stitches all components together in Section 9.7.
9.1
Hardware and Embodiment Taxonomy for Physical AI
A robot opening an unfamiliar drawer must do more than recognize a handle. It must reach it,
establish a grip, and discover how the drawer responds to a pull. Resistance may mean that the
drawer is heavy, jammed, or still locked. Continuing the same movement could damage the handle.
The robot needs evidence that distinguishes these possibilities and a body capable of changing
its action. This connection between physical interaction, observation, and correction is central to
Physical AI.
9.1.1
From Hardware Components to Embodiment
Cameras, motors, encoders, transmissions, and processors are hardware components. Their ar-
rangement gives a robot its embodiment, comprising its shape and mass distribution, available
movements, sensing locations, and ways of making contact. The platform adds power, compu-
tation, communication, and the controllers that regulate those movements. Together, these corre-
spond to the broader notion of the embodiment Bemb in Section 8.1. A change anywhere in this
system can change what an action means. Replacing a rigid fingertip with a soft pad alters both the
grip and the measurements produced during contact.
The drawer example makes these dependencies visible. An external camera may locate the handle
but lose sight of it behind the gripper. Joint encoders describe arm movement, while force or tactile
measurements can reveal resistance or slip. A small initial pull then serves two purposes by moving
the drawer and testing the robot’s prediction about its motion. The outcome can justify continuing,
changing direction, or releasing the handle. Such exploratory actions require suitable force limits
and feedback. Trial and error is useful only when the body can tolerate the trial and the system can
interpret its outcome.
The same mechanics constrain possible corrections. Reach does not guarantee that an arm can
sustain a load, and a grip that supports lifting may fail when twisting a cap. Grasp analysis captures
this distinction through the forces and torques a set of contacts can resist (Ferrari and Canny, 1992).
A mobile robot may reach the handle yet lack room to reposition or sufficient support to resist the
pull. Planning must therefore consider how to remain controllable after the first movement, as well
as whether that movement is possible.
Useful feedback must also arrive before the opportunity to correct is lost. A detailed image deliv-
ered after an object has slipped provides evidence for later learning but cannot rescue that grasp.
Sensor placement and task-state observability (Section 9.2.3) must be considered together with con-
trol delay and actuator response (Section 9.2.2). Better inference can extract more from available
signals. Sustained performance still depends on obtaining the right evidence and acting within the
body’s limits.

example of a fixed instrument. An arm on a wheeled base is a mobile manipulator. A biped with

Autonomous laboratories illustrate why capability often comes from a combination of bodies. In-

connect embodiment to the system-level agents in Section 8.2.
9.1.2
Embodied Model-Hardware Co-Design and Multi-Embodiment Adaptation
Model-hardware co-design starts from a coupled choice. The body determines which states can be
observed and which actions can be realized, while the model and controller determine how much
of that capability is used. A camera added to expose a contact changes the policy’s inputs and
training data. A softer fingertip changes contact dynamics and may reduce the precision the policy
must achieve. A larger model can improve inference yet lose that advantage if its delay exceeds the
time available to correct a slip. These choices must therefore be evaluated as a system, against the
same physical task and operating limits.
A model influences the world through a control interface. It may request a tool movement, joint
positions, or forces. Local controllers translate those targets into actuator behavior. An embodiment
adapter handles the robot’s command conventions, coordinate frames, and limits. Figure 9.1 shows
three arrangements of these responsibilities. All require a return path from the physical outcome
to the next decision.
A modular pipeline estimates an object’s pose, plans a motion, and tracks it with a controller. Its in-
termediate quantities make some failures easier to locate. The object may have been misidentified,
the path may have been infeasible, or contact may have differed from the prediction. An end-to-
end vision-language-action policy learns a more direct mapping from images and instructions to
actions, as in OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2025b). It can exploit visual cues without requiring an explicit
object pose at every step, but its output still has the units and physical consequences defined by the
controller. Without incorporating new observations, neither arrangement can revise its task-level
response to an unexpected event.

An agentic hierarchy adds task-level decisions, such as selecting a tool or deciding to retry. Systems
that compose skills from language illustrate this separation (Ichter et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2023a).
During drawer opening, a fast controller may limit contact force while the higher-level system
decides whether resistance calls for another strategy. A completion message from a skill is useful
only insofar as it is supported by evidence about the drawer. Execution checking in Section 9.4 and
reliability assessment in Section 9.5 develop this requirement further.
Transfer to another robot changes the relationship between observation and action. Knowledge
that a drawer translates along a guide may remain useful. Camera appearance, reachable poses,
finger contacts, motor limits, and the forces generated by a command may all change. Expressing
a desired movement relative to the tool can reduce dependence on a laboratory’s coordinates, but
does not make the new robot mechanically equivalent. The receiving body must still support the
intended motion and contact.
Training across robots can reveal useful shared regularities.
The Open X-Embodiment study
demonstrates benefits from combining data across robots (Open X-Embodiment Collaboration,
2024). Octo supports adaptation to new observation and action spaces through fine-tuning (Ghosh
et al., 2024), while HPT combines a shared model with embodiment-specific input and output mod-
ules (Wang et al., 2024c). These approaches organize what can be shared and what must be adapted.
Their physical value must be established on the receiving robot, including its contact behavior and
recovery from errors (Section 6.4). Success on familiar images alone does not establish that the
transferred commands produce the intended forces.
Hardware design can make this adaptation easier. ALOHA’s matched leader and follower arms
give demonstrations a direct relationship to robot joint movements (Zhao et al., 2023). UMI coor-
dinates a handheld gripper, camera geometry, and action representation to support transfer from
portable demonstrations (Chi et al., 2024) (Section 9.2.1). A compliant fingertip can also tolerate
small placement errors, while tactile sensing reveals how the contact develops. Joint optimization
can extend to the mechanism itself. Chen et al. (2021) optimize mechanical and control parame-
221


ters together and build an underactuated hand from the resulting design. Such optimization still
depends on whether the modeled contacts and actuator response describe the physical machine.
For the drawer task, a useful co-design cycle begins by identifying the failed correction. If the han-
dle disappears behind the fingers, changing the viewpoint or adding touch may resolve missing ev-
idence. If resistance is measured but force cannot be reduced promptly, transmission, compliance,
and controller bandwidth become the relevant design variables. If the state is observed and the
action is feasible but the policy chooses poorly, additional training may be the appropriate change.
Each candidate requires data collected or transformed for its own observation and action inter-
face, followed by evaluation on held-out physical trials. Comparing an unchanged policy across
bodies measures transfer. Allowing each body the same adaptation budget tests the quality of the
co-designed system. Reporting both prevents a favorable match to one policy from being mistaken
for a universal hardware advantage. The final comparison is cost per valid output, including col-
lection, computation, interventions, and maintenance, as developed below and in Section 9.5.

Selecting a robot begins with a complete task, including the measurements that establish success.
Reach and payload can exclude an unsuitable arm, but do not establish whether it can thread a cap
without damaging a vial. Figure 9.2 moves from requirements to tests of individual operations,
complete workflows, and continued use. Failures can motivate a change in the policy, sensing,
mechanics, or protocol.
Candidates should meet the same requirements for workspace, load, precision, contact force, time,
and recovery. Among feasible options, the cost per valid output introduced in Section 1.5 gives a
useful comparison. Divide the fully allocated average cost of an attempt by the measured fraction
that produces a valid result. The cost includes failed attempts, human interventions, and recovery.
Early estimates remain provisional until tested under the intended workload.
A laboratory preparing metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), porous materials built from metal-
containing units and organic linkers (Furukawa et al., 2013), provides a concrete example. A syn-
222


thesis workflow may involve opening vials, transferring solids and liquids, heating, separation,
and loading instruments (Tom et al., 2024). Successful motion is insufficient. The sample must re-
tain its identity, composition, and integrity. A balance may verify a transfer that the arm’s camera
and encoders cannot establish by themselves.
Consider opening a sealed vial, dispensing a specified quantity, and seating the vial in an instru-
ment. Table 9.2 compares four possible configurations through the questions these operations raise.
Their exact arms, grippers, sensors, and controller settings must be specified before testing. Addi-
tional fingers or lower transmission ratios change the possibilities for interaction. Their practical
benefit depends on how well that interaction is observed and controlled.
Tests should use the same protocol, object batches, starting-condition distribution, and definition
of success. Repeated trials distinguish a reliable advantage from a fortunate grasp (Section 9.5.1).
Recording observations, commands, and measured outcomes helps explain failures by distinguish-
ing whether the robot lacked information, chose an unsuitable action, or could not physically real-
ize it. The diagnosis then guides a concrete change and another test.
The preferred solution may combine specialized machines, provided their transfers and coordina-
tion remain reliable. Continued operation must then test calibration drift, worn contact surfaces,
thermal limits, and recovery after interruptions. This closes the design loop. Experience changes
the model and, where necessary, the body that supplies its evidence and carries out its decisions.
9.2
Sensors, Actuators, and Intelligent Materials
To lift a glass vial, a robot must first find it, then recognize contact, and finally hold it firmly with-
out breaking it. A camera helps with the approach. Joint encoders report how the fingers and arm
have moved. Touch and force measurements reveal what happens when the fingers meet the glass.
Electric motors supply the motion, but their response depends on the transmission, the controller,
and the load. Physical AI emerges through this interaction. The robot acts, measures the conse-
quences, and adjusts its behavior. A model can infer an object’s properties from experience only
when the hardware exposes useful evidence and can carry out the resulting decisions.
The relevant hardware therefore extends from visible cameras and grippers to the electronics inside
a joint, including encoders, current sensors, power transistors, and local control processors. These
components determine both what a learning system can observe and how its actions affect the
world. Figure 9.3 connects the measurements collected during learning to the feedback used during
execution. Section 3.2 discusses sensor physics and fusion more generally. Here the emphasis is on
their consequences for robot learning and physical interaction.

9.2.1
Acquiring Physical Experience for Learning
Before a robot can learn from a recorded movement, its sensors must agree on where and when
that movement occurred. Camera calibration relates image coordinates to the robot. Joint positions
and a kinematic model locate the tool. For a wrist camera, hand-eye calibration identifies the fixed
relationship between camera and gripper (Zhang, 2000; Tsai and Lenz, 1989; Park and Martin, 1994).
Timing is equally important. A 20 ms mismatch for a tool moving at 0.5 m/s corresponds to 1 cm of
displacement. Hardware triggering, synchronized clocks, and measured delays help align images,
joint states, and forces. A receipt timestamp is not necessarily the acquisition time. These details
can determine whether a demonstration teaches the robot to react to contact or, mistakenly, to a
state that occurred afterward.
A useful trajectory records observations, measured body state, and the commands sent to the con-
troller together. It also preserves their units, coordinate frames, calibration, and control mode. A
command to advance the tool by a centimeter means something different from a command to ex-
ert a force. Even identical position targets can produce different contact behavior under different
controller gains. Changes to the camera, gripper, or controller consequently change the learning
problem, not just the equipment inventory. If actions are normalized numbers or relative tool mo-
tions, deployment must preserve the same scaling and coordinate conventions when converting
them into controller targets.
Different collection methods preserve different parts of this physical experience. Robot teleopera-
tion, as in ALOHA and DROID (Zhao et al., 2023; Khazatsky et al., 2024), records demonstrations
through a robot’s own body and controller. Handheld devices such as UMI make collection more
portable by combining a gripper with a camera and motion estimation (Chi et al., 2024). Their
trajectories can describe real contact, but the human holding the device does not have the robot’s
inertia, reach, or torque limits. Human video supplies broader examples of activities and object
use, while motion-tracking gloves and exoskeletons add hand or arm kinematics (Grauman et al.,
2022; Wang et al., 2024a; Fang et al., 2024a).
Surface electromyography (sEMG) adds a different kind of observation. Electrodes on the skin
record the electrical activity associated with muscle recruitment (Farina et al., 2014). This is the
modality denoted EMG (electromyography) in Figure 9.4. It can reveal motor intent when move-
ment is slight or visually occluded, making it a useful complement to video during demonstration
collection (Kaifosh et al., 2025). Its interpretation nevertheless depends on the person, posture, and
electrode placement. Neither visible motion nor muscle electrical activity directly specifies the con-
tact forces a robot must reproduce. Recordings should therefore synchronize EMG with kinematics
and video, preserve the electrode configuration and calibration, and include force or tactile mea-
224


surements when contact-force supervision is required. These sources complement robot recordings
rather than serving as mechanically interchangeable substitutes.
The data pyramid in Figure 9.4, motivated by GR00T N1 (NVIDIA et al., 2025c), places abundant
human video below synthetic and robot-free demonstrations, with robot execution at the top. Its
distinction is the kind of evidence available, as well as its volume. Simulation can supply complete
robot actions while approximating friction and contact. Human recordings contain real interactions
without the robot’s execution dynamics. A weighted training objective retains these differences

9.2.2
Closing the Loop from Measurements to Motion
When a finger touches a hard surface, force may rise before a large model has processed another
image. The robot must therefore respond at several timescales. A learned policy can choose a
grasp, a movement, or a desired compliance. A local controller follows that target. The motor drive
regulates electrical current. Fast joint feedback remains useful even when the policy is learned end
to end. Playing a predicted sequence of actions rapidly is also different from reacting rapidly to
new evidence.
The electronics make this distinction concrete. A drive switches power transistors to apply voltages
to the motor windings. Current-sensing circuits and analog-to-digital converters report the result-
ing currents. An encoder or other rotor-position sensor tells the controller how the rotor is oriented.
The drive adjusts these voltages to produce the desired torque. Filtering suppresses noise but intro-
duces delay, and electrical switching can contaminate small sensor signals. Consequently, sensing,
computation, and power delivery must be designed together (Muthalagu et al., 2025; Kollmorgen,
2020).
The total delay includes sensing, communication, inference, and actuation. In a linearized feedback
loop, a delay ∆adds a phase lag ω∆at angular frequency ω. The controller increasingly acts on
an outdated state. This explains why contact regulation usually stays close to the hardware, while
slower reasoning can run elsewhere (Section 9.3). Each interface must specify reference frames,
units, timestamps, control modes, and limits. The return path should report the measured motion
and available forces or currents, together with faults and temperature. Without this feedback, a
learning system can confuse a saturated actuator or a delayed measurement with an incorrect plan.
9.2.3
Task-State Observability: Cameras, Encoders, and Contact Sensing
The camera is often the most recognizable sensor on a physically intelligent robot. An RGB cam-
era measures light and provides the appearance cues used to recognize objects, interpret a scene,
and connect language to action. Depth cameras add geometric information. Stereo systems com-
pare two viewpoints. Structured-light systems observe a projected pattern. Time-of-flight systems
estimate distance from the travel time or phase of returned light. These approaches have differ-
ent sensitivities to distance, illumination, and surface appearance. An integrated RGB-D sensor
makes color and depth available together, as illustrated by the RealSense architecture (Keselman
et al., 2017). However, transparent glass, shiny metal, and low-texture surfaces can leave missing or
misleading depth. ClearGrasp addresses one such problem by inferring geometry for transparent
objects (Sajjan et al., 2020). Inferred geometry still requires validation when an action can damage
the object.
Placement determines what the camera can contribute. A head or external camera sees the overall
workspace but may lose the contact behind the hand. A wrist camera follows the approach and

between an image and a successful action. Calibration aligns geometry. Training must still account
for the change in appearance.
While cameras look outward, encoders measure the body’s own movement. A rotary encoder
converts shaft rotation into an electrical position reading. Optical encoders read a patterned disk.
Magnetic encoders sense the orientation of a magnet. Inductive designs use electromagnetic cou-
pling. Incremental encoders count changes and generally need a reference after startup, whereas
absolute encoders identify position within their specified measurement range. More digital counts
do not by themselves guarantee more accurate position. Mounting error, alignment, mechanical de-
formation, and calibration also matter (HEIDENHAIN, 2023). Velocities are often estimated from
successive position measurements, which introduces a trade-off between noise and delay.
A motor encoder and a joint-output encoder observe different shafts. With an ideal rigid gearbox,
motor angle divided by the reduction ratio gives joint angle. Real transmissions have friction, lost
motion, and elastic deformation. An output encoder can reveal movement errors that the motor
encoder misses, particularly during reversals and under load. Joint measurements and the robot’s
geometry then estimate the tool’s pose, but do not directly reveal whether an object is slipping
between the fingers. On a walking or mobile robot, an IMU adds angular velocity and specific
force from gyroscopes and accelerometers. Combined with joint and contact measurements, it
helps estimate body motion. Integration alone accumulates error, and gravity must be accounted
for when interpreting acceleration. Figure 9.5 presents examples of cameras, encoders, and current-
sensing shunts.

Touch becomes especially valuable once the hand hides the contact. In a vision-based tactile sensor,
a small camera looks inward at a soft surface rather than outward at the scene. Pressing an object
against that surface changes its shape and, in some designs, moves printed markers. GelSight uses
controlled illumination to recover fine contact geometry. DIGIT packages a related optical approach
into a compact fingertip (Yuan et al., 2017; Lambeta et al., 2020). Figure 9.6 shows why optics and
material design are inseparable here. The camera observes the deformation of a purpose-built skin.
Images can support estimates of local shape, shear deformation, and incipient slip. They are not
direct force maps. Recovering force requires calibration or a learned model of the skin and its
loading.
This information changes what a policy can learn. A gripper can tighten when the contact patch
starts to slip, or adjust the direction of insertion when an edge presses unevenly. A compliant
skin may also wear, creep, or change with temperature, shifting the relationship between image
and force. Other tactile technologies measure changes in resistance, capacitance, or magnetic field.
ReSkin, for example, uses a deformable magnetic skin (Bhirangi et al., 2022). The choice is therefore
between useful measurements, spatial coverage, durability, and processing demands, rather than
between a sensor that “has touch” and one that does not.

(b) Sensor assembly
(c) Camera and LEDs
