Force sensing complements this local picture. A six-axis wrist force-torque sensor measures three
force components and three moments transmitted through the wrist. Strain gauges detect tiny de-
formations of an elastic structure. Calibrated combinations of their signals recover the load. The
reading includes the tool’s weight and inertial loading, which must be compensated when estimat-
ing contact force (ATI Industrial Automation, n.d.). A joint torque sensor measures twisting load
about one joint axis, often on the output side of the transmission. Its location matters. A sensor
upstream of a lossy gearbox does not measure the same load as one downstream. Multiple joint
measurements can support estimates of external contact, but these depend on the robot’s dynamics
and contact assumptions. Specialized joint force-torque sensing has even supported touch local-
ization over a robot’s body (Iskandar et al., 2024). An ordinary single-axis torque sensor does not
automatically provide that capability.
Current sensors offer another source of evidence already needed by the drive. A small shunt resis-
tor produces a voltage proportional to current. Magnetic current sensors infer it from the surround-
ing magnetic field. For a suitable motor model, torque-producing current estimates motor torque.
It does not directly measure force at the fingertips. Friction, acceleration, gravity, and transmis-
sion losses contribute to the same signal. Current remains valuable for control, overload detection,
and learning about loading, provided these ambiguities are recognized (Muthalagu et al., 2025;
Wensing et al., 2017).
The purpose of combining sensors is to resolve uncertainty that matters for an action. In the Jenga
experiments of Fazeli et al. (2019), vision locates blocks and force measurements during interaction
help infer how they can move. The contact supplied information unavailable from an image alone.
A similar principle applies when opening a drawer or seating a connector. The robot must distin-
guish free motion from resistance, then decide whether to continue, change direction, or retreat.
This is task-state observability in practical terms. The most useful sensor is the one that reveals the
distinction in time to change the action, at a precision appropriate to the task.
9.2.4
Electric Motors and the Mechanics of Actuation
An actuator converts supplied energy into mechanical work. Electric motors are a practical default
for many robot arms, grippers, mobile bases, and legged platforms because electrical power is
readily distributed, motor drives are mature, and feedback can regulate motion and torque. These
advantages depend on scale and duty. Hydraulic, pneumatic, and material-based actuators remain
useful where their force capacity or mechanical behavior better fits the task.
Inside an electromagnetic motor, current in windings interacts with a magnetic field to turn a ro-
tor. The stationary part is the stator. Sustained rotation requires the winding currents to change
as the rotor turns, a process called commutation. In a brushed direct-current (DC) motor, physical
brushes and a segmented commutator perform this switching. Such motors are straightforward
to drive and remain useful in compact or inexpensive mechanisms, but the brushes wear and cre-
ate electrical noise. A coreless brushed motor removes the iron core from the rotating winding,
reducing rotor inertia and cogging. It still needs careful thermal design. “Coreless” describes con-
struction, rather than a separate feedback control method (FAULHABER, n.d.).
Brushless permanent-magnet motors place commutation in the electronics. The rotor carries mag-
nets and the stator carries windings. The drive energizes the phases according to rotor position.
Eliminating brushes removes a wear mechanism and enables efficient, controllable drives, at the
cost of more complex electronics. The labels brushless direct-current (BLDC) motor and permanent-
magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) describe closely related motor families. In a common conven-
tion, BLDC designs are associated with trapezoidal back-electromotive force and block commuta-
tion, whereas PMSMs are associated with sinusoidal waveforms. Products and control methods
overlap, so the label alone is insufficient to predict torque quality. Field-oriented control regulates
current components relative to the rotor field, allowing smooth torque control over a useful oper-
ating range (Sidelsky, 2020; Muthalagu et al., 2025).
Packaging creates further options within these families. An inrunner places the rotor inside the
stator. An outrunner rotates an outer shell, often providing a larger torque-producing radius. A
228


frameless motor supplies the rotor and stator for integration into the robot’s own bearings and
housing. A hollow center can accommodate cables, while different winding and rotor designs trade
speed, torque, inertia, cooling, and space. These are engineering choices rather than a universal
ranking. An easily accelerated rotor can benefit a responsive finger, whereas a large joint must
also carry sustained load and reject heat. Figure 9.7 illustrates motor construction and feedback
integration.
A stepper motor also uses electronically switched windings, but is designed to advance through
discrete angular equilibria. Counting commanded steps can provide simple positioning in lightly
loaded fixtures, dispensers, and laboratory mechanisms. The count is a command history, however,
not proof of actual position. An overloaded open-loop stepper can lose steps. Microstepping makes
the commanded motion smoother without guaranteeing correspondingly finer absolute accuracy.
Closed-loop steppers add feedback, and the best choice depends on speed, load, efficiency, and
required disturbance response (Oriental Motor, n.d.). For Physical AI, this distinction affects the
data as well as the motion. A dataset should not silently treat requested steps as measured joint
states.
The word servo describes feedback-controlled operation, not a unique electromagnetic motor type.
A servo system combines a motor, a drive, a position or velocity sensor, and a controller. It may
also contain a gearbox (Kollmorgen, 2020). A small hobby servo and an industrial brushless servo
share this principle while differing greatly in precision, torque control, response, and access to
measurements. For a learning system, the interface matters. Position-only commands offer dif-
ferent possibilities from current or torque commands, and a nominally identical target can behave
differently under another drive’s limits and gains.
The transmission then converts motor motion into joint motion. Planetary, strain-wave, and cy-
cloidal gearboxes are transmission mechanisms, not types of motor. They allow a relatively fast
motor to turn a slower joint with greater torque. Direct drive couples the motor to the load with-
out reduction. Quasi-direct drive combines a high-torque motor with a modest reduction. Neither
approach is free of trade-offs. Removing reduction requires the motor itself to supply more torque,
often increasing its size or thermal burden. Under an idealized constant-efficiency approximation,

These effects become apparent when a foot lands or a hand meets an unexpected obstacle. A trans-

friction can improve this response and make motor current more informative about joint loading,
as explored in the MIT Cheetah’s proprioceptive actuators (Wensing et al., 2017). High-reduction
joints can instead use output torque sensing and feedback to yield under external load, as in the
DLR lightweight robot (Albu-Schäffer et al., 2007). A series elastic actuator places a spring in the
force path. Its calibrated deflection estimates transmitted torque and cushions disturbances, while
introducing additional dynamics that the controller must handle (Pratt and Williamson, 1995).
Peak torque is only part of the operating envelope. Winding heat grows approximately with cur-
rent squared times resistance, so a joint may produce a large torque briefly but be unable to sustain
it. At higher speed, the motor’s back-electromotive force and the supply voltage limit the current
the drive can establish. A policy that repeatedly asks for unavailable torque experiences delayed
or incomplete movement. Temperature-dependent limits can make an identical command behave
differently later in a task. Training and evaluation should therefore include the relevant torque-
speed limits, thermal duty, friction, and control delay, rather than treating an actuator as an unlim-
ited source of prescribed motion (Kafader, 2024; Gealy et al., 2019). In the ANYmal experiments
of Hwangbo et al. (2019), a learned actuator model helps bridge this gap by representing the real

For contact, the controller must also decide how strongly to resist position error. Impedance control
makes a robot respond like a chosen spring and damper (Hogan, 1985). A softer response can
absorb a small alignment error. A stiffer response may be needed to support a load. In a simple,

control. This is how a learned intention to “insert gently” acquires a measurable physical meaning.
9.2.5
Fluid Power, Compliance, and Functional Materials
Electric motors do not cover every useful form of actuation. Hydraulic systems use pressurized
liquid to move pistons or hydraulic motors. Large force can be generated in a compact actuator,
making fluid power attractive for demanding loads, but the complete machine also needs pumps,
230


valves, seals, and fluid routing. Valve dynamics, leakage, friction, and fluid temperature affect
the response a controller must learn or model. Electrically powered pumps and local hydraulic
circuits can combine electrical distribution with hydraulic force generation. “Hydraulic” does not
necessarily mean a remote central pump.
Pneumatic systems use compressed gas. Air can inflate a soft finger that wraps around an object
with relatively simple mechanics, but its compressibility, flow restrictions, and material hysteresis
complicate precise positioning. Pressure is useful feedback, yet does not uniquely determine the
fingertip force when shape and contact change. Both fluid technologies therefore need sensing
appropriate to their dynamics, rather than relying on pressure commands alone (Rus and Tolley,
2015; Laschi et al., 2016).
Functional materials offer an emerging route to combining actuation, sensing, and compliance
within the body. They remain under active investigation alongside the motor-driven platforms
discussed above. Thermal and electrochemical artificial muscles offer distinctive combinations of
strain, force, and response time (Mirvakili and Hunter, 2018), but their value for physical intel-
ligence depends on the interaction they enable. Hydraulically amplified self-healing electrostatic
(HASEL) actuators, for example, use electrostatic forces to redistribute a liquid dielectric inside
flexible pouches, producing motion. Changes in capacitance also reveal deformation (Acome et al.,
2018). By integrating driving electronics, capacitive self-sensing, and computation, Ly et al. (2021)
demonstrate feedback control of a Peano-HASEL-powered arm. The actuator therefore supplies
both mechanical work and a measurement that can guide the next action.
Figure 9.8 connects this component behavior to task feedback. A compliant finger may accom-
modate an object’s shape mechanically, while its deformation provides evidence for adjusting the
grasp. Yet compliance alone does not reveal whether the object is secure, slipping, or being com-
pressed excessively. That distinction requires calibrated sensing and a controller whose response re-
mains useful under changing loads. High-voltage electronics, nonlinear mechanics, material drift,
and fatigue must be considered together with control bandwidth and replacement needs. Progress
should therefore be measured through repeatable task performance, including sensing, power de-
livery, and maintenance, as well as the properties of an isolated material sample.
Even without an unusual actuator, the body’s structure can simplify control. A compliant insertion
fixture can guide a misaligned peg, and an underactuated hand can conform to an object using
fewer motors than moving joints (Whitney, 1982; Dollar and Howe, 2010). This is a practical form
of sharing the work between mechanics and computation. The same softness that accommodates
contact can make shape harder to estimate. Electronic skins and learned sensing models help ad-
dress that problem (Shih et al., 2020). For physical intelligence, the useful question is which part of
an interaction the body can handle reliably, and which changing circumstances still require obser-
vation, inference, and a new action.
The following cases examine a hand and a humanoid as complete sensing and actuation systems
(Figure 9.9). Section 9.6 then compares three dexterous hands at the level of actuation, tactile sens-
ing, and demonstration hardware.
9.2.6
Case Study: RobotEra XHAND 1
RobotEra’s XHAND 1 illustrates the measurement-motion loop at the level of one component. Its
host sends joint targets, controller gains, and torque limits. The hand returns joint positions, motor-

optional fingertip sensors are fitted (RobotEra, n.d.; 2024). Section 9.6.3 compares the mechanism,
loading capacity, and communication timing with other hands. The question here is how these
signals support correction during a grasp.
Vision can locate an object before contact, while joint feedback records how the fingers move to-
ward it. Once a finger meets the object, target position alone no longer describes the interaction.
Controller gains, effort limits, and transmission mechanics determine the load. Tactile measure-
ments, when available, can reveal changes in contact that require a revised finger target. Motor

9.2.7
Case Study: Unitree G1 and Perceptive Locomotion
Gallant illustrates how a humanoid’s useful workspace depends on the sensing and control sys-
tem built around its body (Ben et al., 2026). The task is to move a 29-degree-of-freedom Unitree
G1 through stairs, gaps, narrow passages and overhead obstacles. Two torso-mounted LiDARs
provide complementary views of the surrounding geometry. A head-mounted Livox Mid360 sup-
ports localization. A voxel representation preserves the vertical structure that a ground-height map
discards, allowing the controller to account for both footholds and body clearance.
The software connects point-cloud processing, proprioception and learned control on an onboard
NVIDIA Orin NX. A convolutional encoder extracts spatial features, which are combined with
the robot state to generate joint commands. Sensor placement and the representation used during
training must therefore remain consistent at deployment. Changing the visible space changes the
information available for each action. In the initial deployment, LiDAR traffic and robot-state mes-
sages share a software pipeline and incur substantial communication delay. Restricting transmitted
point clouds and using shared memory reduce this overhead (Ben et al., 2026). These changes con-
cern the age of the feedback reaching the controller, rather than the size of the policy alone.
The real-robot evaluation uses 15 trials per terrain and compares the full system with perception
and training ablations (Ben et al., 2026). This provides evidence for the integrated locomotion loop
within the tested environments. On approach to a low ceiling, observed clearance and current body
configuration must jointly determine posture. A correct map delivered too late cannot support that
correction. The useful capability belongs to the complete perception-action loop.
9.3
Device-Edge-Cloud Collaboration and Real-Time Communication
9.3.1
Distributed Architecture
The purpose of Physical AI is to enable intelligent agents, under finite computational resources,
to interact continuously with the physical environment through perception, decision-making, and
action and to accomplish a given physical objective in real time, effectively and safely. Resources
in computation, energy, storage, communication, and control cycles must be allocated across per-
ception, state estimation, prediction, planning, policy generation, and execution control at different
nodes. These functions have different temporal scales, resource requirements, and spatial distances.
This creates a central challenge for Physical AI. High-level computation tends to be low-frequency,
computationally intensive, and spatially remote, whereas physical perception and interaction must
be high-frequency, computationally limited, physically proximate, and temporally continuous.
The device-edge-cloud distributed architecture provides a way to balance these requirements (Fig-
ure 9.10). It decomposes a unified perception-decision-action loop according to distinct timescales,
spatial scopes, and responsibility boundaries (Lee et al., 2026), organized around validity deadlines, dis-
tributed networks, and responsibility horizons. The device connects directly to the body, sensors, and
actuators. It handles the fastest state perception, servo control, contact responses, and safety con-
straints so that the minimum safety-critical loop does not depend on the network. The edge op-
erates at the physical site with greater computational resources. It performs multimodal fusion,
local world modeling, policy inference, trajectory generation, action-chunk generation, and coor-
dination of multiple bodies, transforming site-level state into executable commitments that remain
valid. The cloud operates over longer timescales across tasks, devices, and sites. It supports goal
decomposition, experimental design, long-term memory, experience accumulation, model updates,
and cross-site orchestration. Computation can migrate according to task requirements, but physical
responsibility cannot migrate arbitrarily. The closer a responsibility is to a physical consequence,
the more it must be assumed by a trusted node close to the body.
Accordingly, device-edge-cloud collaboration is better understood in terms of migratable responsibil-
ity boundaries rather than as a fixed three-layer computational hierarchy. When real-time communi-
cation is healthy, prediction, planning, and policy generation can migrate toward the edge or cloud
in exchange for stronger model capabilities. When real-time communication becomes abnormal,
responsibility must contract toward the physical object and switch to validated degraded modes.
233


Furthermore, device-edge-cloud collaboration exchanges node state and commitments with phys-
ical semantics. At least three categories of state should be distinguished. Physical state includes
pose, joint state, force, contact, limits, environmental conditions, and execution mode. It must
carry sampling time, coordinate frame, units, and effective range.
Action state includes action
chunks, task phase, resource occupancy, execution progress, and version information. It must dis-
tinguish among “generated,” “sent,” “received,” “acknowledged,” and “physically acted upon.”
Evidence state includes credit, measurement identity, experimental conditions, execution confirma-
tion, anomalies, and recovery records. It determines whether a result is sufficiently grounded to
be treated as a fact by subsequent reasoning. Confusing these categories produces characteristic
failures in Physical AI closed loops, including treating a plan as a fact, transmission as execution,
or an old observation as the current state.
The following sections address four questions within this Physical AI framework. What informa-
tion must the device maintain, and what must it guarantee? How does the edge transform site-
level state into valid action? How does the cloud provide low-frequency, high-level intelligence?
How can real-time communication ensure that information transferred across these responsibility
boundaries remains physically valid?
9.3.2
Device-Side Computing
The device is the computational and control node closest to the point of physical action in the
Physical AI loop. It typically includes sensor interfaces, actuator interfaces, body-state estimation,
safety control, local policies, and an adaptation layer for real-time communication with higher-level
systems (Ortega-Kral et al., 2026). Device-side computing must ensure that the physical system
does not enter an unacceptable state simply because it is waiting for remote information, even
under the worst real-time communication conditions. Hosting the largest model is secondary to
this requirement.
The device must first establish a time-aligned multimodal state. Cameras, encoders, force sensors, tac-
tile sensors, and motor feedback do not inherently share the same sampling instant. A visual-frame
timestamp may correspond to exposure or acquisition time. Joint state may originate from a con-
troller cycle. Force signals may contain additional delay introduced by filtering, transmission, and

mechanical response. Device state should therefore be represented by states carrying timestamps,
source identities, safety attributes, spatial coordinate frames, units, and quality indicators, rather
than simply by a collection of “current values.” Only then can the system determine whether differ-
ent trusted observations describe the same contact event and, when a sensor is missing, represent
the state as “unknown” rather than incorrectly reusing the previous frame.
The device must also maintain a local execution state machine. The state machine should at least dis-
tinguish standby, preparation, execution, constrained execution, pause, fault, and recovery, while
specifying which actuator actions are permitted in each state. Its purpose is to make device-native
safety enforcement independent of interpretation by a high-level model. A policy model may rec-
ommend “continue grasping,” but if a joint is approaching its limit, force exceeds a threshold, or
the real-time communication lease has expired, the device-side state machine must be able to reject
the action. Policy output and execution permission are distinct. The policy proposes an action,
whereas the safety layer determines whether it is currently allowed.
For real-time control, the device typically uses a fixed-period or event-triggered local closed loop.
The real-time communication layer provides references, targets, parameters, or action chunks. It
should not require every servo cycle to wait for a remote system to generate the next joint com-
mand. This prevents network jitter from entering the innermost control loop and turns network
failure into an explicit operating state rather than an accident handled only after it occurs. Based on
the remaining validity of an action chunk, local state, and safety rules, the controller can continue
execution, execute in a degraded mode, perform a controlled stop, or stop immediately, thereby
implementing device-native safety.
Device computation is also constrained by physical considerations. Larger models imply higher
memory consumption, power draw, thermal load, and computational latency, and may also alter
the weight distribution, power capacity, and onboard compute budget of a mobile system. Model
size therefore cannot be discussed independently of the control cycle. For tasks requiring rapid
contact feedback, a more complex but slower model may be unsuitable for direct participation in
the execution loop. It can instead support slower action generation, candidate selection, or anomaly
interpretation, while the fast loop remains the responsibility of lightweight models, controllers, and
safety logic.
9.3.3
Edge-Side Computing
Edge-side computing provides site-level computation and coordination. It is closer to the physical
process than the cloud while offering substantially more computational and coordination capability
than the device. Edge nodes are well suited to policy inference, local world models, trajectory
generation, resource coordination, and multimodal fusion (XPolicyLab Community et al., 2026).
These computations, however, have physical control value only when their outputs still correspond
to the current state of the site.
In this architecture, an action chunk serves as a time-bounded execution commitment with explicit
semantics. An action chunk should include, at minimum, the target device or body identity, refer-
ence time, validity interval, sequence number, control units, execution mode, and necessary con-
straints. The device can then determine whether the action still belongs to the current task, whether
it has expired, and whether it has been superseded by a newer version. The key metric for an edge
closed loop is not average inference time, but the end-to-end interval between the observation reference
time and the instant at which the action begins to take effect. This interval must be shorter than the
validity deadline permitted by the physical action, rather than merely satisfying a requirement that
model inference itself be fast enough. Loss of an action chunk must not be interpreted by default
as “continue executing the previous chunk,” because doing so hides communication failure inside
the control state. A more appropriate execution rule uses a lease. When the lease expires without a
new valid commitment, the device enters a predefined safe state.
The edge should also keep the world model decoupled from the controller. A world model may predict
“what might happen if this grasp continues,” but that prediction does not thereby acquire direct
control authority. Its output can condition action generation, candidate-action selection, or risk es-
235


timation, while final execution must still pass through the device-control interface and safety state
machine. This allows independent checks before execution and lets the world model be upgraded
independently.
In site-level distributed collaboration, the edge is better suited to maintaining resource semantics
than to replicating all internal device data. For example, when multiple robots compete for the
same tool, the edge needs information about tool occupancy, reservation expiry, task priority, and
current execution phase. It does not need to continuously aggregate high-frequency joint data from
every robot. Resource state can be encoded using leases, version numbers, or monotonic sequence
numbers, making “who owns the resource” a state that can be checked rather than a conclusion
inferred from whichever message arrives last.
9.3.4
Cloud-Side Agents
Cloud-based agents operate on the longest time scale and are suited to processing information
across experiments, devices, and sites. They can maintain long-term memory, compare histori-
cal results, generate scientific hypotheses, plan resources, and select subsequent tasks, but should
not directly assume millisecond-scale contact control. Communication between the cloud and the
physical site therefore primarily concerns task state and evidence state, rather than the next joint com-
mand.
The cloud must distinguish plan, request, confirmation, and fact. A plan describes what is intended to
happen. A request specifies what the site is asked to execute. A confirmation indicates that the site
has accepted the request. A fact originates from an identified, timestamped physical measurement.
These four concepts cannot substitute for one another. For example, when the cloud generates
a task to “close the valve,” this does not mean that the valve has closed. Even if the actuator
reports “completed,” sensor evidence may still be required to confirm the final physical state. Only
states supported by site-level measurements should enter the evidence set used for subsequent
experimental reasoning.
Accordingly, communication between cloud and site is better implemented through event-driven
state synchronization than through continuous replication of all raw signals. High-frequency data
can be aggregated, compressed, or selectively uploaded on site. The cloud receives task-relevant
measurements, summaries, anomalies, and evidence. For experiments that must be reproducible,
uploaded records must also carry identities for samples, devices, experimental conditions, and
software versions. Otherwise, historical results become difficult to interpret reliably.
When the cloud becomes unavailable, an action that has already started should not be extended
indefinitely while waiting for a cloud response. The site should complete, pause, or stop according
to device- and edge-level state. After recovery, the cloud should first re-read site-level facts and
only then select the next action. In particular, “the last transmission succeeded” must never be
interpreted as “the experiment has completed.”
9.3.5
Real-Time Communication
The central metric for real-time communication in Physical AI is the physical validity of infor-
mation when it arrives relative to the physical process, rather than throughput alone. Average
latency, average bandwidth, and average packet-loss rate are therefore insufficient to characterize
a physical closed loop. At minimum, one must also consider latency bounds, jitter, queueing time,
observation age, action validity, reordering, duplication, and the duration of disconnection (Sajid
et al., 2026).
A simple serial end-to-end real-time constraint (Diao et al., 2025) can be written as
Te2e = Tsensor + Tencoder + Tuplink + Tcompute + Tdownlink + Tdecoder + Tactuator.
(9.4)
The terms correspond, in order, to the stages of one remote closed loop, namely on-device sens-
ing, observation encoding, uplink transport, computation at the edge or in the cloud, downlink
236


transport, command decoding, and the onset of actuation. For one observation and its resulting
action, the stage intervals cover sensing start to actuation onset without gaps or overlaps, includ-
ing any queueing time. Their sum is Te2e, with stage boundaries specified and timestamps mapped
to a common clock domain. Tdeadline is not an arbitrary parameter chosen by the real-time com-
munication system, but a deadline determined by the physical process, and Te2e must be strictly
less than it. Contact, balance, and high-speed motion may require deadlines close to the control
cycle, whereas experimental steps and resource scheduling may tolerate delays of seconds, min-
utes, or even longer. A distributed physical AI can therefore contain multiple real-time classes
simultaneously. A single “real-time/non-real-time” label cannot adequately describe all of its com-
munication.
In device-edge-cloud collaboration, asynchronous execution and queueing affect which observa-
tion an action uses. The age of information (AoI) (Yates et al., 2021) complements end-to-end latency
by measuring information freshness. At an evaluation time, standard AoI is the interval since
generation of the freshest state update available at the receiver. The observation age of an action
measures the interval from generation of the observation actually used for that action to the ac-
tion’s execution. Both age calculations use timestamps mapped to a common clock domain. For
the same update stream and receiver, the two ages coincide at action execution if the action uses
the freshest available update. The action’s observation age is greater if it uses an older update.
These quantities should not be conflated with the simple serial latency estimate above. A backlog
of action chunks can make nominal network latency appear normal while delaying execution and
increasing the age of the observation used by the current action, potentially beyond its validity pe-
riod. For real-time action generation, skipping queued observations that are no longer useful to the
current control computation can prevent queue buildup. Older observations may still be retained
for state estimation, sensor fusion, or historical analysis. For example, a model requiring only 5 ms
for inference can still produce an unusable action if its input waits 100 ms in a queue. Conversely,
a slower model may be entirely acceptable for second-scale task planning.
The action side requires complementary execution rules. An action prefix that has already begun
execution generally cannot be arbitrarily rolled back, whereas an unexecuted suffix can be regen-
erated according to new observations. This distinction avoids excessive action oscillation while
allowing new information to modify future behavior. When an action chunk expires, the system
should stop extending the commitment rather than repeatedly copying the last action.
Real-time communication must also handle semantic loss. Undetected message loss can leave the re-
ceiver with an incorrect view of task or safety state. Losing a frame used only for visualization may
be harmless, whereas silently losing an event indicating that a device has entered a safe state could
cause the cloud to schedule the next experiment incorrectly. Communication protocols must there-
fore distinguish discardable information from information that requires acknowledgment, and pro-
vide the latter with confirmation, sequence numbers, timeouts, and idempotent semantics (Zhang
et al., 2024; Klüner et al., 2025; Chovet et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2023b).
In multi-body collaboration, real-time communication should likewise not force all bodies to share
a single high-frequency state. When two robots compete for the same tool, the edge must make tool-
occupancy and release events visible before a conflict occurs. If occupancy information arrives late, its
effect is equivalent to having no information. Force feedback within a body should remain in a local
closed loop, because elevating it to an inter-body network only increases real-time communication
latency and the risk of failure.
A real-time communication system with explicit responsibility boundaries should provide at least
four capabilities, including timestamping, state versioning, validity control, and explicit fault representa-
tion. Timestamping identifies when a state was observed, versioning identifies the plan or policy
that produced it, and validity control determines whether it remains usable. Explicit fault repre-
sentation identifies who is responsible for entering the safe state when the information is no longer
usable. Together, these capabilities establish state and responsibility semantics for maintaining the
Physical AI closed loop in addition to transporting messages.
237


9.3.6
Self-Driving Laboratories
A self-driving laboratory (SDL) provides a validation setting for device-edge-cloud collaboration
(Gao et al., 2025). A typical dry/wet experimental SDL simultaneously contains millisecond-scale
device control, second-scale experimental operations, and minute-to-hour-scale scientific decision-
making. Instruments and robots must execute rapidly. The site must continuously maintain the
state of samples, devices, and the environment, while higher-level scientific-discovery agents typ-
ically operate in a relatively predefined experimental world, running a “hypothesis, execution, mea-
surement, and next selection” loop. The objectives, workflow, instruments, and basic interpretive
framework for measurements are specified before an experimental campaign begins, and the sys-
tem primarily optimizes parameters and actions within those predefined boundaries.
An open-governance architecture for SDLs emphasizes a transition from closed-loop optimization in a
predefined world to open-world scientific discovery. This motivates designing the InternLab platform (Li
et al., 2026e) to advance Physical AI from a single-laboratory closed loop to a governable capability
network across laboratories and institutions.
InternLab’s device-edge-cloud distributed architecture organizes physical capabilities into a gov-
erned network without centralizing all laboratories into a single cloud. Scientific agents can use
it to discover and compose experimental capabilities dynamically from nodes across the devices,
sites, and cloud systems of multiple laboratories and institutions. Its three mutually coupled layers
are Physical Intelligence & Distributed Network (the capability layer), Lab OS Runtime (the execution
and orchestration runtime connecting the capability and governance layers), and Native Governance
(the governance foundation).
The Capabilities Network Layer transforms “equipment owned by a laboratory” into “capabilities
callable by a network.” Robotic manipulation, scientific instruments, analytical models, and ex-
perimental skills are no longer merely private components within a site. They can be described as
capabilities with explicit applicability conditions. The Capability Graph describes which nodes can
provide which capabilities under which conditions. Scheduling & Routing selects qualified nodes ac-
cording to sample state, temporal constraints, instrument availability, and governance conditions.
The Composition Engine combines multiple capabilities serially or in parallel into an experimental
route.
The Lab OS Runtime Layer transforms continuously changing scientific intent into executable physi-
cal actions and brings the resulting outcomes back into the scientific loop. Its core can be abstracted
into four runtime functions, namely Task Routing, Live State, Authorization Checks, and Trace Return.
Task Routing delivers tasks or action chunks to bodies, instruments, or sites with the required capa-
bilities, rather than requiring every servo cycle to wait for a remote command. Live State maintains
site state with timestamps, coordinate frames, and validity intervals, enabling higher-level deci-
sions to determine whether observations remain fresh. Authorization Checks verify the necessary
governance prerequisites before an action enters the physical system. Trace Return brings execu-
tion results, anomalies, and recovery information back into the next round of scientific reasoning.
The Native Governance Layer is the foundation that enables InternLab to move from a conventional
automation network to an open experimental network. InternLab explicitly contains at least five
inseparable conditions, including Permission, Safety, Calibration, Provenance, and Credit. Permission
specifies who may invoke a capability, for what purpose, over which sample scope, and within
which risk boundary. Safety is not a local property of a single action, but an end-to-end property
spanning hardware, environmental monitoring, action validation, and fail-safe recovery. Calibra-
tion determines whether an instrument or sensor is currently in a measurement state that can be
trusted. Provenance records sample identity, protocol version, data source, and operational chain
so that cross-site evidence can be audited and reproduced. Credit preserves attribution for contri-
butions across institutions. Most importantly, the design goal is not merely “post hoc auditing,”
but governance-native execution. Governance conditions are part of the interface when a capabil-
ity is defined and invoked, and they propagate together with the execution context. When any
prerequisite fails, the capability should be rejected, degraded, re-authorized, or escalated to human
handling.
238


The two InternLab pilot deployments (Li et al., 2026e) demonstrate that the device-edge-cloud col-
laboration and responsibility model extends to an open spatial scale. The local safety loop at the
device, site-level state and resource coordination at the edge, and long-horizon scientific reasoning
in the cloud therefore do not disappear when collaboration becomes cross-site. They become em-
bedded within a network of capability discovery, task routing, governance checks, and evidence
return. The evolution from SDL to the InternLab design extends Physical AI from a single, prede-
fined, closed experimental loop to an open-world loop that spans bodies, sites, and institutions and supports
re-planning, re-composition, and governance-native execution. This makes device-edge-cloud collabora-
tion and real-time communication operational infrastructure for open-world, distributed Physical
AI.
9.4
Software Stacks and Development Infrastructure
A robot carrying a vial cannot wait for a language model to finish reasoning before responding to a
slipping grasp. Nor does a completed arm trajectory establish that the vial reached the correct rack.
These two observations define the software problem. Physical regulation must continue at the rate
required by the body, while task execution must remain accountable to measured outcomes. Soft-
ware connects these timescales through interfaces that specify what a component may command,
what evidence it consumes, and what happens when that evidence or the component itself becomes
unavailable.
Section 9.3 establishes where computation can run across the device, edge, and cloud. This section
examines the software boundaries that make that distribution workable. The architecture com-
prises nested feedback loops, hardware and data interfaces, a runtime for controllers and learned
policies, and a task execution framework. This chapter uses Embodied Intelligence Harness as its or-
ganizing term for the last of these. It brings together established mechanisms for skill composition,
state management, execution monitoring, and recovery. The term denotes their integration for this
chapter rather than a new middleware standard.
9.4.1
Layered Software Architecture and Physical Interaction Loops
Robotics software separates perception, estimation, planning, and control because these functions
have different computational and physical requirements. Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) pro-
vides a widely used framework for composing such components through explicit interfaces (Ma-
censki et al., 2022). Learning changes what can be implemented inside a component, and founda-
tion models expand how tasks can be specified and decomposed. Neither change removes the need
to assign ownership of state, control authority, and failure responses. A hierarchy is useful only if
its feedback paths and failure boundaries are equally explicit.
Figure 9.11 distinguishes three loops. The task loop interprets instructions, selects skills, checks their
applicability, and evaluates their effects. It can revise a plan when a rack is occupied or an object’s
identity is uncertain. The local control loop regulates motion or contact using measurements avail-
able on the device. Its execution period follows the plant dynamics and the controller design. The
protection path detects conditions requiring intervention and can inhibit or limit actuation within its
specified response time. It may use drive electronics, a separate controller, or other independently
provisioned hardware. These functions can exchange evidence without sharing a single execution
path.
The task loop admits a request such as “transfer vial A to slot B” while the local controller processes
encoder samples and motor updates. At admission, the executor assigns a skill instance a lease,
which grants authority to issue task commands until a deadline on the executor’s monotonic clock.
Each command or action chunk also has an expiry determined by its intended execution interval
and the validity of its observations. The executor applies task commands only while both the
lease and the command remain valid. A new policy output cannot renew the lease. An admitted
segment must fit within this joint interval. The executor begins its preconfigured fallback no later
than expiry, allowing for detection and switching delay. That fallback has separate local authority
and a specified completion or holding limit.

Crash, stall, and network partition exercise this boundary differently. A crashed Harness stops
renewing its lease. A stalled task monitor must also stop renewal, even if a separate heartbeat
thread is alive. Renewal follows a completed monitoring cycle with valid evidence. A partition
can leave both sides running with divergent state. The executor therefore checks skill identity,
supervisor epoch, sequence, and freshness before accepting a renewal. One implementation uses
an executor-issued challenge with a local response deadline. Delayed responses cannot start a
fresh lease merely by arriving. Expired or superseded authority requires re-admission. The lease
duration must accommodate the admitted renewal delay while leaving time for the tested fallback.
Until expiry, locally available regulation and protection continue within the existing authority.
The correct fallback depends on the physical state. A moving base may brake. A loaded grip-
per may need to maintain a limited holding force. A gravity-loaded joint may require controlled
braking rather than abrupt removal of torque. Holding has thermal and energy limits and needs
an escalation or unloading procedure. If sensing or the controller fails, an independent protec-
240


tion channel handles the faults assigned to it. Merely placing two processes on the same com-
puter does not establish independence from kernel failure, power loss, or resource exhaustion. A
task-level cancellation request is not an emergency-stop mechanism. Industrial implementations
specify and validate the safety-related control and drive functions under applicable standards, in-
cluding ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2 (International Organization for Standardization, 2023a; In-
ternational Electrotechnical Commission, 2016). The required functions follow the machine’s risk
assessment.
Runtime assurance provides a related logical architecture. An advanced controller operates while a
monitor retains authority to transfer control to a verified fallback under stated assumptions (Desai
et al., 2019). Its guarantees depend on the plant model, measurements, recovery region, and timely
execution of the monitor and fallback. Implementing that logic in a separate fault domain is an
additional engineering decision. The local sensing, compute, power, and actuation paths must sur-
vive the faults for which continued operation is claimed. This separation preserves the autonomous
device loop emphasized in Section 9.3 while slower layers improve task selection and recovery.
9.4.2
Hardware Abstraction, Sensor Data, and Robotics Middleware
A hardware interface should hide transport details while exposing the physical properties on which
correct action depends. The ros2_control framework, for example, separates controllers from
hardware components through state and command interfaces, with a controller manager coordi-
nating the read-update-write cycle (ros2_control Development Team, n.d.). An interface named
“position” is still incomplete without joint units, coordinate conventions, limits, supported modes,
calibration state, and the conditions for switching modes. A simulated actuator and a physical
drive can satisfy the same software signature while differing in delay, saturation, compliance, and
failure behavior. Closed-loop substitution consequently requires testing the dynamics as well as
the API.
Sensor interfaces need similar precision. An observation should carry its acquisition time, clock
domain, frame, calibration identity, and validity information alongside the measurement. Covari-
ance or another uncertainty representation is needed when the estimator relies on it. Receipt time
alone conceals camera exposure, transport, and queueing delays. Combining a recent force sample
with an old image can create a plausible state that never existed. The estimator must either align
the measurements to a common time, propagate them using an explicit motion model, or mark
the combination as unsuitable for the intended decision. Missing and invalid measurements must
remain distinguishable from a measured zero.
Sensor validity can be expressed on the executor’s clock. Let ˆts be the mapped acquisition time,
with a clock-mapping error bounded by ϵsync. The estimated age of this particular observation at
use time t, rather than standard AoI for the latest available update, is
∆age(t) = t −ˆts,
∆age(t) + ϵsync ≤∆max

(9.5)
where ∆max
age is a configured age limit for the particular observation and use. It can differ for a
cached object label and a force estimate. The test applies at admission and at each intended actu-
ation time, so age continues to grow across an action chunk. For commands that depend on this
observation, it limits expiry to ˆts + ∆max
age −ϵsync. Additional constraints may shorten the interval. If
the clock mapping or its error bound is unavailable, the receiver needs another validated freshness
mechanism or must reject the observation for that use. ROS 2 distinguishes ROS time, which can
follow simulation, from steady time (Foote, 2018). Physical watchdogs and leases use the latter.
Simulation tests must state how their virtual timing maps to that mechanism.
Middleware carries these interfaces but does not supply their physical meaning. ROS 2 offers top-
ics for streams, services for request-response interactions, and actions for longer operations with
feedback and cancellation (Macenski et al., 2022; Biggs et al., 2020). The Data Distribution Ser-
vice (DDS) specifies data-centric publish-subscribe communication and quality-of-service (QoS)
policies, including reliability, history, deadline, and liveliness (Object Management Group, 2015).
Zenoh combines publish-subscribe with query-based data access, and rmw_zenoh integrates it be-
241


neath ROS 2’s middleware interface (Eclipse Zenoh, n.d.; ROS 2 Project, n.d.). These technologies
occupy different layers. ROS 2 defines the action protocol above the underlying DDS or Zenoh
transport.
QoS choices should follow the consequences of delay and loss. A high-rate state stream may benefit
from a shallow queue that favors recent samples. A configuration transaction may require acknowl-
edged delivery. Retransmission can improve delivery while increasing age, and a growing queue
can turn a responsive estimator into a consumer of historical data. DDS deadline and liveliness
events make some communication failures observable. They do not stop a motor or prove that a
task is progressing. Backend support also differs. The Jazzy implementation of rmw_zenoh does not
implement deadline or lifespan policies. A design that depends on those policies must verify the
selected release and enforce the necessary command-expiry behavior locally (ROS 2 Project, n.d.).
The resulting boundary is practical. Middleware transports typed information. The application
establishes freshness, ownership, and permissible use. A command should identify its producing
skill and sequence, its coordinate and control modes, and its validity interval. The receiver rejects
incompatible or expired commands before they enter the actuator path. Configuration changes
are versioned and checked before activation. These conventions allow a developer to distinguish
a transport failure from a stale observation, a conflicting controller, or an invalid request, each of
which calls for a different response.
9.4.3
Real-Time Runtimes and Learned Policy Integration
A controller needs its next input before a deadline, whereas a learned policy may have variable
inference time. Running both in one callback chain makes physical timing depend on model exe-
cution, memory allocation, and accelerator contention. ROS 2’s real-time guidance identifies page
faults, dynamic allocation, and indefinitely blocking synchronization as hazards in a time-critical
path (Kay, 2016). Deployment therefore separates the bounded control cycle from inference, log-
ging, visualization, and network-facing task services. Separation may require dedicated threads,
priorities, memory discipline, processor allocation, or a separate controller. The necessary arrange-
ment depends on the faults and interference the system must tolerate.
For a periodic local update, a useful timing budget is
Cmax + Bmax + Jmax < Tdeadline ≤Tc,
(9.6)
where Cmax bounds computation and input/output (I/O) on the selected path, Bmax bounds block-
ing and scheduling interference, Jmax bounds release jitter, Tdeadline is the deadline, and Tc is the
control period. This is an accounting condition for that path, not a complete schedulability or sta-
bility proof. The bounds require evidence for the actual workload and hardware. A finite bench-
mark’s largest observed latency is not automatically a worst-case bound. A complete assessment
also includes sensing delay, communication, actuator response, and the controller’s tolerance to
missed updates.
Learned policies fit this structure through explicit adapters.
OpenVLA illustrates a vision-
language-action model that maps observations and instructions to robot actions (Kim et al., 2025b).
ACT predicts sequences of actions for fine-grained manipulation (Zhao et al., 2023). Their out-
puts may be joint targets, end-effector increments, or other embodiment-specific commands. The
adapter must preserve the model’s normalization, reference frames, action period, and control
mode, and establish compatibility with the receiving controller. Position, velocity, and force checks
constrain admission. Collision avoidance and contact stability additionally depend on the con-
troller and its operating envelope.
Figure 9.12 shows an asynchronous arrangement. An inference worker consumes a timestamped
observation and produces a candidate action sequence with a sequence identity and validity hori-
zon. A local executor continues its fixed-rate cycle from an already admitted buffer while the can-
didate is computed. Before a buffer switch, the receiver checks observation age at the scheduled
use times, command order, frame, operating mode, lease, and relevant limits. It rejects late results
whose assumptions are no longer valid. The gate also applies a controller-specific continuity rule

velocity, force, or target pose. To avoid fallback, a replacement must finish inference, transport, and
admission before the current buffer expires. When inference runs at the edge, the freshness budget
includes both outward observation transport and returning commands. A small learned controller
with a demonstrated execution bound can instead run inside the periodic path and is subject to

Action chunks reduce the frequency at which a model must be invoked, but they also commit
the robot to predictions made from an earlier observation. A longer chunk can absorb inference
delay while delaying the response to a changed scene. Real-time chunking addresses this inter-
face by generating a new chunk asynchronously while accounting for actions committed during
inference (Black et al., 2025b). It coordinates policy execution under delay through a continuation
consistent with the committed prefix. Deployment still requires measurement and validation of the
complete runtime. Contact-sensitive control and protection still require timely local measurements,
even when the high-level action sequence remains valid.
The runtime should make buffer expiry, inference overrun, and observation dropout first-class
events. Repeating the last action indefinitely can be especially dangerous when the action is a
velocity or torque. At the earlier of lease and command expiry, the executor begins the plant-
specific fallback described above, records the transition, and prevents a delayed response from
restoring authority. Resumption requires fresh state and an explicit re-admission. Thus learning
243


can change the motion strategy without making the availability of a large model a prerequisite for
every control update.
9.4.4
The Embodied Intelligence Harness and Skill Contracts
The Harness governs the task loop across these interfaces. It maintains the current goal and ev-
idence, resolves requests against available skills, arbitrates resources, and tracks execution to an
observable result.
Hierarchical reinforcement learning formalizes temporally extended actions
through initiation, policy, and termination components (Sutton et al., 1999). Behavior trees pro-
vide established mechanisms for composing and monitoring robot behaviors (Iovino et al., 2022).
These precedents explain much of the required machinery. Language-conditioned skill selection
with affordance scoring, as in SayCan, provides a concrete precedent for connecting model propos-
als to robot capabilities (Ichter et al., 2023). In the framework used here, the model proposes skills
and arguments. Admission, monitoring, and completion decisions follow explicit contract checks
over timestamped evidence.
A skill contract gives the supervisor something more precise than an action name. Table 9.3 devel-
ops one example for moving a capped vial between known fixtures. Its parameters and conditions
are illustrative design choices, to be set from the actual robot, payload, and procedure. The exam-
ple separates request acceptance, physical progress, and completion evidence. A ROS 2 action can
carry the goal, feedback, result, and cancellation protocol, but resource ownership, physical pre-
conditions, command leases, and evidence requirements remain application responsibilities (Biggs
et al., 2020).
Admission checks establish that a skill can start. Execution monitoring determines whether its as-
sumptions continue to hold (Pettersson, 2005). A fresh target pose may become stale during an
approach. Another device may occupy a reserved region. A grasp may be established and then
lost. The monitor should therefore associate each predicate with evidence and a validity interval,
and distinguish false from unknown. Unknown identity or destination occupancy cannot be con-
verted to success merely because the motion controller reports completion. Learned perception
can misidentify a vial or occupancy state. Completion thresholds need calibration, and consequen-
tial decisions may require complementary sensing or repeated observation. Conflicting evidence
triggers re-observation or a recovery whose own conditions are checked.
Cancellation also has physical semantics. A ROS 2 action server may accept a cancellation request
while the underlying mechanism still needs time to decelerate or secure its load. The Harness
should wait for the executor’s terminal state and physical evidence before allocating its resources
to another skill. If communication fails after a vial has been placed but before the result arrives,
a timeout leaves the outcome uncertain. Retrying the transfer immediately could act on an empty
fixture or move a second object. Persistent request identities, execution records, and observation
of the fixtures allow the supervisor to reconcile state after reconnection. Reliable message delivery
alone cannot provide exactly-once physical effects.
Restarting the Harness reconstructs task state from the executor and fresh observations before
any new authority is issued. The application-level “outcome unknown” state describes missing
physical evidence or a missing result. It is distinct from the unset status represented by ROS 2’s
STATUS_UNKNOWN.
9.4.5
Development Infrastructure and Evidence for Deployment
Development infrastructure should test the boundaries just described. A reproducible episode
records acquisition and actuation times, frame and calibration versions, model and controller iden-
tities, skill requests, authority changes, and the evidence used to declare completion.
Tracing
the path from a sensor event through callbacks to a command helps distinguish inference delay
from scheduling or transport delay. ros2_tracing provides instrumentation for such analysis in
ROS 2 (Bédard et al., 2022). High-rate recording itself consumes resources, so its effect on the con-
trol workload must be measured or isolated.

Recorded-data replay is valuable for comparing estimators and diagnosing failures, but an un-
changed sensor log cannot establish the closed-loop outcome of a changed policy. Different actions
would have produced different observations. Software-in-the-loop (SIL) testing runs the relevant
software against a simulated plant to examine logic, interfaces, and responses to modeled dis-
turbances. Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing runs target firmware on target control electronics
against a simulated plant, exposing processor and scheduling effects. Sensor and actuator I/O
may still be emulated through a different link, as in PX4’s hardware-in-the-loop (HITL) arrange-
ment (PX4 Development Team, n.d.). The test report must identify which physical interfaces were
exercised. Gripper friction, camera exposure, and the complete machine’s stopping response re-
quire physical trials.
Figure 9.13 organizes these stages around explicit claims. For the vial-transfer skill, SIL can inject
a stale pose, a duplicated request, or a lost acknowledgment. HIL can expose queue growth, in-
ference contention, and watchdog delay. Bounded hardware trials can test grip loss and verify a
loaded stop. Terminating the Harness, suspending its monitoring loop while a heartbeat remains
alive, and partitioning the network are particularly informative. Local regulation and assigned
protection must remain available, command authority must expire as specified, and reconnection
must reject queued commands and renewals from obsolete epochs. Tests should also challenge
sensor loss and the shared resources that could defeat the intended isolation.
The evidence should include the operating conditions, observed latency distribution and misses,
age at actuation, time to fallback, recovery outcome, and the physical criterion for success. A re-
lease bundles the policy weights, preprocessing and action adapter, controller settings, middleware
configuration, firmware, calibration, and skill schema used to obtain that evidence. Changing one
of these can invalidate a previously established interface or timing assumption. Regression tests
and staged physical trials determine whether the affected claims still hold. Binding evidence to
this configuration provides the software basis for the sustained reliability and fleet deployment
considered in Section 9.5.

9.5
Reliability and Deployment at Scale
A vial-handling robot may complete a demonstration and still fail to produce usable samples over
a working day. A cap slips after the fingers warm up, a dispenser delivers less liquid than com-
manded, or a restart repeats a transfer already completed. Each failure breaks a different connection
between an intended action and its physical result. Reliable Physical AI requires that connection to
remain observable and correctable. The system must detect a deviation, determine what can still
be recovered, and verify the result before proceeding. Experience from these events can improve
subsequent behavior, provided the cause is identified and the change is tested. This section follows
that loop from one task to a fleet of machines.
9.5.1
From Successful Attempts to Sustained Physical Output
Reliability concerns continuity of correct service. Availability concerns whether a system is ready
to work (Avizienis et al., 2004). For a physical task, correct service needs an observable endpoint. A
sample is valid only if its identity, quantity, and required process conditions are preserved. Com-
mand delivery, completed trajectories, and apparent grasps are intermediate events. Their success
matters only through the result they enable. A robot that remains powered throughout a shift but
repeatedly requires a person to rescue its samples has poor autonomous productivity.
The measurements should therefore follow the task. Encoders establish arm configuration, touch
can reveal loss of contact, and a balance can verify a transfer. Agreement among several signals is
useful when they provide independent evidence. Several estimates derived from the same incorrect
calibration may agree while the sample is wrong. The task-state observability of Section 9.2.3 thus
becomes a reliability requirement. The system must distinguish states that call for different actions
while there is still time to intervene. Table 9.4 links this evidence to the scale of correction.
Small errors accumulate over long procedures. Fifty independent steps that each succeed 98% of the
time give only about 36% success for the whole sequence (0.9850 ≈0.364). Detection and recovery
can change this outcome. Let pk be the initial success probability at stage k, ddetect

A system can eventually succeed yet produce little usable work per hour. Full-workflow tests must
therefore measure both outcome and time.
Finite trials also limit what can be claimed. Twenty successes without a failure leave an exact one-
sided 95% upper confidence bound of about 14% on failure probability, under independent trials
with a fixed protocol (Hanley and Lippman-Hand, 1983). Evaluation should state the workload,
initial conditions, trial count, allowed assistance, and stopping rules. All attempted tasks, including
aborted ones, belong in the record.
9.5.2
Detecting and Diagnosing Failures from Physical Evidence
A monitor must recognize both an abnormal interaction and a missing task result. Rising torque
with little movement may indicate a jam. Ordinary joint motion with an unchanged balance read-
ing may indicate an empty transfer. The first can require a rapid local response, while the second
requires knowledge of the process. The sensor and actuator interfaces in Section 9.2 provide the
measurements. The runtime in Section 9.4 must associate them with the action being attempted
and its expected outcome. A successful command acknowledgment closes neither loop.
Detection is easier to interpret when it compares a prediction with a measurement tied to the task.
A dynamics observer can compare expected and measured joint loading, subject to its calibration
and model assumptions (Haddadin et al., 2017). A task monitor can check whether a cap rotated,
a vial moved with the gripper, or mass changed by the required amount. These checks should be
conditional on the current phase. Resistance is expected when tightening a cap but may indicate
a fault before the threads engage. A fixed threshold applied without that context can either stop
useful contact or overlook an abnormal one.
Learned monitors can supplement these checks. Sentinel combines action consistency tests with
vision-language assessment of task progress (Agia et al., 2025b). It provides evidence for detecting
failures during execution. Detection alone does not establish a correct recovery. Likewise, a plau-
sible explanation from a model remains a hypothesis. A stopped finger may reflect an obstructed
object, a current limit, overheating, or loss of communication. Synchronized images, encoder read-
ings, currents, temperatures, and command records help separate these causes. Their timestamps
matter because evidence collected after the robot has withdrawn may no longer describe the failed
contact.

Detection quality should be measured where it changes the physical outcome. Report missed fail-
ures, false stops per scheduled operating hour, and the time from a detectable deviation to the
protective response. Delays include sensing, transport, inference, and actuation, as discussed in
Section 9.3. An alarm raised after a fragile vial breaks has a different value from one that allows
the grasp to be corrected. Evaluate monitors on representative faults as well as normal contact
transitions. High accuracy on a dataset dominated by uneventful motion is insufficient.
9.5.3
Recovering Progress and Handling Irreversible Actions
Recovery begins by establishing what is still true. After a slipping cap, the vial may remain sup-
ported, the cap may have moved, and the threads may already be partly disengaged. Returning
the arm to a previous pose does not restore that state. The system should first preserve support and
limit further loading, then acquire enough evidence to choose a feasible continuation. A new view,
a gentle probing action, or a quantity check can be more useful than another full attempt. These
actions use interaction to reduce uncertainty, which is a central capability of Physical AI.
A recovery should change the conditions responsible for failure. A missed grasp may permit a
revised approach. A jam may require controlled withdrawal and realignment. A thermal limit
may require reduced duty or cooling. Force, travel, retries, and elapsed time need task-specific
bounds. If the cause remains unresolved or those bounds are reached, the robot should stop or
request assistance. The physical checks required to resume belong to the recovery procedure itself.
Long tasks need checkpoints defined by verified physical outcomes. After a transfer, the system
records sample identity, measured quantity, and completion status outside the policy’s transient
state (Section 8.3). On restart, it reconciles that record with the scene before issuing a new com-
mand. Otherwise, replaying a command whose acknowledgment was lost can double a dose. An
operator may also have moved the container, or a sample may have exceeded its usable holding
time. The checkpoint preserves what was verified. Renewed observation establishes what remains
valid now.
Some actions admit no useful rollback. Mixing the wrong reagent cannot be undone by restoring
a software version. Before an irreversible step, the system should verify its identity and process
preconditions and resolve uncertainty while correction is still possible. Action-conditioned world
models can simulate candidate interactions. UniSim uses predicted visual outcomes to train plan-
ners and control policies (Yang et al., 2024b). These predictions may still omit contamination, weak
248


contact, or damage invisible in an image. They should guide investigation, while the actual process
supplies the evidence for committing the action and accepting its result.
9.5.4
Learning from Operation Without Concealing Hardware Drift
The same command can produce a different interaction as pads wear, a camera mount shifts, or
actuator temperature rises. Changes also arise from new objects and from states reached after
the policy’s own mistakes. These forms of distribution shift demand different remedies. A loose
camera mount requires repair and recalibration. Repeated failure on a correctly observed new cap
geometry may justify additional demonstrations or a revised control policy. Retraining on every
deviation risks teaching the model to compensate for a deteriorating machine.
The operating record should retain the observation, intended action, measured response, hardware
and software configuration, intervention, and verified outcome. A successful human rescue is
especially informative when it records which state prompted the intervention and what changed.
DAgger addresses learning from states visited by the learner through expert feedback (Ross et al.,
2011). Sirius studies learning from robot execution with human monitoring and interventions (Liu
et al., 2023b). These approaches support improvement from experience. Intervention frequency
and operator time remain part of the deployment result, including the monitoring Sirius requires.
Simulation can test a proposed correction across variations that are costly to reproduce physically.
RialTo reconstructs real environments for simulation-based policy improvement (Villasevil et al.,
2024), while dynamics randomization varies physical parameters to reduce dependence on one
nominal model (Peng et al., 2018b). The relevant variation should follow the diagnosed mecha-
nism. Friction is relevant to slip, delay to late correction, and camera placement to an observation
mismatch. Randomizing unrelated parameters cannot establish that the observed failure has been
addressed.
SIMPLER evaluates agreement between simulated and real policy performance within tested ma-
nipulation settings (Li et al., 2025b). Such agreement makes simulation useful for screening can-
didates, but a favorable ranking does not establish adequate absolute reliability. A revised policy
needs fresh physical trials on the failure conditions, earlier successful tasks, and representative
operating variation. Development episodes and acceptance trials must be separated. Fast control
feedback corrects the current interaction. Learning changes future behavior and therefore requires
this additional validation loop.
9.5.5
Deploying Compatible Configurations Across a Fleet
Scaling a policy means preserving its observation-action relationship on multiple physical ma-
chines. Differences in camera placement, fingertip wear, controller gains, and firmware can change
that relationship even when robots share a model name. Common collection procedures, as used
in DROID, help make experience comparable across sites (Khazatsky et al., 2024). Deployment ad-
ditionally requires evidence that each supported configuration still produces the intended physical
outcome under its assigned workload.
Consider a new cap-opening policy for a fleet of vial-handling robots. The release manifest identi-
fies model weights, observation preprocessing, action units and scaling, controller code and gains,
drive firmware, and supported hardware revisions. It also binds each robot to its own checked
camera, tool, and force-sensor calibration, using a specified calibration procedure and tolerances.
Calibration values cannot be copied between machines merely because their parts have the same
names. The validated unit is the compatible configuration. Installing new weights with an old
action convention can turn a useful learned correction into an unintended movement.
After interface, replay, simulation, and hardware-in-the-loop checks, a small subset runs super-
vised trials spanning the intended hardware and workload. Robots on the previous release pro-
vide a concurrent comparison. Acceptance criteria are fixed beforehand and cover sample quality,
completion, contact loads, temperature, interventions, and recovery time. The trials include re-
peated cycles and warm actuators. Expansion depends on adequate exposure to these conditions,
249


rather than a few successful picks. Results should be separated by configuration. An improved
fleet average can conceal a regression on one gripper revision.
Suppose cap slip increases after the update. Further rollout stops and affected robots are removed
from the scheduler. Each preserves its load and reaches a validated stopping state where possible.
Uncertain samples are held for inspection. Logs retain the complete configuration and the physical
evidence around the event. Recovery restores the previously validated compatible configuration
where supported, checks calibration, and runs a physical acceptance sequence before returning the
robot to service. Firmware that cannot be reversed needs a tested recovery image or maintenance
procedure. Software restoration and sample recovery are separate obligations. A spilled sample
remains lost after rollback.
Table 9.5 connects these trials to sustained productivity. Faults still unresolved at the reporting
cutoff must remain visible, rather than disappearing from recovery-time statistics. Over the same
reporting period, the cost per valid output introduced in Section 9.1 is

including its interruptions. Those records then identify whether the next improvement belongs in
the policy, the sensing and actuation hardware, or the operating procedure.
The cases in Section 9.6 examine this requirement at the contact level. A demonstrated manipula-
tion skill becomes useful within a larger task only when its entry conditions, physical result, and
recovery requirements are preserved.
9.6
Case Studies in Dexterous Hand Hardware
A hand holding a spray bottle must support the bottle while another finger moves the trigger
and the wrist maintains the spray direction. Rotating an object within the palm instead requires
changing the contacts that keep it under control. In both cases, what a learned policy can achieve
depends on which contacts the hardware can make, sense, and adjust.
Applying Sections 9.1 and 9.2 at the finger level, the following cases examine RobotEra XHAND 1,
the first-generation Wuji Hand, and Sharpa Wave W01 through their task requirements, mecha-
nisms, sensing and control interfaces, and demonstrated capabilities. The emphasis is on the hard-
ware conditions under which a result holds. Learning methods are covered in Section 6.6, and
low-level hand controllers in Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5.
