9.6.1
Manipulation Tasks and Contact Requirements
Dexterous tasks place different demands on the hand. Grasp acquisition establishes contact with
an object. Transport preserves its relation to the hand. In-hand manipulation changes that relation.
Tool operation additionally changes another object or process. Their evaluation boundaries matter.
A policy tested with an object already in its palm has not thereby been tested on acquiring it from
a table, and reaching a tool pose does not necessarily establish that the tool performed its intended
operation.
To move the index finger around a cylinder, the remaining fingers must first sustain the load. Exces-
sive squeezing can prevent rotation, while premature release can lose support. Rolling, sliding, and
breaking contact permit different motions. The controller must coordinate the transition between
them, as well as the finger positions (Lynch and Park, 2017). In tool use, it must also resist the re-
action to pressing, cutting, or twisting. A grasp that supports the tool’s weight may be inadequate
once the tool meets its target.
Each of these demands is partly a hardware question. Holding a load while another finger moves
takes enough independent joints and enough sustained fingertip force. Regulating squeeze instead
of position takes a drive that accepts force or impedance commands, or at least torque limits. Catch-
ing the onset of sliding takes a contact sensor fast enough to act before the grasp is lost. Resisting a
tool’s reaction takes force capacity, and an arm that can carry the hand’s own mass.
9.6.2
Hand Design and the Observation-Action Interface
The hands differ in their independently controlled coordinates (Table 9.6), excluding the arm and
wrist (RobotEra, n.d.; Wuji Technology, n.d.c; Sharpa Robotics, n.d.a). Thumb opposition, finger
spread, joint limits, and available contact surfaces determine what those coordinates can accom-
plish. More coordinates enlarge both the possible contact arrangements and the coordination prob-
lem. They do not alone rank task performance.
Figure 9.15 compares a MANO human-hand mesh with the actual robot geometries and locates
their rotational coordinates. MANO represents each of its 15 finger joints by a three-parameter
rotation. Its 45-dimensional hand pose is a model parameterization, not a count of independently
actuated anatomical motions (Romero et al., 2017). Reconstructed human landmarks and robot
joints are different representations. A tracked fingertip need not correspond to one motor, and
equal joint-vector dimensions need not imply equal fingertip motion. For a thumb-index pinch,
the useful correspondence concerns fingertip separation and opposition relative to the object. Re-
producing them may require different combinations of finger flexion, lateral motion, and wrist
placement. Moving the wrist can compensate for limited finger reach, but also moves the other
contacts.
The retargeting objective in Eq. (6.23) must be constrained by collisions and contact. A small fin-
gertip error does not guarantee that a tool can be held under load.
The observation interface requires the same care. A fingertip contact flag can detect contact without
resolving shear load or object pose, while an external camera can locate an object without seeing its
supporting contacts. Coverage also matters. A dense fingertip sensor does not observe a load borne
by the palm. Rotating without Seeing illustrates the alternative of distributing binary contact sensing
over the fingers and palm, supporting learned reorientation on real objects (Yin et al., 2023). Sensors
should therefore be compared by the contact decisions they support, not by resolution alone.
Policy targets also differ from actuator response. A finger stopped by an object cannot track every
requested position. Its loading depends on gains, transmission, and effort limits. A study therefore
has to report both the policy’s targets and the observations it actually used. A tactile sensor listed
in a hand’s specification may be absent from a particular policy input. Hardware revisions and
additional software development kit (SDK) capabilities should likewise remain separate from the
experimental configuration being discussed.

9.6.3
Actuation, Sensing, and Electrical Interfaces
Table 9.6 lists manufacturer specifications for the cited versions, rather than measurements from the
learning studies. Their implications depend on the load, contact geometry, and feedback required
by the task.
Mass, Size, and Force Capacity
All three hands approach human hand size, but their masses
differ by more than a factor of two (Wuji Technology, n.d.c; Sharpa Robotics, n.d.a). Hand mass
consumes arm payload before an object is lifted and adds to wrist inertia. It must therefore enter
the arm’s dynamics model. Maximum fingertip-force ratings do not specify how long a force can
be sustained. For a stiff trigger, the relevant test is continuous force within the motor’s thermal
limits, evaluated in the geometry of the actual grasp.
Drive and Compliance
The three drives give a policy’s joint target different physical mean-
ings. Wuji’s rotary direct-drive joints operate under position control and are specified as self-
locking (Wuji Technology, n.d.c). Active yielding to an external load requires the controller to adjust
the position target from feedback. Sharpa Wave instead exposes position, admittance, impedance,
and zero-force modes, the last being backdrivable for manual guidance (Sharpa Robotics, n.d.a).
Under impedance control, a blocked finger produces a force that grows with its position error and
the stiffness selected, as in the series-compliance relation of Eq. (9.3). Under zero-force mode an
operator can move the fingers directly, which is one route to kinesthetic demonstration. XHAND
accepts joint targets together with controller gains and torque limits from the host (Section 9.2.6).
Joint targets alone therefore underspecify an action. The control mode, gains, and effort limits used
during collection must be logged and reproduced at deployment.
Sensing Load at the Joints
Sharpa Wave estimates joint torque from motor current by default
and also provides five torque sensors at the thumb carpometacarpal and four metacarpophalangeal
joints. Their full-scale ratings are 5 and 3 N m, respectively, with a stated total error of ±(1% of full

perature. A dedicated torque sensor measures the load through its joint but still does not locate the
contact. Section 7.4.5 examines control using such joint-torque force estimates.
253


Tactile Sensing: Coverage, Rate, and Latency
Each Sharpa Wave fingertip uses an internal cam-
era to image a compliant surface. It reports force, surface deformation, and contact location, with a
30 N force measurement range (Sharpa Robotics, n.d.a). For control, their timing is critical. In the
standard mode these outputs are computed on board at 30 Hz with a reported nominal latency of
about 50 ms. In the high-performance mode raw images stream at up to 180 Hz with a reported
nominal latency of about 20 ms and are processed on a host GPU. The joint loop, by comparison,
runs at 500 Hz. The reported nominal tactile latencies of 20 to 50 ms correspond to 10 to 25 joint-
control periods at 500 Hz. Tactile updates at 30 to 180 Hz arrive approximately 3 to 17 times less
frequently than joint-control updates. Systems such as T-Rex therefore refine finger targets asyn-
chronously from tactile history while a separate servo thread tracks them (Section 7.4.5). Sensing
latency remains part of the end-to-end budget in Eq. (9.4). XHAND’s optional arrays report finger-
tip force and temperature (RobotEra, n.d.). The first-generation Wuji Hand has no tactile sensing.
Pressure measured by its companion glove belongs to the operator’s contacts, not the robot’s. In
all three cases the palm and the inner finger segments are uninstrumented, so loads that the policy
routes there remain unobserved.
Electrical Interfaces, Bandwidth, and Power
The joint interfaces in Table 9.6 impose different
update periods (Wuji Technology, n.d.c; RobotEra, 2024). Sensor transport can impose a separate
constraint. Sharpa Wave’s hand control and 30 Hz tactile outputs fit within 100 Mb/s Ethernet,
whereas its 180 Hz raw tactile stream requires gigabit Ethernet (Sharpa Robotics, n.d.a). Choosing
raw images thus moves computation to the host and raises network load, linking sensing to the
device-edge placement decisions of Section 9.3. Power follows the same logic. Sharpa Wave speci-
fies 100 W average and 180 W peak per hand, and 200 W average for a pair. Wuji’s supplied adapter
is rated for 420 W 10 ms transients (Sharpa Robotics, n.d.a; Wuji Technology, n.d.c). On a mobile
manipulator, two hands draw from the same battery as the base and arms, and peak currents dur-
ing simultaneous grasps must be within the supply’s transient capacity.
Durability and Maintenance
The rated hand lifetimes concern unloaded motion, whereas the
tactile-skin rating specifies loaded cycles (Sharpa Robotics, n.d.a; Wuji Technology, n.d.c). These
conditions matter in contact-rich learning. Fingertip skins become consumables, and pressure-
induced tactile drift calls for recalibration within the maintenance loop of Section 9.5, separate
from model updates. Neither stated ingress rating specifies liquid-ingress protection. Covers or
gloves needed for spills in kitchen or laboratory tasks also alter friction and tactile response.
The specifications alone already limit what can transfer between hands, whatever the learning
method. A policy trained on Sharpa fingertip deformation images cannot run on a hand without
tactile sensing. A controller that relies on impedance mode cannot be transferred unchanged to a
position-only interface. A refinement loop designed for a 500 Hz joint interface must be retimed
for a 12 ms bus update. Section 6.6.3 asks the complementary question of what a shared action
representation can transfer.
9.6.4
Demonstration and Data-Collection Hardware
For dexterous hands, data collection must capture wrist motion, articulated finger motion, and
contact together. The same tracker and glove can record a person directly manipulating an object
or provide commands to a robot. The resulting records describe different bodies and interactions.
Human pretraining data include egocentric video with estimated hand motion and instrumented
demonstrations with measured tracking signals. CAIP uses both pose-estimated video and labora-
tory human recordings with MANUS Metagloves Pro and Vive Ultimate Trackers (Sharma et al.,
2026b). Instrumented capture reduces dependence on reconstructing occluded fingers, but still re-
quires the hand model and the retargeting of Section 6.6.1. Robot teleoperation additionally records
how the deployed arm and hand respond to the mapped commands. This response is the extra evi-
dence needed when a geometrically plausible demonstration does not produce the intended grasp.
A representative teleoperation arrangement pairs a wrist tracker with a data glove. The tracker
estimates the hand’s position and orientation in the tracking space. The glove resolves the fingers
254


relative to the hand. MANUS Core supports external tracker poses, including HTC Vive devices,
with calibrated offsets between tracker and glove (MANUS, n.d.b). In CAIP’s Sharpa setup, Vive
wrist motion drives relative arm targets, while MANUS finger keypoints are retargeted into hand-
joint targets (Sharma et al., 2026b). The two measurements solve separate parts of the arm-hand
coordination problem. Finger tracking alone cannot tell the arm where to place the hand in the
workspace.
Wuji’s official teleoperation interface likewise supports Vive tracking with Wuji Glove or MANUS
as the hand input (Wuji Technology, n.d.b). Wuji Glove combines electromagnetic fingertip track-
ing, a fitted hand model, and pressure sensing on the palmar side (Wuji Technology, n.d.a).
MANUS also distinguishes raw sensor measurements from its solved hand skeleton and retar-
geted output (MANUS, n.d.a). For supervision, this means that a model-derived joint angle is not
an independently measured robot joint angle. Likewise, pressure recorded while the wearer holds
an object describes human-side contact. During free-hand teleoperation, the glove does not ac-
quire the remote robot’s contact forces. Those require robot-side sensing. Measuring pressure and
rendering force feedback to the operator are separate capabilities.
Calibration has two distinct roles. Tracker-to-hand and tracking-to-robot transforms establish wrist
targets, while hand-shape calibration and retargeting establish finger targets. A misplaced wrist
tracker shifts every fingertip even when finger articulation is estimated accurately. Recording is-
sued targets alongside measured robot motion helps distinguish this error from failure to reach a
target under load.
Exoskeleton interfaces move part of this correspondence into the mechanism. Linkages and en-
coders relate the operator’s motion to the demonstration hand, and mechanically matched designs
can make collected contacts closer to those available during deployment. DexEXO illustrates this
approach with a wearable linkage driving a passive hand whose appearance and kinematics match
the deployed hand. Aligned wrist-camera images can then be used directly for policy training (Zhu
et al., 2026). The benefit must be weighed against fit, range of motion, and access around a tool. A
bulky finger attachment can prevent a valid demonstration even when the robot itself fits the tool.
Passive coupling also differs from an actuated interface that returns robot forces to the wearer. An
exoskeleton does not, by itself, imply bidirectional force feedback.
XHAND: Shaping the Collection Interface to the Mechanism
XHAND approaches the corre-
spondence problem from the collection side. A lower-dimensional hand changes which demon-
strated finger motions can be reproduced independently, as Figure 9.15 shows. DexUMI investi-
gates this problem on XHAND and Inspire hands. It combines a wearable exoskeleton fitted to
the target hand’s kinematics, measured joint motion, matched tactile sensing, and visual replace-
ment of the human hand and device with the robot hand (Xu et al., 2025c). Mechanical alignment
constrains the motion before it becomes training data. Observation alignment makes the same in-
teraction more recognizable after deployment. Neither step alone ensures that the robot can sustain
the demonstrated load. The paper also reports tactile drift after high pressure and an inconsistent
motor-to-fingertip mapping (Xu et al., 2025c). Collection and deployment may use nominally iden-
tical devices that differ in loading history, so recalibration and loaded tests are part of keeping the
demonstration interface valid.
A second XHAND study addresses the difficulty of coordinating the arm and fingers during collec-
tion. In the shared-autonomy framework of Cui et al. (2025), a person guides a UR3e arm through
virtual reality (VR) while DexGrasp-VLA uses vision and touch to control the 12-DoF hand. This
division reduces the number of decisions the operator must make simultaneously. The person
chooses the approach and places the wrist, and the hand controller handles contact. The benefit
depends on that controller. If it closes too early, the demonstration records the error unless the
operator corrects it. A useful collection system must therefore expose who controlled each interval,
how an intervention changed the action, and whether the resulting grasp served the task. Sec-
tion 6.6.4 discusses the learning results of both studies, including where tactile input helped.
Figure 9.16 organizes these routes by where the physical interaction occurs.

Contact transitions make timestamp alignment consequential. Pairing finger closure with an image
acquired after contact changes the state on which the action appears to depend. Records must
distinguish pre-contact intent, measured contact, and subsequent correction.
9.6.5
From Demonstrated Skills to Integrated Tasks
Each learning result built on these hands covers one piece of a task. EgoScale learns a target-robot
policy from human data (Section 6.6.2), WM-Craftnet rotates a held object, SimToolReal follows
object-pose goals, and Play2Perfect adapts to assembly (Sections 7.4.4 and 7.4.5). Sharing a hand
does not make them composable. The skill interfaces of Section 8.3.2 require the state produced by
one behavior to support the next. An acquired grasp must permit the required finger movement,
the object must remain observable, and the transition must preserve its support.
Consider using a tool after picking it up. A grasp that permits lifting may occupy the finger needed
to operate the handle. Integration then requires reorientation, a changed grasp, or placement on a
support surface before operation can begin. An in-hand rotation result supplies evidence about one
of these transitions under its tested initial conditions. It does not establish the complete acquisition-
operation sequence. This is where the runtime interfaces of Section 9.4 must connect policy outputs
to measured contact and task state. Finishing a motion command is not by itself permission to begin
the next skill.
Feedback also has to reach the right level. Recent touch can correct finger targets while the visual
goal stays valid, but losing a usable grasp calls for a new task-level decision, and the runtime must
route the event accordingly (Section 9.3). With tactile latency spanning ten or more joint-control
256


periods in the reported modes (Section 9.6.3), a faster servo cannot make up for a policy that never
receives the evidence of slip.
The reported endpoints (rotation completion, progress along a tool trajectory, insertion success,
and accumulated success in a kitchen sequence) do not support a controlled comparison between
hands (Section 6.6.5). Complete-task evidence requires grasping, contact transitions, operation, and
recovery to succeed together under a declared protocol, with assistance costs reported alongside
success.
Across the cases, reusable motor knowledge becomes useful only through a specific sensing and
control interface. What transfers may be human coordination, an object-level goal, or a functional
finger action. What has to be checked is the contact behavior on the deployed hand. Transfer to
another hand, adaptation to assembly, and continued operation through wear are separate achieve-
ments. On a humanoid, this interface also depends on the moving body that supports the hand.
Section 9.7 extends the analysis to that integrated system.
9.7
Case Studies in Humanoid System Integration
Carrying an object across a room connects almost every component considered in this chapter. The
hands maintain the grasp, arm motion redistributes the load, stepping changes the support con-
tacts, and the moving cameras must still provide useful observations of the destination. Recent
systems built on the Unitree G1 show how these components can be organized for teleoperation,
data collection, and autonomous whole-body interaction. They make the co-design problem in Sec-
tion 9.1 concrete. The task model must express the required movements, and the robot’s mechanics,
sensing, and computation must support their execution in closed-loop interaction. The comparison
follows a common set of questions concerning what the task demands from the body, how observa-
tions and commands cross the interfaces, what was demonstrated, and which operating conditions
bound that evidence. G1 provides a common platform for comparing these integration choices.
9.7.1
Embodiment and Whole-Body Coordination
A humanoid’s manipulation workspace depends on how it positions and supports its body. In
G1’s 29-DoF configuration, six joints per leg, three at the waist, and seven per arm provide mul-
tiple ways to reach and orient an object. Hand joints are counted separately (Unitree Robotics,
2026). Waist and arm motion can extend a reach, but the resulting posture and load must remain
compatible with the supporting contacts. The hand’s contact capabilities therefore need to be con-
sidered together with the body motions required to use them, extending the hand-design problem
in Section 9.6 to the complete robot.
This coupling shapes the division of control between a task model and a motor controller. A task
model may specify hand and arm motion while leaving the supporting legs to a local feedback
policy. When a foot also manipulates an object, the task interface must convey that contact objective
as well. HOMIE and SONIC implement these divisions of control on G1 (Ben et al., 2025; Luo et al.,
2026). Both depend on a motor controller that produces the expected physical response from the
assembled robot.
9.7.2
From a Learned Policy to Physical Execution
For a joint-target policy, motion depends on the interaction between its outputs, feedback gains,
and actuator mechanics. As the actuation analysis in Section 9.2 explains, matching target angles
alone does not match the robot’s response. ASAP addresses this problem on G1 by learning a
correction to the simulated action-response relationship from measured robot trajectories, with a
focus on the ankle linkage. The correction is used during policy fine-tuning in simulation. The
resulting policy executes on the robot without that additional correction model (He et al., 2025a).
Physical measurements thus change the dynamics against which the policy is trained, improving
transfer without adding that model to the online control loop.
257


Policy execution also depends on the state estimates and timing of its feedback path. Beyond-
Mimic’s G1 motion-tracking stack combines a 500 Hz state estimator with a 50 Hz policy, whose
onboard CPU inference takes less than 1 ms (Liao et al., 2026). The estimator updates the body-state
estimate between policy evaluations, while the policy uses that estimate to update joint targets. Pol-
icy frequency, inference latency, and estimation frequency therefore describe different parts of the
physical loop. This separation implements the multirate execution discussed in Section 9.4. Timely
movement depends on the complete sensing-computation-actuation path, including the stages out-
side neural-network inference.
9.7.3
Connecting Body Control, Hands, and Task Models
In whole-body manipulation, the division of control determines which aspects of motion a person
or task model specifies and which the local controller supplies. HOMIE and SONIC provide two
concrete answers (Figure 9.17). Both connect a task-command source to body and hand execution,
but they expose different levels of control over the supporting legs.

gets with velocity, turning, and torso-height commands to a learned lower-body controller. Its
autonomous visual policy predicts arm, hand, and height targets. In SONIC’s whole-body VLA

representation (Ben et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2026)
HOMIE: A Shared Interface for Demonstration and Autonomous Execution
HOMIE connects
an isomorphic arm exoskeleton, motion-sensing gloves, and foot pedals to a G1 equipped with
Dex3-1 hands (Ben et al., 2025). The exoskeleton supplies arm-joint targets. The gloves command
the hands. The pedals specify forward or backward velocity, turning rate, and torso height. A
learned lower-body controller uses robot feedback to walk or squat as the upper-body posture
changes. This allocation reduces the operator’s burden. The person directs the reach and grasp
while the lower-body policy supplies the compensating motion discussed in Section 7.3. The op-
258


erator receives no force feedback, however, limiting direct assessment of contact loads through the
teleoperation interface.
The same allocation connects data collection to autonomous execution. HOMIE records images,
joint states, and task commands during teleoperation, then trains a visual policy to produce arm,
hand, and height targets. Its local locomotion policy runs at 50 Hz on the robot’s Jetson Orin. For
autonomous manipulation, head- and arm-mounted cameras and joint feedback supply a visual
policy on an external RTX 4080 computer through wired Ethernet. This upper-level loop runs
at 10 Hz. The task model can therefore replace the operator while retaining the controller that
regulates body motion. After collecting 50 demonstrations per task, the system succeeds in 11 of 15
trials of squatting to pick a tomato from a low sofa and 12 of 15 trials of tabletop pick-and-place (Ben
et al., 2025).
SONIC: Exposing Coordinated Body Motion to a VLA
Some tasks require the task model to
choose a foot contact as deliberately as a grasp. Opening a pedal-operated bin while holding
an object, for example, requires placing one foot on the pedal while the other supports the body.
SONIC connects a fine-tuned GR00T N1.5 VLA model to a reusable whole-body controller through
a learned motion representation (Luo et al., 2026). In its whole-body mode, the VLA predicts a
64-dimensional motion token and 14 hand-joint targets. The token conditions coordinated body
motion. The hand targets command finger configurations. Teleoperated demonstrations populate
this same action representation, connecting the motor pretraining discussed in Section 7.4 to task
learning.
The G1 motion stack controls 29 body joints and runs onboard a Jetson Orin. Its learned controller
updates at 50 Hz, while an independent 500 Hz command publisher streams the latest joint targets
to the low-level interface (Luo et al., 2026). Separating these operations sustains command delivery
between policy evaluations. At the task level, the VLA-driven system completes the sequence of
picking up a can, walking to a bin, pressing its pedal, and disposing of the can in 6 of 10 trials after
training on 1,000 multi-object demonstrations. It also places a drill in a box and carries the box to
a shelf with both hands in 7 of 10 trials after 300 demonstrations. These are complete-task results.
Grasping, locomotion, and changes in support must succeed within the same execution.
The two interfaces support different task demands. HOMIE assigns the operator or visual policy
direct control of the arms and hands and leaves leg coordination to a command-conditioned con-
troller. SONIC’s motion representation also lets the task model request coordinated leg motions,
including a foot’s interaction with an object. In both cases, reusing a motor controller becomes
useful through an interface that expresses the movements needed to establish and maintain task
contacts.
9.7.4
Physical and Perceptual Conditions for Task Execution
A task interface connects learned models to coordinated movement, but the range of executable
tasks also depends on the robot’s end effectors, the states it can observe, and the demands of re-
peated operation. AdaPT’s G1 tennis experiments expose the coupling between the first two. Serv-
ing requires both a body capable of the swing and timely observations of the ball (Huang et al.,
2026a).
For professional-style serving, AdaPT combines a task-specific racket mount with a lightweight
parallel gripper that holds and tosses the ball. The heavier Unitree hand, termed Dex-3 in the
AdaPT study, is evaluated with simpler amateur motions because the tested configuration cannot
maintain balance with that hand during the professional serving motions (Huang et al., 2026a). The
choice of hand thus changes which whole-body movements are feasible, even though its immedi-
ate role is to hold and release the ball. End-effector selection must account for the dynamic task
performed by the complete body as well as the local grasp.
Executing the swing also requires observations that arrive early enough to coordinate racket-ball
contact. AdaPT’s principal experiments use a 35-camera motion-capture system to track the robot
and ball. In a separate field deployment on the Dobot Atom humanoid, stereo vision and HTC
259


VIVE Ultimate Trackers provide ball observations and robot localization, respectively (Huang et al.,
2026a). The motor skill is therefore evaluated together with a particular source of task-state in-
formation. The same dependence appears in locomotion. Gallant’s confined-terrain case in Sec-
tion 9.2.7 requires three-dimensional geometry over the space occupied by the body. In both set-
tings, sensing must resolve the geometry relevant to making or avoiding contact. Intercepting a
moving ball additionally requires predicting where contact occurs.
Sustaining these motions over repeated trials adds thermal and mechanical constraints to those of
a single execution. ASAP reports motor overheating and partial damage to two G1 robots during
its high-dynamic-motion data collection, limiting the real-world data available for adaptation (He
et al., 2025a). This connects the actuator limits in Section 9.2 to the operating-life considerations in
Section 9.5. Physical learning depends on how often the assembled robot can repeat the contacts
and accelerations needed to collect experience.
9.7.5
From Integrated Demonstrations to Sustained Operation
HOMIE and SONIC demonstrate that a shared command interface can connect data collection, task
models, and local body control. Their reported task trials test whether grasping, movement, and
changes in support can succeed in one execution. The different tasks, demonstration sets, and trial
protocols do not provide a controlled comparison between the two systems. Nor do those trial
counts describe how either system performs over a working shift. The measures in Section 9.5
extend the evaluation to valid output, assistance, downtime, and recovery under a declared work-
load.

each answer a different part of the system question.

For a humanoid carrying an object, this distinction becomes concrete when the task computer or its
communication link becomes unavailable. A local body controller may still receive proprioceptive
feedback, but that alone does not specify whether the last task command remains authorized or
how the object is secured. The runtime must define command expiry and the locally executable
response for the relevant physical state, as in Section 9.4. Trials then need to establish the response
under the faults assigned to that design, including the conditions for resuming the task. These
260


fault-response tests form part of deployment validation. The task trials summarized above do not
establish their outcomes.
The hand and humanoid cases bring the chapter’s five questions together. The body determines
which contacts and loads are feasible. Sensing makes their consequences observable. Compu-
tation must finish while that evidence remains useful. Software assigns authority and connects
commands to measured outcomes. Deployment preserves these relationships through repetition,
wear, and updates. A change in fingertip material, payload, camera placement, or command tim-
ing can alter several of these relationships at once. The unit to validate is therefore the assembled
observation-action system under its intended workload. Hardware and software become a de-
pendable physical capability when they repeatedly produce the required result and retain a tested
means to detect, contain, and recover from deviations.

Part III
Future Outlook
"The real problem of humanity is the following: we have
paleolithic emotions; medieval institutions; and god-like
technology."
— Edward O. Wilson
262


10
Physical AGI
The preceding chapters examine the basic concepts of Physical AI together with perception, data,
world models, foundation models for robot manipulation, foundation models for whole-body mo-
tor control, agents, and hardware systems. These technologies provide the foundations for systems
that perceive, reason, and act in the physical world. The question for this chapter is whether these
foundations can support more than a growing repertoire of predefined physical tasks. This mono-
graph focuses on intelligence that can interpret unfamiliar situations, develop new ways of acting,
and take part in creating and maintaining the material conditions of human life. It calls the ultimate
goal of this line of research physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI). This term denotes an
artificial system that integrates broad understanding, learning, and reasoning with reliable action
in the physical world and can solve unfamiliar real-world problems across many domains at a level
comparable to capable humans.
The qualifier physical gives this goal its specific meaning. An agent must connect its task-relevant
knowledge to what its body can actually do, reason about the consequences of intervention, and re-
vise its understanding when the world responds unexpectedly. Recognizing an object or describing
a plausible plan is only the beginning. The agent must also find out how the object is supported,
what changes once contact is made, and which uncertainties matter for execution. The physical
world is thus more than the place where an intelligent system is tested. It supplies evidence, con-
strains reasoning, and is the medium through which the system achieves its goals.
Physical grounding, a complete technical stack, a larger task repertoire, and greater model scale
do not by themselves establish generality. Chollet defines intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency
relative to priors, experience, and generalization difficulty, and thereby separates it from achieved
skill (Chollet, 2019). High task performance may reflect effective learning, extensive prior training,
or both. The relevant contrast is between a fixed repertoire and the ability to meet unfamiliar de-
mands by reusing knowledge and acquiring what is missing. Scale can improve both, and Sutton
identifies search and learning as general methods that keep benefiting from increasing computa-
tion (Sutton, 2019). For Physical AI, what must be shown is that these gains translate into better
understanding, transfer, execution, and adaptation.
Physical AGI must therefore act effectively across tasks, environments, and embodiments, and ac-
quire further competence when existing knowledge falls short, without being redesigned for each
task. Section 10.1 makes this requirement precise. It examines what separates such a system from
today’s Physical AI and characterizes competence along four dimensions, namely breadth, depth,
plasticity, and continuity. As Figure 10.1 shows, the subsections that follow trace four pathways to-
ward Physical AGI, namely systematic generalization, human-robot collaboration, collective Phys-
ical AI, and self-evolution, each of which relaxes an assumption of current Physical AI. A con-
cluding subsection considers the proposed purposes of Physical AGI in scientific discovery and in
engineering beyond human limits.
10.1
Core Capabilities of Physical AGI
Most Physical AI systems today are built and evaluated for a stated set of tasks, settings, and
platforms. Within that set they can be highly capable, but their competence is bounded by the scope
anticipated by training and engineering, and a new demand typically calls for new data, retraining,
or redesign. Physical AGI differs from such systems in generality, the “G” in AGI, rather than in
higher performance on the same tasks. A Physical AI system is characterized by the skills it has.
Physical AGI is characterized by how far it can carry those skills, and extend them, beyond the
conditions covered by its preparation.
This chapter takes generality in this sense to mean the capacity to reuse knowledge and problem-
solving processes across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments, and to acquire or revise
competence efficiently when existing knowledge is insufficient. Generality is always relative to a
stated scope, performance standard, and resource budget, not to all conceivable tasks.

Fig. 10.1 Overview of physical artificial general intelligence (Physical AGI). Building on Physical
AI, Physical AGI is described by the four capability dimensions of breadth, depth, plasticity, and
continuity. It is pursued through four pathways, which are systematic generalization, collabora-
