advance scientific discovery and to enable engineering beyond the reach of human capability
What makes this definition physical is the relationship between knowledge and intervention. An
agent must reason about objects, materials, spatial structure, forces, and its own body well enough
to act on them, and it must link an abstract objective, such as repairing an object or assembling a
mechanism, to the physical conditions under which that objective can be met. The link runs both
ways, since interaction can expose unknown constraints and change how the agent understands
the problem. Physical AGI thus acts with available knowledge and also uses action to acquire
knowledge for later tasks.
The definition covers both the use of existing competence and the acquisition of new competence,
and many unfamiliar conditions call only for the former. A robot may grasp an object with an un-
seen surface texture using a policy it already has. A narrower container opening may call for a new
grasp or a contact-guided insertion, which planning with existing knowledge may still find. New
learning becomes necessary only when knowledge and available skills both fall short. The deciding
question is whether existing competence still suffices, not whether the situation is unfamiliar.
For the same reason, a large but fixed repertoire is weak evidence of adaptability, and fast learning
within a narrow task family is weak evidence of breadth. Generality also does not mean freedom
from human help. Demonstrations, feedback, and manual adjustments needed for a new task count
toward its adaptation cost. The criterion is whether the system’s own adaptation and learning
can meet new demands within its physical, computational, and safety limits, without task-by-task
redesign.
To describe both the competence a system has and its capacity to develop further, this chapter
uses four dimensions. Breadth and depth describe present capabilities, following the distinction
between generality and performance (Morris et al., 2024). Plasticity and continuity describe how
competence is acquired and accumulated through experience.
Breadth is the range of physical conditions over which a system acts effectively, including variation
in tasks, objects, scenes, tools, dynamics, and embodiments. Counting task names is a poor proxy
for this range. Many differently named tasks rely on the same grasp and motion, while a small
change in friction can demand quite different control. Breadth should therefore be described by
264


the physical variation over which competence holds. Open X-Embodiment shows that training
across robotic platforms can improve performance by transferring experience between them (Open
X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024), and π0.5 performs household manipulation in homes absent
from its training data (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025). Both results demonstrate breadth under
their evaluation conditions, but neither addresses arbitrary changes in dynamics or morphology.
Sharing parameters across robots makes transfer possible, but whether transfer actually occurs is
an empirical question.
Depth is how well the system performs within that range, including its accuracy, compliance, effi-
ciency, reliability, and coordination over long horizons. In physical tasks these qualities are tightly
linked. A grasp must support transport, transport must leave the object in a state from which it can
be placed, and a small slip can alter the conditions for every later action. Deep competence there-
fore includes detecting disturbances, maintaining the conditions that later actions depend on, and
recovering when those conditions are lost. Hierarchical planning supports long-horizon coordina-
tion by decomposing an objective into subgoals and reusing existing policies for familiar low-level
actions (Sutton et al., 1999; Kaelbling and Lozano-Pérez, 2011). A system with many fragile skills
and one with a few reliable skills are limited in different ways, and describing either requires both
dimensions.
Plasticity is the capacity to acquire or revise competence when existing behavior is inadequate. A
change in payload or friction may force the agent to revise its model, adjust its control, or learn
a different interaction. Plasticity is measured by the experience, time, computation, supervision,
and risk that adaptation requires. Two systems may reach the same success rate after very different
numbers of physical trials, and their plasticity then differs even though their final performance
does not. Plasticity is also distinct from retention. Dohare and colleagues show that standard deep-
learning methods can gradually lose the ability to learn in continual-learning settings (Dohare et al.,
2024). Forgetting concerns what a system can no longer do, whereas loss of plasticity concerns what
it can no longer learn.
This chapter treats plasticity as a property of the whole embodied system, not only of its param-
eter updates. Memory, model-based replanning, and newly generated procedures can all support
adaptation (Hafner et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024b). Replanning with unchanged knowledge may
produce an unfamiliar solution without any new competence being acquired, while new knowl-
edge can be stored in memory or executable procedures without changing network weights. This
chapter therefore judges plasticity by whether new experience leads to effective behavior, whatever
mechanism carries the change.
Learning accumulates only if the results of adaptation outlast the episode and can be recalled when
needed. This chapter calls this accumulation of useful competence across encounters continuity. It
involves keeping skills that remain valid, revising assumptions that no longer hold, and preserving
the ability to keep learning. Elastic Weight Consolidation, for instance, restricts changes to param-
eters that matter for previously learned tasks (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). This can reduce forgetting,
but it leaves open when a physical failure calls for learning, which part of the system should change,
and when a retained skill should be used. These are system-level decisions, and this chapter mea-
sures continuity by the lasting benefit of experience rather than by how long parameters persist.
None of the four dimensions is sufficient alone. Zero-shot success can show breadth without plas-
ticity, and rapid adaptation can occur without continuity. Assessing them jointly is therefore a
longitudinal matter. It asks whether experience lastingly extends the conditions under which the
system acts effectively, without demanding new learning in every successful encounter.
To make this criterion operational, this chapter introduces the capability boundary, the limit of the
conditions under which a system meets a specified performance standard, with computational re-
sources, interaction budgets, human assistance, and safety constraints held fixed. Prior training
and accumulated experience should be reported separately from any resources added during eval-
uation. Success on a task the evaluator has not tried before may reveal competence that was already
present, so novelty to the evaluator is not, on its own, evidence of capability expansion.
265


This chapter distinguishes three outcomes. Direct transfer applies existing competence without
acquiring task-specific knowledge, although it may involve substantial search or planning. Episodic
adaptation resolves the current difficulty but does not retain the useful change. Persistent capability
expansion retains changes that let the system meet the standard under previously unsupported
conditions. Claiming it requires evidence of better performance, or of lower interaction, time, or
assistance costs, under comparable constraints, together with evidence that valid skills and the
ability to keep learning have been preserved. Gains within conditions the system already handled
improve performance or efficiency but do not expand the boundary.
Current Physical AI typically assumes that operating conditions resemble those covered by train-
ing, that a person specifies the task and the robot merely executes it, that the robot acts alone in
a single body, and that people design and run its learning process and fix its physical configu-
ration. Each of these four assumptions confines the capability boundary in a different direction.
In the case of collaboration, the boundary in question is that of joint human-robot action rather
than of the robot alone. Relaxing each assumption defines a pathway toward Physical AGI, a pro-
posed system independent of all four assumptions. The next four subsections take the pathways in
turn, covering systematic generalization (Section 10.2), human-robot collaboration (Section 10.3),
collective Physical AI (Section 10.4), and self-evolution (Section 10.5). The four dimensions and the
distinction among direct transfer, episodic adaptation, and persistent capability expansion serve as
a common yardstick for all four.
10.2
Systematic Generalization in Open-World Settings
The first pathway relaxes the assumption that operating conditions resemble those covered by
training. Here the distinction between transfer and capability expansion shapes how generaliza-
tion tests should be read. Many out-of-distribution evaluations vary objects, positions, or task
combinations within a predefined family while the basic form of the problem stays the same (Koh
et al., 2021). Success shows transfer within the family but says little about what happens when the
sources of change are themselves unknown.
Under open conditions, an agent may first need to work out which factors have changed and
whether the knowledge behind its current policy still applies, and only then decide what to learn. A
drawer that does not open may be latched, jammed, or poorly grasped, and each explanation calls
for a different response. The lack of motion alone does not distinguish these cases, whereas a con-
strained probe can provide additional evidence. Evaluations of open-world generalization should
therefore state the changes introduced, the feedback available, and the adaptation permitted.
The same issue arises when systematic generalization is framed, as it usually is, through combina-
tions of familiar constituents. Lake and Baroni show that meta-learning can support such general-
ization in controlled sequence-learning tasks (Lake and Baroni, 2023). Recombination works when
the constituent operations keep their meaning and effectiveness. In physical tasks the operations
themselves can fail. A change in friction may break a grasp that sits in exactly the right place in the
task sequence, and reordering the sequence does not repair it.
This chapter therefore defines system-level systematic generalization as the capacity to identify
changes, preserve reusable structure, and find effective solutions when the conditions support-
ing existing policies no longer hold. It extends the compositional notion to perception, internal
models, decision processes, and control without replacing it. A local failure may require changing
only part of the system while the rest of its knowledge continues to serve the task. The agent must
decide whether and where revision is needed, acquire or repair the missing competence, and test
the result.
The structure retained for this purpose need not reproduce every observable detail. World mod-
els can predict in an abstract representation space without reconstructing future observations in
full (Garrido et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025), and temporal abstractions support prediction over
extended actions (Sutton et al., 1999). Such a representation must preserve the information needed
to evaluate possible outcomes across tasks and changing conditions. Learned largely from obser-
vation, it can supply reusable physical knowledge before a new task arrives, so that not all useful
266


structure has to be acquired through reward-driven trial and error (Hafner et al., 2019). Abstraction
of this kind is one plausible route to generalization, but it is not part of the definition.
Representations alone do not explain how a system responds when its current solution fails. This
chapter distinguishes five functions in that response, namely competence assessment, change charac-
terization, composition and acquisition, interactive validation, and knowledge consolidation. Together they
lead from recognizing a difficulty to building, physically testing, and retaining a revised solution.
They are roles rather than software modules or a fixed sequence, and they may share representa-
tions and recur as new evidence arrives. Not all five are always needed, since existing competence
may suffice.
Competence Assessment
The agent judges whether continued execution is likely to remain effec-
tive and safe. Unexpected contact forces, mismatches between predicted and observed motion, or
uncertain outcomes can warrant further observation, constrained probing, targeted assistance, or
a safe stop. Prediction error rises, for instance, when a video shows an event that violates learned
physical expectations (Garrido et al., 2025). Such a discrepancy is a reason to reassess but offers
no safety guarantee, and visual familiarity does not show that a policy remains reliable, because
friction can change with no visible sign. An assessment is useful only if it changes behavior early
enough, which can happen before the cause of the difficulty is known.
Change Characterization
Detecting a difficulty does not identify its cause. The agent must de-
termine which assumptions need revision and which knowledge remains usable, since holding on
to invalid assumptions invites repeated failure and discarding valid knowledge makes adaptation
more expensive. The principle of Independent Causal Mechanisms supports selective revision,
because under suitable assumptions a change in one mechanism need not require revising the oth-
ers (Schölkopf et al., 2021). Whether a learned representation has captured the relevant factors is
a separate question. The agent may need informative actions to tell competing explanations apart,
and it can act on a partial causal account as long as the remaining uncertainty constrains what it
does. Learning can then concentrate on the affected parts of the system.
Composition and Acquisition
The agent builds a candidate solution from the knowledge that re-
mains valid and identifies any competence still missing. A world model, drawing on memory and
current perception, can predict the outcomes of candidate action sequences and score them against
a task objective. Searching over these sequences at inference time can yield an unfamiliar solution
without changing the model or learning a new skill (Hafner et al., 2019; Assran et al., 2025). A new
objective may still need a learned readout from the representation, as reward prediction does in la-
tent model-based control (Hafner et al., 2019), and such training counts toward the adaptation cost.
SayCan combines language-model proposals with value functions that estimate whether learned
robotic skills can be executed (Ichter et al., 2023), so its choices are limited to the skills it already
has. When a required interaction is missing or no longer works, the task structure can isolate it as
a local learning problem, and the agent can acquire or revise that interaction without relearning
the whole task. The new competence then becomes available for other combinations, although any
solution built from it still requires physical validation.
Interactive Validation
The agent tests the candidate solution under the physical conditions in
which it must work. Limited probes, which must themselves respect force, motion, and safety
limits, can reveal resistance, contact constraints, or errors in the state estimate. Predicted trajec-
tories can be checked against task goals and safety constraints before execution (Wabersich and
Zeilinger, 2021), but only real feedback shows whether the predictions and constraint estimates
hold. Inner Monologue uses success detection, scene descriptions, and human feedback to revise
robotic plans (Huang et al., 2023b). Feedback may also show that the diagnosis itself was wrong
and send the agent back to assessment or characterization. A successful recovery resolves the im-
mediate difficulty but remains episodic adaptation unless its benefit is consolidated.
267


Knowledge Consolidation
The system retains useful experience in a form that can inform later
decisions, whether in policies, world models, memory, or executable procedures. Verified con-
straints and failed strategies are worth retaining alongside successful actions, together with the
conditions under which each applies, so that retrieval can judge whether a skill fits the current
situation. Consolidation need not take place in model weights. Voyager keeps executable skills
in a retrievable library without fine-tuning its underlying language model (Wang et al., 2024b),
although its Minecraft setting leaves open how the approach would fare on physical robots. In
robotics, RECAP improves π∗
0.6 over successive rounds of data collection and training that use au-
tonomous experience and human corrections (Amin et al., 2026). Neither system constitutes a fully
autonomous lifelong-learning process, and establishing persistent capability expansion for either
would require the longitudinal evidence specified in Section 10.1.
This account extends generalization from unfamiliar samples and task combinations to the whole
perception, cognition, decision, and action system. The four capability dimensions specify which
improvements to assess, and the five functions describe how experience can produce and preserve
them. Because actions can obtain the evidence needed to revise a model or establish a new solution,
the functions also connect systematic generalization to physical inquiry. Collaboration with people,
the second pathway, supplies another source of such evidence, as well as a setting in which the
resulting competence must work.
10.3
Human-AI Collaboration and Social Intelligence
The second pathway relaxes the assumption that a person specifies the task and the robot merely
executes it. When people and robots share a task, both act on the world, and each changes the
conditions under which the other can proceed. One partner’s operation may change access to the
workspace, the state of an object, or the support needed for a later action, so a robot can carry out its
own step correctly and still leave its partner unable to continue. Joint execution therefore requires
coordination between two active participants, and the robot must consider how its actions affect
the person as well as the objects and the environment.
Coactive Design distinguishes individual taskwork from the teamwork needed to manage interde-
pendence (Johnson et al., 2014). Its requirements of observability, predictability, and directability
concern access to relevant information, expectations about the other participant’s actions, and the
ability to influence the interaction. For a robot, this means making its progress and limitations
visible enough for the person to respond as the task unfolds. The participants need the informa-
tion and physical conditions required to act, not identical internal models or continuous verbal
communication.
How an action is performed also matters for coordination. Dragan and colleagues distinguish pre-
dictable motion, which matches what an observer expects given a known goal, from legible motion,
which helps the observer infer the goal (Dragan et al., 2013). Their experiments show that motion
design affects collaboration even when the movements accomplish the robot’s immediate task (Dra-
gan et al., 2015). A trajectory both changes the physical state and informs the partner’s next action,
and a robot should choose how to move with both effects in mind.
At the task level, Chaski selects and schedules robot actions within a shared plan, accounting for
the human’s progress and idle time (Shah et al., 2011). The person need not command each step,
yet the person’s own choices still constrain when the robot can act and which operations can follow.
Scheduling should therefore aim at joint progress rather than at finishing the robot’s own work as
quickly as possible.
In direct physical interaction, the participants’ control behaviors are coupled as well. Li and col-
leagues combine estimation of the human’s control strategy with a differential-game controller (Li
et al., 2019b), treating human behavior as part of the coupled dynamics rather than as a fixed tra-
jectory or an external disturbance. Many collaborations involve no direct contact, however, and do
not need this form of control.
268


Coordination can also change with repeated interaction. Nikolaidis and colleagues model un-
certainty about how willing a person is to adapt and incorporate it into the robot’s decision-
making (Nikolaidis et al., 2016). In cross-training, participants swap roles to improve coordination
within a shared plan (Nikolaidis and Shah, 2013). Both methods help the partners’ actions fit to-
gether during a task, but improvement within one encounter remains episodic unless it is shown
to persist or transfer.
Evaluating these interactions therefore requires attention to how the work is coordinated as well as
whether it is completed. Hoffman’s notion of collaborative fluency describes how well the partici-
pants’ activities mesh and treats it as distinct from task efficiency (Hoffman, 2019). Useful measures
include task outcomes, coordination delays, and the effort needed to keep the interaction working.
The person’s physical work is part of the joint task and should be reported separately from effort
spent compensating for avoidable system shortcomings.
Tests of generality should vary the collaborators as well as tasks and environments, since perform-
ing well with a familiar partner does not demonstrate the same ability with a new one. Evalua-
tions should report prior joint training and the additional coordination needed when the pairing
changes, separate team competence from the robot’s own competence, and identify gains that come
from changes in human behavior. The resulting evidence characterizes the capability boundary of
the team and the cost of forming new coordination, which a count of predefined collaborative rou-
tines cannot capture.
The longer-term goal proposed here is a physical collaborator that takes part in developing a project
instead of merely executing delegated movements. Such a system would help clarify an under-
specified goal, explain what it has learned about the environment, propose feasible alternatives,
and acquire new methods through joint work. In a repair or construction project, the person and
the robot might diagnose a problem together, redesign part of the procedure, and verify the result.
Collaboration in this sense concerns participation in shared reasoning and action and does not re-
quire a human-like appearance. It also makes the preservation of human initiative, understanding,
and authority a design requirement for future Physical AI systems.
Such projects can run for weeks under changing conditions. The system would need to remember
why earlier decisions were made, distinguish temporary workarounds from completed repairs, and
revise its plans when new evidence undermines an earlier assumption. Shared memory would hold
agreements, open questions, and causal context in addition to observations, so that later actions
build on earlier decisions instead of treating each encounter as a new task. Such projects rarely
involve a single robot, and the same need for shared context arises when competence is distributed
across several bodies.
10.4
Multi-Agent Systems and Collective Physical AI
The third pathway relaxes the assumption that the robot acts alone in a single body. Once several
embodied agents are involved, the organization of physical competence becomes a question about
the group. This chapter defines collective Physical AI as Physical AI in which a group achieves phys-
ical objectives through coordinated sensing, action, and interaction. Capability is then assessed at
the level of the group and depends on how individual skills are organized, what information is ex-
changed, and how the bodies interact. Control may be centralized or distributed, and coordination
may partly emerge from local self-organization. The number of robots and the control architecture
do not by themselves indicate generality.
Members need not each possess everything the group can do. Prorok’s mixture-of-robots perspec-
tive argues for specialized, interdependent components instead of the same generalist model in
every robot (Prorok, 2025), which makes the distribution of competence across bodies a design
choice. Shared capabilities let one member substitute for another, while specialized capabilities
allow contributions tied to a particular embodiment or role (Gerkey and Matari´c, 2004). Bettini
and colleagues report benefits from heterogeneous policies and communication in multi-robot re-
inforcement learning on simulated and physical tasks with heterogeneous requirements (Bettini
269


et al., 2023), although their results do not show that diversity by itself improves performance. Spe-
cialization enables complementary action but also makes the group depend on particular members.
Pooling robot experience to train a policy is a different use of multiple bodies. Shared data can im-
prove a policy that each robot later runs on its own, without any coordinated behavior at deploy-
ment. Collective competence instead rests on what members achieve by acting together. Assessing
it means measuring how much the observation, manipulation, or control conditions provided by
their organization contribute to the outcome.
Such organization depends on coordinating information, since a single robot’s observations may
not suffice for the group’s decisions. Tolstaya and colleagues train local controllers by imitating
a centralized controller that has global information during training, and at execution time the
learned controllers rely on local observations and communicate over graphs that change as the
robots move (Tolstaya et al., 2020). CoViS-Net pools visual information across robots for relative
pose estimation and has been evaluated in real-world multi-robot formation control (Blumenkamp
et al., 2025). As robots move, the observations available for later decisions and the coordinated
actions that remain feasible change with them (Olfati-Saber et al., 2007). The system must decide
what to communicate, when local information is sufficient, and how missing or inconsistent in-
formation affects group behavior. Members’ internal representations need to support the task but
need not agree in every detail. Evaluations should distinguish the information available during
training from that available at deployment.
Sensing networks extend this organization beyond the sensors on individual robots. The term
sensing network here denotes connected sensing resources distributed across agents, objects, and
environmental infrastructure, building on research on cooperative observation through distributed
sensing, local processing, and communication (Akyildiz et al., 2002). A sensing node need not be an
autonomous agent. It contributes information about physical conditions that another component
needs to understand or act on. The research opportunity for collective Physical AI is to organize
such networks around the decisions and interventions they support. In an instrumented workshop,
a fixed sensor might detect a change outside a robot’s field of view, a mobile agent might approach
to resolve the uncertainty, and a manipulator might then test or repair the affected mechanism,
which in turn changes what the network needs to observe next. This requires tracking the origin,
timing, and uncertainty of each observation, maintaining local operation when communication or
sensing fails, and keeping access to observations of people and shared spaces subject to explicit
authorization.
Bodies and environmental structure can also coordinate collective behavior without any explicit
exchange of plans. In TERMES, Werfel and colleagues derive locally executable rules whose ex-
ecution by robots with local sensing produces a specified global construction, with coordination
passing through the changes the robots make to their shared environment (Werfel et al., 2014). In
particle robotics, Li and colleagues build loosely coupled particles that cannot move individually
but move collectively through local oscillations modulated by a global signal (Li et al., 2019a). No
single component executes a complete locomotion policy, so describing such a system requires an
account of its contact relationships and spatial organization as well as its controllers.
Understanding collective behavior thus involves both predicting the outcomes of local interactions
and designing interactions that achieve a given objective. Stable behavior under one set of condi-
tions shows only that a particular mechanism works. Generality requires further evidence that the
relationship between local behavior and global outcome can be maintained or adjusted when ob-
jectives, component capabilities, or physical conditions change. Physical coupling belongs in this
analysis as a mechanism whose contribution to task competence needs to be measured.
That relationship also depends on the membership of the group. Stone and colleagues formulate ad
hoc teamwork as collaboration without prior coordination, distinguishing cooperation within an es-
tablished team from cooperation with unfamiliar partners (Stone et al., 2010). In a physical group,
a member that leaves or is impaired may remove an observation, a manipulation capability, or a
source of support on which the task relies, and reassigning task labels cannot restore these condi-
270


tions. Reconfiguration must find a feasible organization of the remaining capabilities or recognize
that none exists.
Scalability, resilience, and generality therefore need separate evidence. Scalability concerns ef-
fective operation as group size changes, resilience concerns preserving or restoring function af-
ter disruption, and generality requires testing unfamiliar combinations of members, capabilities,
and task dependencies. Comparisons should account for hardware, computation, communication,
and preparation costs, because adding resources can raise performance without any improvement
in how they are organized. Collective generality is ultimately judged by the group’s capability
boundary and by the cost of establishing the relationships it requires.
Looking further ahead, collective Physical AI could operate at the scale of a home, a laboratory, or
an infrastructure network, with sensing resources tracking local conditions while heterogeneous
agents investigate, maintain, and repair different parts of the environment. An observation made
by one component could guide an experiment carried out by another, and the resulting knowledge
could inform work elsewhere. Its physical reach would depend on the relationships among models,
bodies, people, and infrastructure, without every component being generally intelligent or every
decision being made centrally. The research challenge is to keep evidence, decisions, and physical
consequences consistent as sensing and action pass between components. A related question is how
the participating systems might help improve the knowledge, skills, and physical organization on
which their collective competence rests.
10.5
Autonomous Evolution
The fourth pathway relaxes the assumption that people design and run the learning process and
fix the system’s physical configuration. In both individual and collective settings, the question is
then how a system can take part in developing its own competence over time. Here, self-evolution
of Physical AI denotes the sustained development of physical understanding, prediction, and action
through experience that the system increasingly helps to select, acquire, and use. Its objectives, au-
thorization, and resource limits remain explicit. The definition includes learning with a fixed body
and with ongoing human support, and it requires neither biological evolution nor unrestricted
self-modification. Progress is measured by lasting changes in physical competence.
Tegmark’s Life 3.0 offers a broader frame for this possibility (Tegmark, 2017). In this conceptual clas-
sification, Life 1.0, exemplified by bacteria, has its physical organization and behavioral programs
shaped largely by biological evolution. Life 2.0, exemplified by humans, retains an evolved body
but acquires much of its behavioral repertoire through learning and culture. Life 3.0 is a prospective
technological form of life that can redesign both its software and its hardware. The classification
concerns how behavior and physical organization can change, not levels of task performance.
Within a physical system, change can occur in perceptual representations, predictions of action
outcomes, knowledge of the body’s capabilities, control policies, or reusable skills, and these com-
ponents may change at different rates. Bongard, Zykov, and Lipson demonstrate a robot that builds
a predictive model of its own body through interactions chosen to discriminate between competing
models, and that uses the model to generate locomotion before and after damage (Bongard et al.,
2006). Cully and colleagues instead use a repertoire generated before deployment to guide trial-
and-error adaptation after damage (Cully et al., 2015). Both studies recover a lost function, which
differs from acquiring a broader repertoire. Gupta and colleagues evolve morphology jointly with
learned control and examine how evolved bodies affect the learnability of new tasks (Gupta et al.,
2021), but only in simulation, so their results do not show that deployed robots can redesign their
own hardware.
From the standpoint of Life 3.0, learning a new policy on fixed hardware addresses only the be-
havioral side. A more ambitious system would use experience to identify a physical limitation,
propose a change to its sensing or actuation, and test whether the revised configuration enables
new competence. Experience with deformable objects might show, for example, that a system can-
not distinguish contact states with its current sensors. Instead of collecting more of the same data,
it could propose an additional sensing modality, design an experiment to measure its value, and
271


adapt its control to the new information. The studies above each supply one ingredient of such a
process, whether learning, self-modeling, or body-controller co-design. Their integration would be
an early technical step toward the co-development of intelligence and its physical substrate, but
none of the studies achieves it, let alone artificial Life 3.0. Within authorized limits, such a process
might begin with selecting tools or replacing modules and later extend to designing and validating
new physical configurations.
A system that helps organize its own learning must also decide which uncertainties, interactions,
and skills are worth investigating. Oudeyer, Kaplan, and Hafner use learning progress to direct ex-
ploration toward situations in which a robot’s predictive competence can improve (Oudeyer et al.,
2007). High prediction error alone is ambiguous, since it may reflect a learnable regularity, noise,
or missing information that the available interactions cannot supply. The value of an exploratory
action lies in the learning it makes possible, and novelty is only one factor in that judgment. Ob-
servation can further reduce how much must be learned through direct intervention. V-JEPA 2
learns first from video by self-supervision and then from robot trajectories with action condition-
ing, a combination that supports physical planning (Assran et al., 2025). A self-directed learner can
likewise use accumulated physical knowledge to select targeted interactions and keep task-specific
trial and error to a minimum.
Every physical attempt changes the environment, and automatic resets are not always available.
Eysenbach and colleagues learn task and reset policies jointly and use estimates of recoverability to
avoid states from which recovery is difficult (Eysenbach et al., 2018). Resets, recovery, and requests
for help belong in the reported cost of learning, and the acquisition of experience must preserve the
conditions under which further learning is possible.
Within these limits, current policies can also collect data for their own later training. RoboCat
uses a trained multi-task robotic agent to gather experience for subsequent training iterations and
evaluates adaptation across tasks and embodiments (Bousmalis et al., 2024). RECAP combines
demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and expert corrections to improve a vision-language-action
policy (Amin et al., 2026). In both systems, tasks, data, or supervision are still supplied externally,
so claims of autonomy should be tied to specific stages of the process. As the system takes on a
larger role in acquiring and using experience, reliable external criteria for judging improvement
need to remain in place.
Whether these learning processes help must be checked against later physical behavior, using the
criteria of Section 10.1. Changes in prediction loss, policies, or memory count only if they im-
prove later task outcomes, reduce the experience needed for further adaptation, or make previ-
ously unsupported conditions achievable, while valid skills and the ability to keep learning are
retained (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Dohare et al., 2024). Tests confined to the most recently practiced
task cannot determine whether development is cumulative. Persistence, transfer, and autonomy
each require separate evidence, since an improvement that persists may be specific to the condi-
tions in which it was learned. Progress need not be monotonic on every task, but gains and re-
gressions should be reported over a stated range and time horizon, together with the costs of data
collection, computation, resetting, correction, and physical recovery.
The same assessments decide which updates to accept. Updates selected with success detectors,
reward models, or predictive models must be checked against the physical objectives those signals
stand in for, including under conditions not used to select them. A verified fallback and the option
to intervene or suspend can limit the damage of an unsuccessful update, but any safety claim
still rests on the assumptions under which the fallback is valid (Wabersich and Zeilinger, 2021).
Long-term development should be judged by retained physical competence and by the system’s
measured role in organizing its own learning, and continued operation or repeated retraining is
not evidence of either.
The horizon extends beyond continual policy improvement. A developing Physical AI system
would take a growing part in deciding what to investigate, which capabilities to acquire, and which
tools or bodily configurations would enable further progress, and each change to its means of
272


interaction would open new opportunities for understanding. This reciprocal development, more
than learning alone, gives the Life 3.0 analogy its concrete content.
10.6
Toward the Ultimate Goal of Physical AGI
The preceding subsections examine how Physical AI might extend its capability boundary. This
subsection considers what such an extension could enable, with Physical AGI as a long-term re-
search goal. Two prospects illustrate why extending this capability boundary could matter. The
first is scientific discovery, where claims about the physical world will ultimately be tested against
empirical evidence. The second is engineering at scales, levels of precision, and speeds beyond
direct human capability, or in environments inaccessible to people. In both domains, the examples
discussed below illustrate progress within problem settings and infrastructures largely defined by
people. The prospect envisioned here is a shift toward more open-ended spaces, where systems can
formulate new problems, revise their approaches, and test solutions through physical interaction.
Progress toward generality would also require transferring these abilities across unfamiliar tasks
and environments, supported by coordinated advances across the four pathways discussed above.
Experimental science provides a concrete setting for acquiring knowledge through action. Its cy-
cle of hypothesis, experiment, and revision links reasoning to empirical validation. Parts of this
cycle are already automated. The Robot Scientist Adam generated and tested hypotheses in yeast
functional genomics (King et al., 2009). A mobile robot chemist searched for photocatalysts us-
ing instruments built for human researchers (Burger et al., 2020). Coscientist demonstrated the
use of large language models to plan and run chemical experiments (Boiko et al., 2023). Kitano
frames the long-term aim as an AI Scientist that conducts research at the level of the best human
scientists (Kitano, 2021). These experimental demonstrations establish components of autonomous
inquiry, while leaving research goals and much of the experimental infrastructure under human
specification.
Physical AGI points toward inquiry in which that space is itself open. Such inquiry offers no stan-
dard answer to imitate, its feedback may take months, and failure is the normal outcome. This
chapter therefore identifies three necessary shifts, from data-driven learning to world interaction,
from immediate feedback to long-horizon reasoning, and from imitating correct results to learning
from failure. This chapter also regards embodied autonomous exploration as a necessary route
to Physical AGI. Attaching a large model to a robot is not enough, because embodied intelligence
requires physical feedback that keeps revising the model. Physical Recursive Self-Improvement
(Physical RSI) offers a framework for investigating how experience from physical interaction can
produce persistent changes to both task capabilities and the procedures that improve them (Zhou
et al., 2026). Its recursive objective is to make subsequent improvement more effective across tasks.
In the vision considered here, this could contribute to Physical AGI by enabling systems to refine
how they design experiments, acquire skills, and develop new tools. An artificial experimentalist
must decide which uncertainty justifies an experiment, design probes that discriminate between
explanations, and retain negative results with the conditions that produced them. When existing
instruments cannot resolve a question, it may need to build and calibrate a new one, so that the
instruments themselves become part of the space of possible designs.
Engineering illustrates how specialized robotics and control can extend human physical reach. A
reinforcement-learning controller has demonstrated control over diverse plasma configurations in
a tokamak (Degrave et al., 2022). Research on untethered microrobots explores the potential for
procedures inside the body (Nelson et al., 2010). The underwater robot Ocean One has extended
an operator’s visual and tactile access through teleoperation in challenging underwater environ-
ments (Khatib et al., 2016). These examples illustrate specialized control, prospective medical ap-
plications, and human-robot collaboration. Extending such capabilities to unfamiliar tasks and
operating conditions remains a challenge.
Physical AGI would open this space in two ways. The first is generality in operation, where a
Physical AGI system running a fusion device or a planetary outpost would recognize when con-
ditions have moved outside the scope of its controllers’ design and adapt, sometimes faster than a
273


human engineering cycle. The second is open-ended design. When no tool or procedure solves a
problem, the system would translate the goal into functional requirements, design and fabricate a
candidate, and verify it under the conditions in which it must work. Such work is collective over
years of operation, and people unable to act on site still set goals, weigh trade-offs, and authorize
interventions. Human intent thus reaches regimes that human bodies cannot.
The two prospects share one arc, from operating within a predefined space to opening it, through
new instruments in science and new tools and mechanisms in engineering. They also reinforce
each other, since new instruments raise new questions and new understanding enables new en-
gineering. Their value depends on reliable results and on actions that remain safe when they are
hard to reverse. This monograph adopts the principle it calls the AI-45◦Law (Yang et al., 2024a).
Over the long term, capability and safety should advance together, with short-term fluctuation
permitted but neither persistently outpacing the other. For systems that operate in laboratories,
power plants, and natural environments, meeting these requirements is an operational necessity
as well as a responsibility of governance. AI may accelerate the expansion of knowledge, but this
monograph holds that the compass of scientific exploration should remain human curiosity and
human values. Physical AGI, as proposed here, would enlarge what people can investigate and
build without displacing their judgment about what is worth pursuing. These capabilities have not
yet been demonstrated. Today’s Physical AI systems lay the foundations, and progress toward the
goal is measured by the physical results they achieve.
274


11
Evaluation, Safety, and Governance for Physical AI
Physical AI turns decisions into changes in the world, making reliable goal pursuit, bounded con-
sequences, effective human control, and accountability essential to its practical value. This chapter
develops an evidence-based framework linking physical-agent evaluation, action and system safety, and life-
cycle governance. These concerns are inseparable because competence and risk emerge from inter-
action among models, software, hardware, embodiment, and the environment. Task completion
alone cannot establish safe or autonomous operation. Evaluation and safeguards must therefore
address the complete agent under specified operating conditions, with requirements proportionate
to its authority and potential physical effects.
Figure 11.1 illustrates this framework around the agent’s perception-decision-action-outcome loop.
Physical-world evaluators (Section 11.1) establish evidence for capability assessment, benchmark-
ing, and application readiness (Section 11.2). These findings inform operating limits and action
alignment (Section 11.3), while system safety and risk governance (Section 11.4) sustain safeguards
through fault containment, monitoring, updates, and maintenance. Law, ethics, standards, and
global governance (Section 11.5) provide overarching responsibilities, ethical boundaries, and over-
sight. Field evidence feeds back into evaluation and governance, supporting reassessment as the
agent and its operating conditions change.

11.1
Physical-World Evaluators
The chapter’s approach begins with evidence about what a physical agent actually does.
A
physical-world evaluator observes goal-directed, autonomous or semi-autonomous interaction,
compares behavior and outcomes with stated requirements, and produces judgments grounded
275


in recorded evidence. Its evaluation unit is the complete agent acting through its embodiment and
responding to environmental feedback. The physical significance of model outputs depends on
their role in this closed-loop interaction. Intended behavior, issued commands, measured execu-
tion, and final physical outcomes may not align.
This section establishes a common framework for the chapter. It first organizes evaluation around
reliability, safety, operational controllability, and traceability, linking these concerns to Sections 11.2
to 11.5. It then explains how evidence from the physical agent and its environment can be col-
lected, interpreted, and combined to support assessment, diagnosis, and improvement. A cup-
transfer task illustrates the connection between general evaluation objectives and concrete physical
evidence.
11.1.1
Evaluation Objectives and the Chapter Framework
The Complete Physical Agent as the Evaluation Unit
Component tests remain useful within
physical-agent evaluation. For example, visual recognition benchmarks such as ImageNet measure
classification and detection performance (Russakovsky et al., 2015). These measurements character-
ize a perceptual capability under specified inputs. They do not establish whether a physical agent
can select a feasible grasp, execute it reliably, detect slipping, and recover without damage. RL-
Bench extends evaluation to interactive manipulation tasks with explicit success conditions (James
et al., 2020). Nevertheless, completion alone can conceal retries, human assistance, excessive con-
tact force, or delayed damage. Achieving a goal and avoiding unwanted consequences are distinct
requirements (Amodei et al., 2016).
The evaluation unit is therefore a complete interaction episode. Perception informs decisions, em-
bodied action changes physical states, and the resulting observations guide subsequent behavior.
The sequence perception-decision-action-outcome describes recurring stages within this feedback loop.
Evaluation should examine whether the physical agent recognizes discrepancies and appropriately
continues, replans, requests assistance, or stops. This perspective applies to modular and end-to-
end architectures without prescribing their internal organization.
Claims about autonomy must also match the responsibilities assigned to the physical agent. A trial
in which an operator selects every grasp examines a different capability from one in which the
agent receives only a goal and selects its own strategy. Evaluation must state which decisions are
autonomous, which information is supplied externally, and when assistance is permitted.
Four Objectives Connecting Evaluation, Safety, and Governance
The chapter develops four
connected concerns introduced here. Each provides a guiding question and a principal connec-
tion to one of the following sections.
• Reliability (Capability Evaluation and Benchmarking (Section 11.2)) Can the physical agent ac-
complish its goals repeatedly, with a declared degree of autonomy, under specified oper-
ating conditions? This question motivates assessment of perception, reasoning, manipu-
lation, mobility, long-horizon execution, and generalization. Section 11.2 develops the ca-
pability tests, benchmarks, and application evaluations needed to establish what the agent
can do and where that competence remains dependable.
• Safety (Physical Safety and Action Alignment (Section 11.3)) Does the physical agent pursue
goals within authorized and physically acceptable limits? Successful completion may coex-
ist with unsafe contact, excessive force, object damage, or harmful environmental changes.
Section 11.3 examines how security, environmental safety, and action alignment constrain
the perception-decision-execution loop so that useful behavior remains consistent with in-
tended and permitted consequences.
• Operational Controllability (System Safety and Risk Governance (Section 11.4)) Can protective
mechanisms and authorized supervision keep the physical agent within operating lim-
its, intervene in time, and establish an appropriate fallback state under faults or chang-
ing conditions? Section 11.4 develops this concern through cross-layer failure analysis,
276


fault containment, runtime protection, and lifecycle risk management. Here, controllabil-
ity concerns effective operational intervention, including automatic protection and human
takeover, rather than only the availability of a stop command.
• Traceability (Law, Ethics, Standards, and Global Governance (Section 11.5)) Can system config-
urations, decisions, actions, interventions, and updates be reconstructed and connected to
responsible actors? Section 11.5 relates this evidence to accountability, meaningful human
control, privacy, fairness, standards, and international coordination. Traceable records sup-
port investigation and responsibility reviews. They do not independently determine legal
liability or acceptable use.
These connections identify the main emphasis of each section, while the concerns remain interde-
pendent. Reliable capability informs operating limits. Action-safety requirements guide system
protection. Traceability connects evidence from all three to oversight and accountability. Human
control, for example, requires both effective intervention mechanisms and legitimate authority.
Section 11.1 supplies the common evidence framework, which Sections 11.2 to 11.5 develop into
capability assessment, safe action, sustained system protection, and accountable deployment.
Conditions and Limits of Evaluation Claims
Every conclusion should identify the tested em-
bodiment, task, degree of autonomy, permitted assistance, and operating conditions, including
lighting, payload, and human proximity. The evaluator’s own limitations, such as camera occlu-
sion or missing force measurements, must also be reported. Detecting a hazard does not itself
establish that the physical agent can respond safely. Communication, intervention authority, and
the physical response must be assessed as well.
11.1.2
Evidence-Based Evaluation of Physical Agents
The four objectives become assessable through a connected process of specifying requirements,
collecting evidence across the interaction, applying appropriate assessment methods, and using
the results for diagnosis and renewed testing. This process connects component measurements to
judgments about the complete physical agent.
Specify the Task and Record the Interaction
In a cup-transfer task, requirements may specify
the correct cup, target region, permitted spillage, completion time, and stability period after re-
lease. Safety limits, termination rules, and permitted human assistance should be fixed before test-
ing. Records should preserve timestamps for observations, task-relevant state estimates, selected
actions, issued commands, measured motion, and interventions. Commands document intended
behavior. Physical measurements establish what actually occurred.
Table 11.1 links the interaction stages to evaluation evidence.
Records should also capture
feedback-driven changes, such as a revised grasp, an additional observation, or a protective stop.
External tracking or independently reviewed video can help check the physical agent’s own es-
timates. Controlled variations should test its response to disturbances. A shifted cup tests state
updating and grasp adjustment, a blocked route tests replanning, and slipping tests detection and
recovery.
Link Evidence Across Components, Embodiment, and Environment
A common timeline and
configuration record should connect the physical agent’s models and decision functions, software,
hardware, and integrated embodiment with its environmental conditions. Decision records reveal
perception, task-relevant memory, and action selection. Software records reveal message delays
and data freshness. Hardware measurements reveal sensing and actuator response. Complete-task
observations reveal coordinated motion, grasping, stopping, and supervisory response. Environ-
mental records identify changes in lighting, friction, object properties, and human activity.
These are complementary diagnostic perspectives, not a prescribed architecture.
The environ-
ment remains the agent’s interaction context, while its embodiment provides the physical means

Apply Complementary Assessment Methods
Rules, sensor analysis, multimodal assessment,
and optional world-model predictions interpret the shared record for different purposes. Models
used by the evaluator are assessment tools and should be distinguished from components of the
physical agent being evaluated.
Executable rules test target-region membership, speed or force limits, and prerequisites such as
grasp confirmation before lifting. RLBench illustrates task-specific, machine-checkable success con-
ditions (James et al., 2020). Physical trials require corresponding measured inputs. Each rule should
specify thresholds, units, temporal scope, and the treatment of missing or uncertain measurements.
Images and depth measurements reveal position and motion, force and tactile signals reveal contact
or slipping, and joint measurements reveal execution. Calibration, coordinate frames, timestamp
alignment, and data loss must be checked before scoring. Estimates derived from the same sensor
should not automatically be treated as independent confirmation.
Instructions and video can support judgments about object selection, action order, and task
progress.
RoboVQA demonstrates video-based reasoning about success, previous events, and
possible future actions (Sermanet et al., 2024). Such judgments require explicit rubrics, support-
ing frames or timestamps, and an “uncertain” option. They should be validated against human-
reviewed cases and should not override calibrated measurements that establish a physical con-
straint violation.
A world model may estimate the consequences of a candidate action as

quality is validated for the relevant conditions. Predicted consequences must remain distinct from
observed events. Alternative rollouts suggest hypotheses rather than independently establishing
causation. World models are optional tools, not a defining requirement of physical agency.

Scoring rules should be fixed before
testing. Binary requirements may receive 0 or 1, while continuous measurements can be normalized
to [0, 1], with higher values consistently indicating better performance. If required evidence is

A confirmed critical violation gives a failed safety assessment even if the task is completed. Missing
or conflicting critical evidence gives a “review required” result unless a violation is already con-
firmed. In either case, withhold the aggregate while retaining individual measurements. Report
completion, safety status, interventions, and evidence quality separately. Across repeated trials,
state the trial count and whether completion times include only successful trials. Autonomous and
assisted completion must remain distinguishable, as illustrated by RoboVQA’s treatment of cog-
nitive and physical interventions (Sermanet et al., 2024). A high score does not establish safety
outside the tested scope.
Diagnose Failures and Verify Improvements
Suppose the physical agent identifies the correct
cup and selects a feasible route, but the cup slips during transport. Force and tactile records locate
the onset of slipping. Video identifies the task stage. Command timestamps and actuator measure-
ments reveal timing and grip response. Environmental observations indicate whether the cup was
wet. The evaluation should also examine whether the agent detected the discrepancy, adjusted its
grip, placed the cup down, requested help, or continued despite evidence of failure.
Diagnosis links the failed requirement and earliest abnormal event to these records, while separat-
ing confirmed events from possible causes. If delay is suspected, a controlled repeat can correct it
while keeping the cup, route, and other conditions as consistent as practical. Persistent slipping
motivates further checks of grip response and surface conditions. A language model may summa-
rize the evidence, but its explanation requires validation. The evaluator itself should be checked
for missed failures, false alarms, disagreement, and incomplete evidence.
After changes to learned components, software, or embodiment, repeat relevant component tests
and complete interaction episodes. Simulation can broaden scenario coverage, while physical tri-
als address contact and execution effects it does not reproduce. This connects evaluation to im-
provement of the complete physical agent and supplies evidence for the capability, safety, system-
protection, and governance questions developed in the following sections.
11.2
Capability Evaluation and Benchmarking
Building on the evidence framework of Section 11.1, capability evaluation asks what a physical
agent can accomplish, how independently it can act, and under which operating conditions its
competence holds. Such competence emerges through coordinated perception, reasoning, manip-
ulation, mobility, memory, and adaptation. Benchmarking makes these claims comparable by spec-
ifying tasks, embodiments, assistance, and resource budgets. Simulation supports scalable capability
diagnosis, while real-robot evaluation provides indispensable evidence of executed behavior and physical con-
sequences. Together, they connect capability profiles to claims about autonomous completion, exe-
cution quality, recovery, and deployment readiness.
This section develops a layered capability framework, compares simulation, real-robot, and hybrid
benchmarks, and connects their evidence to application evaluation and governance. Figure 11.2
relates benchmark coverage to progressively demanding physical test settings, illustrated by au-
tonomous laboratories, industrial production lines, and agricultural work. The discussion explains
how simulation guides diagnosis, why deployment claims require physical trials, and how proto-
279


cols should account for assistance, uncertainty, and operational variation. These capability bound-
aries provide the basis for Section 11.3’s treatment of physically safe and appropriately authorized
action.
11.2.1
Layered Capability Evaluation of Physical Agents
A physical agent must convert observations into feasible decisions and coordinated actions, pre-
serve progress over time, and respond to changing conditions. The following capability layers
organize these observable responsibilities without prescribing a particular internal architecture.
Their integration is the central evaluation problem. An agent must select, combine, and revise its
skills as a task unfolds. Generalization and adaptation apply across the layers, while sustained
closed-loop autonomy requires evidence that their coordination remains reliable during operation.
The Physical Agent as the Evaluation Unit
The evaluation unit determines what a result can es-
tablish. Model-level tests assess a policy under specified observations, actions, and computational
resources. System-level tests assess the coupled sensing, decision-making, control, hardware, and
protective functions of the physical agent. Application-level tests add sustained workflows and
the human effort needed to maintain service. Fixed-platform comparisons help isolate policy dif-
ferences. Cross-embodiment comparisons assess combined model and hardware capabilities. Re-
ports should identify which responsibilities are autonomous and which depend on external soft-
ware or operators. Where accessible, both proposed and executed actions should be recorded to
reveal interventions by protective controllers. Capabilities outside an embodiment’s scope should
be marked as not applicable, with the supported operating conditions stated.
Perception and Active State Understanding
Perception evaluation concerns task-relevant geom-
etry, affordances, and interaction states under partial observability. Recognizing a container, for
example, does not establish whether its handle is obstructed or its grasp is stable. Tests should
examine whether the agent changes viewpoint or performs a permitted diagnostic action when ob-
servations are insufficient. Controlled changes in occlusion, lighting, calibration, and latency can
reveal state-estimation accuracy, responses to uncertainty, and the cost of acquiring useful informa-
tion. Required precision should be determined by the subsequent physical operation.
Reasoning and Physical Consequence Prediction
Reasoning evaluation examines goal interpre-
tation, prerequisite recognition, feasible action sequences, and revision after unexpected outcomes.
Embodied Agent Interface distinguishes goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action se-
quencing, and transition modeling (Li et al., 2024). Agent-level claims require testing these de-
cisions through execution. Paired trials can preserve visual appearance while changing mass, fric-
tion, or physical constraints, revealing whether decisions respond to their consequences. Verbal
explanations alone provide limited evidence of physical understanding. Behavioral tests establish
whether an agent acts appropriately without assuming a particular internal representation.
Manipulation and Adaptive Physical Interaction
Manipulation evaluation spans grasping,
placement, assembly, tool use, compliant contact, and deformable-object handling.
A capable
agent should adjust its interaction strategy as physical properties become observable. Tests can
vary mass, friction, stiffness, geometry, tolerance, and pose while measuring placement accuracy,
contact forces, damage, and output conformance. Unfamiliar tools and altered contact conditions
further test whether strategies transfer beyond practiced object-action combinations.
Mobility and Embodied Coordination
Mobility evaluation covers navigation, obstacle avoid-
ance, transport, balance, and whole-body coordination under changes in payload, floor conditions,
and clearance. Successful navigation must deliver a usable configuration for the next operation.
Reaching a room while remaining beyond grasping range leaves the workflow incomplete. Tests
should therefore assess route choice and final base pose together with subsequent interaction, in-
cluding revisions when access or stability changes.

Fig. 11.2 A proposed layered framework connects benchmark coverage with real-robot evaluation
settings. Each benchmark is shown once at its highest represented layer, indicating partial and
overlapping coverage rather than a universal difficulty ranking. Illustrative laboratory, industrial,
and agricultural settings show where actions, feedback, and physical consequences must be mea-
sured. Claims of sustained deployment require closed-loop evidence from the intended working
environments
Long-Horizon Goal Pursuit and Memory
Long-horizon evaluation examines subgoal formation,
progress verification, memory, and transitions between operations. CALVIN evaluates supplied
chains of language-conditioned manipulation tasks (Mees et al., 2022). Autonomous decomposi-
tion of a high-level objective imposes additional responsibilities. Tests with interruptions, delayed
observations, or revised goals can assess whether the agent preserves valid achievements, updates
its task state, and avoids unnecessary repetition. Complete-workflow success and dependence on
assistance remain essential measures. Multiplying isolated skill success rates does not generally
predict mission reliability, because sensing errors, state changes, and recovery decisions couple
successive operations.
Generalization and Learning Through Interaction
Generality must be evaluated under declared
shifts in objects, sites, physical properties, task compositions, and embodiments. LIBERO studies
transfer and retention during sequential learning (Liu et al., 2023a). Frozen-policy transfer, bud-
geted adaptation, and task-specific training should be reported as distinct evaluation conditions.
Learning through interaction additionally requires measuring how efficiently experience improves
later decisions and whether prior competence is retained. Data, compute, interaction, and memory
budgets make these improvements interpretable. Held-out task compositions test whether familiar
capabilities can be reorganized without demonstrations of the complete workflow.
Capability Integration and Diagnostic Tests
Table 11.2 connects capability claims to controlled
tests and observable evidence. Isolated trials help locate weaknesses. Integrated missions test co-
ordination under dependencies and uncertainty. A failed retrieval, for example, may originate in
281


perception, planning, navigation, contact control, or their interaction. Diagnosis requires interven-
tions that distinguish these explanations.
Controlled substitutions and matched interventions can support diagnosis, provided any privi-
leged information or external assistance is declared. Systematic variation in visibility, precision,
contact complexity, task dependencies, and disturbance magnitude helps establish an operating
envelope. The resulting profile should distinguish limitations in individual skills from failures of
coordination, rather than infer general physical competence from an aggregate success score.
11.2.2
Benchmarking Physical Agents: Current Paradigms and Future Directions
Benchmarks operationalize capability claims through specified tasks, embodiments, environments,
and scoring procedures. Existing suites provide complementary evidence, from controlled skill
diagnosis to physical execution and multi-stage workflows. Comparing their scope clarifies both
what current scores establish and what remains to be tested for agents that pursue unfamiliar goals,
adapt through interaction, and operate over extended periods.
Simulation Benchmarks: Controlled Diagnosis and Coverage
Tables 11.3 and 11.4 compare rep-
resentative benchmarks by task scope, setting, metrics, and training conditions. CALVIN evalu-
ates supplied skill chains, while LIBERO studies transfer and retention during sequential learn-
ing (Mees et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023a). SIMPLER examines correspondence between aligned sim-
ulated evaluation and real-world policy performance in validated settings (Li et al., 2025b). These
protocols support controlled diagnosis, but their task definitions and observation interfaces deter-
mine which agent responsibilities are exercised.
Recent simulation suites broaden this coverage. LIBERO-Plus introduces seven perturbation fam-
ilies to expose vulnerabilities hidden by nominal success (Fei et al., 2026). RoboCasa365 expands
household mobile-manipulation tasks and supports multiple learning protocols (Nasiriany et al.,
2026). The 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge evaluates 100 household workflows using goal-predicate
completion and efficiency measures under onboard-observation restrictions (BEHAVIOR Team,
2026). Comparisons should distinguish the full task catalog, the evaluated task panel, and the
available training resources, since these quantities describe different aspects of coverage.
RoboLab is a robot- and policy-agnostic simulation platform built on Isaac Lab. Its RoboLab-120
suite comprises 120 tasks organized around visual, relational, and procedural competencies (Yang
et al., 2026b). Its analysis extends binary success with graded completion, execution errors, tra-
jectory quality, and sensitivity to environmental variation. The reported evaluation emphasizes
policies trained on real-world data without task-specific simulation co-training. These results char-

EBench diagnoses generalist manipulation policies through 26 tasks covering mobile pick-and-
