Iocchi et al., 2015). Their results remain conditional on the selected physical tasks and protocols.
RoboDojo combines simulation and physical evaluation in one infrastructure, with 42 simulated
tasks and 18 physical tasks across three real robot embodiments (Chen et al., 2026a). Its simulation
dimensions cover generalization, memory, precision, long-horizon execution, and open-vocabulary
instruction following. Success and partial-progress scores expose different failure patterns, while
Open tasks exclude task-specific simulation demonstrations. The simulated and physical suites
provide complementary coverage rather than one-to-one matched task pairs. A shared interface
therefore improves evaluation access and consistency without, by itself, measuring direct sim-to-
real transfer.
Why Real-Robot Evaluation Is Indispensable
Simulation permits controlled variation, inexpen-
sive repetition, and targeted diagnosis. Even high-fidelity simulation evaluates a computational
representation whose contact parameters, sensing model, actuator response, and timing require
physical validation. SIMPLER demonstrates useful simulation-real correspondence within vali-
dated settings (Li et al., 2025b). Such correspondence supports screening within that regime rather
than unrestricted extrapolation. EBench similarly reserves deployment claims for subsequent phys-
284


ical evaluation (Gao et al., 2026). The value of simulation lies in exposing hypotheses and weak-
nesses that can then be examined on the deployed system.
Real-robot evaluation is indispensable because it observes the coupled physical system whose deployment
performance is being claimed. A simulated placement may succeed while a physical cup slips be-
cause surface properties, grip response, or command timing differ from the model. Physical trials
can measure contact forces, object damage, sensing errors, stopping behavior, and recovery effort,
including consequences that persist after the last commanded motion. They also reveal the opera-
tional costs of resets, interventions, wear, and downtime. This evidence records what the hardware
executed and what happened in the world.
Physical evidence remains bounded by the tested conditions and exposure. A laboratory demon-
stration does not establish unrestricted field autonomy, and incident-free trials do not establish uni-
versal safety. A credible evaluation strategy combines simulation screening, standardized physical
trials, and external or distributed sites, with uncertainty and coverage reported explicitly. Relative
rankings, complete-task success, and partial-progress scores answer different questions and should
be interpreted within their respective protocols.
Capability Coverage and Progressively Demanding Physical Settings
Figure 11.2 organizes
evaluation from perception and feasible decisions to coordinated manipulation, mobility, long-
horizon execution, and sustained autonomy. This ordering is a guide to increasing integration and
responsibility, not a universal difficulty scale. A precision assembly task may be harder than a par-
ticular long-horizon mission. The physical settings on the right show how each responsibility can
be tested through observable actions and consequences.
Each benchmark is displayed once at the highest layer probed by its represented task scope, with
RoboDojo identified as a hybrid suite. Placement indicates evidence for dimensions within a layer,
not comprehensive coverage or mastery by evaluated agents. Suites shown at higher layers may
also test underlying skills, while generalization cuts across the framework. The open gap at the
top concerns sustained field autonomy, which episode-level success and robustness tests cannot
establish on their own.
Physical settings make these responsibilities observable through controlled changes and integrated
work. Cluttered observation tests sensitivity to occlusion, lighting, and calibration. Changed pre-
requisites test feasibility and replanning. Contact-rich tasks vary fit, friction, payload, and compli-
ance, while shared-space work varies routes, access, and human activity. Interrupted workflows
probe memory, resumption, and recovery. Sustained operation across jobs, sites, and days adds
evidence about adaptation, wear, service quality, and human effort. The application illustrations
show possible working environments rather than results from a particular benchmark.
Simulation can test reasoning, memory, generalization, and long-horizon behavior within its mod-
eled domain. Physical trials establish whether those capabilities remain effective under the cou-
pled sensing, contact, timing, and operational conditions of deployment. Resuming a simulated
sequence, for example, does not establish recovery after a fixture moves, a sensor drifts, or an oper-
ator changes the job. Sustained autonomy, useful adaptation, and dependable recovery require closed-loop
validation on real robots in the working environments covered by the claim. Simplified scenes provide ini-
tial measurements. Integrated and longitudinal trials examine whether these measurements sup-
port dependable service.
A Real-Robot Evaluation Workflow
The following workflow synthesizes standardized, auto-
mated, and distributed evaluation approaches (Zhou et al., 2025; Atreya et al., 2025; Ma et al.,
2026b). It is a proposed procedure for this section, rather than the official protocol of every listed
benchmark.
1. Declare the protocol. Fix goals, quality requirements, operating conditions, model and
system versions, training exposure, trial budgets, permitted retries, assistance, and termi-
nation rules. Specify whether the claim concerns frozen-policy transfer, adaptation, or a
complete product system.
285


2. Calibrate and prepare. Check sensors, coordinate frames, timestamps, control interfaces,
end effectors, payloads, and protective functions. Prepare reproducible initial states and
record unavoidable variation. Keep calibration and operator preparation distinct from au-
tonomous task execution.
3. Execute and record. Run repeated closed-loop trials under the stated protection and su-
pervision. Log observations, proposed and executed actions where accessible, physical
outcomes, stops, failures, retries, and all interventions. Preserve unsuccessful episodes
and verify the state after each reset.
4. Adjudicate and measure.
Validate success detectors against independently reviewed
physical evidence. Report autonomous completion, execution quality, forces or damage
where relevant, intervention burden, recovery, and resource use. Automated scoring and
reset errors require their own assessment (Zhou et al., 2025).
5. Replicate and report. Randomize or counterbalance policy order and repeat across days,
task variations, embodiments, or sites as required by the claim. Report uncertainty, expo-
sure, exclusions, and per-condition results. Use discrepancies and field failures to refine
scenarios, models, and subsequent physical tests.
Challenges of Authentic Physical Evaluation
Authentic physical evaluation faces variation that
a nominal reset cannot eliminate. Object placement, friction, lighting, battery state, temperature,
calibration, and wear may change during a campaign. Reset success must therefore be verified,
and comparisons should control or record these changes. Distributed evaluation increases envi-
ronmental coverage, but site and operator differences require stratified reporting (Atreya et al.,
2025). Shared hardware and remote access improve comparability without removing dependence
on the tested task distribution.
Protective functions and human intervention also affect what trials reveal. A stop may prevent
harm while leaving the outcome of the unmodified policy unknown. Reports should distinguish
proposed actions, applied safeguards, observed outcomes, autonomous recovery, appropriate han-
dover, and assisted completion. Cost and safety exposure constrain sample size, especially for
long-horizon and contact-rich tasks. These constraints motivate targeted scenario selection, val-
idated measurements, transparent trial budgets, and uncertainty estimates. They do not make
simulation a substitute for deployment evidence.
Limitations of Current Physical Agent Benchmarks
The first limitation is incomplete assign-
ment of autonomous responsibility. Supplied instruction chains, fixed catalogs, prepared initial
states, and external resets may leave goal decomposition, preparation, and sustained recovery out-
side the test. RoboDojo adds memory and open-task evaluation, while BEHAVIOR extends house-
hold workflows, but no listed result alone establishes broad, continuing autonomy. Reports must
identify which responsibilities the agent actually performs.
The second limitation is restricted evidence about generalization and physical understanding. High
success in familiar settings may depend on narrow scene or instruction distributions. LIBERO-Plus
exposes fragility under controlled perturbations (Fei et al., 2026). Visual variation, altered physical
properties, novel task compositions, and new embodiments test distinct forms of transfer. Evalua-
tion should separate these factors, examine their interactions, and establish whether observations
and instructions influence behavior when they change the required action.
The third limitation is incomplete comparability and consequence measurement. Training expo-
sure, sensor access, retry budgets, evaluators, and hardware can alter scores independently of pol-
icy competence. Repetition improves precision within tested conditions but does not automatically
broaden coverage. Success and progress measures also leave execution quality, efficiency, safety, re-
covery burden, and uncertainty only partly characterized. Episodic trials with fresh resets provide
limited evidence about accumulated failures, retained memory, and adaptation during prolonged
operation.
286


A Framework for Future Physical Agent Benchmarks
Future benchmarks should link capability
claims to a declared coverage matrix spanning goals, physical conditions, embodiments, and conse-
quences. Three complementary test levels are needed: diagnostic skill trials, integrated missions in
intended working environments, and longitudinal sequences of changing tasks. High-level goals,
partial observations, interruptions, and recoverable failures should be introduced under specified
initial conditions, assistance rules, and acceptance criteria. Coverage can then be assessed against
the intended application domain.
Stable anchor tasks support comparisons over time, while sequestered missions and controlled
interventions test generalization and adaptation. Holdouts should cover the sites, object fami-
lies, physical properties, and task compositions relevant to the claim. Frozen-policy, budgeted-
adaptation, and continual-learning tracks need distinct rules for exposure and memory retention.
Matched interventions can probe consequence-sensitive decisions and active information acquisi-
tion. Adaptive challenge selection requires reproducible rules and comparable resource budgets.
Evidence should connect simulation, genuinely matched physical trials, and independent sites,
identifying where correspondence holds and where rankings change. Hybrid suites with differ-
ent simulated and physical tasks provide complementary coverage rather than matched transfer
measurements. Consequential weaknesses found in simulation should guide physical tests, which
should be repeated after changes to sensing, contact, timing, or protection. Reports should combine
autonomous task completion with efficiency, quality, robustness, safety, recovery, and adaptation
cost. Success detectors and resets need independent validation, and partial progress remains diag-
nostic when mandatory conditions fail. Eq. (11.5) specifies the protocol fields needed to document
these comparisons.
Maintained benchmarks also require declared roles, exposure records, controlled feedback, adju-
dication procedures, uncertainty estimates, and reviewable trial evidence. Changes to tasks, hard-
ware, or scoring should be versioned and connected through anchor comparisons. Operational
failures should inform revision. These proposed requirements extend a benchmark from a static
score to a maintained account of what an agent can do, how efficiently it adapts, and where its
reliability has been established.
11.2.3
Application Evaluation and Governance for Physical Agents
Application evaluation turns capability evidence into a decision about a defined product role. Eval-
uation governance makes that evidence traceable and comparable across scenarios, embodiments,
and tasks. The connection depends on explicit responsibilities, measurable physical outcomes, and
clearly bounded deployment claims.
Application Evaluation in Product Scenarios
Product evaluation begins with the intended work-
flow, users, operating environment, and accepted output. It specifies autonomous responsibilities,
permitted human involvement, quality tolerances, resource budgets, and conditions for stopping or
handing over control. Acceptance concerns the integrated model-software-hardware-embodiment-
environment system. A successful motion matters only if it delivers the required physical result
under those conditions. Simulation can guide stress-case selection and development, while accep-
tance requires trials on the physical configuration and operating conditions covered by the claim.
Success, quality, efficiency, and reliability should be assessed together. For Neval > 0 protocol-valid

Industrial evaluation emphasizes assembly quality, cycle time, and tolerance variation. NIST task
boards provide reproducible test artifacts (Kimble et al., 2020). Household evaluation combines
navigation, manipulation, and interaction under unfamiliar layouts and changing requests, draw-
ing on RoboCup@Home (Iocchi et al., 2015). Autonomous laboratories additionally require pro-
cedure ordering, sample identity, precision, contamination control, and traceability. Agricultural
work adds changing crop geometry, access, and handling requirements. Across these domains,
integrated trials should test whether the agent diagnoses disruptions, preserves valid progress,
revises its workflow, and seeks appropriate assistance while meeting product requirements.
Unified Evaluation Governance Across Diverse Settings
A common evidence framework can
support scenario-specific evaluation modules. Shared definitions establish task terminology, metric
meanings, protocol fields, assistance rules, and evidence requirements. Each module specifies its
goals, difficulty, operating distribution, and acceptance thresholds. NIST’s test-method program
illustrates the separation of repeatable capability measurements from mission-specific performance
requirements.9 This principle supports comparability while preserving the physical requirements
of different applications.

Results should be stratified by goal type, difficulty, physical conditions, and embodiment before
matched groups are compared. Per-group performance, uncertainty, and coverage should precede
aggregation. Equal-task averages characterize breadth, whereas deployment-weighted averages
characterize a specified use distribution. Both require a common task panel and declared weights.
Denominators, exclusions, and adaptation budgets should be published, with consequential low-
frequency conditions retained. Cross-platform policy transfer and independently optimized prod-
uct systems also require distinct comparison tracks.
Governance assigns stewards to maintain protocols, operators to prepare trials, evaluators to ad-
judicate outcomes, and reviewers to examine disputes. Combined roles and conflicts should be
disclosed. Automated judgments and resets need validation against independently checked trials.
Randomization or counterbalancing, declared stopping rules, and treatment of clustering across
sites and days make comparisons interpretable. Incident reports should state severity and expo-
sure. For Neval > 0 independent Bernoulli trials with a common incident probability, zero observed

Evidence records should link configurations, observations, actions, interventions, and judgments,
with appropriate access controls for private information. Permitted learning experience must re-
main separate from hidden scoring feedback. Material changes to software, hardware, tasks, or
scoring require versioning and targeted re-evaluation, while shared anchor tasks connect succes-
sive assessments. This structure supports both a comparable capability profile and an application-
specific acceptance decision, keeping each claim tied to observed physical behavior under declared
conditions.
11.3
Physical Safety and Action Alignment
The capability evidence developed in Section 11.2 must be complemented by constraints on how
goals are pursued. In Physical AI, an erroneous decision can become motion, contact, or an envi-
ronmental change before correction is possible. Safety therefore depends on the evolving relation
among human intent, the agent’s decisions, physical feasibility, and permitted consequences. This
includes both preventing hazards created by the agent and ensuring that actions intended to re-
duce existing environmental hazards do not introduce new ones. Detecting danger, possessing the
means to intervene, and having authority to act are separate requirements.
This section first explains the transition from content safety to physical action safety, examining sep-
aration, contact force, energy, object integrity, persistent environmental effects, and hazardous task
interpretations. It then develops multi-layer action alignment from task reasoning through plan-
ning, real-time control, and actuator safeguards. Shared action contracts connect intended effects,
preconditions, operating bounds, and termination conditions across these layers. The discussion
shows why successful task completion can coexist with unsafe or unauthorized behavior, and why
warning, clarification, assistance, or safe termination may be appropriate outcomes. These action-
level requirements provide the basis for the integrated-system and lifecycle assurance developed
in Section 11.4.
11.3.1
Physical Agent Security
The security of a physical agent concerns its ability to maintain the integrity of perception, decision-
making, and action under malicious interference. As defined in Chapter 8, a physical agent is a
goal-directed system that integrates sensing, computation, physical embodiment, execution, and
feedback. Its security cannot therefore be reduced to the robustness of an individual foundation
model. An adversary may influence the agent through its observations, instructions, learned com-
ponents, communication interfaces, or control commands. Unlike attacks on purely digital appli-
289


cations, successful interference with a physical agent may propagate into unauthorized motion,
inappropriate contact, or other physical consequences. Security must consequently be considered
across the complete perception-decision-execution loop.
Threat Models and Attack Surfaces
Security threats should first be distinguished from ordinary
uncertainty and physical failure. For example, a sensor may produce an incorrect measurement
because of noise or occlusion, whereas an adversary may deliberately manipulate the observed
scene to induce a particular decision. Similarly, a policy may fail on an unfamiliar object without
being attacked, while a compromised model may exhibit malicious behavior when a specific trig-
ger appears. The distinction matters because defenses against distribution shift do not necessarily
protect against an adaptive adversary. A useful threat model should specify the attacker’s objec-
tives, accessible interfaces, permitted modifications, and intended effects on the agent. Relevant
security properties include the integrity of observations and commands, authenticity of instruc-
tions, availability of essential functions, and preservation of authorized decision-making. Safe-
ClawArena evaluates system-level security in persistent software agents, including failures arising
from interactions among their components (Niu et al., 2026b).
Adversarial Perception Attacks
Perception provides an important attack surface because physi-
cal agents depend on observations that may originate outside their trusted computational bound-
ary. Adversarial perturbations can influence learned perception without requiring access to the
model’s parameters. Eykholt et al. (2018) demonstrate that physical modifications to traffic signs
can induce incorrect visual classifications under varying viewpoints and environmental conditions.
Such results illustrate how deliberately constructed physical inputs may alter downstream deci-
sions. For a physical agent, the consequences depend on the role of the compromised perception
output. An incorrectly identified object may affect grasp selection, while a manipulated environ-
mental feature may influence navigation or task planning. Possible defenses include multimodal
consistency checks, temporal verification, detection of abnormal observations, and conservative re-
sponses when critical state estimates are unreliable. Their effectiveness must be established against
specified attack conditions rather than assumed from improved nominal perception accuracy.
Prompt Injection and Instruction Manipulation
Physical agents increasingly use language mod-
els to interpret commands, decompose tasks, and select actions. This creates a security boundary
between authorized instructions and information obtained from less trusted sources. Text detected
in the environment, retrieved documents, external messages, or tool responses may contain in-
structions intended to redirect the agent. RoboPAIR (Robey et al., 2024) and BadRobot (Zhang
et al., 2025b) investigate adversarial attacks against robotic systems controlled by large language
models (LLMs), demonstrating that manipulated instructions can induce harmful physical-action
decisions under the evaluated conditions. These findings motivate explicit separation between
task authority and contextual information. An agent may use external content to understand its
surroundings, but such content should not independently authorize new objectives, override op-
erational restrictions, or disable protective mechanisms. Memory adds a temporal dimension to
safety risks in LLM agents, as information accumulated during benign interactions can contribute
to violations on later, unrelated tasks through temporal memory contamination, even without ad-
versarial input (Al-Tawaha et al., 2026).
Model Backdoors and Supply-Chain Attacks
Security risks also arise before deployment. Phys-
ical agents may incorporate pretrained models, third-party skill libraries, training datasets, and
remotely maintained software components. An attacker with influence over these resources may
introduce hidden behaviors that are difficult to identify through ordinary testing. BadNets (Gu
et al., 2017) demonstrates how malicious training procedures can insert trigger-dependent behav-
ior into learned models while preserving apparently normal performance. This attack mechanism
provides a threat model for learning-enabled components in physical agents. Practical safeguards
include verifying model and data provenance, restricting component permissions, validating soft-
ware updates, and testing for suspicious behavior under controlled trigger conditions. These mea-
sures should extend to the interfaces connecting learned models with executable robot skills.
290


Security vulnerabilities may also occur outside the learned models. Sensor spoofing, unauthorized
remote commands, communication interference, and compromised middleware can modify the in-
formation or control signals exchanged among agent components. A perception model may func-
tion correctly while receiving falsified measurements, and a planner may generate valid commands
that are subsequently altered before reaching the controller. Protecting the foundation model alone
is therefore insufficient. Authentication, integrity checks, access control, interface isolation, and
monitoring of command consistency provide complementary safeguards.
The key challenge is that attacks can propagate across layers. A manipulated observation may
change a high-level objective, which leads to a plausible plan and is then faithfully executed by an
otherwise functioning controller. Security evaluation should therefore examine complete attack-
to-action pathways, including whether the agent detects suspicious inputs, preserves authorized
objectives, rejects unauthorized commands, and prevents compromised decisions from producing
unacceptable actions. Independent physical constraints provide an additional boundary when up-
stream components fail, but they do not replace protection against unauthorized control. Physical
agent security is ultimately concerned with maintaining trustworthy agency. The agent should act
according to authorized objectives despite malicious attempts to alter its perception, decisions, or
execution.
11.3.2
Layered Environmental Safety and Action Alignment
Physical agents can contribute to environmental safety by perceiving hazardous conditions, select-
ing appropriate responses, and executing interventions that reduce physical risk. This role extends
beyond ensuring that the agent itself is not attacked or compromised. The surrounding environ-
ment may contain unstable objects, moving machinery, excessive temperatures, leakage, obstructed
pathways, or unsafe interactions among people and equipment. Such hazards can arise indepen-
dently of the agent’s behavior. Environmental safety therefore concerns whether the agent can rec-
ognize relevant physical conditions and influence their evolution without introducing additional
risks.
A physical agent’s contribution to environmental safety depends on the coordination of several
capabilities. Perception provides evidence about the current state. Foundation models and task
reasoning connect observations with safety objectives. Planning identifies feasible interventions.
Control and actuation realize those interventions under physical constraints. Feedback determines
whether the intended safety improvement has occurred. These functions may be implemented
through separate modules or integrated learned policies, but their responsibilities remain distin-
guishable. The relevant alignment problem is to maintain consistency among human intent, agent
decisions, physical feasibility, and environmental safety requirements throughout execution.
Environmental Perception and Hazard Identification
Environmental protection begins with
identifying physical states that may lead to unacceptable consequences. Relevant observations
include geometry, object stability, contact relationships, human proximity, equipment motion, tem-
perature, pressure, vibration, and other process-specific variables. A single visual observation may
reveal an obstruction but provide insufficient evidence about its mass or stability. Likewise, an
abnormal equipment image may not establish whether a mechanical failure is developing. Multi-
modal sensing and temporal state estimation can provide complementary evidence, while uncer-
tainty estimates help determine whether additional observations are required.
AnomalyGPT (Gu et al., 2024) illustrates how vision-language models can support industrial
anomaly detection and localization. Such methods provide a possible perceptual foundation for en-
vironmental safety agents, particularly when hazardous conditions have recognizable visual mani-
festations. However, anomaly recognition is not equivalent to hazard assessment. The system must
relate the detected condition to physical consequences, operating requirements, and the potential
development of the environment. A physical agent should therefore distinguish observed abnor-
malities from evidence-supported risks and unresolved conditions that require further inspection.
291


Foundation-Model Reasoning and Safety Objectives
After identifying a potential hazard, the
agent must determine what response is appropriate. This requires connecting physical observa-
tions with task objectives, human intentions, operating permissions, and safety priorities. A house-
hold agent may detect a spill near electrical equipment, while an industrial agent may observe that
a person has entered a machinery workspace. In both cases, the desired response depends on
context rather than object recognition alone. Possible responses include warning nearby people,
restricting access, delaying the current task, requesting assistance, or initiating an authorized phys-
ical intervention.
Foundation models can assist by interpreting safety-related observations and decomposing high-
level objectives into executable steps. SayCan (Ichter et al., 2023) illustrates a mechanism for com-
bining language-based action selection with estimates of robotic skill feasibility. For environmental
protection, a related approach can associate safety-oriented skills with explicit preconditions, per-
mitted interactions, and expected outcomes. An agent may identify that an obstruction should be
removed while determining that its available manipulation skills are insufficient to move the object
safely. In such cases, requesting assistance can be more appropriate than executing a semantically
plausible but physically unsupported action.
Human intent and environmental safety requirements must also remain aligned. An instruction to
transport an object does not authorize passing dangerously close to a person, exceeding contact-
force limits, or disturbing hazardous equipment. Conversely, detecting a hazard does not automat-
ically grant the agent permission to perform unrestricted intervention. A practical implementation
can distinguish the requested objective, the agent’s authorized actions, and mandatory environ-
mental constraints. These elements define the permissible scope within which autonomous deci-
sions can be made.
Safety-Constrained Planning
Planning converts safety objectives into physically realizable ac-
tions. Candidate interventions should be evaluated for reachability, collision, stability, contact
conditions, workspace restrictions, and possible effects on surrounding objects or people. Vox-
Poser (Huang et al., 2023a) illustrates how language-level constraints can be grounded in three-
dimensional spatial representations to support manipulation planning. Such representations pro-
vide one possible mechanism for translating environmental safety requirements into motion-
related objectives, although their use does not independently guarantee safe execution. Safe re-
inforcement learning complements planning by incorporating safety requirements into policy op-
timization. Constrained Policy Optimization optimizes expected return under bounds on expected
discounted cumulative costs (Achiam et al., 2017), with a multi-agent extension for multi-robot
control (Gu et al., 2023).
Environmental protection requires considering both intervention and non-intervention. Moving
an unstable container may reduce one hazard while increasing the probability of spillage. Sim-
ilarly, an agent approaching malfunctioning machinery may expose itself or others to additional
risk. A safety-aware planner should therefore compare alternative responses according to their ex-
pected consequences and uncertainty. Observation, warning, isolation, or human assistance may
be preferable to direct manipulation when the available evidence is insufficient.

Control and Physical Execution
Even an admissible plan may become unsafe when environmen-
tal conditions change during execution. A person may enter the workspace, an object may slip, or
the contact dynamics may differ from those assumed during planning. Low-level control must
therefore monitor the actual physical state and adjust commands when motion, force, or proxim-
ity approaches a safety boundary. Control barrier functions provide one established mechanism
for enforcing such constraints. Ames et al. (2017) formulate safety-critical control through barrier
functions and quadratic programming, allowing nominal commands to be modified when nec-
essary to preserve a specified safe set. Their guarantees depend on the assumptions concerning
system dynamics, state information, and available control authority.
The actuator and hardware layer supplies further physical protection through joint limits, torque
limits, compliant mechanisms, braking systems, and protective stops. These mechanisms bound
the physical consequences of commands that pass through higher-level decision-making. They
also determine which environmental hazards the agent can address. A robot may recognize a high-
temperature or heavy object without possessing the mechanical protection, payload capacity, or
sensing required for safe manipulation. The ability to identify a hazard should therefore not be
confused with the capability to remove it.
Cross-Layer Action Alignment
Environmental safety requires these layers to operate under con-
sistent conditions. One possible mechanism is an action contract specifying the intended inter-
vention, required preconditions, authorized contacts, physical limits, termination criteria, and ev-
idence needed to verify the outcome. Foundation-model reasoning identifies the safety objective,
planning establishes a feasible intervention, control constrains its execution, and feedback deter-
mines whether the relevant hazard has been reduced.
This organization also clarifies why task completion alone does not establish safe behavior. An
agent may remove an obstruction while damaging nearby equipment or exposing a person to an-
other hazard. Conversely, an agent that declines direct intervention because the available evidence
is insufficient may be acting appropriately. The objective is not unrestricted autonomous inter-
vention, but the reliable realization of authorized safety objectives under physical and operational
constraints.
11.3.3
Predictive Safety and Degradation
Conventional safety mechanisms often respond after a hazardous condition has been detected, for
example when a collision occurs, a contact-force threshold is exceeded, or an emergency stop is
activated. Such mechanisms remain necessary, but their effectiveness may be limited when phys-
ical consequences develop faster than corrective action can be applied. A more capable physical
agent should anticipate risks before execution, monitor whether its assumptions remain valid, and
modify its behavior while safer alternatives are still available. This progression applies both to pre-
venting unsafe agent behavior and to protecting the surrounding environment from developing
hazards.
Risk Prediction
Predictive safety begins with estimating how the physical state may evolve un-
der candidate actions or existing environmental conditions. Geometric checks, dynamic models,
contact prediction, and learned representations can assess collision, instability, excessive force, or
inadequate stopping distance. The prediction horizon should reflect the relevant physical process
rather than only the next control step. A grasp may remain stable during initial lifting but become
unsafe during subsequent acceleration, while a navigation trajectory may become hazardous as
nearby agents move. Evaluating these possibilities before execution allows the physical agent to
compare actions according to their expected consequences.
For environmental protection, prediction also considers how a hazard may develop without inter-
vention. An inspection agent may observe increasing equipment temperature or vibration, while
a mobile agent may estimate whether moving objects are approaching a dangerous configuration.
The agent can then compare continued observation, warning, physical intervention, and human
escalation. Prediction should include uncertainty because physical environments are partially ob-
293


servable and their dynamics are not always known. When uncertainty can be reduced through
additional sensing, the agent may change its viewpoint or acquire another measurement. When
further observation is insufficient or delay is dangerous, conservative constraints or restricted op-
eration may be more appropriate.
Self-Checking and Execution Verification
Prediction alone cannot establish safety because the
predictor may itself be incorrect or compromised. A physical agent should therefore verify crit-
ical conditions before, during, and after execution. Before acting, it checks task preconditions,
relevant permissions, and the current physical state. During execution, it compares observed mo-
tion, contact, and environmental changes with expected behavior. After execution, it determines
whether the intended outcome occurred and whether unintended effects remain. Inner Mono-
logue (Huang et al., 2023b) demonstrates how environmental and task feedback can inform the
revision of language-based robotic plans. This provides one possible route toward closed-loop
decision revision, although safety-critical conclusions still require reliable physical evidence.
Self-checking should use evidence that is sufficiently independent of the mechanism generating
the action. A policy that proposes a trajectory and then evaluates its own safety using the same
potentially incorrect representation provides limited protection against shared errors. Indepen-
dent geometric checks, force or tactile measurements, redundant state estimates, and separately
implemented monitors can expose discrepancies. For security-sensitive agents, these mechanisms
can also help detect inconsistencies between authorized instructions, received observations, and
executed commands.
A practical runtime process can therefore follow a predict-execute-verify cycle. The agent evalu-
ates a candidate action, executes it while monitoring relevant constraints, and verifies the resulting
state before proceeding. For environmental protection, the corresponding process extends to an
observe-predict-intervene-verify sequence that identifies a potential hazard, estimates its develop-
ment, selects a justified intervention, and confirms that the hazard has been reduced. If observa-
tions differ substantially from prediction, the agent should revise its plan rather than continue an
obsolete action sequence.
Safe Degradation and Fallback Control
When a physical agent cannot maintain its nominal op-
erating conditions, it should reduce its capabilities in a controlled manner instead of continuing
unrestricted operation. Possible degraded modes include reducing speed, restricting workspace
access, disabling contact-intensive skills, increasing human supervision, or transferring control to
a simpler policy. SOTER (Desai et al., 2019) illustrates a runtime-assurance architecture combining
an advanced controller with a safety-oriented fallback controller, with switching governed by spec-
ified conditions. Such mechanisms provide a possible implementation of controlled degradation,
but their guarantees remain conditional on the validity of the safety specifications and controller
assumptions.
Degradation must also apply to agents performing environmental safety functions. An inspection
agent with unreliable localization may continue collecting local measurements while suspending
autonomous navigation near hazardous equipment. An agent that detects a dangerous condition
but cannot determine a safe manipulation strategy may issue a warning or request assistance in-
stead of intervening directly. Likewise, when the integrity of critical observations or commands
cannot be established, the agent should restrict actions that depend on the affected components.
The available operating modes should reflect the information and control capabilities that remain
trustworthy.
Importantly, entering a degraded mode must not create a new physical hazard. Immediate stop-
ping may be inappropriate when a manipulator is carrying a heavy load or a mobile system is
maintaining dynamic stability. The agent may first need to secure the object, reduce stored energy,
or reach a stable configuration. Similarly, an intervention intended to protect the environment
should not be abandoned in a state that increases the original risk. Returning to normal operation
should require evidence that the conditions responsible for degradation have been resolved.
294


Experience from near misses, rejected actions, unexpected environmental changes, and unsuccess-
ful interventions can provide evidence about declining safety margins. These observations may
reveal weaknesses that are difficult to identify through ordinary task-success measurements. They
can inform improvements to risk prediction, sensing, action constraints, and regression testing. The
objective is not to assume that a physical agent can prevent every failure, but to recognize emerg-
ing hazards before they produce unacceptable consequences, preserve appropriate control under
uncertainty, and reduce autonomous capability when safe continuation cannot be established.
11.4
System Safety and Risk Governance
Action alignment for a highly intelligent physical agent depends on an integrated physical system
whose sensing, computation, communication, control, actuation, and power remain adequate for
the task. Even correct AI-model decisions can be undermined by delayed commands, unreliable
observations, degraded actuators, or interacting failures across these layers, compromising the con-
straints developed in Section 11.3. Conversely, an incorrect model output need not cause physical
harm if independent safeguards can constrain or prevent unsafe execution. Safety assurance must
therefore examine how the complete agent detects faults, contains their propagation, and preserves
an appropriate physical state. It must also account for changes in hardware condition, software,
task permissions, and operating environments, because evidence from initial testing may no longer
describe the deployed agent.
As illustrated in Figure 11.3, system safety and risk governance follow the three connected stages of
cross-layer risk analysis, risk-driven assessment, and lifecycle safeguards. Cross-layer failure anal-
ysis first investigates how local faults propagate into hazardous physical outcomes and how inde-
pendent safeguards can interrupt this process. These failure pathways then motivate system-level
safety assessment, which examines observable degradation, evaluation indicators, and protective
responses across the hardware and software layers of a physical agent. Beyond these immediate
risks, lifecycle risk governance connects hazard analysis and pre-release verification with deploy-
ment, maintenance, and operational reassessment. Continuous safety assurance is integrated into
this lifecycle perspective through runtime monitoring, protective intervention, user-facing fault
communication, field feedback, controlled software updates, and physical remediation. As phys-
ical agents move toward increasingly autonomous operation in homes, factories, and public en-
vironments, these mechanisms shift safety evaluation from a one-time test result toward a con-
tinuously maintained body of evidence throughout the product life cycle. They also establish the
technical records and responsibilities needed for the broader legal, ethical, and institutional gover-
nance discussed in Section 11.5.
11.4.1
Cross-Layer Failures and Cascading Risks
Perception and Timing Cascades
A local fault becomes a physical hazard when it propagates
through the perception-planning-control-actuation chain. A mobile robot moving from a dim room
into strong illumination, for example, may receive temporarily saturated camera frames while au-
tomatic exposure adjusts. Industrial-camera documentation confirms that exposure changes may
take effect only after subsequent frames have been acquired (Basler AG, n.d.). Benchmarks of vi-
sual depth estimation further document sensitivity to lighting, sensor, and data-processing corrup-
tions (Kong et al., 2023). If these observations are treated as reliable, obstacle detection may fail and
a seemingly coherent navigation decision may increase collision risk. A different cascade begins
in real-time scheduling. As a hypothetical example, a controller nominally updated every 10 ms
may experience a delay of 100 ms because of thread contention or blocking. Meanwhile, momen-
tum, gravity, and contact continue to change the robot state. Research on control timing explains
why execution delays must be analyzed with closed-loop dynamics rather than average processing
speed alone (Cervin et al., 2003).
Shared Infrastructure and Physical Actuation
Processor overheating may activate thermal
throttling, protecting a chip while reducing the computation available for time-critical deci-
sions (NVIDIA Corporation, n.d.).

worked control systems (Baglietto et al., 2020). Undervoltage or power interruption may simul-
taneously disable multiple subsystems, making the robot’s power-loss behavior a distinct safety-
verification concern. At the joint level, an unsafe position target is not identical to a motor current.
A controller translates tracking error into drive demand, which a motor driver regulates under the
actual mechanical load. If a joint is obstructed, persistent error may sustain high demand. With-
out suitable protection, overheating, transmission damage, or loss of support may follow. Existing
drivers demonstrate current regulation, overcurrent protection, and thermal shutdown (Texas In-
struments, 2019), while surveys of robotic fault-tolerant control document the broader need to de-
tect and accommodate actuator faults (Milecki and Nowak, 2023). These functions must be verified
for the specific actuator rather than assumed universally.
Containment Under Degraded Conditions
The appropriate response depends on the remaining
physical capabilities. Command-age checks, watchdogs, current and torque limits, thermal protec-
tions, and independent safety supervision can interrupt some cascades, but a generic emergency
shutdown may create another hazard. Abrupt removal of joint power can destabilize a balanc-
ing humanoid or cause a load-bearing manipulator to drop its payload. Safe intervention may
instead require controlled deceleration, support retention, a designed braking mechanism, or an
energy-independent mechanical fallback. The appropriate stopping function and residual hazards
must be specified for the application, rather than inferred from the existence of an emergency-stop
device (International Organization for Standardization, 2015; Bi et al., 2021). Loss-of-power behav-
ior must be tested before deployment. Fault analysis should therefore record the initiating event,
propagation path, physical consequence, and intended protective barrier. System-theoretic acci-
dent analysis complements component-oriented methods by identifying hazardous interactions
that need not begin with a defective part (Leveson, 2004). The resulting failure pathways provide
296


the basis for the risk-driven safety assessment that follows. Each path must be associated with an
observable precursor, a protective requirement, and a physically meaningful verification outcome.
11.4.2
Risk-Driven System Safety Assessment
From Failure Pathways to Safety Evidence
Task-success rates, perception accuracy, and track-
ing errors quantify useful capabilities but do not establish what happens after corrupted observa-
tions, missed deadlines, or degraded actuators. A defensible safety claim concerns the complete
physical agent, its authorized tasks, the exposure of people and equipment, and the conditions un-
der which protective functions remain effective. It should distinguish an action proposed by the
model, the command actually admitted and applied, and the resulting physical state. Surveys of
safety-critical robotics and safeguarding of autonomous systems identify the need to state assump-
tions, adopt suitable safety mechanisms, and examine evidence across heterogeneous application
domains (Guiochet et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2022). Research on testing standards for integrated
robots likewise identifies limitations of component-centered performance tests when systems com-
bine multiple functional modules (Bi et al., 2020). Assessment should consequently be derived from
the fault pathways described above, with explicit acceptance criteria for both component degrada-
tion and end-to-end physical outcomes.
Observable Indicators Across System Layers
Perception cascades motivate tests of image sat-
uration, dropped measurements, timestamp consistency, estimator residuals, and behavior when
observations are unreliable. Robust-perception benchmarks explicitly test lighting, sensor, and
processing corruptions, although they do not by themselves establish the safety of the complete
robot (Kong et al., 2023).
Fault-tolerant robotics research also addresses failures in sensor in-
formation and state estimation (Milecki and Nowak, 2023). Timing cascades require tail latency,
deadline-miss rate, control jitter, and command freshness. Real-time control research relates tim-
ing to closed-loop performance, while ROS 2 guidance identifies blocking, memory allocation, and
priority inversion as sources of execution-time nondeterminism (Cervin et al., 2003; Kay, 2016).
Processor and supply degradation motivate thermal, clock-frequency, voltage, and interruption
tests. Hardware thermal-management documentation establishes why computation may degrade
under overheating (NVIDIA Corporation, n.d.). Communication assessment should measure la-
tency, loss, and timeout behavior, drawing on networked-control fault-detection research (Bagli-
etto et al., 2020). Actuator assessment must examine current, temperature, joint and torque lim-
its, stall detection, and the resulting physical response. Existing driver protections and robotic
fault-tolerance studies provide corresponding engineering foundations (Texas Instruments, 2019;
Milecki and Nowak, 2023). Table 11.5 synthesizes these candidate measurements and associated
protective responses. Their thresholds and applicability should follow the robot’s risk assessment.
Even published safety-related test guidance for personal care robots does not treat every test as
universal (International Organization for Standardization, 2020; Müller et al., 2022).
End-to-End Protection Verification
Measurements become safety evidence only when they are
tied to the physical response of the integrated system. Fault injection should introduce exposure
faults, delayed commands, packet loss, thermal or computational degradation, actuator restric-
tions, and loss of power under representative tasks. Systematic reviews of robotic testing, valida-
tion, and verification, together with research on integrated-robot testing, provide a foundation for
selecting complementary test methods and reporting their coverage (Araujo et al., 2023; Bi et al.,
2020). Evaluation should measure detection and intervention latency, the ability to isolate a failing
component, and whether the robot can enter a state whose residual risk is acceptable. Work on
interpretable runtime monitoring demonstrates how predicted unsafe states can trigger corrective
replanning, while safety-critical control research develops explicit constraints on admissible system
behavior (Di Franco and Bezzo, 2020; Ames et al., 2017). Safety-related control design supplies fur-
ther principles for protective functions whose effectiveness must be validated independently of the
nominal policy (International Organization for Standardization, 2023b; Bi et al., 2021). The goal is a
traceable relationship between an identified hazard, a tested safety requirement, and the observed
outcome, not a context-free aggregate safety score.

11.4.3
From Pre-Deployment Verification to Post-Deployment Safeguards
Safety-by-Design Before Delivery
Risk governance starts before a product is placed into use.
Developers should identify foreseeable operating environments, human proximity, loads, task per-
missions, misuse, and failure combinations, then translate them into safety requirements and in-
dependent protection functions. Recent robotics safety reviews emphasize risk assessment across
both design and deployment (Adesiji et al., 2026). Simulation, hardware-in-the-loop testing, cross-
module fault injection, environmental stress testing, and controlled physical trials should verify
both nominal performance and behavior under degraded conditions, using complementary tech-
niques whose limitations have been surveyed in the robotic testing literature (Araujo et al., 2023).
The corresponding evidence must record hardware and software versions, model or policy con-
figuration, operating limits, residual risk, and what was not tested. ISO 12100 and ISO 13849-1
provide established foundations for machinery risk assessment and safety-related control design.
ISO 13482 and ISO 10218-1 illustrate additional requirements for particular robot applications, not
universal certification rules for every physical agent (International Organization for Standardiza-
tion, 2010; 2023b; 2014; 2025).
Release as an Evidence-Based Transition
Acceptance testing should validate not only whether a
robot can complete its assigned tasks but whether its safety monitors, limits, fallback controllers,
brakes, and any emergency energy provisions work together when a fault occurs. The need to
test the integrated configuration and select risk-dependent test methods is reflected in integrated-
robot testing research and application-specific ISO guidance (Bi et al., 2020; International Organi-
zation for Standardization, 2020). A release record should link the tested product configuration to
its operating envelope, protective functions, acceptance criteria, and outstanding hazards. Wear,
new payloads, changed environments, repaired components, and updated policies may invalidate
the assumptions documented in the release record. Post-deployment safeguards must therefore
maintain and revise the evidence created before delivery rather than replace it with an unrelated
monitoring process (Guiochet et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2022).
298


Runtime Detection and Protective Action
After delivery to the user or operator, the robot should
monitor whether observations remain trustworthy, commands are fresh, and control deadlines are
met. It should also monitor whether actuator, computing, communication, and power subsystems
retain adequate capacity. Where justified by the hazard analysis, an independent safety supervisor
should restrict commands or transfer control when the nominal policy is unavailable or wrong.
Runtime monitoring and corrective replanning have been demonstrated for autonomous robotic
operation, while control-barrier methods illustrate how physical safety constraints can be imposed
on control inputs when their modeling assumptions hold (Di Franco and Bezzo, 2020; Ames et al.,
2017). Predictive checking and measured feedback should support graduated responses, including
limiting speed or workspace, disabling contact-rich actions, reducing payload, requesting confir-
mation, or moving into a validated protective mode. In an emergency, local protection must act
within the required response time rather than wait for a user decision. The chosen safe state must
respect the actual mechanics. A dynamically balancing robot or one supporting a heavy load may
need controlled motion or braking before torque is removed. Protection must also recognize when
insufficient power or sensing makes autonomous recovery impossible.
User-Facing Warnings and Operational Responsibility
A deployed safety system must commu-
nicate consequential faults, not merely store engineering logs. Research on human-robot collabora-
tion identifies operator awareness and effective visual, acoustic, and other notification channels as
important interface design concerns (Grushko et al., 2021; Bi et al., 2021). Operators or household
users should receive an intelligible account of the affected capability, the protective action already
taken, and the appropriate next step. For example, the account should explain that a joint has
overheated, forceful manipulation has been disabled, and servicing is required before that func-
tion resumes. Notifications should distinguish informational maintenance advice from an urgent
restriction on continued use, without exposing users to raw diagnostics they cannot interpret. In
higher-risk settings, a warning may need to be paired with physical isolation, a lockout, or esca-
lation to an authorized operator. Such interaction supports accountable operation but must not
substitute for automatic, timely safety intervention.
Validated Updates and Physical Remediation
Some defects can be corrected by over-the-air
(OTA) software or firmware updates, but changing perception, scheduling, control logic, or model
capabilities may invalidate safety assumptions. Future update processes should verify provenance
and integrity, assess hardware-software compatibility, test affected safety functions, stage deploy-
ment, and provide recovery or rollback where feasible. The software-update-management princi-
ples of UN Regulation No. 156 offer an automotive precedent, not a law automatically applicable to
robots (United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, 2021). Other defects require inspection
or replacement. Motors, gearboxes, brakes, sensors, batteries, and power electronics can wear or
fail in ways software cannot correct. When a common defect affects a product batch, the manufac-
turer may need to identify affected configurations, contact users, restrict risky operation, provide
repairs, or initiate a recall. Automotive recall practice offers a relevant governance analog.10 OTA
maintenance is not a substitute for on-device protection during an unfolding hazard.
Continuous Improvement Across the Product Life Cycle
Incident and near-miss reports, safety-
filter interventions, maintenance histories, and configuration records should connect field observa-
tions to the original hazard analysis and qualification tests. Comparing evidence across deployed
robots may reveal emerging combinations of temperature, wear, environmental conditions, and
task behavior that were not covered before release. Data collection should remain proportional to
the safety purpose, particularly in private environments. Updated risks must result in reviewed
corrective decisions, re-validation of affected configurations, and, where necessary, revised operat-
ing permissions or withdrawal from service. Linking risk analysis to subsequent tests is consistent
with existing safety-assessment and robotic verification research (Adesiji et al., 2026; Araujo et al.,
2023). The objective is not to guarantee the absence of all faults, but to maintain a credible and revis-
10NHTSA, Check for Recalls: Vehicle, Car Seat, Tire, Equipment.
299


able basis for safe operation as physical agents and the environments in which they work continue
to evolve.
11.5
Law, Ethics, Standards, and Global Governance
The preceding sections have examined how to evaluate the behavior and competence of physical
agents, constrain their actions, and maintain safety evidence throughout operation. These tech-
nical foundations inform deployment decisions, but they do not by themselves determine who is
responsible, which uses of autonomy are acceptable, or what oversight is required. Because Physi-
cal AI connects perception and decision-making to actions in the physical world, governance must
address the deployed system rather than the model in isolation. Law, ethics, standards, and inter-
national coordination connect technical evidence to obligations and acceptable uses, extending the
chapter’s focus from measurable behavior and safety assurance to accountable deployment.
This section first addresses responsibility allocation and traceability, then examines human control,
privacy, fairness, and ethical boundaries. It next considers legal and regulatory frameworks from
technical, ethical, and application perspectives, connecting these issues to safety standards and
the book’s illustrative risk-tiered governance framework. Finally, it explores global cooperation
through compatible evaluation evidence, incident records, and investigation procedures.
11.5.1
Responsibility Allocation and Traceability
Learning-based systems may behave in ways that designers and operators cannot fully anticipate,
creating difficulties associated with the responsibility gap (Matthias, 2004). Responsibility conse-
quently extends beyond the person exercising immediate control. Model developers should doc-
ument capabilities, limitations, and versions. Hardware manufacturers should address mechan-
ical and electrical hazards. Integrators should validate interfaces and operating limits. Opera-
tors should maintain safeguards and intervention procedures. Maintenance providers must track
safety-relevant updates and configuration changes. These engineering duties support accountabil-
ity but do not themselves determine legal liability.
This allocation depends on what each party supplies or changes. For example, replacing a model,
increasing permitted speed, or changing an end-effector can alter different parts of a safety argu-
ment. Documentation should identify who approved the change, which assumptions were recon-
sidered, and what evidence supports continued operation.
Product-liability law provides a complementary perspective. Directive (EU) 2024/2853 includes
software and addresses safety-relevant updates and upgrades. Its rules apply to products placed
on the market or put into service after December 9, 2026 (European Parliament and Council of the
European Union, 2024b). The significance for Physical AI is that assessment cannot stop at initial
delivery. Subsequent changes may alter the behavior of the deployed system.
Accountability also depends on reconstructing what occurred.
A safety-relevant event record
should connect system and model identity with perception states, decisions, executed actions,
safety settings, and human interventions, together with update, maintenance, and cybersecurity
histories. Recording should serve investigation and safety improvement rather than unrestricted
surveillance. Data minimization, access controls, encryption, and proportionate retention are there-
fore part of traceability design, not exceptions to it.
11.5.2
Human Control, Privacy, Fairness, and Ethical Boundaries
Meaningful human control requires more than the presence of a supervisor. A person must under-
stand relevant capabilities and limitations, receive usable information, possess intervention author-
ity, and have sufficient time to act. An override that cannot bring the system into a safe state within
the available response time offers little practical control. Human oversight and accountability are
also central to the UNESCO and OECD AI ethics frameworks (UNESCO, 2021; Organisation for
Economic Co-operation and Development, 2019).
300


The appropriate form of oversight depends on the task. A supervisor may authorize a sequence in
advance, monitor execution, or intervene when an exception occurs. These roles require different
information and response times. Where physical dynamics are faster than human reaction, protec-
tive functions must constrain the system without waiting for an operator to diagnose the problem.
Physical sensing extends privacy concerns beyond direct users. A domestic robot may observe vis-
itors or neighbors who have neither purchased nor authorized it. Privacy by Embodiment, used here
as a design principle, connects privacy protection to sensing and actuation. Under this principle,
systems should process data locally where feasible, minimize raw-data retention, protect sensitive
information, and communicate active sensing and remote access. User authorization does not by
itself resolve bystander exposure.
Fairness likewise concerns physical outcomes, not only balanced prediction accuracy. Differences
in mobility, body characteristics, or speech may change whether users can interact safely or ob-
tain timely assistance. Evaluation should therefore examine accessibility and failure consequences
across intended users, particularly children, older people, and people requiring care. Greater au-
tonomy does not remove the need for human judgment where actions threaten safety, dignity,
or essential services. Physical AI may also displace workers, while newly created jobs may not
benefit those affected. Fair deployment should therefore consider worker participation, retraining
opportunities, and the equitable distribution of productivity gains (UNESCO, 2021; Organisation
for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2019).
11.5.3
Legal and Regulatory Frameworks for Physical AI
Technique
Technical regulation connects responsibility allocation, change management, and
traceability to legal accountability. The EU AI Act’s high-risk framework addresses risk manage-
ment, technical documentation, event logging, and cybersecurity, subject to its scope and applica-
tion dates (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024a; 2026). Directive (EU)
2024/2853 complements this framework by covering software and addressing safety-relevant up-
dates in product liability (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024b). As
discussed in Section 11.5.1, model replacements or changes in speed and tooling should prompt
reassessment, with records identifying who approved each change and what evidence supports
continued operation. Event records should connect deployed versions, actions, interventions, and
maintenance histories. These engineering duties support accountability but do not themselves es-
tablish legal liability.
Ethics
Meaningful human control, Privacy by Embodiment, and fairness require safeguards for
people affected by deployment. The EU AI Act’s high-risk framework addresses effective over-
sight, while practical intervention must remain feasible within the available response time (Euro-
pean Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024a; 2026). The GDPR addresses lawful
processing, data minimization, and protection by design. China’s Personal Information Protection
Law addresses sensitive information and fairness in automated decision-making (European Par-
liament and Council of the European Union, 2016; Standing Committee of the National People’s
Congress, 2021). Article 5 of the AI Act prohibits specified manipulative practices and exploita-
tion of vulnerabilities where its statutory conditions are met (European Parliament and Council of
the European Union, 2024a; 2026). Legal compliance does not exhaust the ethical responsibilities
identified in Section 11.5.2, including equitable access to safe assistance and support for workers af-
fected by automation (UNESCO, 2021; Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development,
2019).
Application
Application-level regulation depends on intended use, system boundaries, and ju-
risdiction. Industrial robot installations fall under applicable machinery rules, while qualifying
medical robots are subject to medical-device regulation (European Parliament and Council of the
European Union, 2006; 2023; 2017). The EU AI Act separately classifies high-risk systems through
Article 6 and Annex III, subject to their statutory conditions (European Parliament and Council
of the European Union, 2024a; 2026). Table 11.6 presents the book’s illustrative five-tier frame-
301


work, considering harm severity, human exposure, tooling, autonomy, safeguard reliability, and
user vulnerability (International Organization for Standardization, 2010; Tabassi, 2023). These tiers
are neither legal categories nor an international standard and do not map directly onto the AI Act.
Classification must record operating assumptions and be reassessed when conditions change. A

11.5.4
Global Cooperation and Governance
Models, components, integrators, and operators may span jurisdictions, while responsibility for an
incident must remain traceable across their interfaces. Building on the obligations and safeguards
discussed in Section 11.5.3, international cooperation should seek compatible safety evidence and
investigation procedures rather than identical legal systems. The practical objective is to preserve
the responsibility chain described in Section 11.5.1 when development, integration, deployment,
and maintenance take place in different countries.
The UNESCO and OECD frameworks provide shared ethical principles, while the Council of Eu-
rope AI Framework Convention connects AI governance with human rights, democracy, and the
rule of law (UNESCO, 2021; Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2019;
Council of Europe, 2024). The 2023 Bletchley and 2024 Seoul declarations emphasize safety co-
operation alongside broader development goals (Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit, 2023;
Participants Attending the Leaders’ Session of the AI Seoul Summit, 2024). China’s 2024 Shanghai
Declaration and 2025 Global AI Governance Action Plan likewise advocate safe, inclusive develop-
ment and international cooperation (World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI
Governance, 2024; World Artificial Intelligence Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI
Governance, 2025). These declarations and policy initiatives are not binding international safety
302


regulations. Their value for Physical AI lies in supporting cooperation on the shared concerns of
human control, privacy, fairness, and accountability identified in Section 11.5.2.
Practical cooperation would include common incident categories, interoperable event records, re-
liable model and system identification, compatible evaluation methods, cross-border safety noti-
fications, and coordinated corrective updates. Evaluation evidence should preserve the operating
assumptions, system configuration, and safeguards under which it was obtained, so that inves-
tigators can determine whether it remains relevant in another deployment. Shared investigation
procedures should make it possible to connect a reported event with the organizations responsible
for the affected model, hardware, integration, and subsequent modifications. These mechanisms
would support investigation and improvement across borders without presuming agreement on
every regulatory choice or automatic recognition of another jurisdiction’s approval.
Interoperability does not require publishing every operational record.
Shared formats can de-
scribe the system, event, and applicable safeguards while access to personal data, security-sensitive
information, and other protected evidence remains controlled.
Consistent with Sections 11.5.1
and 11.5.2, cooperation should preserve both investigative usefulness and proportionate informa-
tion protection. The practical test of global governance is whether an incident can be investigated
across organizational and national boundaries without losing the chain of responsibility or expos-
ing sensitive information unnecessarily.
303


12
Strategy and Civilizational Outlook
The preceding chapters have examined the concepts, technical foundations, models, and systems
of Physical AI. This final chapter considers how these advances might develop into capabilities
that shape the longer-term course of human civilization. The central question is how intelligence
grounded in physical interaction can expand humanity’s ability to discover, produce, build, and
sustain the systems on which it depends.
The chapter first identifies development priorities for the coming decade and beyond, including the
convergence of digital and physical foundation models, self-evolving agents, hardware-software
co-evolution, an Internet of Physical Agents, and the scientific and technological ecosystem sup-
porting their development. It then examines how local achievements can become shared physi-
cal services, allowing verified capabilities to accumulate across teams, locations, and generations.
From this foundation, the discussion extends to planetary energy and infrastructure associated
with a Type I civilization, and to the autonomous construction, resource use, and long-duration
operation that proposed stellar-scale development requires.
These possibilities depend on progress in both intelligence and its physical foundations. Energy,
materials, equipment, and maintenance remain essential constraints. The civilizational significance
of Physical AI therefore rests on its ability to turn knowledge into reliable action, preserve useful
capabilities over time, and support further discovery under increasingly demanding conditions.
12.1
Development Strategies for Physical AI
The development of Physical AI requires advances in models, learning systems, hardware, and the
infrastructure through which capabilities are shared. Over the next five to ten years and beyond,
these advances should support a common objective of systems that can undertake increasingly var-
ied physical tasks, learn from their operation, and transfer useful capabilities with less additional
engineering. Figure 12.1 summarizes five priorities that follow from this objective, including the
convergence of digital and physical foundation models, self-evolving agents, hardware-software
co-evolution, an Internet of Physical Agents, and a scientific and technological ecosystem that al-
lows progress to accumulate.

12.1.1
Converging Digital and Physical Foundation Models
Digital foundation models and physical foundation models should develop through increasingly
close integration. Digital foundation models learn broadly reusable representations and capabili-
ties from language, code, images, and other digitally represented information. Physical foundation
models seek reusable capabilities grounded in physical states, dynamics, interventions, and inter-
action.
The strategic opportunity lies in connecting the breadth of digital knowledge and reasoning with
the grounding required for physical action. A system working in the real world must interpret
objectives, draw on prior knowledge, recognize physical constraints, anticipate the consequences
of its actions, and revise its decisions after observation. Digital and physical capabilities need to in-
form one another throughout this process. Physical evidence can correct an assumption made dur-
ing reasoning, while semantic knowledge can help identify which variables to measure or which
intervention to attempt.
The integration of large multimodal models and world models is one important example. Multi-
modal models can connect observations to concepts and task descriptions, while world models can
predict how a physical state may change under an intervention. Other combinations include code-
generating models coupled with executable control interfaces, reasoning models linked to scientific
simulators, and general-purpose planners working with embodied action models. These examples
suggest a broader research direction involving foundation-model systems that connect knowledge,
prediction, and action across digital and physical domains.
Integration can proceed through explicit interfaces before requiring a unified architecture. Mod-
els can exchange task objectives, state estimates, candidate actions, predicted outcomes, and un-
certainty. Shared representations and joint training may subsequently reduce inconsistencies and
improve transfer. Analytical models, numerical solvers, and simulators should remain available
where they provide useful structure or more reliable estimates. The choice between a single model
and a coordinated set of models should depend on performance, adaptability, latency, and cost.
The longer-term goal is a foundation-model system that participates actively in acquiring knowl-
edge. It should recognize when available evidence is insufficient, select a useful observation or
intervention, and incorporate the result into subsequent decisions. Progress should be assessed
through the quality of those decisions, the physical trials required to reach them, and the ability to
reuse knowledge under new conditions.
12.1.2
Self-Evolving Agents for Open-Ended Tasks
Physical AI should support agents that extend their capabilities through experience. Here, self-
evolution refers to a controlled process of identifying capability gaps, acquiring evidence, and im-
proving memory, skills, models, or policies. Objectives and operating constraints remain explicit,
and changes to deployed behavior require evaluation.
This approach treats the environment as data. The operating environment is a continuing source of
learning opportunities, rather than merely a destination for a pretrained model. An agent’s actions
influence which observations become available. A failed grasp may reveal an incorrect estimate of
friction. An unexpected measurement may expose a missing variable. A successful recovery may
suggest a reusable procedure. Such experience becomes useful training evidence only when it is
recorded with sufficient context, checked for quality, and interpreted with appropriate attention to
uncertainty and alternative explanations.
The resulting cycle (Figure 12.2) is learning-action-discovery-relearning. Existing knowledge guides
action. Action exposes the agent to physical outcomes. Discrepancies and new observations reveal
gaps or regularities. Subsequent learning revises the relevant capability. Discovery in this cycle
may be modest, such as a changed equipment response, a previously unrecognized task constraint,
or a more effective action sequence. The value of the cycle depends on whether these findings
improve later performance.
305


Adaptation during execution should be distinguished from persistent learning. Updating a state
estimate, revising a plan, or retrieving another skill may be sufficient to complete the current task.
Changes intended to improve future tasks require retained evidence, failure analysis, candidate up-
dates, and evaluation against established competencies. Physical exploration must remain within
defined safety and resource limits, and updates should be introduced in stages with a means of
rollback.
Composable skills make this process more economical. Capabilities for movement, manipulation,
measurement, inspection, and recovery should describe their preconditions, expected effects, and
failure modes. Agents can then assemble workflows from existing components and learn the miss-
ing parts. Composition still requires testing, since the timing and physical effects of one skill can
invalidate the assumptions of another.
A useful measure of progress is the cost of acquiring the next capability. Learning across tasks,
environments, and embodiments should reduce the additional demonstrations, trials, engineering
changes, and human assistance needed in a new setting. Comparisons with frozen systems should
account for these costs, as well as retained performance and the reliability of long-horizon execu-
tion.
