12.1.3
Hardware-Software Co-Evolution
Hardware-software co-evolution in Physical AI spans computing resources, physical terminals,
and the infrastructure in which they operate. Hardware includes edge processors and communi-
cation devices, sensors and actuators, robots and scientific instruments, and installed systems such
as cameras and traffic signals. Their design determines what algorithms can observe, how quickly
they can respond, and which actions are physically possible.
Edge computing should be developed alongside model architectures and execution requirements.
Memory capacity, energy consumption, thermal limits, and latency constrain the models that can
run near a device. Model compression, task allocation, and the division of computation between
306


local and remote resources should reflect these constraints. Time-critical control and essential pro-
tective functions need dependable local execution when communication is delayed or unavailable,
while less urgent reasoning and learning may use shared computing resources.
For robots and other terminals, morphology and function should be considered together with mod-
els and control algorithms. Joint arrangement, actuator characteristics, mechanical compliance,
sensor placement, and end-effector design affect both task performance and learning difficulty. A
hardware change may simplify a control problem or make a previously hidden state observable.
Conversely, improvements in perception or control may allow a simpler mechanical design. Co-
design should evaluate these trade-offs against task coverage, reliability, energy use, and mainte-
nance requirements.
The same reasoning extends to physical infrastructure. Camera placement can be optimized jointly
with perception and state-estimation methods, taking account of coverage, occlusion, calibration,
and privacy constraints. The layout and configuration of traffic signals can be studied together with
sensing, prediction, and coordination algorithms, subject to engineering and safety requirements.
In such settings, the environment’s instrumentation and configuration become part of system de-
sign. Software performance should be assessed against the infrastructure it requires, including
installation and operating costs.
Over approximately five years, priorities should include reliable edge deployment, instrumented
platforms, and reproducible integration and testing. Over five to ten years, modular terminals,
reusable interfaces, and coordinated infrastructure design could reduce the cost of supporting new
tasks. More distant research may investigate reconfigurable bodies, adaptive sensing systems, and
brain-computer interfaces that connect human neural signals with computational and physical sys-
tems. The latter remains an exploratory direction, with substantial questions concerning signal sta-
bility, biocompatibility, privacy, and safe operation. It should not be treated as a prerequisite for
near-term progress.
Across these horizons, access to physical testing remains essential. Computing resources need com-
plementary support from equipment, calibration, maintenance, consumables, and technical exper-
tise. Co-evolution is useful when changes in hardware and software jointly improve sustained
performance or reduce total resource requirements.
12.1.4
The Internet of Physical Agents: Architecture and Sustained Operation
The Internet of Physical Agents is a proposed federated infrastructure through which agents, models,
data, computing resources, physical equipment, and human participants cooperate. Its architecture
(Figure 12.3) should support the circulation of observations, knowledge, task requests, actions, and
verified outcomes among heterogeneous participants. A node may consume one capability while
providing another, and its role can change from one task to the next.
Three interacting components provide a useful architectural starting point. Physical nodes combine
local perception, computation, control, and equipment interfaces. Shared capability services pro-
vide models, skills, datasets, simulation, computing, and evaluation. Coordination services sup-
port discovery, resource matching, task decomposition, scheduling, authorization, and evidence
exchange. These are logical functions that may be distributed or replicated across sites, rather than
fixed levels in a centralized hierarchy.
Information and capability should move in multiple directions. A robot may receive a task and
invoke a shared model, while also collecting measurements, identifying an unexpected condition,
and supplying evidence that helps another agent. An instrument can execute an experimental pro-
cedure and return observations that change the procedure itself. One node’s findings may update
a shared resource, inform a peer directly, or trigger a request for further measurement elsewhere.
The network therefore links execution with sensing, interpretation, and learning through several
interacting loops.
Local autonomy remains necessary within this distributed architecture. Physical nodes retain time-
critical control, equipment protection, and bounded execution. Network services coordinate activ-
307


ities whose timing and dependencies permit wider cooperation. Capability interfaces should spec-
ify operating conditions, uncertainty, latency, resource requirements, and failure handling. Prove-
nance and version information are needed so that recipients can determine whether an observation,
model, or procedure is suitable for their own setting.

The Scientific Internet is one proposed implementation case. It would connect scientists, scientific
literature, datasets, models, laboratories, instruments, and computing resources across disciplines
and locations to support interdisciplinary autonomous scientific discovery.
A workflow could
move from literature analysis to hypothesis generation, simulation, physical experimentation, and
revised investigation. Experimental results would feed back into hypotheses and models, while
unresolved questions could redirect work to other facilities. Scientists would define objectives and
assess significance, and scientific claims would remain subject to independent verification.
Sustained operation requires clear permissions and controlled updates. Equipment access, result
sharing, and permission to learn from operational data should be specified separately. Changes to
shared models or services need compatibility tests, staged deployment, monitoring, and rollback,
since an update can affect dependent nodes. Participation also depends on practical arrangements
for maintenance, cost sharing, and contribution recognition. Expansion should follow evidence
that capabilities can be reused by other teams, coordination produces a net benefit, and service
quality persists beyond the support of the original developers.
12.1.5
Building the Scientific and Technological Ecosystem for Physical AI
The reach of Physical AI depends on the maturity of the technologies and practices around it.
Models require suitable instruments, reliable equipment, manufacturing capacity, energy supplies,
communication infrastructure, and people who can integrate and maintain them. Development
strategies should identify these complementary requirements and the bottlenecks that limit useful
deployment. The limiting factor may be a model in one setting and measurement quality, equip-
ment reliability, or integration effort in another.
A productive ecosystem makes results easier to reproduce and capabilities easier to extend. Shared
test facilities, documented datasets, reference implementations, and interoperable interfaces can
308


reduce repeated engineering work. Evaluation methods should support meaningful comparison
across systems while leaving room for different architectures. Training and collaboration should
connect AI research with control, equipment engineering, domain expertise, and operations. These
connections are particularly important when moving from a successful prototype to a system that
another team can use and maintain.
Scientific research provides one example of how Physical AI could strengthen this broader techno-
logical base. Better instruments and experimental methods can produce more informative evidence
for learning. Models and agents can, in turn, help design experiments, investigate materials, im-
prove fabrication processes, and diagnose equipment failures. Improvements can thus propagate
between research tools, scientific knowledge, and engineering capability. Their value depends on
reproducible findings and usable technologies, including cases where experiments reject a hypoth-
esis or reveal a method’s limits.
Similar feedback can occur in manufacturing, logistics, maintenance, and energy operations. De-
ployment reveals drift, wear, resource constraints, and interactions that are difficult to reproduce in
isolated tests. When this experience is documented and returned to development, it can improve
both the intelligent system and the processes that support it. Longer-term investment should pre-
serve the ability to investigate unresolved problems while also developing the interfaces, equip-
ment, and operating practices needed for reliable reuse.
Technological maturity should therefore be assessed beyond model-level benchmarks. Relevant
measures include the cost of adaptation, intervention frequency, operating lifetime, recovery time,
and useful output relative to total resource consumption. Reproducibility across sites and contin-
ued operation after the original developers leave are important tests of whether a capability has
become broadly usable.
At a larger scale, Physical AI could extend the ability to investigate, construct, operate, and main-
tain physical systems. The significance of that extension depends on what can be accomplished,
across how much space, for how long, and with what expenditure of energy, materials, and hu-
man effort. A capability acquires enduring value when it delivers useful work reliably, survives
changing conditions, and can be recovered and passed on to others.
12.2
Physical AI and Human Civilization
Physical AI connects computation, perception, and action. Questions about civilizational scale
therefore depend on energy, materials, and infrastructure. The level a civilization can reach de-
pends on how much energy it can obtain and organize, how effectively it can turn that energy into
stable production and services, and whether those capabilities can continue to operate, be repaired,
and be inherited across locations and generations. Larger models and more computation become
civilizational capabilities only when they enter equipment, energy systems, and real environments
and are tested through physical feedback.
Physical AI as a Service (PAIaaS) is used here to describe how such capabilities can be organized.
Model as a service separates model inference from individual applications and lowers the cost
of using digital intelligence. PAIaaS extends this idea to experiments, manufacturing, inspection,
energy operations, and maintenance. Users can call on real equipment and operating procedures
without rebuilding the full facility at every site. Physical capabilities can then be shared across
locations and combined into more complex tasks.
The development of Physical AI is therefore connected to the growth of civilization. Reaching Type
I requires organizing energy, production, and infrastructure across Earth. Reaching Type II requires
infrastructure beyond Earth that can obtain resources, manufacture components, and operate for
long periods. The discussion below first considers how physical capability can be measured and
then examines the role of physical AI in progress toward Type I and Type II civilizations.
309


12.2.1
Civilizational Scale and the Physical Basis of Intelligence
Civilizational scale requires energy measures to be interpreted together with practical capability.
The Kardashev index provides a power scale, but power alone says how much energy a civilization
continuously directs, not what that energy enables. A physical measure must also account for the
area a system can serve, the duration for which it can operate, and its ability to recover from failures
and changing conditions.
Civilization as a Physical Measure
In the continuous convention, the Kardashev index is written
as
Kciv = log10(Ppower/W) −6
10
,
(12.1)
where Ppower is the power continuously used by a civilization. Under this convention, Type I,
Type II, and Type III correspond to approximately 1016, 1026, and 1036 W, respectively. Using 2019
global total energy supply, Jiang et al. (2022) estimate humanity’s index at about Kciv = 0.73. Using
this rounded index in the continuous convention gives a Type I power level about 102.7 ≈501 times
the baseline (Kardashev, 1964; Sagan, 1973). A small change in the index can therefore correspond
to a large change in the energy base.
Power is an entry point for measuring civilizational capability. The same power can support dif-
ferent levels of production, transport, computation, and public service, or it can be consumed by
inefficient conversion and maintenance. A fuller account should combine power with duration,
spatial coverage, reliability, and recovery. A remote facility that operates for several hours has a
different physical capability from one that can work for years without a local human team.
Energy Use and Energy Acquisition
Overall energy efficiency is determined by two efficiencies
working together. Energy-use efficiency describes how much of the energy already obtained be-
comes useful service. Energy-acquisition efficiency describes the equipment, materials, land, and
maintenance required to bring new energy into the usable energy system. Higher use efficiency
allows the same energy supply to support more service. Higher acquisition efficiency allows more
resources to become available. A limitation at either stage constrains the expansion of a civiliza-
tion’s energy base.
Both efficiencies are physical. Use efficiency depends on equipment, materials, conversion pro-
cesses, transmission networks, and operating conditions. Acquisition efficiency depends on re-
source location, environmental conditions, tool lifetime, operational safety, and resupply. Infor-
mation processing alone cannot establish either one. Both have to be tested through equipment,
field operations, and long-term maintenance. Energy systems should therefore be evaluated by the
useful service delivered over a defined period, together with the full requirements for equipment,
computation, materials, and personnel.
Civilization develops in two directions at once. It must make better use of energy already available
and continue to obtain or create new energy sources. Digital systems rest on the same physical
base. Computation requires electricity, chips, materials, cooling, and equipment maintenance. The
expansion of digital capability is therefore supported and limited by physical conditions.
From Digital Information to Physical Action
Digital systems process information, while civi-
lizational capability is realized through physical processes. A model can propose a design, predict
demand, or generate a control policy. Such results become testable changes only when they en-
ter equipment and an environment. More information, model parameters, or computation cannot
replace energy conversion, material processing, equipment assembly, or field maintenance.
Physical processes also change the meaning of a computation. Equipment may respond differently
from the model’s prediction, materials may degrade, and environmental conditions may shift. A
system must update its judgment from observations and check whether the result meets require-
ments for safety, performance, and lifetime. Physical AI concerns this continuing interaction. Com-
310


putation proposes an action, equipment carries it out, the environment provides feedback, and the
system adjusts its next action.
The basic unit of Physical AI is therefore a physical system that combines perception, computation,
execution, verification, and maintenance. An isolated model cannot provide this capability by
itself. A computational capability acquires civilizational significance when it can reliably change a
real process and remain interpretable and recoverable under different conditions.
From Local Capability to Shared Physical Services
Physical capability usually begins with one
set of equipment at one site. It performs a task under particular material, environmental, and
operating conditions, while also generating calibration, failure, and maintenance experience. To
move the capability to another site, its dependencies must be identified, transferable steps must be
separated from site-specific ones, and the new setting must provide its own evidence.
When the experience, models, interfaces, and equipment can be used by another team, a local ca-
pability becomes a shared capability. Sharing includes equipment access, task execution, result
verification, and maintenance support, not only a model file. A user specifies a physical task, a
provider performs it under agreed conditions and returns evidence, and the parties define permis-
sions, responsibilities, and failure handling.
PAIaaS is the service form of this shared capability. It makes experiments, measurements, manu-
facturing, energy operations, and maintenance available on demand. This lowers the threshold for
using specialized facilities, improves equipment utilization, and allows services at different loca-
tions to be combined. A local success that has been validated can then be inherited by more teams
and later generations.
Physical services remain constrained by resources, equipment, and operating environments, so
they cannot be copied without limit like digital interfaces. A service must be usable by a new team,
its results must withstand verification, and its facility must continue operating after the original
developers leave. When these conditions are met, local experience can become a civilizational
capability that remains available over time.
12.2.2
Toward a Type I Civilization, Planetary-Scale Physical Systems
Moving from this estimated level toward Type I begins on Earth. The first task is to organize energy
and infrastructure at planetary scale. Physical AI supports continuous improvement of the energy
system, beginning with more effective use and acquisition of existing energy, continuing with new
energy processes, and extending to controlled fusion as a stable facility. Every stage depends on
perception, control, diagnosis, maintenance, and iteration in real environments.
Existing Energy Systems
Fossil fuels, wind, solar, hydropower, and nuclear fission already form
the energy base of modern society. Here, the focus is on operating and maintaining facilities already
in service. Physical AI can support coordinated dispatch, equipment inspection, fault diagnosis,
and maintenance across the chain from resource acquisition to final use. For nuclear fission facil-
ities, these tasks also involve monitoring material degradation and planning maintenance within
independently verified safety limits.
Large energy networks depend on connected equipment.
Wind and solar output varies with
weather and location, while transmission and storage constrain dispatch. A local improvement
can create congestion elsewhere. Physical AI can adjust generation, transmission, and demand
using equipment state, weather, and changing loads. The relevant measures are reliable supply,
recovery from failure, and sustained service.
Energy extraction is part of the same system. Oil, gas, coal, minerals, deep-sea resources, and nu-
clear fuels require exploration, collection, transport, processing, and maintenance. Wind, solar, and
hydropower require dispersed equipment that must also be built and maintained. Local conditions
in deep-sea, underground, and high-temperature or high-pressure facilities often exceed what de-
311


sign documents describe. Physical AI can use field observations to adjust an action, conduct a
limited probe, or suspend a task when the risk becomes too high.
Records of extraction and maintenance should inform later construction. Repeated failures under
particular conditions can expose problems in materials, site selection, or maintenance plans. Phys-
ical AI can identify such patterns and use them to improve equipment design and operation. Each
operating cycle can then inform the next round of infrastructure.
Developing Advanced Energy Technologies
The focus now shifts from operating existing facil-
ities to developing and validating new materials, devices, and processes, including advances in
photovoltaics, wind power, storage, and nuclear fission.
Physical AI can support this development by connecting design proposals to physical experiments.
In photovoltaic research, a system could select material compositions and fabrication conditions,
prepare samples, and compare measured performance with model predictions. Similar workflows
could examine storage materials, turbine components, or materials intended for nuclear systems.
The experimental objective is to establish how a proposed change affects performance, durability,
and operating limits.
Results from these experiments should guide subsequent tests and revisions to materials, struc-
tures, and control plans. Progress toward deployment requires evidence from prototypes and ex-
tended operation, together with independent verification of relevant safety requirements. Physical
AI can help carry knowledge from one development stage to the next, while controlled fusion
presents a particularly demanding example of this process.
Controlled Fusion on Earth
Controlled fusion is a key energy process on the path to Type I.
The Sun continuously produces energy through fusion. On Earth, the challenge is to create and
maintain an extreme plasma state while managing magnetic fields, heating, wall materials, energy
output, and component lifetime.
Tokamak plasmas change rapidly and involve many control variables, so fixed rules cannot cover
every operating state. Degrave et al. (2022) show that reinforcement-learning controllers can move
from simulation to a real TCV tokamak and control several plasma configurations magnetically.
The experiment shows how Physical AI can turn a theoretical configuration into an operable and
measurable experiment.
Fusion development must extend from research into engineering and operation. Models should
be updated from experimental observations, follow-up experiments should be selected, equipment
should be improved, and long-term stability should be tested. Sustained generation and safe main-
tenance require evidence from real devices. Physical AI can shorten the path from physical discov-
ery to engineering iteration and carry the knowledge from one experiment into the next device.
Planetary Coordination and Long-Term Maintenance
When energy systems expand to plane-
tary scale, one facility can affect other regions and infrastructures. Reservoir operation can change
downstream water and ecological conditions, while large energy facilities can alter land use, water
use, and regional industry. Models must represent these connections and be tested against obser-
vations at the relevant scale.
Physical AI can help identify missing data, compare operating plans, and schedule monitoring and
maintenance. Models cannot replace public decisions or remove the physical consequences of inter-
vention. Climate intervention in particular requires a clear distinction between mechanism studies
and large-scale deployment, together with explicit treatment of uncertainty, risk, and responsibility.
Type I civilization requires energy and infrastructure services to continue over long periods. In-
spection, repair, and replacement should occur before failures spread, and efficiency should be
evaluated across the full service cycle. More complex control can increase sensor and computation
requirements, while equipment that cannot be repaired locally can increase dependence on remote
312


supply. The maturity of Physical AI is assessed by stable energy supply, continuing maintenance,
and rapid recovery across the planet.
12.2.3
Toward a Type II Civilization, Space Infrastructure and Stellar-Scale Energy
Type II civilization extends physical activity to stellar scale. One reason for this transition is that
energy development and large infrastructure on Earth face increasing constraints from space, en-
vironmental effects, and social coordination. New computing, energy, and manufacturing facilities
occupy public space and can conflict with local communities and other industries. Moving parts of
energy production, computation, resource extraction, and manufacturing to orbit, the Moon, Mars,
and other bodies may provide another way to expand civilizational capability.
Space facilities must do more than complete a single mission. They need to build themselves, use
local resources, produce replacement parts, manage failures, and operate with little direct human
presence. Physical AI allows these activities to continue despite communication delay, extreme
environments, and incomplete information.
Deep-Space Autonomy and Continual Learning
Earth-Mars one-way light time varies with or-
bital configuration from roughly 3 to 22 min (National Aeronautics and Space Administration,
2023). Urgent actions must be performed locally, equipment diagnosis can wait longer, and changes
to mission objectives generally require ground review. Perseverance’s AutoNav illustrates this ar-
rangement by supporting onboard navigation and hazard avoidance while the ground team plans
routes and mission activities (Jet Propulsion Laboratory, 2021). Remote autonomy can begin with
defined local tasks, while validated control, local adaptation, and ground supervision handle deci-
sions at different timescales.
Deep-space missions encounter environments that cannot be fully covered during preparation on
Earth. Javed and Sutton’s Big World Hypothesis describes agents whose capacity is limited relative
to the environments they encounter (Javed and Sutton, 2024). Such agents cannot maintain a com-
plete world description and must understand the parts relevant to their current goals. A model
trained on Earth therefore omits features that matter at a particular site. New observations may
require a revised state estimate, a different existing plan, or a change to the model and policy.
Continual learning needs evidence from local experiments. A rover can first probe low-risk ground
and then decide whether to enter more difficult terrain. The probe should change the next decision,
while the risks of immobilization, energy use, and tool damage remain acceptable. Some unknowns
cannot be resolved safely, so the system must be able to postpone an objective. Long-duration
construction also requires constrained physical self-improvement in tools, experiments, and local
control. Such changes need field tests, regression checks, and rollback procedures.
Adaptation Under Unfamiliar Physical Conditions
Deep-space autonomy must also address
physical conditions that differ from those encountered during development on Earth. The broad
gravitational conditions of the Moon and Mars are already characterized, but local terrain, contact
properties, and equipment responses may remain incompletely known. The challenge is to deter-
mine how transferable physical models apply at a particular site and when their assumptions cease
to support reliable action.
Reduced gravity changes the relationship between equipment weight, available traction, and the
reaction forces generated by tools. An excavator or assembly robot may move or lose stable contact
when applying forces that a terrestrial platform could resist. NASA’s RASSOR excavator illustrates
the resulting need for different mechanical arrangements. Opposing, counterrotating bucket drums
reduce the net reaction forces associated with excavation.11 Physical AI would need to estimate
support conditions and coordinate tool motion with vehicle posture, anchoring, or other means of
stabilization.
11NASA Kennedy Space Center, Regolith Advanced Surface Systems Operations Robot (RASSOR) Excavator,
technology-transfer page.
313


Illumination creates a different set of coupled constraints. Low solar angles near the lunar south
pole produce long shadows and strong contrasts that complicate terrain interpretation (Litaker
et al., 2025). A route that appears geometrically accessible may offer insufficient visibility or solar
energy for continued operation. Physical AI should therefore combine terrain estimates, sensing
confidence, illumination forecasts, and energy reserves when selecting routes and work periods.
Surface interaction introduces further uncertainty. Friction alone is insufficient to describe whether
a vehicle slips, sinks, or remains supported, or whether a tool can penetrate the ground. Local
estimates must also account for bearing capacity, cohesion, and the response of material to repeated
contact. Limited traverses or shallow tool interactions could provide evidence for revising these
estimates, provided that the system retains sufficient resources and a feasible recovery option.
Future research should examine how Physical AI can identify these conditions from limited obser-
vations and interactions, adapt control without losing previously validated capabilities, and recog-
nize when further probing would be too costly. Evaluation should include the physical interactions
required before reliable operation, the energy and equipment wear incurred during adaptation, and
recovery when an environmental estimate proves incorrect.
Planetary Construction and Underground Habitats
Space construction is harder than a single
measurement because each action changes the setting for the next one. Lunar and Martian facilities
may benefit from underground spaces, which can provide radiation protection and stable tem-
peratures while reducing exposure to surface conditions. Construction must proceed from local
observations and repeatedly adjust excavation, support, and inspection.
A lunar energy facility would pass through transport, positioning, installation, inspection, and
connection. Each installed component must be checked before later work can rely on it. The sys-
tem cannot simply execute a design prepared in advance. It must establish step by step that the
emerging structure can support further construction and operation.
Space-based solar power provides a concrete object for studying these dependencies. NASA’s 2024
assessment identifies major gaps in orbital assembly and maintenance, autonomous operation, and
power transmission (Rodgers et al., 2024). An orbital collector becomes an energy service only
when its associated equipment can be deployed, repaired, and operated continuously. Physical AI
must connect construction planning, state inspection, failure handling, and later task scheduling.
Local production can reduce resupply, but raw material alone does not create manufacturing capa-
bility. A remote facility must repeatedly produce components that meet performance requirements
and verify that they are fit for their intended roles. Materials processing, quality verification, and
equipment maintenance must form a continuous local process.
Long-Duration Operation with Limited Resources
Decision autonomy and resource indepen-
dence are different properties. A facility may schedule months of work while still depending on
Earth for a critical component. Better planning can extend limited supplies, but it cannot replace
missing materials or tools. The autonomy of a remote facility must therefore be described together
with its remaining dependence on resupply, communication, and maintenance.
Long-duration operation requires choices between current tasks and future capability. When re-
sources are scarce, equipment status is uncertain, or external support is interrupted, postponing
an experiment may preserve more useful work. A remote facility should leave later missions with
usable energy, tools, data, and maintenance conditions rather than forcing every mission to start
again from Earth.
Stellar-Scale Infrastructure and Dyson Swarms
A Dyson swarm is a hypothetical arrangement
of independently orbiting collectors for harvesting stellar radiation (Wright, 2020). Its relevance
to Physical AI lies in the construction and maintenance tasks that such an arrangement would
impose. Components would have to be manufactured, transported, assembled, inspected, and
replaced across widely separated sites, with limited opportunities for direct human intervention.
314


Physical AI could support these tasks by connecting local observations to physical action. Dur-
ing assembly, a robotic system would need to estimate component pose and deformation, adjust
contact forces, and verify each completed connection before further construction proceeds. Dur-
ing operation, each facility would need to diagnose degradation and adjust energy collection and
use within equipment and thermal limits. Repair would require identifying a fault, selecting an
available intervention, and checking that the repaired equipment can safely resume its role.
Coordination across the swarm would also require Physical AI at multiple scales. Local systems
would handle immediate control and fault response, while broader coordination would allocate
transport, manufacturing, and maintenance resources using delayed information. Construction
and repair records should preserve the conditions under which earlier designs were validated,
allowing later systems to assess compatibility when replacing components or extending facilities.
These requirements define a speculative research setting for autonomous construction, distributed
coordination, and maintenance across successive generations of equipment. Physical AI could help
identify and operate workable arrangements, but those arrangements would still require suitable
materials, manufacturing capacity, and sufficient heat rejection. Their capability would be demon-
strated through verified construction, recovery from failures, and sustained useful operation.
12.3
Summary and Outlook
This chapter has considered Physical AI over the long time horizon of human development and
civilizational change. Physical AI requires stable infrastructure and systems in which equipment,
data, computation, and people can continue to work together. The value of a project lies in its
results and in the models, interfaces, methods, and operating experience that later teams can verify
and reuse.
The development of Physical AI can begin in scientific research and engineering practice. Shared
models and data, connected experimental facilities, cross-institutional service interfaces, and de-
ployment of validated capabilities all contribute to the accumulation of physical capability. PAIaaS
offers an organizing form for this process. Experiments, manufacturing, inspection, energy opera-
tions, and maintenance can become services that other teams call when needed. Physical capability
can then grow from a single site into a broader network of cooperation.
At the scale of civilization, humanity must first improve the acquisition and use of energy on Earth,
develop new energy and nuclear systems, build planetary infrastructure, and advance controlled
fusion. A more distant stage requires deep-space infrastructure that can operate with communica-
tion delay, continual learning, autonomous construction, local manufacturing, and long-duration
activity. Civilizational level is ultimately reflected in whether energy, equipment, materials, and
maintenance can continue to work across larger ranges and longer periods.
This monograph has examined the foundations, methods, systems, and applications of Physical
AI, and has considered the perception, action, learning, and adaptation required by Physical AGI.
These discussions show that Physical AI requires systems to understand environments, act in them,
bear the consequences of action, and change their later behavior from real experience. A digital
model becomes a component of a Physical AI system only when it is integrated into this closed-
loop process.
Future progress must be tested in concrete equipment and real tasks. Laboratories, factories, energy
facilities, and deep-space systems impose different constraints and expose unresolved weaknesses
in current models and methods. Progress toward Physical AGI depends on whether systems can
gain reliable experience under these constraints, turn local experience into transferable capability,
and remain safe, interpretable, and maintainable over long operation. Physical AI may become an
important technical basis for humanity’s transition to a higher civilization, but reaching that future
requires sustained work by researchers, engineers, and infrastructure operators.
